How College Education Divided America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:57:01 UTC
23:57:01 KST

Shortly after pandemic-era travel restrictions eased, I flew to Washington, D.C., for a meeting with leaders from left-leaning foundations. The topic was close to my heart: combating inequality and constructing a new narrative about reversing huge and widening income disparities. I expected the focus to be on the jarring increase in earnings inequality over the last four decades, led by the declining wages of workers, and especially men, without college degrees.
To my surprise, nobody seemed to comment on the stagnation and decline in the wages of non-college workers. Nor was there any discussion of how inequality between residents of small cities and large metropolitan areas had surged. Instead, commentator after commentator talked about gender inequality, racial inequality, and inequality affecting sexual minorities. These are all important topics, of course, but if our aim was to understand the surge in inequality at the aggregate level, much of the story was about jobs and opportunities for Americans without college education.
As I was traveling back to Boston, another event crystallized my unease about American political trends. Seeing that my flight was delayed by an hour, I decided to get a drink. At the bar by my gate, the only opening was next to a burly gentleman around my age. As I ordered a beer, he asked me whether my flight was also delayed. I nodded ruefully and said it wasn’t too bad. He proceeded to talk about football, a topic I know little about. But I welcomed the distraction, and over the next hour, we broached several other topics: the annoyances of air travel, beer, the challenges of the small business he was running, politics, and basketball, about which I knew a little more than football.
It was only later that I realized how rare such an event had become, where I spoke to somebody with a very different education profile, occupation, and interests from mine. This made me consider what would have happened if, on my other side at the bar, there had been somebody with a Ph.D. and an occupation similar to mine (academic, financier, consultant, lawyer, etc.). Whom would I have chosen to initiate a conversation with? Whom would the participants in the workshop I attended have chosen? The answer seemed almost too obvious, and not completely unrelated to why the plight of manual workers was less than top of mind for many college-educated policymakers, activists, and civil servants.
I later embellished the choice a little and offered it to several friends and participants at various conferences: If stranded at an airport, with a professional with a Ph.D. from a faraway land (China, India, Brazil, Nigeria) on one side and an American high school graduate on the other, to whom would you look forward to talking for the next hour? Many took the question to be rhetorical, because the answer was, again, too obvious.
There is nothing natural about the educational segregation that has emerged in the United States. But it has become a reality, with far-reaching consequences for postindustrial politics. It is emblematic of weakening ties within communities—and within the nation. It may explain how, as they became more politically influential and assertive, the well-educated became less understanding of the woes of those with lower levels of education. It is a big part of the story of how left-leaning, well-educated liberal elites started deviating from the premises of liberalism that had generated its past success.
The political rise of the college educated is related to the phenomenal growth in the number of people with college degrees. But even more important, it is a consequence of the rising status of the college educated, which is itself rooted in their meteoric economic climb—while automation, offshoring, globalization, and related sectoral trends have reduced the availability of good jobs for non-college workers. As the college educated have become politically more powerful, they have also diverged further from the less educated in their geographic locations and their social lives, reducing their ability to empathize with the latter’s problems and creating a major cultural rift between the two groups. In the process, a coalition between different segments of the college-educated and the tech sector has formed. I would argue this coalition has completely turned its back on the economic priorities of the less educated and has come to focus on cultural and global issues.
Cultural politics, promoted from both left and right, has further alienated the working class.
Excerpted with permission from What Happened to Liberal Democracy: Remaking a Politics of Shared Prosperity by Daron Acemoglu, published by Dutton, an imprint of Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House, LLC. Copyright (c) 2026 by Daron Acemoglu.

Amid public backlash, surveillance tech company Flock announces platform changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:53:02 UTC
23:53:02 KST

Amid public backlash, surveillance tech company Flock announces platform changes
RICHMOND, Va. (AP) — Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company increasingly under scrutiny from lawmakers, civil liberties advocates and citizens across the U.S., announced Thursday it is making changes to its platform intended to quell privacy concerns and address documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement.
The company is one of the nation’s largest providers of automated license plate readers, which document plate data and other vehicle characteristics as automobiles pass Flock’s cameras. The thousands of law enforcement agencies that contract with the company can search and share that data across jurisdictions to inform investigations.
Police have credited the technology as an important crime-fighting innovation that has helped locate missing people and track suspects in violent crimes. But dozens of cities and agencies have nixed their relationships with Flock amid concerns that the data can be accessed for immigration enforcement or used in unauthorized surveillance, after a flurry of examples surfaced of law enforcement officers misusing the technology for personal searches.
CEO says changes will drive accountability
In an interview, Flock CEO Garrett Langley said many of the product changes will make what were once optional guardrails mandatory for its users to implement by Jan. 1.
Among them: All law enforcement customers will have to implement an audit tool that’s intended to flag abnormal search behavior. When the system detects abnormal behavior, the user would be locked out pending an internal review, the company said in a description of the changes provided ahead of Thursday’s announcement.
Flock, which says its customers own the data that the cameras record, is also shortening the standard data retention window from 30 days to seven. It said it will allow data to be preserved for longer when it is evidence tied to a case number.
Law enforcement users will now also be required to enter a code from their records management system tying each search to a specific case before it is run, something Langley said civil liberties advocates have long been calling for. Overrides for emergencies would be automatically flagged for review, the company said.
Customers will also be allowed to decide which offense types — such as homicide or arson — outside agencies can search their data for, which would allow a customer to block outside searches related to immigration enforcement, the company said.
Langley said that change will give individual cities and departments control to use the system in a manner “consistent with community values.”
Critics say updates still leave room for abuses
Critics of the company reacted skeptically to the changes, which they said appeared designed to address the growing bipartisan anger about the cameras but could still leave room for police to abuse the system.
The American Civil Liberties Union said in a blog post that the shortened evidence retention window could be “a step in the right direction,” but it characterized the other changes as “retreads” of inadequate safety measures.
Robert Frommer, a senior attorney at the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm that’s led closely watched litigation over the technology, called the changes “window dressing” from a company in “panic mode.”
“This is window dressing that doesn’t address the fundamental problem, which is that police officers are the ones deciding who and when to search, and that should be done by judges with real warrants,” he said.
Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a professor at the George Washington University Law School whose scholarship has focused on policing, big data surveillance and the Fourth Amendment, said he’s been surprised to see the “growing community backlash” against Flock specifically, given the technology is not new and other companies sell it as well.
But Flock and the movement against it have “captured people’s sense that maybe they don’t want to be surveilled all the time,” said Ferguson, a former public defender who earlier this year published a book about policing and surveillance.
More than 50 agencies or jurisdictions canceled, suspended or rejected a contract or deactivated their cameras since the beginning of the year, according to a tracker maintained by DeFlock, a grassroots group formed to track the use of license plate reader technology and push back against it.
In Congress, Republican representatives filed at least two bills aiming to restrict the use of the technology in July.
Ian Adams, an associate professor of criminology at the University of South Carolina currently working on a Flock-related research study, said many of the concerns raised about how the company’s data can be used are not new concerns in law enforcement.
“Anyone with policing experience could have reasonably foreseen that what have been termed as ‘curiosity searches’ by officers, searches for private reasons not related to police work, were going to be a problem this technology faced,” he added, noting that other technologies and platforms like the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information had faced those issues.
Successes and failures have captured attention
Flock, based in Atlanta, Georgia, often posts to its website what the company deems to be everyday examples of success stories for its cameras, including finding missing seniors and catching car thieves. But the tech has also been used in high-profile cases that have garnered national attention, such as the search for a suspect in a fatal shooting at Brown University and in tracking and arresting a former North Carolina police officer who authorities say had made threats that he planned to carry out a mass shooting at a festival in Louisiana.
Abuses have also drawn widespread attention. The Washington Post reported earlier this month finding nearly 50 instances of police officers charged or accused of using the cameras for unauthorized purposes, many for tracking current or former romantic partners or family members.
Just this week, six employees — including four officers — of the Savannah Police Department in Georgia were fired after they were accused of searching for friends and family using the tool and allowing an officer from an outside agency to use the city’s cameras.
The Savannah department said it was made aware of the misuse through Flock’s voluntary audit function.
___
Lauer reported from Philadelphia.

Mali pardons French official sentenced to 20 years in prison

The Malian government said in a statement posted to Facebook that the clemency "does not call into question the facts established by an adversarial judgment rendered during a trial".

Ukrainian city authorities preparing for worst-case winter scenario, but hoping for better
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:50:12 EEST
23:50:12 KST

Lviv First Deputy Mayor Andriy Moskalenko has said the city is preparing for the most difficult scenario for the 2026-27 winter heating season and that Ukrainian cities are ready to help one another.
"We very often hear that this winter will be difficult. And this is not just words, this is the experience we had last winter, and the experience of what the enemy is doing by attacking Ukrainian cities now… Lviv is preparing for winter. We have approved our city resilience plan. This is 96 separate projects... Of course we need to prepare for the most difficult scenario, to have the mental readiness to accept that the worst could happen," Moskalenko said during a discussion titled "Winter is coming: are the state and society ready?" at the Interfax-Ukraine press center on Thursday.
According to him, active meetings in residential buildings will begin in Lviv from next Monday so that every resident knows the algorithm of actions.
"And of course, when there is a difficult situation, every Ukrainian city helps another. In particular, this past winter more than 50 specialists worked in Kyiv for more than five weeks, helping with the restoration of housing stock... So we, Ukrainian cities, will always support one another. And here, I think, the question is about being close, exchanging information, and preparing for the most difficult things," Moskalenko said.
Poltava Acting Mayor Kateryna Yamshchykova said the city is also implementing a resilience plan, in particular actively repairing water drainage networks, while stressing the importance of ensuring the resilience of all networks so they can operate under blackout conditions.
"We have also introduced a separate resilience program for educational institutions in the community… There is also an additional program for launching solar power plants at municipal enterprises of critical infrastructure. This is not only about energy resilience in terms of having our own generation, it is also about the fact that such plants must have storage stations, batteries that can be charged not only from the sun but also from the general grid," she said.
Regarding mutual support between cities, Yamshchykova said Poltava utility workers took part last winter in major work to "de-freeze" multi-story buildings in Kyiv and gained relevant experience. "Of course we would never want this to be repeated anywhere. But our teams gained additional experience working through these difficult procedures," she said.
Serhiy Shmyhol, a deputy of the Cherkasy City Council and member of the commission on rules, health care and housing and communal services, said the city is "more or less prepared" for the heating season and already has a fairly well-established diversified generation network and about 20 MW of reserve capacity.
"The second scenario is a hardcore option, if we don't have gas… Most likely, we will be able to keep buildings in a non-freezing regime. And hospitals, as a base – separate methods and scenarios are now in place to provide them with heat," he said.
The deputy said the city is preparing for non-standard scenarios and the possibility that the winter will be difficult. "Thanks to the fact that we have a very powerful company, Cherkasyteplokomunenerho, which provides heat, plus a large enterprise, Cherkasyteploelektrotsentral, the former Khimvolokno, which generates electricity and heat for part of the city, having such a system we are relatively well provided with heat, and, God willing, we will get through this winter more or less normally," Shmyhol said.
During the discussion, the Civil-Military Movement (CMM) NGO presented its "Winter. The City Will Hold" project, which envisages comprehensive preparation of communities for the 2026/2027 heating season – from risk assessment to specific action algorithms in the event of shelling, prolonged blackouts, loss of heat and water supply, and other emergencies. The second stage of the project will begin with the onset of cold weather and will be aimed directly at helping community residents.

Ukraine hits Russian US$100m radar in Sevastopol that detects aircraft and missiles
Ukraine's defence forces struck a Russian long-range Nebo-U radar station in temporarily occupied Sevastopol on the night of 12-13 August.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook
Details: The General Staff reports that the Nebo-U is a Russian long-range three-coordinate VHF-band radar station. It is designed to detect and track aerial targets, including aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles.
"Striking the station reduces the capabilities of Russian forces to control airspace and detect aerial assets in a timely manner," the report states.
An infographic published by the General Staff estimates the cost of the Nebo-U radar at approximately US$100 million.
In addition, on the night of 12-13 August, Ukraine's defence forces struck a drone ground control station near Myrne in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a fuel and lubricant depot near Dovzhansk in Luhansk Oblast.
An ammunition depot near Novyi Hai in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a logistics depot near Kalanchak in Kherson Oblast were also hit.
On the territory of the Russian Federation, Ukrainian forces struck a cluster of Russian troops near Butyrki in Belgorod Oblast.
The General Staff emphasised that striking these targets weakens the capabilities of Russian forces, disrupts their logistical support and reduces their ability to stockpile and deploy ammunition, equipment and personnel.
Background: On 12 August, Ukraine's defence forces struck a cluster of Russian personnel from an unmanned systems unit near Marivka in Luhansk Oblast, as well as other Russian assets.

WOG has launched a mobile application for business customers
Kyiv • UNN
WOG has introduced the "WOG Business" application for managing fuel cards and accounts.
WOG continues to digitize its services for corporate clients. The company has launched the "WOG Business" mobile app, giving business customers access to key personal account services from their smartphones. The new tool allows users to manage fuel cards, accounts, and financial transactions in real time, regardless of their location, reports UNN.
One of the app's key advantages is the WOG PC Pay feature, which has no equivalent among fuel services in Ukraine. It allows a corporate account administrator to pay remotely for a driver's refueling if the fuel card has been lost, damaged, or is temporarily unavailable. As a result, vehicles will not be forced to stop, and the company's logistics processes will remain uninterrupted.
"We strive to make fuel resource management as simple, fast, and accessible as possible for our business clients. That is why we created a mobile app that allows company executives and managers who work with fuel and vehicle fleets every day to perform important operations in just a few clicks. This is another stage in the development of WOG's digital ecosystem for business, which helps our clients work more efficiently and without unnecessary risks", says Oleh Kushil, WOG's Director of Digital Transformation.
The app also significantly simplifies the management of financial transactions. In particular, users can:
-  quickly top up accounts via Apple Pay or Google Pay and monitor their balance in real time; 
-  instantly generate invoices and send them via messengers. 
Particular attention was paid to convenience, intuitiveness, and access security. Authorization is carried out using a phone number and a one-time OTP code, so users no longer need to remember complex logins and passwords.
The new "WOG Business" app can be downloaded from the App Store and Google Play.
Another digital solution for corporate clients is a joint WOG and eDilo project—an online service created using Activitis fintech infrastructure. From now on, WOG business clients can purchase quality fuel with deferred payment of up to 90 days. The new option is available at online.wog.ua in the personal account, where companies manage fuel cards and balances.
The new solutions are part of the development of WOG's digital ecosystem for business, which is intended to simplify the management of quality fuel, vehicle fleets, and financial transactions.

The Most Spectacular Photos of Europe's Total Solar Eclipse

People jumping from the diving platform at Kolovare Beach in Zadar, Croatia during the total solar eclipse, August 12, 2026
People jumping from the diving platform at Kolovare Beach in Zadar, Croatia during the total solar eclipse, August 12, 2026Zvonimir Barisin—PIXSELL/Sipa USA/Reuters
On Aug. 12, the luckiest 15 million people in the world were those living in a narrow band measuring approximately 5,100 miles long and 180 miles wide, stretching from northern Russia, down through Greenland, then Iceland, then Spain, then a tiny nip of Portugal, before passing into the Mediterranean Sea. That strip represented the path of totality for the recent total solar eclipse—the first visible from Europe in 27 years.
The eclipse did not take long to play out, lasting just 4.4 hours before it at last extinguished its fires in the Mediterranean waters. But it made an enduring impression—and will continue to, thanks to the uncounted astronomers and lay folk who photographed the event with ordinary cameras, great observatories, and even a NASA chase plane. Here is just a sampling of the work these eclipse-watchers produced.

Authorities in Siberia’s Novosibirsk region have arrested an activist who documented rare local farmer protests this year on charges of calling for terrorism online, her supporters said Thursday.
Armed officers raided the home of Larisa Mikhailova, using power tools to cut through the activist’s front door before taking her into custody, her daughter said in a video published by the activist group Agrarian Council.
Mikhailova is an activist with the Agrarian Council, which documented cattle culls in the Novosibirsk region mandated by the regional administration. Local farmers accused the authorities of secrecy and failing to adequately compensate them for their slaughtered livestock.
Novosibirsk’s Tsentralny District Court later put Mikhailova in pre-trial detention for two months.
“I believe this is payback for my mother’s active civic stance,” Mikhailova’s daughter said in the Agrarian Council video.
Mikhailova’s hearing took place behind closed doors.
Mikhailova’s allies believe the charge stems from online references to “The Internationale,” a 19th-century socialist anthem that served as the Soviet national anthem from 1922 until 1944.
Russian authorities have previously used modified versions of the anthem to bring terrorism charges against political dissidents and opposition figures linked to Svetlana Lada-Rus, a prominent anti-government activist and occult healer who remains wanted by Russian authorities.
Lada-Rus herself has not been seen in person since 2016, when she fled Russia while facing investigation on charges of large-scale fraud and causing grievous bodily harm through negligence, both of which she denies.
Her exact whereabouts remain unknown and she no longer speaks to the press. Last November, a court in Samara sentenced Lada-Rus in absentia to eight years in prison.

Egypt denies link to ship targeted off Yemen, condemns Red Sea attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:47:21 UTC
23:47:21 KST

Egypt has denied any link to a ship targeted off Yemen earlier this week, while condemning attacks on ships and maritime navigation in the Red Sea.
The country’s transport ministry said on Thursday that reports linking the targeted vessel to Egypt or its ports were false.
The denial came after media outlets and social media platforms reported that Yemen’s Houthi group had targeted a ship off the Yemeni coast and that the operating company’s address was in Alexandria, northern Egypt.
“The vessel was flying the Tanzanian flag, owned by a Yemeni national and operated by a company based in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates,” the ministry said.
It added that the ship was not registered with Egyptian shipping chambers and had not received a licence to conduct maritime agency work through Egypt’s maritime transport and logistics sector.
“The ship had never entered Egyptian ports, was not heading to Egypt and did not carry any cargo belonging to Egyptians,” the ministry said.
Separately, Egypt’s foreign ministry said Cairo “condemns the targeting of ships in the Red Sea.”
It cited a Yemeni commercial ship flying the Tanzanian flag that was attacked Tuesday with missiles while sailing off Yemen’s coast south of Mokha port in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, as well as a Saudi oil tanker targeted on July 25.
“Such attacks represent a serious threat to the security and safety of navigation in the Red Sea,” the ministry said, adding that it is one of the world’s most important international waterways.
Egypt renewed its “categorical rejection of all acts targeting ships and civilian facilities or threatening the security and freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and international waterways.”
Attacks in the Red Sea often reduce traffic through Egypt’s Suez Canal, causing financial losses for Cairo as ships divert to alternative routes to avoid security risks.
Since July 20, tensions have escalated in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden after the Houthis announced a “naval blockade” on ships linked to Saudi Arabia.
Three days later, Riyadh said one of its ships had come under attack and, the following day, carried out strikes on Houthi sites in Yemen’s western Hudaydah province, saying they were used to threaten maritime navigation.
Saudi Arabia also announced the formation of a defensive naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including the US, Yemen, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan, Sudan, Morocco, the Maldives, Bangladesh and New Zealand.

Suicide attempts, broken toilets and rationed food: crisis deepens aboard USS Abraham Lincoln
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:46:31 UTC
23:46:31 KST

The strain aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln has become so severe that several sailors have reportedly tried to jump overboard as the aircraft carrier remains at sea in the Middle East after nearly nine months of continuous deployment.
Reports by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes describe worsening mental health conditions aboard the ship, where about 5,000 sailors and Marines have spent roughly 250 consecutive days at sea without a port call, a modern-era record for a U.S. aircraft carrier.
Families of some of the sailors met Navy officials in San Diego last week to voice their concerns.
One woman among roughly 200 people at the meeting said her husband had texted her that same day saying he “hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow.”
Annabel Luma told the Navy Times that her husband tried to jump into the water after learning that his deployment at sea had once again been extended.
“He’s scared,” she said. “He thinks he’s going to get kicked out of the military in disgrace just because he’s worn down, and a 13-year career is being destroyed just like that. It’s not fair, it’s not right. That’s not what he should be worrying about right now.”
Natalie Oliverio, the journalist behind the Navy Times report, later told CNN that Luma had not heard from Navy representatives for weeks and remained deeply concerned about her husband’s condition.
The Navy Times also cited the wife of another service member aboard the Lincoln who said her husband had attempted to jump into the sea.
The USS Abraham Lincoln left San Diego on November 21, 2025, originally bound for the Pacific but was redirected to the Middle East after the war with Iran began.
Since then, its roughly 5,000 personnel have had only two days ashore, one in Guam in December and another in Oman in July.
The deployment was originally expected to end in May but has been extended several times during the ongoing war.
By April, complaints about conditions aboard the carrier were already spreading publicly. Images shared on social media showed what appeared to be severely rationed, poor-quality meals, while reports described water shortages, moldy showers and broken washing machines.
The current crisis comes after another carrier, the USS Gerald R. Ford, earlier this year broke the previous record for the longest aircraft carrier deployment since the Vietnam War.
A fire in the Ford’s laundry compartment in March took crews about 30 hours to extinguish, and roughly 600 sailors temporarily lost access to their berths because of the damage.
On the Lincoln, lawmakers are now demanding answers about both the length of the deployment and conditions aboard the ship.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat and member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, wrote to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth expressing “serious concern” over the deployment.
“Shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing problems, deteriorating mental health, concerns about shipboard safety” have all been reported, Blumenthal wrote, along with disruptions to the mail system that allegedly caused packages bound for the ship to go missing for months.
Rep. Mike Levin, a California Democrat, described conditions aboard the carrier in similarly stark terms.
“They are using moldy showers and broken toilets, enduring long periods without hot water, a meal that consisted of half a cup of rice and two tortillas. No soap, deodorant or toothpaste,” he said.
After Hegseth dismissed the reports as “more fake news,” Levin responded sharply.
“These men and women went to serve their country,” he said. “The least their country owes them is hot water, working toilets and a real meal. Hegseth can’t even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their family members in the eye and call them liars.”
The U.S. Navy more broadly has been grappling with burnout among sailors and naval aviation personnel, from pilots to maintenance crews, with many leaving the service.
A study conducted last year by the University of Oxford examined stress factors faced by sailors on deployment and found that among the most common were excessive noise, insufficient rest and inadequate physical and mental health care.
Nearly half of those surveyed said they were not receiving enough help managing stress at sea.
The researchers concluded that, given the high suicide rates among military personnel, including within the Navy, there was an urgent need to improve access to health services aboard ships.
At the meeting with families in San Diego, Vice Adm. Joseph Cahill, commander of Naval Surface Forces, acknowledged the growing concern.
“We hear you loud and clear about the impact this is having on families, on service members and on our ability to preserve the health of our force over the long term,” he said.

WSJ: Ukrainian drone operators ‘easily defeated’ U.S. troops in military exercise
Ukrainian servicemen from the 412th Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) regiment “defeated” a U.S. armored brigade during an exercise this spring, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing its own sources.
American troops attacked positions defended by a mock enemy backed by USF, with the attacking side equipped with standard electronic warfare and counter-drone systems.
One participant told the newspaper that the heavy armored vehicles kicked up clouds of dust that made them easy targets for Ukrainian drones. Another source said the drones destroyed the vehicles so fast that “eliminated” American vehicles had to be rotated back in as fresh formations just to keep the exercise running.
The training scenario was repeated several times over two weeks, and the Americans gradually improved, according to a U.S. Army representative — dispersing more effectively, camouflaging their positions, and making better use of electronic warfare equipment. Halfway through the exercises, Ukrainian servicemen were sent to support the American side, and USF proved just as effective in offensive operations.
The U.S. Army was not the first to lose to Ukrainian drones, according to WSJ sources. In May 2025, Ukrainian Armed Forces drone operators “easily defeated” British, Estonian, and other NATO forces during an exercise in the Baltic region, and in another exercise this spring, USF defeated troops from Sweden and other NATO countries.
The Combined Resolve exercise ran from April 9 to May 10 at the training range in Hohenfels, Germany, and involved about 3,500 American troops. The number of Ukrainian servicemen who took part was not disclosed.
President Volodymyr Zelensky ordered the creation of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces in June 2024, and Robert Brovdi (call sign “Madyar”) has led the force since June of last year. In recent months, USF has carried out regular strikes on Russian facilities, including oil refineries, vessels in Russia’s “shadow fleet,” and Wildberries logistics centers.

Gulf Stream collapse could depend on rate of warming, scientists warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:43:44 UTC
23:43:44 KST

Aysu Bicer
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
A possible collapse of the Gulf Stream may depend more on how quickly the climate warms than on reaching a specific temperature threshold, according to Dutch climate scientists.
The findings suggest the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), a major system of ocean currents, could reach a tipping point even without global temperatures reaching levels previously thought necessary to trigger such a collapse.
Scientists had previously estimated that an irreversible collapse could begin at around 2.5C of warming, potentially as early as 2060. The new study, however, suggests that the rate of warming may be more important than the temperature itself.
“The collapse occurs due to the rate of warming rather than reaching a specific temperature,” researcher Rene van Westen told public broadcaster NOS.
A shutdown could have major consequences. The Netherlands could become colder and drier, while sea levels and the risk of storm surges could rise. Rainfall patterns in the tropics could also shift, bringing drought to some areas and wetter conditions to others.
Van Westen said faster action was needed to prevent further weakening of the circulation.
Oceanographer Femke de Jong of NIOZ said the findings showed a need for greater caution.
“You cannot say that below a certain temperature there is no risk of the AMOC shutting down.”
She said the effects could last for hundreds of years, even if carbon dioxide levels returned to pre-industrial levels.
Scientists said more monitoring and research are needed, while policymakers should prepare for potentially severe climate changes. Preventing a collapse, they said, remains the best and least costly option.

The head of the Mykolaiv regional Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center was detained for a $15,000 bribe — Prosecutor General
Kyiv • UNN
The head of the Mykolaiv regional Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center was detained while receiving $10,000. In total, the receipt of $15 thousand in undue benefit was documented.
Today, the head of the Mykolaiv Regional Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center was detained while receiving an illicit benefit, and a notice of suspicion is being prepared. Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko reported this, according to UNN.
Details
According to the investigation, the official received US$10,000 for not taking mobilization measures against three persons liable for military service, removing them from the wanted list in the "Oberih" system, and creating conditions for their subsequent unhindered reservation through their place of employment.
The Prosecutor General added that earlier, as part of the same proceedings, the receipt by him of another US$5,000 had been documented. In exchange for this money, he was supposed to prevent a mobilized man from being sent to a military unit and return him for a repeat military medical examination. In total, the receipt of US$15,000 in illicit benefits has been documented.
The official was detained pursuant to Article 208 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine. Searches are being conducted at his place of service and residence, as well as other initial investigative actions. A notice of suspicion is being prepared in connection with the receipt of an illicit benefit. The prosecution will request that the suspect be held in custody and suspended from office. We continue

PM: Land joining Madise in race 'should make the election interesting'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:43:00 UTC
23:43:00 KST

PM: Land joining Madise in race 'should make the election interesting'
Ülle Madise is now backed by more than 60 MPs, but Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) still believes TalTech rector Tiit Land will also enter Estonia's presidential race.
Michal said he supports Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise and believes she would make a good president.
"We have one candidate with the support of about 60 MPs, and more signatures are gradually coming in," Michal said Thursday, calling it good news. "This means the presidential election has its first candidate eligible to be elected in the Riigikogu."
The prime minister said said parties are still in talks with Land, the rector of Tallinn University of Technology, and Mart Helme, the founder and deputy chair of the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE), but expects Land to be nominated.
"That should make the election rounds in the Riigikogu interesting," he added.
'I don't understand what's stopping them'
Minister of Education and Research and Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas said the political expectations surrounding the election do not reflect the constitutional system established for electing the president.
"The idea that Estonia's president is simply appointed or that this is a contest between top officials makes a mockery of our constitutional order," Kallas said, emphasizing that the president's role in Estonia as head of state isn't significant enough to require such a broad public mandate.
"The law provides for the president to be elected by the Riigikogu," she added. "We don't have nationwide campaigns, debates or public forums."
Kallas praised the work the Riigikogu has put into the process over the summer, noting that the process is less a traditional election and moreso an agreement on who will represent Estonia for the next five years.
With more than 60 MPs agreeing by now that that should be Madise, Kallas urged other parties to skip any political games, show good statesmanship and join in her support.
"If the other parties say they have no reservations or fundamental ideological objections to Madise, I don't understand what's stopping them from supporting her," the Eesti 200 chair said. "Our job is to come together and elect a president."
She added that Madise's international standing and strong knowledge of the Constitution would make her well suited to the role.
'This isn't some game'
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said every MP in his party's parliamentary group has already signed in support of Madise. "Eesti 200 stands 100 behind what we've said," he said.
He urged parties to put aside political maneuvering connected to the 2027 Riigikogu elections and focus first on their responsibility to Estonia.
"This isn't some domestic political game where it's all fun and games and we take shots at one another," Tsahnka continued. "Look around you — we haven't seen geopolitical turmoil like this since the Soviet Union, and it affects our security as well. Never forget that independence cannot be taken for granted."
The Riigikogu will convene to elect the next president of Estonia on September 2, with candidates to be formally nominated August 21–24.

SBU Busts Russian Spy Network Tracking F-16s, Mirage 2000s and Their Flight Schedules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:41:54 UTC
23:41:54 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
SBU Busts Russian Spy Network Tracking F-16s, Mirage 2000s and Their Flight Schedules
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) says it has dismantled a 14-person Russian military intelligence network that was collecting information on Ukrainian air bases hosting F-16 and Mirage 2000 fighter jets, potentially helping Russia plan missile strikes against the aircraft and the infrastructure supporting them, SBU reported on August 13.
The operation was carried out by SBU military counterintelligence under the coordination of Oleksandr Poklad, the agency said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to investigators, members of the network photographed Ukrainian airfields, combat aircraft, flight crews, and maintenance personnel. They also collected information on takeoff and landing schedules that could have helped Russian military intelligence determine when and where aircraft were most vulnerable.
The SBU said the intelligence gathering was specifically aimed at air bases used by Ukraine’s F-16 and Mirage 2000 fighters.
The alleged network consisted of 14 people living in different regions of Ukraine.
“Countering Russian intelligence services that seek to destabilize Ukraine from within is one of the SBU’s main priorities today. Anyone who agrees to work in Russia’s interests should understand: the SBU will inevitably hold you accountable,” Poklad said.
According to the investigation, Russia’s GRU initially recruited a resident of Lviv who administered a Telegram channel focused on military aviation.
The man allegedly drew the attention of Russian intelligence after posting photographs of Ukrainian combat aircraft in pro-Kremlin online groups.
To carry out the assignments, the agent then involved 13 subscribers to his channel, reportedly without telling them that the information was ultimately being collected for Russian intelligence.
Many of those subscribers lived near Ukrainian military aviation facilities and owned professional or high-quality camera equipment.
They were allegedly instructed to photograph Ukrainian air bases, aircraft, crews, and technical personnel, as well as record the approximate timing of takeoffs and landings. The participants were told the material was being collected for the Lviv blogger’s aviation-focused Telegram channel.
According to the SBU, some members of the group used professional cameras while hiding in abandoned buildings or positioning themselves in open areas near military airfields.
The photographs were then uploaded to an online storage service that the main agent had arranged access to in advance.
Investigators say he subsequently passed the material to a Russian handler whose identity has already been established by the SBU.
The suspected agent was also accused of providing Russia with flight schedules for Ukrainian combat helicopters.
According to the SBU, that information came from a Ukrainian Armed Forces aviation squadron commander who allegedly provided the data on his own initiative.
Such intelligence could have allowed Russian forces to build a more detailed picture of Ukrainian aviation activity, including when aircraft were present at particular bases and when flight operations were underway.
That information would be especially sensitive for Ukraine’s Western-supplied fighter fleet, including F-16s and Mirage 2000s, which Russia has repeatedly sought to locate and destroy on the ground.
During searches of the suspects’ homes, SBU officers said they recovered smartphones and digital photography equipment containing evidence of alleged cooperation with Russia, along with images of Ukrainian military aviation facilities.
The agency also blocked four Telegram channels and 10 specialized groups that had been used to distribute photographs and other information concerning Ukrainian aviation units.
Earlier, reports emerged that the Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) has systematically coordinated with Russia’s FSB security service to identify and punish priests who oppose the war against Ukraine.

Ukraine Just Put VR Goggles in an APC—Meet the New OWL Built for the Drone War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:41:38 UTC
23:41:38 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Just Put VR Goggles in an APC—Meet the New OWL Built for the Drone War
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has codified a new domestically produced armored personnel carrier, the OWL-APC, clearing the vehicle for use by Ukrainian forces alongside the existing MAC OWL armored vehicle, according to the Ministry’s press release on August 13.
The new 4×4 platform combines a rigid V-shaped monocoque hull, advanced mine protection, a modular troop compartment, and a domestically developed 360-degree virtual-reality vision system with night capability.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The OWL-APC was developed by a Ukrainian manufacturer with experience building armored vehicles for the extreme conditions of modern warfare. The same company also produces the MAC OWL specialized armored vehicle, which is designed around particularly high levels of mine protection.
The new APC is intended for a wide range of missions, including troop transport, combat operations, fire support, special operations, patrol duties, training, and emergency-response missions in difficult terrain and hazardous environments.
During testing, the OWL-APC reportedly confirmed its stated tactical and technical characteristics and demonstrated the ability to perform a broad range of military tasks.
Compared with larger armored personnel carriers, the vehicle is designed to be relatively compact and lightweight. Its 4×4 configuration is intended to provide high mobility, while the manufacturer also highlights a longer driving range, higher maximum speed, lower operating costs, and simpler and cheaper maintenance.
The vehicle is also designed to have a relatively low battlefield signature, an increasingly important characteristic as both Russian and Ukrainian forces operate under near-constant drone surveillance.
One of the OWL-APC’s key features is its protection against mines and explosions.
The vehicle uses a V-shaped monocoque hull and double floor, combined with blast-absorbing components and shock-resistant seats intended to reduce the effects of explosions on troops inside.
The modular troop compartment can also be reconfigured into a medical evacuation vehicle within several hours, allowing the same platform to be used either for transporting personnel or evacuating wounded troops from the battlefield.
Perhaps the most unusual feature, however, is the vehicle’s 360-degree VR observation system.
The Ukrainian-developed system includes night vision and allows the driver to put on VR goggles and receive a panoramic view of what is happening around the armored vehicle.
Instead of depending only on conventional viewing ports or individual camera screens, the system is designed to give the driver a continuous picture of the surrounding battlefield while remaining protected inside the armored hull.
Earlier, a Ukrainian firm, Zvook, had for the first time mounted its passive acoustic early-warning sensors on a moving vehicle, testing the drone-detection technology beyond its standard fixed-infrastructure setup during the BATT26 exercises in Latvia.

261 Bodies Returned to Ukraine as Part of Latest Exchange With Russia
Ukraine and Russia have exchanged the bodies of people killed during the war, with 261 bodies returned to Ukraine, according to Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The headquarters said the remains were transferred to Ukraine following joint repatriation efforts involving representatives of the Coordination Headquarters, the Security Service of Ukraine’s Joint Center, the Armed Forces, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ombudsman’s Office, the Commissioner for Missing Persons, the State Emergency Service, and other security and defense agencies.
According to the Russian side, the repatriated bodies belong to military personnel.
Ukrainian investigators and forensic experts will now carry out the necessary procedures to establish the identities of those returned.
The exchange follows a previous repatriation in which Ukraine received the bodies of 501 people whom Russian authorities also claimed were Ukrainian military personnel. The remains were similarly subjected to identification and forensic examinations on July 16.
In some previous exchanges, Russia has also returned the remains of its own servicemen to Ukraine. Ukrainian officials have suggested that such cases could help Moscow avoid compensation payments to the families of fallen Russian soldiers or may reflect negligence in handling the remains of its personnel.
The repatriation comes as hundreds of Ukrainian servicemen remain in Russian captivity. More than 600 members of Ukraine’s Azov Brigade are still being held by Russia, including more than 20 in critical condition, while nearly half have been convicted on what the brigade says are fabricated charges.

Flooding in China displaces thousands as Japan declares highest emergency with 1 killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:40:58 UTC
23:40:58 KST

Islamuddin Sajid
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
- Japan issues Level Five Emergency Warning for heavy rain across 14 cities in Chiba Prefecture
Thousands have been evacuated in China and Japan, with one person killed after torrential rain caused flooding, as authorities issued emergency warnings in parts of the two East Asian countries.
In central China's Henan province, more than 2,000 people have been relocated to safety after a levee along the Beiru River in Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan City, collapsed late Wednesday following extreme rainfall and heavy water releases from upstream reservoirs, according to state-run Xinhua News.
The breach, which measured more than 40 meters wide, caused floodwaters to spread into surrounding areas.
No casualties have been reported so far, authorities said.
Water levels were receding by Thursday morning as emergency crews continued efforts to close the breach.
In Henan, more than 4,500 residents from 10 villages in Luohe City were evacuated as river levels rose and authorities warned of possible flooding.
Luohe received an average rainfall of 270.1 millimeters (10.6 inches) between Monday afternoon and Wednesday afternoon, with the highest recorded at 434.2 millimeters (17 inches).
Authorities activated the highest-level flood-control emergency response as heavy rain continued to threaten the region.
China's National Meteorological Center renewed a yellow alert for heavy rain on Thursday, forecasting further downpours across several areas, including Henan and neighboring Hubei province.
Apart from flooding in China, Japan on Thursday declared a high-level rainfall emergency.
The Japan Meteorological Agency issued its highest-level, Level Five Emergency Warning for heavy rain across 14 cities in Chiba Prefecture, east of Tokyo, according to NHK.
The warning covers Chiba, Ichihara, Sakura, Yotsukaido, Shiroi, Ichikawa, Funabashi, Matsudo, Narashino, Kashiwa, Yachiyo, Kamagaya, Inzai and Abiko.
The Level Five warning is the highest on Japan's five-tier system and indicates that life-threatening disasters may already be occurring.
According to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, one person has died in Ichikawa City in the Chiba Prefecture, due to heavy rain, Kyodo News reported.
Residents in the affected areas have been urged to take immediate measures to protect themselves, including moving to higher floors of buildings or evacuating to designated shelters where possible.
Authorities have issued an evacuation order for 176,988 people in the Ibaraki, Saitama and Chiba prefectures.

These are Europe’s best-value cities for a weekend break - and Poland dominates the top five
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:40:46 UTC
23:40:46 KST

A new study has revealed the best-value European cities for a weekend away, with Polish destinations sweeping the top five and some of the continent’s biggest tourist hotspots proving much pricier.
Planning a last-minute European escape doesn’t have to mean paying a premium.
A new study by virtual card provider Getsby has revealed the best-value cities for a weekend break, analysing data from travel cost site Budget Your Trip across 100 destinations.
It compared the typical daily costs of accommodation, meals and local transport for two people travelling on a mid-range budget, revealing where your money will go furthest.
Flights aren’t included in the final figure, as they can vary hugely but, if in doubt, head to Poland. The Slavic nation takes six out of the top 10 spots, and the entire top five.
Poland reigns supreme
According to the data, Wroclaw in Poland is Europe’s most affordable city for a weekend trip for two people.
If you head to the City of Bridges, you can expect an average daily cost of €41 per person, and a total weekend trip which costs just €163 for two people.
Here, travellers tend to spend around €18.75 on food and €5.85 on local transport costs. There’s plenty to do, too, including a visit to the Rynek, one of Europe’s largest medieval market squares, and the Centennial Hall, a striking UNESCO-listed architectural landmark.
In second place is Poznań, where a weekend trip for two people costs an average of €168.50, or around €42 per person per day.
Travellers can expect to spend roughly €18.75 a day on food and €34 on accommodation, making it another particularly affordable option for a city break.
There’s lots to see without spending a fortune, including the colourful Old Market Square and Poznań Town Hall, where the famous mechanical goats appear each day. Cathedral Island is also worth a visit and is considered the birthplace of the Polish state.
Katowice takes third place, with a weekend for two costing around €239, or €60 per person per day.
Food accounts for about €32.75 a day, while hotels cost an average of €37.50, keeping the overall price relatively low.
The Silesian Museum is one of the city’s standout attractions. Built on the site of a former coal mine, it combines art and history with panoramic views from its observation tower.
Gdańsk comes fourth, with a two-day trip for two costing around €275.25, or €69 per person per day.
Visitors spend an average of €35 a day on food and €54 on hotels, with plenty of sights to fill a weekend.
The picturesque Long Market is a good place to start, while the historic waterfront around the Gdańsk Crane offers a glimpse into the city’s long maritime history.
Kraków rounds out the top five, costing around €295 for two people for a weekend, or €73.75 per person per day.
Hotels account for around €83 of the total, while local transport is particularly cheap at just €7 on average.
Once there, travellers can explore the atmospheric Jewish Quarter of Kazimierz, browse the historic Sukiennice Cloth Hall and visit St Mary’s Basilica, where the famous trumpet call rings out every hour.
Affordability varies across the continent
If you’ve been everywhere in Poland already, fear not – there are other, very affordable options across Europe.
Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria, takes sixth place, with a weekend trip costing around €77.25 per person per day.
Zagreb in Croatia follows in seventh, with the average traveller spending around €95 a day.
Sweden’s Malmö comes next at €105 per day, followed by Budapest in Hungary at €111.
Rounding out the top 10 and it’s back to Poland, namely the capital, Warsaw, a spot where visitors can expect to spend around €112 per person each day.
The least affordable options
At the other end of the scale is Zurich, Switzerland, where a weekend away costs an eye-watering €1,325 for two people, or around €331 per person per day.
Food is a major expense, with travellers spending around €112 a day on meals, while a hotel costs an average of €359.
Switzerland dominates the more expensive end of the ranking too, with Bern and Basel taking second and third place. A weekend for two costs around €1,240 and €1,189 respectively.
Venice and Paris complete the top five most expensive cities, with a two-person weekend costing around €1,180 and €1,133 respectively once food, accommodation and local transport are factored in.

Switzerland submits film about Gaza survivors for Oscars
The documentary Qui vit encore (Who is still alive) is representing Switzerland in the race for an Oscar. In it, Geneva-based director Nicolas Wadimoff has survivors from Gaza tell their stories in an abstract setting.
Qui vit encore is a film that directly addresses the feelings of loss, uprooting and belonging, according to the jury’s statement in a press release issued by the Federal Office of Culture (BAK) on Thursday.
+ Nicolas Wadimoff wins Solothurn Film Festival prize
Earlier this year, the film won Switzerland’s most prestigious film award, the Prix de Soleure, at the Solothurn Film Festival. It is now Switzerland’s official Oscar entry, competing for the Best International Feature Film award at the 99th Academy Awards on March 14, 2027.
The road to the golden statuette is a tough one: in mid-December, the Academy will announce the finalists from all international submissions in a shortlist. From these, five films will then be nominated for an Oscar in the “Best International Feature” category. These will be announced on January 21.

Sybiha condemns Putin's visit to Etorofu, expresses Ukraine's solidarity with Japan
Sybiha stated this on X, according to Ukrinform.
"Ukraine's position is unwavering: Japan's sovereignty over the Northern Territories is grounded in historical facts and international law… Russia uses the same imperial playbook everywhere. It occupies foreign land, militarizes it, threatens its neighbours, and then tries to make the world accept the illegal as irreversible," the Foreign Minister said.
He added that Ukraine knows this model very well and emphasized that it must not succeed either in Europe or in the Pacific region.
Sybiha stressed that Ukraine stands in solidarity with Japan and highly values its support. He called on international partners to clearly condemn Putin's provocative visit, reject any attempts to normalize Russia's occupation, strengthen the aggressor's isolation, and increase sanctions pressure.
As Ukrinform reported, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi protested to Russia following Vladimir Putin's first visit to the disputed island of Etorofu. Motegi stated that the Northern Territories, including Etorofu, are an integral part of Japan both historically and under international law.
Etorofu is part of a group of islands off the eastern coast of Hokkaido Prefecture that were occupied by the former Soviet Union after World War II.
Japan claims the southern Kuril Islands, which it refers to as its Northern Territories, based on the 1855 Treaty of Commerce, Navigation and Delimitation.
Russia, meanwhile, insists that the Kuril Islands became part of the Soviet Union as a result of World War II.
In spring 2022, the Japanese government restored the wording "illegally occupied" in its annual Diplomatic Bluebook in reference to the Northern Territories — the islands of Etorofu, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai Islands.

Settler leaders denounce Kusra violence: ‘This is not our way’

Senior settler leaders on Thursday publicly denounced the violence surrounding the Palestinian village of Kusra, with the chairman of the Yesha Council declaring that the events were “not our way” and the head of the Beit El Council warning they were causing “irreversible damage” to Israel and the settlement movement.
Yisrael Ganz, chairman of the Yesha Council and head of the Binyamin Regional Council, said there was no justification for violence against uninvolved Palestinians or Israeli security forces.
“The events in Kusra are serious and are not our way,” Ganz said.
“There is no place for privately deciding to establish a hilltop outpost in the yard of a house, even when it is an illegal house or there is an attempt to take control of the area,” he said. “There is absolutely no justification for violence against uninvolved people or against the security forces.”
Ganz’s condemnation was joined by Beit El Council head Shai Alon, who gave an unusually blunt assessment of the events in an interview with Ynet on Thursday.
Alon said the violence was causing “irreversible damage” to Israel and to the settlement movement and described those responsible for attacks on innocent Palestinians as criminals.
“These are criminal offenders who take out their rage on an innocent population,” Alon said, adding that the phenomenon had to be eradicated.
Alon said he had warned for years about what he described as a group of “lost youth” in the West Bank and accused the state of failing to deal adequately with the problem before it developed into violence.
“The State of Israel is not doing enough to deal with this phenomenon,” he told Ynet. “It begins with education and welfare, and when it is not dealt with, it reaches the places we are seeing today.”
Alon criticizes Ben-Gvir, Son Har-Melech
Alon also directed criticism at National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit MK Limor Son Har-Melech, saying the young extremists involved in such incidents were politically closer to them.
He argued that greater pressure should have been applied to prevent what he described as the “terrible and horrific scenes” being seen in the West Bank.
Alon also criticized the Israel Police’s Judea and Samaria District, saying that while he respected its officers, law enforcement had not done enough to address the phenomenon. He backed the IDF’s handling of the latest events.
He said West Bank municipal leaders were united in opposing the violence, describing those involved as a relatively small group that did not represent the broader settlement movement.
Alon added that reservists who participate in such incidents while wearing IDF uniforms should immediately remove their uniforms and be released from reserve duty.
The condemnations came after several days of tensions in the Kusra and nearby Jalud areas of the northern West Bank.
The IDF said Israeli civilians had entered Palestinian homes and land in the area earlier this week, describing the activity as “illegal, reprehensible, and unacceptable.” The area was subsequently declared a closed military zone.
Dozens of settler extremists clashed with IDF forces on Wednesday after security forces evacuated an outpost established near Kusra. Footage seen by The Jerusalem Post showed extremists dismantling fences, blocking roads, and surrounding the area.
Security forces demolished two unauthorized outposts near Kusra and Jalud overnight Wednesday, according to the IDF, which said one Israeli was detained. Golani Brigade Battalion 51 was also deployed to the area to carry out patrols and security missions.
Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth visited the area and met with a Palestinian family living there, the IDF said.
Commanders expressed concern over the conduct of Israeli civilians toward the family and ordered measures to restore order.
Ganz: Critics exploiting events against settlements
Ganz said the violence should be condemned regardless of what he described as attempts by opponents of the settlement movement to exploit the events politically.
“There is no doubt that there are those who are exploiting these events for a campaign against the settlement movement, but that must not obscure the simple fact: What happened in Kusra is improper and unacceptable to us,” he said.
Ganz said the Yesha leadership would continue working to expand Jewish settlement through organized and authorized channels.
“We are leading and will continue to lead settlement in Binyamin, Judea and Samaria with determination and responsibility, in an organized and proper manner,” he said.
At the same time, he called on the government to repeal the Oslo Accords and permit regulated Jewish settlement throughout open areas of the West Bank.
“I call on the Israeli government to cancel the Oslo Accords and allow legitimate and regulated Jewish settlement throughout all the open areas,” Ganz said.
The statements from Ganz and Alon placed two veteran settlement officials publicly against those responsible for the violence while rejecting attempts to portray the perpetrators as representative of the hundreds of thousands of Israelis living in West Bank settlements.

2027 UP assembly elections: How parties are vying for Dalit votes amid Mayawati’s shrinking base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:35:31 UTC
23:35:31 KST

As Mayawati's base shrinks, BJP, SP and Congress intensify fight for Dalit votes in UP
NEW DELHI: Dalit politics in Uttar Pradesh is at a crossroads. For a very long time, Mayawati and her Bahujan Samaj Party were synonymous with the idea of Dalit vote in UP. Not any more. Mayawati’s BSP today is a much weaker force. The last three elections in the state have pushed Mayawati, the four-time chief minister of UP, to the margins of state politics. This has opened up the Dalit space and triggered an interesting scramble among political parties for a slice of the Dalit pie in the 2027 assembly elections.So, we have the BJP playing the name-change game in Bhadohi and organising a 7-month campaign to honour 15th-century saint-poet Sant Ravi Das. Then we have Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav announcing 14 extra seats for the Dalits to cement his PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) politics. Congress too is trying to win back voters it lost decades ago. Then there is Chandrashekhar Azad, who is trying to consolidate his own space in the state.As Uttar Pradesh heads towards 2027, the question is: if the BSP continues to lose ground, where does Mayawati’s old support base go and which of her rivals stands to gain the most?
From 206 seats to one: How BSP lost ground
The BSP’s rise in UP politics was as dramatic as its fall. The party was founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984 with the idea of giving Dalits and other marginalized communities an independent voice.
Mayawati, who emerged as his political successor, took the BSP to great heights in Uttar Pradesh. Under her leadership, the BSP won a majority on its own in the 2007 assembly elections, winning 206 seats with a vote share of 30.43%.Dalits, who constitute around 21% of UP’s population as per the 2021 census, have for years been the core base of Mayawati’s Bahujan Samaj Party. But that dynamic has now changed.BSP is a much weaker force today. Mayawati has failed to mobilise Dalit support for her BSP in the last two elections in the state, thereby opening up the space for other political contenders. In the 2022 assembly elections, the BSP could win just 1 seat with a vote share of 12.88%. This was a sharp decline from the 19 seats and a 22.23% vote share that Mayawati had got in 2017.The 2024 Lok Sabha elections went on to showcase that Mayawati’s dismal 2022 performance was not an aberration. The BSP supremo failed to win even one Lok Sabha seat, while her party’s vote share dipped to 9.4% from 19.43% in 2019. Clearly, the results reinforced the gradual decline in BSP’s influence among Dalits.As Mayawati gears up for the 2027 assembly challenge, she faces an uphill road. The BSP chief has not just lost support of voters, but also control over her party. So, when Mayawati issued a stern message that all the candidates for the upcoming poll will be finalised by her and not by her nephew Akash Anand, it was an indication of the internal tussle in her party.Akash Anand, who has been in and out of Mayawati’s favour in the past, launched the party’s 2027 assembly poll campaign from Sadabad in Hathras this week.Mayawati, who has often been accused of helping the BJP, has ruled out any pre-poll alliance. She has claimed that some candidates have already been finalised for the upcoming assembly elections. Mayawati has asked party cadres to start rebuilding the party and drum up OBC support ahead of the polls. The cadres have apparently been asked to remind people of the party's past governance and convince them that the real benefit and welfare of the OBC community lie with the BSP and its "iron lady government".Mayawati, however, must consider that it will be difficult for the BSP to come back to power only by holding on to its core Dalit vote alone. It will have to recreate the Dalit-OBC combination that originally carried Mayawati to power in Lucknow with a majority of her own.
BJP's Dalit outreach gets sharper ahead of 2027
One interesting fallout of BSP’s decline has been the BJP’s aggressive outreach to woo the Dalits. When Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath announced the renaming of Bhadohi district as Sant Ravidas Nagar last month, he put the BJP right at the middle of the Dalit outreach battle ahead of 2027 polls.The move also revived an old political contest over name-change politics. Mayawati was the one who had renamed Bhadohi as Sant Ravidas Nagar in December 1997. Akhilesh Yadav restored the old name in 2014. Now, by bringing Sant Ravidas Nagar back, Yogi sought to make a bigger political point, accusing the SP of erasing a Dalit symbol while positioning the BJP as a party willing to restore it.Mayawati publicly welcomed the decision, a rare moment of agreement with the ruling party. She was quick, however, to remind voters that it was her government that had changed the district's name in the first place and that the decision was later reversed under Akhilesh.The party realises that Dalit votes are up for grabs and hence is going all out to woo them. The party’s 'Samrasta Sankalp Abhiyan’ appears planned to coincide with assembly elections in two key states, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab, early next year.Both these states have a sizeable population of Dalits who play an important role in many constituencies. In the 2022 assembly elections, the BJP and its ally Apna Dal (Soneylal) together bagged 63 Scheduled Caste (SC) seats compared to 20 won by the then Samajwadi Party-led opposition alliance. But the 2024 Lok Sabha polls changed the dynamics, with the SP and the Congress winning 43 of the 80 seats in the state and pushing the BJP to make an aggressive outreach. The loss of Faizabad seat to SP's Awadhesh Prasad, a Pasi leader, was particularly significant and gave Akhilesh Yadav fresh ammunition for his PDA pitch.Earlier this year, the Yogi Adityanath government approved the “Dr B R Ambedkar Murti Vikas Yojna" under which Rs 1 crore is to be allocated to each of the state's 403 assembly constituencies for the beautification and development of statues of social reformers.The BJP's efforts to woo Dalits has also been visible in its recent Cabinet expansion. Of the six new ministers inducted into the Yogi government, two were Dalits, Krishna Paswan from the Pasi community and Surendra Singh Daler from the Valmiki community. Three others were from OBC groups. Two non-Yadav OBC ministers were also given independent charge.The BJP's primary task ahead of 2027 would be to hold on to the non-Jatav Dalit support it built over the past decade and prevent a repeat of 2024.
SP’s Dalit outreach
The 2024 Lok Sabha elections also showed that the Dalits in UP were ready to back other political parties who wooed them. Dalit support played a key role in the spectacular success of Akhilesh Yadav’s Samajwadi Party, which won 37 seats in 2024.Together with its alliance partner Congress, the INDIA bloc won 43 of the 80 seats in the state, pushing the BJP on the back foot. Akhilesh Yadav, who has centred his politics around PDA (Pichhde, Dalits and Aplasankhyaks), gained from his Dalit outreach in the 2024 elections. His Samajwadi Party fielded two Dalit candidates from general seats. While one of them went on to win the all-important Faizabad seat, the other lost by just 10,585 votes to the BJP in Meerut.
How Samajwadi Party performed when they contested independently
Little wonder, in the run-up to the 2027 assembly elections, Akhilesh has already announced plans to field 14 Dalit candidates from general seats. Uttar Pradesh has 84 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and two for Scheduled Tribes. With 14 more candidates on general seats, the total tally of reserved candidates for SP will increase to 100. This will help reinforce his message to the Dalits in line with his PDA politics. The move will also help the SP shed the narrative of being a Muslim-Yadav party.
Congress tries to reclaim lost ground
Rahul Gandhi has made it clear that Dalits would now play a 'central role' in Congress. Before Mayawati and the BSP built their massive Dalit vote bank in the 1990s, Congress was the primary choice for Uttar Pradesh's Dalits. For nearly three decades after that, Congress was almost pushed out of UP politics.Rahul Gandhi has started his road to the UP election by acknowledging that the party had failed to take the right steps for the community in the 1980s and 1990s. He even praised Kanshi Ram for bringing Dalits together and giving the community a sense of confidence.Rahul has also made the Constitution a regular part of his social justice pitch. He is often seen carrying the red book of the Constitution while warning that constitutional rights and reservation are under threat. He has repeatedly invoked BR Ambedkar in the same pitch, asserting that Congress wants to position itself as a guardian of the Constitution.The party has also put a Dalit leader in charge of Uttar Pradesh. Rajendra Pal Gautam, who heads the Congress’s Scheduled Castes Department, has been appointed UP in-charge ahead of the 2027 polls. Interestingly, Gautam had also made an unsuccessful attempt to meet Mayawati at her Lucknow residence earlier this year.Whether the party will be able to translate this outreach into votes remains to be seen.
Chandrashekhar Azad adds another claimant
Then there is Chandrashekhar Azad, whose 2024 victory from Nagina made him a prominent figure in UP’s Dalit politics. Unlike BJP, SP or Congress, Azad is trying to build an independent space outside the BSP. His challenge now is to take that appeal beyond one constituency and build an organisation strong enough to matter across the state in 2027.
That is what makes the coming assembly election in Uttar Pradesh interesting. For decades, politics in Uttar Pradesh has revolved around caste. Political parties build their electoral strategies around social coalitions, loyalty of communities and traditional vote base.Mayawati may no longer command the Dalit vote the way she once did, but that vote bank has not disappeared. It simply has more claimants. And in 2027, where those voters eventually move could make a significant difference.

She also cares deeply about stories around women’s rights and social change, while two very opinionated dogs make sure she never truly switches off.
