Tree lines out, swamps in—Lithuania rethinks how to stop Russian armor at the border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:20:24 UTC
20:20:24 KST

Lithuania's government approved an expanded plan on 12 August to fortify its borders with Russia and Belarus against a possible attack, LRT reports. Lithuania, a Baltic state and NATO member, sits wedged between Russia's Kaliningrad exclave and Belarus. The decision opens a new counter-mobility belt reaching inland from the border, a 20-meter strip that widens to 150 meters where the army marks out areas for operations.
The buildout answers a fear that has gripped the Baltics since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022: that a Russia left unchecked in Ukraine could turn on them next. Western intelligence agencies have warned for years that Moscow could eventually threaten NATO itself, and former CIA director David Petraeus has singled out Lithuania as the likeliest first target, pinned between Kaliningrad and Belarus and sitting beside the Suwałki Gap, the thin land corridor that is NATO's only overland route to the Baltic states.
The decision raises the number of engineering parks, storage depots for obstacles like concrete blocks and roadblocks, from 27 to 50, and gives that work until the end of 2028, more than three years past the original April 2025 target. The state rail company LTG Infra is to store the equipment. The changes could cost an extra €50 million ($58 million) from the State Defense Fund between 2026 and 2030.
Of the Baltic states and Poland fortifying their eastern borders, Lithuania is the most at risk yet the least fortified, according to a satellite review by open-source analyst Clément Molin, even as Belarus keeps testing that border with engineered migrant crossings. The plan is Lithuania's share of the Baltic Defense Line, the joint barrier it launched in 2024 with Latvia and Estonia, alongside Poland's parallel East Shield.
The design comes straight from Ukraine. Lithuania began building counter-mobility parks in 2023, drawing on Russia's war against Ukraine, and much of what it is now putting into the ground, the swamps, ditches, and obstacle fields, was tested first on Ukrainian battlefields, where mud, water, and simple barriers have repeatedly stalled armored advances.
The restored swamps should make some ground impassable to heavy military vehicles within a few years, the Defense Ministry says, with that work due by the end of 2030. Plans for defensive ditches and streams in the Marijampolė municipality were dropped, and the ministry found better sites in the Vilkaviškis and Šakiai districts. Deadlines for obstacles on roads and bridge approaches, and for fitting bridges with holders for explosives, were also moved to the end of 2028.
"Military counter-mobility is an important part of Lithuania's defence preparedness," Deputy Defense Minister Tomas Mikelkevičius said. "We seek to make the best possible use of Lithuania's terrain and engineering measures to impede an adversary's movement if necessary and create more favorable conditions for our armed forces to operate."
Lithuania approved its first counter-mobility plan in July 2024. The plan's original 2024 estimate put the full system at around €600 million ($690 million) over the decade.
Russia's pressure on the Baltic borders
The buildout lands amid steady friction along NATO's eastern edge. Latvia has absorbed the bulk of the migrant crossings funneled from Belarus, and this week found its first used smuggling tunnel under the border. Estonia has switched on the first sensors of a planned drone wall along its Russian frontier and is reallocating €500 million ($575 million) toward air defense and long-range strike. Russia, for its part, has shut seven rail crossings with Latvia, Estonia, and Finland without explanation.
The fortification drive is a bet on time. Estonia's military chief has set a two-year clock, warning Russia could be combat-ready again by 2027, and ISW analysts assessed in May that Moscow was manufacturing pretexts for aggression against the Baltics. Poland's parallel East Shield, meanwhile, has gone up far slower than promised, leaving the region's defenses still thin where the threat is judged greatest.

Finland breaks new ground with English-language upper secondary curriculum
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:19:13 EEST
20:19:13 KST

The first students to study Finland's upper secondary school curriculum entirely in English began classes on Thursday in six cities across the country.
The new track follows a law change introduced last year, which permits upper secondary school students to take all subjects and sit the end-of-school matriculation exams in English.
The reform is aimed at attracting foreign skilled workers with families to Finland, as well as encouraging Finnish expats to return to the country with their children.
The first cohort of English-language curriculum students is due to take the matriculation exam in English in 2028.
"I've been struggling quite a bit"
The new English-language tracks are being rolled out initially in six cities: Vantaa, Helsinki, Tampere, Jyväskylä, Oulu and Pori. Espoo will join the list next year.
At the Aviapolis upper secondary school in Vantaa, 17-year-old Aakash Gamage told Yle that the option to study the upper secondary school curriculum in English is a very welcome development for him.
"I've been struggling quite a bit when I've been doing my studies in Finnish, and it will be much, much easier when I do it in English, and I hope to get better grades," he said.
Gamage moved to Finland with his parents from Sri Lanka less than two years ago, and he completed ninth grade at a Finnish secondary school. The English-language track is open to students who have studied in a Finnish school for less than three years.
Gamage's classmate, 24-year-old Eoghan Donnelly, wants to study at a Finnish university — but he must first sit and pass the Finnish matriculation exam.
"There are a few paths I want to go down. It will be either history, philosophy, or engineering. They are my main choices at the moment," he said.
Donnelly is originally from Ireland but went to school in the UK, and he moved to Finland about 18 months ago.
"If this option hadn't been available, I would have had to completely learn the Finnish language first," Donnelly said.
Lack of material concerns teachers
Although classes have now started, the teachers responsible for providing the curriculum in English have expressed concern about the lack of study materials in English.
Juho-Kustaa Mäkinen, who teaches history, social studies and ethics at Aviapolis, noted that education publishers have seemed reluctant to produce English-language materials that cover the Finnish curriculum.
"Publishers have settled for translation tools. I'd prefer the material to be in English from the start," he said, adding that he has translated the existing material into English himself and finds articles from English-language media to support it.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

Russia returns bodies of 261 fallen Ukrainian soldiers to Ukraine
The Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
"As a result of the repatriation process, the bodies of 261 people who were killed and who, according to the Russian side, are Ukrainian service members have been returned to Ukraine," the agency said.
Law enforcement investigators, together with experts from specialized institutions, will carry out all necessary procedures to identify the repatriated remains.
The Coordination Headquarters said the repatriation was made possible through joint efforts by representatives of the Coordination Headquarters, the Joint Center under the SBU, the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Office of the Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights, the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Persons Missing under Special Circumstances, the State Emergency Service and other bodies within Ukraine's security and defense sector.
The Coordination Headquarters expressed its sincere gratitude to the International Committee of the Red Cross for facilitating and supporting the repatriation process.
The agency also separately thanked personnel of the Joint Center for Civil-Military Cooperation Support of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, which transports the repatriated remains to specialized state institutions and organizes the transfer of the fallen to law enforcement agencies within the Interior Ministry system, forensic medical examination institutions within the Health Ministry system, and representatives of the Armed Forces' civil-military cooperation structures, which provide overall coordination.
On July 16, the Coordination Headquarters said that the remains of 501 people killed in the war had been returned to Ukraine as part of repatriation efforts. According to the Russian side, they may belong to Ukrainian service members.

Pro-Palestine campaigners call for Spider-Man film boycott over producer's Israel support

Pro-Palestinian campaigners in Lebanon, Jordan and elsewhere in the Arab world have called for a boycott of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” over producer Avi Arad’s support for Israel and his rejection of criticism directed at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during the war on Gaza.
The Campaign to Boycott Supporters of Israel in Lebanon urged audiences not to purchase tickets for the film, arguing that financially supporting a production involving figures who have publicly backed Israel amounts to “cultural normalisation.”
“Do we want to support a production involving individuals who have publicly expressed political support for Israel?” the group said in a social media statement ahead of the film’s release.
The campaign called on the public to avoid paid screenings and said its position reflected its opposition to normalising Israel or its policies.
In Jordan, the Taharrak anti-normalisation group issued a separate statement calling for the film to be boycotted and excluded from the schedules of Jordanian cinemas.
The group also urged the Jordanian Artists Syndicate, cinema operators and other relevant bodies to take a position against its screening. The calls have since been amplified by activists and content creators in other Arab countries.
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” released internationally on July 31, stars Tom Holland as Peter Parker and is directed by Destin Daniel Cretton. Marvel lists Arad as one of its four producers alongside Kevin Feige, Amy Pascal and Rachel O’Connor.
Arad served in Israeli army
The campaign focuses on Arad’s political record rather than the film’s plot or its other cast and crew members.
Arad, a former Marvel Studios chief who holds Israeli and US citizenship, served in the Israeli military between 1965 and 1968 and was involved in the 1967 Six-Day War.
In a 2024 letter published by entertainment news outlet TheWrap, Arad rebuked then-US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer after the senator described Netanyahu as an obstacle to peace and called for Israel to hold new elections.
“It’s not your war. It is not your country. And it is not you who is at risk,” Arad wrote, arguing that Schumer had no right to influence Israel’s electoral process. He also described himself as a proud former member of the Israeli military and rejected Schumer’s position on a ceasefire.
Campaigners say those statements demonstrate Arad’s support for Israel’s conduct during its genocidal war on Gaza and argue that ticket purchases contribute financially to a production associated with him.
The effect of the campaign on attendance remains unclear. The film continued to screen in Lebanon despite the boycott call, with a representative of the Grand Cinemas chain telling Lebanese publication L’Orient Today shortly after its release that demand remained high.

Civilian deaths in Ukraine in July hit highest level since May 2022: UN
At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said.
The United Nations has reported that civilian deaths in Ukraine have reached their highest level in July since the opening months of Russia’s invasion in 2022.
“At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, a 30 percent increase compared with the previous month and a 70 percent increase compared with July 2025,” the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said in a statement.

The UN said it has verified the deaths of 16,874 civilians since Russia’s invasion, but warned that this is likely a significant underestimate since it cannot confirm casualties in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russian forces.

Russian military official ‘killed in blast’

Also on Thursday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train in southern Ukraine’s Odesa region, killing two of the train’s crew, according to Ukrainian officials.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of continuing a campaign of “terror” by attacking the train on Thursday, which he said was carrying 340 people.
“Whoever was operating that drone certainly could not have been unaware that the target was entirely civilian,” said Zelenskyy in a post on X.
While two crew members were killed, including the train’s driver, none of the passengers was harmed, said the chairman of the state railway operator, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi.
Video published by Ukrainian emergency services showed a bright fire raging in the train cab, the front of which was blown out and mangled.
Moscow’s forces have repeatedly hit trains throughout the war in what Kyiv claims is an effort to disrupt its logistics and hit civilians.
Zelenskyy said Russia also fired more than 130 attack drones into 11 regions of Ukraine overnight Wednesday into Thursday.
The Russian attacks hit several businesses in Ukraine’s Chernihiv, damaging them, reported Ukraine’s state news agency.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces also seized control of the Ukrainian village of Petrivka in the eastern Donetsk region.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said “asymmetric warfare” that has gone beyond the battlefield to affect logistics lines “has taken its toll on people both in Russia and Ukraine”.
‘More air defence needed’
Zelenskyy has pleaded with allies to deliver more advanced air defence systems – particularly United States Patriots – to fend off intensifying attacks by Russia’s super-fast ballistic missiles, whose trajectory and speed make them hard to stop.
He repeated that plea on Thursday, saying “more air defence support and more pressure on Russia are needed if the world is serious about stopping this war in Europe.”
In Russia, Ukraine’s military struck an oil refinery and petrochemical complex in the republic of Bashkortostan, causing a fire, Ukraine’s military said on Thursday.
It said the complex supplies the Russian military and pledged to continue hitting “key enemy targets”.
Ukraine has increased its own long-range attacks on Russia in recent months – justifying them as retaliatory strikes designed to hit Moscow’s war machine and dent its vital energy revenues.

Number of MPs backing Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president rises to 62
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:13:00 UTC
20:13:00 KST

Number of MPs backing Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president rises to 62
Sixty-two MPs have signed in favor of Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as a candidate at next month's presidential elections, up from the 55 received as of yesterday.
While 21 signatures are required to nominate a candidate during the registration process next week, the 62 in favor received at the time of writing is only six votes short of the 68 votes needed to get the next head of state elected at the Riigikogu.
Madise, who has not yet publicly given her consent to run, was backed by 61 coalition MPs from the Reform and Eesti 200 parties, plus MPs from the opposition Social Democrats (SDE).
This is not quite a clean sweep of all members of those parties — three MPs had yet to give their signatures: Mart Võrklaev, Margit Sutrop (both Reform) and Züleyxa Izmailova (SDE) were yet to sign in favor of Madise at the time of writing.
Võrklaev told ERR that he was still weighing up the matter. "For now, I would prefer to keep those reasons to myself," he said when asked why he had not yet signed in Madise's favor, and mentioned Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) rector Tiit Land as an alternative potential candidate. The Reform Party is to meet with Madise next Tuesday.
In response to ERR's inquiry about whether or not she plans to sign her support signature in the near future, Izmailova also said she will decide on giving her signature to Madise, or not, following a meeting between Madise and the SDE Riigikogu faction set for Monday.
Following departures from parties and their Riigikogu groups, the current Riigikogu has a large number of independent MPs, now 20, none of whom have given their signature in favor of Madise yet.
Some have declared that they will not vote at all, while others have promised to form their position after meeting Land and Madise.
The two newest independent MPs, Kalev Stoicescu and Meelis Kiili, who at the start of this week left Eesti 200 and Reform respectively, have stated they may instead back Land, in the interests of providing a choice and a debate, though Stoicescu added that this would not necessarily mean withdrawing his support for Madise.
As a reminder, as recently as July 23, Stoicescu wrote on his social media account that he was awaiting Madise's consent to run and for the collection of signatures in support of her nomination, and that he would back her.
Isamaa (eight seats) and the Center Party (seven seats) have both said they would potentially sign in favor of Land as a candidate, but they are also due to meet Madise too, and will make their decision after that meeting. With 15 seats combined, however, they lack the number of signatures to nominate Land or any other candidate alone, even if the four independent MPs who vote with those parties are factored in — though Stoicescu and Kiili would hold the balance then and could provide the required 21.
The actual nomination process is open Friday, August 21, the day after the Restoration of Independence Day, and runs to Monday, August 24. The Riigikogu voting takes place Wednesday, September 2 and Thursday, September 3.
Madise's name has been mentioned in connection with a potential presidential bid since the start of July. She would likely need to rescind her role as justice chancellor before running for president, due to conflict of interest issues.
You can read more on the proposed candidates here.

Russia&apos;s economy continues to weaken, with production, domestic demand and investment declining in July — the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:12:28 EEST
20:12:28 KST

Russia's economy continues to weaken, with production, domestic demand and investment declining in July — the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
In July 2026, Russia's economy deteriorated: oil and gas production fell by 9.3%, domestic demand grew by only 1.5%, and investment declined by 2.1%. A downturn was recorded in most regions.
In July 2026, the Russian economy showed a further deterioration in financial activity. The main blow hit the extractive sector, petroleum product manufacturing, and public administration. But the problem is no longer limited to export commodities—domestic demand and investment are also weakening. The Foreign Intelligence Service reports, UNN writes.
The largest decline in revenues occurred in export-oriented industries. In the extraction of oil, gas, and other minerals, they were 9.3% below the average level for the second quarter. In August, pressure will be intensified by settlements for June exports, when global prices for oil, metals, and mineral fertilizers were falling
At the same time, domestic demand is losing momentum. In trade, financial services, insurance, real estate, telecommunications, and other sectors focused on the domestic market, revenues increased by only 1.5%, compared with 6.9% in the second quarter. Support came from financial services, insurance, and real estate. Agriculture and telecommunications, on the contrary, reduced their payments.
Industries dependent on state funding declined even more sharply. In July, their revenues fell by 15.4%, following a 12.6% decline in the second quarter. The largest drop occurred in public administration
Investment activity is also falling. Payments in construction, machine building, equipment manufacturing, and scientific research declined by 2.1%. The largest drop was recorded in electronics, machinery and equipment manufacturing, transport engineering, and specialized construction.
Demand within production chains is also weakening. Revenues from intermediate demand—goods and services that enterprises use in their own production—decreased by 0.9%. The main negative contributions came from agriculture and oil and gas extraction.
Problems are already apparent in most regions. Excluding extraction and public administration, a decline was recorded in the Northwestern Federal District, by 1.5%; the Southern Federal District, by 14.1%; the North Caucasian Federal District, by 4.9%; and the Siberian Federal District, by 3.2%. At the same time, the extractive sector contracted in virtually all federal districts. The commodities-based model that for years ensured the main inflow of money into the Russian economy is beginning to fail across the country

WSJ: Ukrainian drone operators defeat US unit during exercise in Germany
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:11:00 EEST
20:11:00 KST

WSJ: Ukrainian drone operators defeat US unit during exercise in Germany
During the Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, Ukrainian drone operators from the Nemesis unit – the 412th Brigade of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces – quickly detected and simulated strikes on vehicles belonging to a US mechanised brigade, demonstrating their advantage in the use of drones.
Source: European Pravda, citing The Wall Street Journal
Details: The Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, held in April and May, showed that the US troops from Texas taking part were unprepared for the capabilities of Ukrainian drone operators.
Under the exercise scenario, troops from a US mechanised brigade were advancing on the positions of a simulated enemy. Sources told the WSJ that the opposing force included Ukrainian drone operators from the 412th Nemesis Brigade of the Unmanned Systems Forces alongside various other units.
The Americans had standard electronic warfare and counter-drone systems. During the mechanised "assault", the Ukrainian pilots easily detected US vehicles and simulated attacks using drone-dropped munitions and FPV kamikaze drones. No live munitions were used, with a "hit" recorded when a drone manoeuvred extremely close to its target.
Ultimately, the attacking force was "destroyed" so quickly that troops deemed to have been hit were brought back into the exercise as reinforcements to keep the war game going.
Meanwhile, the exercise showed that the US drone operators lacked the skills to troubleshoot problems quickly and prepare drones in conditions resembling actual combat.
The exercise scenario was subsequently repeated, and the US troops learned to disperse more effectively, improve their camouflage and make better use of electronic warfare systems.
During subsequent iterations, the Ukrainian drone operators were moved to the other side and demonstrated how uncrewed technologies could be used in offensive operations.
General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said that this kind of training experience cannot be replicated in the United States and that the changes seen after NATO exercises involving Ukrainians are significant.
According to one US source, this was not the first time Ukrainian troops had demonstrated an advantage while training against US forces. In 2023, one US officer involved in an exercise acknowledged that the US already had much to learn from Ukrainian forces about the use of drones and developed a training programme that was subsequently introduced in US units.
Background:
- In May 2025, Ukrainian drone operators defeated a simulated enemy during exercises in the Baltics, with British, Estonian and US troops on the opposing side (apparently referring to Hedgehog 2025).
- In spring 2026, Ukrainian UAV operators taking part in NATO exercises on Gotland "defeated" the Swedish troops tasked with opposing them.

Amsterdam researchers find remedy for fatal child brain disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:10:44 UTC
20:10:44 KST

Amsterdam researchers find remedy for fatal child brain disease
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Researchers from the Emma Children’s Hospital at Amsterdam UMC have for the first time found a way to treat a rare genetic brain disease found mostly in children – vanishing white matter, or VWM.
According to The Lancet Neurology, which published the findings, VWM is a neurodegenerative disease “with onset mostly in children aged 1–6 years that causes early death and has no effective therapy.” It’s caused by a genetic defect and occurs in 1 in 100,000 people in the Netherlands.
But now the blood pressure drug guanabenz has been found to inhibit the disease.
In a trial at Amsterdam UMC, 33 children from various countries received guanabenz for four years, while the comparison group included 66 children who did not receive it. Children who received the drug stabilised and ended up needing a wheelchair less often and less quickly.
They also lived – as compared to five patients in the comparison group who died.
“We saw that the disappearance of the white matter in the brain slowed down or even stopped,” chief researcher Marjo van der Knaap told broadcaster NOS.
Moving forward, “the disease-modifying effect of guanabenz should be confirmed in a long-term extension study,” wrote the researchers. The drug also needs the approval of the European Medicines Agency to be used as a treatment for VWM.

Unknown Publisher

PAS’ latest sharia law push signals its Malaysian federal power ambition
The move aims to signal to Malay voters that PAS is committed to Islamic values ahead of the next general election, analysts say
In 2024, the country’s apex court ruled that 16 provisions in an earlier raft of amendments to the northern state’s sharia law were unconstitutional as the offences – ranging from sodomy to incest and intoxication – overlapped with common law, the latter of which takes precedence in criminal cases.
The latest amendments work around certain points raised by the federal court. For example, they replace specific descriptions of sexual acts such as sodomy with broader terminology to say that Muslims are prohibited from using their limbs or intimate parts for sexual purposes that run contrary to Islamic law.
But a successful implementation of the new amendments by PAS is less important than ensuring its target audience knows it has strived to broaden sharia law ahead of the next general election, according to analysts.
“PAS knows that Islamic sharia law cannot be implemented by the state as long as the Malaysian constitution is not amended,” said Mazlan Ali, a political analyst with Universiti Teknologi Malaysia.

Türkiye plans lunar mission launch in early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:10:22 UTC
20:10:22 KST

Türkiye plans to launch its lunar spacecraft in the first months of 2027, equipped with a domestically developed hybrid propulsion system, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir said.
Kacir told reporters during the Turkish Scientific and Technological Research Institution's (TUBITAK) Sky Observation Event in the western province of Afyonkarahisar that Türkiye had finalised the launch schedule for its Moon mission.
He said the spacecraft's homegrown hybrid propulsion system had completed all testing phases and that the mission would give Türkiye technological capabilities possessed by only a handful of countries.
Building independent access to space
Kacir said space infrastructure had become a strategic pillar of Türkiye's defence capabilities, pointing to recent satellite projects including Turksat 6A, Imece, Bilsat, Rasat and Gokturk-2.
Türkiye is also working to establish independent and cost-effective access to space through the construction of its own equatorial spaceport in Somalia.
The facility is intended eventually to support launches of domestically developed satellites and spacecraft.
"We're reaching the point where these efforts will enable Türkiye to produce rockets capable of launching our own satellites into space entirely through our own means," Kacir said.
"Equatorial regions offer the opportunity to access space through more cost-effective means, taking advantage of the Earth's rotational speed," he added.
Growing space ecosystem
Kacir said the country's advances were supported by a growing domestic space ecosystem, while a planned space technopark at Middle East Technical University (METU) would bring institutions and companies together for research and development.
Türkiye is also preparing to sign international cooperation agreements to develop and manufacture components for new space stations and is seeking to participate in additional crewed space science missions, he said.
The developments come as the southwestern province of Antalya prepares to host the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) from October 5-9, with around 10,000 participants expected from more than 100 countries.
Kacir said the congress had already broken previous records for pre-registration and paper submissions and was expected to become one of the largest scientific gatherings ever held in Türkiye.
The congress will include a section dedicated to next-generation space startups, while a meeting of parliamentarians and government representatives is expected to culminate in the Antalya Declaration, which will emphasise peace, security and stability amid global geopolitical divisions.

Putin draws Tokyo's ire over 1st visit to contested island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:10:00 UTC
20:10:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a disputed island near Japan Thursday, drawing a strong reaction from Tokyo, which said the move made improving relations between the two countries more difficult.
The island, known in Russia as Iturup and in Japan as Etorofu, is one of four in the Kuril chain, close to Japan's main islands, that Moscow seized in the days after Japan's surrender in World War II.
Tokyo has maintained its claim to them, making their return a condition for concluding a formal peace treaty that would unlock closer economic ties.
It "hurts the feelings of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a televised statement.
"We hope that the Russian side will take the seriousness of this matter fully to heart," she added.
Ties between Moscow and Tokyo soured after Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Japan joined other nations in condemning the attack and imposing sanctions on Russia.
Putin's visit to the island comes two days before Japan marks 81 years since its surrender ended World War II and a day after North Korea fired a missile into the sea separating it from Japan ahead of major joint military exercises by Seoul and Washington.
Dmitry Medvedev was the first Russian leader to visit the disputed territory in 2010.
On Thursday, the Russian and Chinese ambassadors to Japan, Nikolai Nozdrev and Chinese Ambassador Wu Jianghao, issued a joint statement pledging to oppose attempts to revise the results of World War II.
They also warned against remilitarization in the Asia-Pacific, language that echoes Moscow's rejection of Japan's claim to the islands.
On the trip, which state news agency TASS described as Putin's first to the island chain, he visited the Yasny fish-processing plant on the island, after overseeing navy drills in Russia's Far East.
Vesti TV channel images showed Putin in a dark suit, beside two large tuna and a halibut laid out on a table, as two officials spoke about fishing and the migratory behavior of fish. He also stopped to try local fish roe.
"What lovely weather you have there, just like a resort!" Putin told a group of locals.

====================================================================================================

Europe facing strain on resources and services due to heatwaves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:09:59 UTC
20:09:59 KST

Britain is set to face it's fifth heatwave this summer while France has put 80 départements on orange alert.
Large parts of western Europe, especially Britain and France, will be sweltering under another heatwave this Thursday as countries feel the strain on resources, the economy and services.
Forecasters are predicting the mercury to rise as high as 38 Celsius in central and southeast England, falling just short of the August record of 38.5 C, set in 2003.
This will be the country's fifth heatwave this summer.
The Met Office said earlier this week that only average conditions were needed for the rest of August to beat last year's record for the hottest year.
For a country that's largely not equipped to deal with these levels of heat, it's been a particularly uncomfortable few weeks. Air conditioning is a rarity outside of shops and offices.
Working has been particularly difficult in hospitals, where nurses have been known to collapse from heat exhaustion, according to the Royal College of Nursing.
“When nursing staff are collapsing, feeling dizzy, sick or even being admitted to the very hospitals they work in because their workplaces cannot handle the heat, it shows just how badly they are being failed,” said RCN chief executive and general secretary Professor Nicola Ranger.
The bulk of the country is now officially in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment to mitigate, all of whom have to look for mitigations both in the short-term and in the long-term in the face of human-caused climate change.
Most of France on orange alert
In France, the heatwave has placed 80 départements under orange alert until Friday, as the government estimates these successive extreme heat events this summer could cost between 10 and 15 billion euros.
Except for part of the northeast, three Pyrenean départements, Lozère and Haute-Loire (under yellow alert), the rest of France is under orange alert with another day of very high heat. This heatwave episode "is reaching its peak on Thursday and Friday," estimates Météo-France.
The highest temperatures will be recorded from Centre-Val de Loire to Nouvelle-Aquitaine, where highs will range "between 38 and 40°C, or even a bit more at peak points. In Île-de-France they will be close to 38°C," it said.
Access to water is also on the agenda given this extremely hot and dry summer.
"Our first priority remains obviously drinking water supply, which is already under strain in several areas, more specifically today in 50 French départements," said Monique Barbut, the Minister for Ecological Transition.
"More than 40,000" people are affected by tap water cutoffs, according to the government.
Europe is the planet's fastest-warming continent and in some places is ill-equipped to deal with hot weather. Repeated heatwaves have fuelled a historically hot summer of drought and wildfires, and contributed to the deaths of thousands of people so far.
Scientists blame growing heatwaves on human-caused climate change.

Watch: When gunman tried to assassinate Sukhbir Badal at Golden Temple in 2024
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 13, 2026, 16:38 IST

On December 4, 2024, Badal was attacked inside the Golden Temple during a penance ordered by the Akal Takht.
NEW DELHI: Sukhbir Singh Badal’s Thursday attack in Nanded marks the second serious attempt on the Shiromani Akali Dal leader’s life. The SAD leader was also attacked two years ago at the Golden Temple when a gunman opened fire at him while Badal was serving religious punishment at the shrine.On December 4, 2024, Badal was attacked at the entrance of the temple, where he was seated in a wheelchair because of his fractured leg, during a penance ordered by the Akal Takht. Video footage from the incident shows the moment the attacker overpowered him within seconds.The footage showed him dressed in a blue sewadar uniform. He was stationed at the temple entrance as part of the punishment pronounced by the Akal Takht over alleged misconduct during his tenure from 2007 to 2017.As Badal sat with a placard around his neck, a man who was later identified as Narayan Singh Chaura approached him and opened fire. The attempt, however, was foiled almost immediately.In the clip, right after the gunman pulled out the weapon, an alert sewadar, believed to be a volunteer associated with an Akali leader, intervened and pushed the assailant’s arm upward as he attempted to fire. The bullet was discharged harmlessly into the air, and the attacker was quickly overpowered by volunteers and others present at the scene.
Police personnel stationed at the shrine also moved in and apprehended Chaura on the spot. Confirming the swift response, ADCP Harpal Singh said, “No one was injured in the attack.”It was not long after the attempted attack that other sewadars present at the scene assembled together to create a human shield around Badal.Despite the dramatic shooting attempt, Badal remained calm.Still seated in his wheelchair, he continued performing his duties as a sewadar, holding a spear and staying at the temple entrance after the assailant had been detained.In a separate clip, the shooter could be seen being overpowered by the crowd. The people holding the man can be heard asking him his motive for opening fire on the SAD leader.
The religious punishment had been announced on December 2, 2024, by Sikh high priests for Badal and other Akali leaders in connection with incidents of sacrilege and the pardon granted to controversial Dera Sacha Sauda chief Gurmeet Ram Rahim. The tankhah was part of a reconciliation process led by Sikh religious authorities to address long-standing grievances within the community.
With Wednesday’s attack once again putting security arrangements at the Golden Temple under scrutiny, the earlier firing incident has returned to focus as a reminder that this was not the first time Sukhbir Singh Badal was targeted while performing religious service at Sikhism’s holiest shrine.

Lithuania Fortifies Borders With Belarus and Russia With New Defensive Zones and Barriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:07:21 UTC
20:07:21 KST

- Category
- World
Lithuania Fortifies Borders With Belarus and Russia With New Defensive Zones and Barriers
Lithuania’s government has approved a package of measures to strengthen border defenses, including the creation of counter-mobility zones, the restoration of wetlands, and the installation of engineering barriers at key infrastructure.
The announcement was made by Lithuanian Deputy Defense Minister Tomas Mickelkevičius on August 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the plan, Lithuania will establish designated areas for military counter-mobility engineering measures. A 20-meter-wide strip will be created along the borders with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region, while the designated areas in operational zones identified by the Lithuanian Armed Forces will extend up to 150 meters. The measure is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.
The plan also calls for restoring wetlands in areas where natural terrain could serve as a barrier to advancing heavy military equipment. Once their hydrological systems are restored, the areas could remain difficult for heavy vehicles to cross without specialized engineering equipment for several years. The work is expected to be completed by the end of 2030.
The measures extend to critical infrastructure. Reserve barriers are being installed along sections of national roads and at bridge supports identified by the Lithuanian military, while bridges will be equipped with structures that can accommodate explosives if their destruction becomes necessary during a conflict.
Lithuania also plans to amend its bridge-design regulations by the end of this year. New and reconstructed bridges would have to include designated points for attaching explosives and structural features that would facilitate their demolition in a military emergency.
The government is further updating plans for restoring drainage ditches and regulating waterways, adding another layer of obstacles that could slow or restrict the movement of potential enemy forces.
The measures come as Lithuania continues to face security concerns along its border with Belarus. Lithuanian border guards recently discovered an unfinished underground tunnel near the village of Latežeris in Druskininkai municipality.
The passage had been dug from Belarus beneath the border fence and was about 4 meters long and 1.5 meters deep.

Russia’s Starlink Rival Faces Rocket Bottleneck as Rassvet Satellite Network Expands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:07:12 UTC
20:07:12 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Starlink Rival Faces Rocket Bottleneck as Rassvet Satellite Network Expands
Russia is continuing to deploy its “Rassvet” satellite constellation, which is intended to serve as an analogue to Starlink. However, the project requires regular launches of carrier rockets. The first two groups of Rassvet satellites were launched into orbit using Soyuz-2.1b rockets manufactured by the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara.
According to Defense Express on August 13, the production of carrier rockets is one of the key constraints on the deployment of the constellation. The satellites can also be launched from the Plesetsk and Vostochny spaceports in Russia, as well as the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Soyuz-2.1b rockets are manufactured at the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara. The facility is located in a large industrial area on the southwestern outskirts of the city. Its production complex consists of workshops with a combined length of about one kilometer.
The facility manufactures rocket fuselages and individual components and also carries out final assembly. According to the information provided, Progress can produce up to 20 carrier rockets annually, the outket reported. Production follows an assembly-line process, with several rockets simultaneously undergoing different stages of assembly. The facility also conducts bench testing of individual components and assemblies.
The assembly of the Soyuz-2 relies heavily on manual labor and the qualifications of its personnel. The rocket is an evolution of the Soviet Vostok launch vehicle and consists of three stages powered by liquid-fuel engines, along with a payload fairing.
The Soyuz-2 is more than 50 meters tall and has a launch mass of about 313 tons. The rocket is currently produced in two main versions: the Soyuz-2.1a, designed to launch Soyuz spacecraft, and the Soyuz-2.1b, used to place satellites and other spacecraft weighing up to 7.4 tons into orbit, according to Defense Express.
After all rocket components are manufactured and tested, they are loaded onto seven freight railcars and transported to the designated spaceport. There, the components are assembled, the payload is integrated, and the rocket is installed on the launch pad, fueled, and prepared for launch.
Since 2022, Russia has conducted an average of six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches per year. In 2026, according to the information provided, four such launches had been conducted so far.
Russia has announced that the Rassvet constellation will require at least 288 satellites for full operational capability. Since one Soyuz-2.1b can launch 16 of these satellites at a time, 18 launches would be required to reach that number.
At the same time, four months passed between the first two launches of Rassvet satellites.
Rockets of the Soyuz family are used not only to launch Rassvet satellites but also to deploy other military, civilian, and scientific spacecraft.
Russia also has another launch option for satellites: the Angara family of carrier rockets, which are manufactured at the Polyot plant in Omsk.
The planned expansion of Rassvet has also prompted discussion over how the constellation could be countered. However, Defense Express reported on August 5 that targeting individual satellites would likely be an ineffective and potentially counterproductive approach.
Unlike earlier military space systems that depended on a limited number of high-value spacecraft, modern satellite constellations are built around hundreds of interconnected satellites. As a result, the loss of individual Rassvet satellites would have a limited effect on the network as a whole.

5% of US Interceptors Could Help Ukraine Survive Russia’s Winter Missile Campaign
Receiving 5% of the US stockpile of interceptor missiles would help Ukraine get through the winter and save lives, while securing 10% would provide enough capacity to effectively counter Russia’s ballistic missile attacks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on August 13.
Russian ballistic missile attacks have intensified in recent weeks, with Kyiv among the areas hit particularly heavily, while Ukraine’s stocks of Patriot interceptors have been reduced to critically low levels.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy said that securing 5% of the US interceptor stockpile would be enough for Ukraine to make it through the winter, while obtaining 10% would provide sufficient capacity to counter all Russian ballistic missile attacks.
According to the United Nations, July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022. Zelenskyy said repeated nightly attacks and several large-scale strikes each month are placing additional pressure on civilians.
“This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025. Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before., the President stated. “Each night you have attacks, and four or five times per month we have massive attacks… terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they (are) tired.”
He said that obtaining 5% of the US stockpile would allow Ukraine to get through the winter and protect lives, while 10% would be enough to intercept all Russian ballistic missiles. However, Zelenskyy said Ukraine currently has access to only 1%.
Zelenskyy also described his ongoing efforts to secure additional air-defense interceptors, saying negotiations with allies had become a central part of his daily work.
“This is what I live each day: from 1% to 5%. I have some months, and million phone calls… I try to exchange something to missiles … I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s outside of the law. But I can’t speak about it,” the President said.
He also expressed uncertainty over plans for Ukraine to eventually produce its own Patriot interceptor missiles, despite an apparent commitment from US President Donald Trump to support the initiative.
“I hope that I will get it. I don’t have now 5% and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me is a big challenge, one of the biggest I had from the very beginning of this war,” Zelenskyy added.
Several days earlier, the President announced that Ukraine could begin domestic production of Patriot air-defense systems and components within a year. However, reaching full-scale production could take several years because of licensing requirements, technology transfers, and dependence on international supply chains.

Putin Lands on Disputed Kuril Island for First Time, Triggering Sharp Protest From Japan
Unknown

2026-08-13

- Category
- World
Putin Lands on Disputed Kuril Island for First Time, Triggering Sharp Protest From Japan
Russian leader Vladimir Putin made his first visit to Iturup, one of the disputed southern Kuril Islands claimed by Japan, prompting Tokyo to lodge a strong protest.
Released footage showed Putin visiting the island, known in Japan as Etorofu, where he toured the Yasny fish-processing plant and was shown products including tuna and halibut, according to the Kremlin press service on August 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He also visited the Kuril Central District Hospital and a local school before meeting Sakhalin regional governor Valery Limarenko.
After leaving Iturup, Putin traveled to Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, where he met residents.
The trip drew an immediate response from Japan, which regards Iturup and several neighboring islands as sovereign Japanese territory.
Japan’s foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Tokyo had lodged a formal protest, according to Japan Wire.
“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu, are an inherent part of the territory of Japan both historically and under international law. Japan strongly protests this visit,” he said.
Japan claims Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets, collectively referred to in Japan as the Northern Territories. Russia currently controls all four.
The dispute has remained one of the principal obstacles preventing Moscow and Tokyo from signing a formal peace treaty more than eight decades after World War II.
The Soviet Union seized the islands at the end of the war. In 1956, Moscow and Tokyo signed a joint declaration under which the Soviet Union agreed that Shikotan and the Habomai islets could be transferred to Japan after the conclusion of a peace treaty.
The two countries never reached such an agreement, however, while Japan later continued to press its claim to all four disputed territories.
Russia maintains that the outcome of World War II settled its sovereignty over the islands and cannot be reconsidered.
Speaking shortly before his visit during Russian Pacific Fleet exercises, Putin claimed Moscow previously had constructive relations with former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and other Japanese leaders over the territorial dispute but accused Tokyo of changing its position.
Relations deteriorated sharply after Russia launched its full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine in 2022 and Japan joined Western sanctions against Moscow.
Russia subsequently suspended negotiations with Japan over a peace treaty.
Japan, in turn, returned in 2022 to describing the disputed islands as territory “illegally occupied” by Russia, terminology Tokyo had not officially used since 2003.
Earlier, the Japanese government had lodged a formal protest after Russia announced plans to conduct live-fire exercises near the disputed Northern Territories from August 1 to September 1.

====================================================================================================

Lesson of the UAE, Abraham Accords: Lasting peace begins in the classroom - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:07:01 UTC
20:07:01 KST

Today, six years ago, on August 13, 2020, the Middle East changed. US President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Mohamed bin Zayed, announced an agreement for full normalization between Israel and the United Arab Emirates.
For the first time in more than a quarter-century, another Arab country chose to establish full relations with the State of Israel. A month later, the Abraham Accords were signed at the White House.
At the time, most of the attention was focused on the political breakthrough – and rightly so. The agreement broke a concept that had dominated Middle Eastern diplomacy for decades: the claim that Israel could not reach true peace with the Arab world before resolving the Palestinian conflict.
But six years later, after the Middle East has gone through one of the most turbulent periods in its history, a deeper lesson can be identified. The UAE’s lesson is that true peace does not begin at a signing ceremony. It begins in the classroom.
Since August 2020, relations between Israel and the Emirates have faced intense tests that none of the signatories to the agreement could have predicted. The October 7 massacre, the war in Gaza, and the regional turmoil created immense pressure on Israel’s relations with the Arab world.
The UAE sharply criticized Israeli policy on various issues. There were disagreements, tensions, and periods in which the warmth that characterized the beginning of the relations was replaced by caution.
But relations were not severed.
The embassies remained open, channels of dialogue were maintained, and economic and institutional ties continued to exist. It is precisely the disagreements that illustrate the importance of the achievement.
Peace is not measured when everything is quiet. It is measured at the moment when the sides disagree, the public is agitated, and the political cost of maintaining relations rises.
Here lies the first lesson of August 13: an agreement that holds up only during periods of quiet is a temporary arrangement. True peace is tested by its ability to survive a crisis.
Peace cannot be built on decades of education toward hatred.
For decades, the international community in the Middle East focused almost entirely on leaders and agreements. Presidents met. Diplomats drafted. Governments signed. International money flowed. Institutions were established.
But the most important question was asked too rarely: What does the Muslim child learn in the classroom the morning after the agreement is signed?
You can bring a leader to the negotiation table through interests and pressure. You can establish an embassy by a government decision. You can even create security and economic coordination mechanisms.
But if the education system continues to teach the next generation that the Zionist entity is an eternal enemy, that its history is forged, that its religion is inferior, and that its very existence is illegitimate, an agreement has been signed between governments, but peace has not been built between peoples.
The UAE offers a different model.
On my visits to the UAE, I found an extensive emphasis on tolerance, coexistence, and acceptance of other cultures and religions – including a magnificent synagogue in the Abrahamic Family House complex in Abu Dhabi.
Studies by the IMPACT-se research institute that examined the Emirati education system also found positive changes regarding Judaism and Israel, and the Abraham Accords themselves were integrated into the learning materials.
This does not mean that all disagreements have disappeared, but it teaches that a country seeking to create long-term peace cannot settle for changing its foreign policy. It must gradually create a cultural infrastructure that allows the next generation to accept peace itself as legitimate. This is a strategic lesson, not just an educational one.
The Palestinian comparison that cannot be ignored
And here lies the difference that the State of Israel and the West must learn from.
Since the Oslo Accords, vast sums have been invested in building Palestinian institutions. Governance and security mechanisms were established, agreements were signed, and international aid was transferred on a massive scale. The assumption was that building institutions, improving the economy, and political progress would gradually create an incentive for peace.
But for years, research and reviews pointed to inciting content in the Palestinian education system, including the glorification of “martyrs,” content hostile toward Israel, and a consistent absence of education that recognizes the State of Israel and the Jewish people as legitimate neighbors with a historical connection to the land.
The West sometimes sought to build peace from the top down, while beneath it, mechanisms continued to exist that passed the conflict on to the next generation.
You cannot expect a child who is educated for years to view Israel as an illegitimate entity to become a natural partner for reconciliation at age eighteen just because leaders signed a document.
The Emirates teaches the other side of that same equation.
When leadership changes the public discourse, encourages religious tolerance, recognizes Judaism, and presents cooperation with Israel as part of a possible future, it creates an additional protective layer for relations even when severe political disagreements arise.
Peace through strength, interests, and awareness
The Abraham Accords also proved another principle: Peace does not have to be born out of weakness or out of giving up national interests. On the contrary.
The agreements were born out of a recognition of shared interests. Israel and the Emirates identified shared regional threats and understood the benefits inherent in cooperation in the fields of security, technology, trade, energy, innovation, and tourism.
Instead of the old concept according to which the parties must first resolve all disagreements and only then start cooperating, the Abraham Accords offered the opposite logic: cooperation itself can become an engine of stability.
But the past six years add a third layer to the equation.
Strength creates deterrence.
Interests create profitability.
Education creates resilience.
All three components are necessary.
Peace that is not backed by strength is liable to invite aggression. Peace that lacks shared interests is liable to become an empty document. And peace that is not supported by an educational and cultural infrastructure is liable to collapse when the first crisis arrives.
The lesson for the day after
This lesson has special meaning right now.
In any future discussion on regional arrangements, on expanding the Abraham Accords, on relations with the Palestinians, and on the future of Gaza, the State of Israel and its partners must not repeat the mistake of measuring peace through signatures alone.
Textbooks must also be measured.
When the international community invests billions in reconstruction, it must ask not only how many schools were built, but also what is taught inside them.
When new institutions are established, one must examine not only who runs them, but what worldview they convey to the next generation.
Does Israel appear on the map?
Is the Jewish people presented as a people with a history and a right to self-determination?
Is terrorism presented as heroism or as a disaster?
These are not marginal questions. These are questions of national security.
You can defeat an army on the battlefield. You can dismantle a terrorist organization. You can eliminate commanders and destroy infrastructure. All of these are necessary for the defense of the state. But long-term victory also requires preventing the ideology that birthed the war from passing intact to the next generation.
This is the greatest lesson of August 13, 2020.
The achievement of the Abraham Accords is not only that Israelis fly to Dubai, that Israeli and Emirati companies do business, and that an Israeli flag flies over an embassy in an Arab country.
The more important achievement is proving the possibility of creating a different model in the Middle East.
A model in which countries do not have to agree on everything to live in peace. A model in which shared interests replace the politics of boycott. A model in which tolerance is not just a diplomatic slogan, but a value that a country seeks to pass on to the next generation as well.
Leaders can sign a peace agreement in one day.
Strength and interests can preserve it in times of crisis.
But for peace to last for generations, it must be taught in the classroom.
This is the lesson of the United Arab Emirates, and it should also be the lesson for any future arrangement in the Middle East.
The writer is the deputy head of the Security Policy Institute of the Israel Defense and Security Forum (IDSF/Habithonistim), and former policy adviser to strategic affairs minister Ron Dermer.

NATO to Deploy Battle-Tested AI Drone Fleet From Ukraine to Defend Eastern Flank Against Russia
Unknown

2026-08-13
11:06:53 UTC
20:06:53 KST

- Category
- World
NATO to Deploy Battle-Tested AI Drone Fleet From Ukraine to Defend Eastern Flank Against Russia
NATO is shifting its approach to future warfare by prioritizing drones, satellites, sensors, and artificial intelligence, Bild reported on August 12.
The alliance’s push for automation draws from the battlefield in Ukraine, where forces have already begun deploying AI-guided drone swarms capable of identifying targets, communicating with one another, and executing strikes autonomously—even when Russian electronic warfare severs human control.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
To protect against potential Russian aggression, NATO plans to establish a unified surveillance and defense system along its eastern flank—stretching from Finland to the Black Sea. The system is designed to quickly detect and help repel incoming attacks.
The development of these new technologies is heavily influenced by Ukraine’s battlefield experience. Bild notes that the Ukrainian military is already actively using AI for drone control, navigation, and precision strikes.
US Army Major Ben Schiff, who oversees NATO's digital systems, explained the pressing need for automation to Bild.
“Humans decide what the drone does. But they don’t necessarily have to fly it themselves, because we don’t have a million pilots. We can’t launch a million drones simultaneously,” Schiff told the publication.
In the future, autonomous machines are expected to take over various battlefield tasks. Aerial drones will independently search for targets, while ground robots will handle supply deliveries and perform dangerous missions instead of deploying human soldiers, Bild wrote.
However, NATO emphasized that the ultimate goal of this automation is not to replace humans in warfare. Instead, the focus is on reducing the physical risks to military personnel while maintaining strict human oversight and control over the deployment of weapons.
Demonstrating how Ukrainian tactics are already shaping defenses along NATO's eastern flank, Germany’s 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania recently equipped its Leopard 2 tanks and Fuchs armored personnel carriers with improvised anti-drone screens.
Spotted during the Freedom Shield 2026 military exercises near the Belarusian border, the vehicle crews designed the protective cages directly from Ukrainian combat experience to defend against FPV drones and dropped munitions.

A landslide swept away houses in the remote Thawang village of Rolpa district in western Nepal, killing at least five people and leaving eight missing, a senior official told Anadolu on Thursday.
"Locals have recovered the bodies of five of the 15 people who went missing in the landslide, while two were injured. The location of the missing people is still unknown," Rishi Keshav Budha Magar, chairperson of Thawang Rural Municipality, which includes the landslide-affected area, said.
Around 8 pm on Wednesday (1415GMT), a landslide swept away 11 houses and sheds for cows and buffalo on sloping mountain areas.
Thawang, a remote village in the district, was once widely known as the Maoist insurgents' hinterland during the conflict, which lasted until 2006, when a peace agreement was signed.
Rescuers continue to struggle to reach the area.
"Since the landslide-affected area is not well connected to the road network, excavators mobilised for rescue couldn't reach there," Magar told Anadolu over the phone. "The Chief District Officer has just arrived at the incident site. I'm also walking on foot for rescue and recovery operations."
Rescuers from the Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have launched a search and rescue operation to locate missing people.
Poorly developed roads and inadequate disaster preparedness lead to fatalities during each monsoon season, which begins in June and lasts until September.
As of Wednesday, 43 people had been killed in monsoon-related disasters such as landslides, floods and heavy rains, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the state-run authority responsible for disaster response.

Eurovision 2027: A guide to Burgas, Bulgaria’s sunny seaside host city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:03:50 UTC
20:03:50 KST

Burgas has been announced as the unexpected host of next year’s Eurovision. Here’s everything you need to know ahead of a visit to the Bulgarian beach city.
Many of us thought that Bulgaria winning the Eurovision Song Contest would mean the capital, Sofia, would be hosting in 2027.
However, it’s now been revealed that Burgas will play host.
Far less known internationally, it’s already one of the country’s best-loved seaside escapes and Eurovision’s arrival next May will put its beaches, buzzing waterfront and relaxed summer atmosphere firmly on the international map.
While the contest will bring the crowds, there’s plenty here beyond the Eurovision bubble, from long sandy beaches and leafy parks to seafood restaurants, cultural sights and a lively arts scene.
Whether you’re heading over for the show or simply want to see what all the fuss is about, here’s how to make the most of Burgas.
How to get there
Burgas, the fourth-largest city in Bulgaria, is located on the Black Sea, known for its sandy beaches and clear blue seas.
It’s about 400 kilometres from Sofia and just under 150 kilometres south of Dara’s – 2026’s Eurovision winner – hometown of Varna.
Burgas airport is actually better served than you might think.
It’s located just 10 kilometres from the city centre, and welcomes direct flights from many European hubs including London, Rome and Berlin. Getting to the city centre from the hub is simple, as there’s a frequently-running bus route between the two.
If you’re combining a trip to Burgas with a visit to Sofia, trains run about eight times a day, with the fastest journey taking just five hours and 43 minutes.
Buses are even faster, taking a minimum of five hours from Sofia to Burgas. They run on average six times per day.
When you arrive in Burgas, e-bike rental is everywhere and the city has a decent public transport network, with Burgasbus the easiest to navigate.
Where to stay
Eurovision’s arrival in a city is notorious for driving up accommodation prices, but Burgas is actually usually very affordable when it comes to hotels.
A spot check by the Euronews Travel team found private rooms from €32per night in August, and four-star hotels from €67 a night.
It’s also possible to secure a one-night stay at the five-star beachfront Hotel Residence Promenade for €130.
What to see in Burgas
No trip to the city is complete without a visit to one of its beaches – and there are spots for every vibe.
Central Beach and Northern Beach are buzzy and packed with restaurants and bars, while Sarafovo Beach and Kraymorie Beach are more laidback and known for their natural beauty.
The Pier of Burgas is a must see after a day at the beach, offering great views of the city and an ideal place to watch the sunset.
Nearby, you’ll find the Sea Garden, a 5km-long route of paved walking trails through a vast public park.
It’s also suitable for bicycling and visitors can catch a glimpse of exotic plant species, cultural monuments and see some of the most impressive Balkan architecture in the region.
Burgas’ Old Town is pedestrianised and boasts endless restaurants, bars and shops as well as the Orthodox Church of Saints Cyril and Methodius.
Culture is a big deal here, too. The Sand Sculptures Festival runs from the beginning of July to the end of September, and showcases the best of international pop culture.
Spice music festival is another highlight, with ‘Despacito’ singer Luis Fonsi having headlined earlier in August.
What to eat and drink
Bulgarian cuisine might not be as famous as eats from other parts of Europe, but there’s still plenty to try, and Burgas has its own local specialities to sample.
Being coastal, fish is obviously a favourite and midi po burgaski, local mussels cooked in their shells with onions, tomatoes, peppers, and savoury herbs, is particularly popular, as is Black Sea turbot, which is served grilled.
Burgas is also a great place to try foods from wider Bulgaria, including strandzhanski dyado, a traditional cured, spiced meat, and the national dish of Shopska salata, made with diced tomatoes, cucumbers, onions, and peppers and topped with grated sirene, a white brine cheese.
When it comes to beverages, don’t miss Burgas 63, a rakia made with local grapes, Bulgarian wines including the well-bodied red Mavrud, and local lagers Burgasko, established in Burgas in 1971.
Food and drinks here are remarkably inexpensive. According to cost-of-living data platform Numbeo, a meal at an inexpensive restaurant will set you back an average of €12.39, while half a litre of local draft beer €1.79, and a meal for two at a mid-range restaurant – that’s three courses, without drinks – is €40.90.

Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) has dismantled a 14-member Russian intelligence network that was gathering information on Ukrainian airfields hosting Western-supplied F-16 and Mirage 2000 fighter jets, the agency said Thursday.
The network was allegedly working for Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, and collected information that could help Moscow plan strikes on Ukrainian air bases.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Blogger recruited 13 spotters
According to the SBU, the GRU first recruited a Lviv resident who ran an aviation-focused Telegram channel. Russian intelligence reportedly noticed him after he posted photographs of Ukrainian military aircraft in pro-Kremlin online groups.
The man then recruited 13 of his subscribers, allegedly without telling them they were working for Russian intelligence.
The group members lived in different parts of Ukraine, including near military aviation infrastructure, and had access to high-quality cameras. They were instructed to photograph airfields, fighter jets, aircraft crews and maintenance personnel, while also tracking takeoff and landing times.
The suspects reportedly used professional cameras while hiding in abandoned buildings or open areas near air bases.
Spy network tracked aircraft movements
The photographs were uploaded to an online storage service and later passed to a Russian handler, whose identity has been established by the SBU.
The Lviv-based agent also allegedly provided Russia with schedules for military helicopter takeoffs and landings. The information reportedly came from a Ukrainian Armed Forces aviation squadron commander who voluntarily shared it with the agent.
SBU Says Russia Using 'Honey Traps' to Assassinate Ukrainian Soldiers
During searches, investigators found smartphones, digital cameras and photographs of Ukrainian military aviation facilities that allegedly documented the suspects’ activities.
The SBU also blocked four Telegram channels and 10 groups allegedly used to distribute photographs and other information about Ukrainian aviation units.
The Lviv agent, his accomplice and the Ukrainian serviceman have been charged with crimes against Ukraine’s national security. The investigation is ongoing as authorities work to identify and prosecute the remaining participants.
