Romania began on Thursday the complete shutdown of its only nuclear plant after water levels in the Danube, used to cool the site, fell to a record low, the national nuclear energy company said.
Nuclearelectrica already shut down last month one of the two reactors at the Cernavoda power plant, which usually generates a fifth of the Eastern European country's total electricity.
The second needed to shut as well "due to the significant and ongoing drop in the water level of the River Danube", it said in a statement.
"Nuclearelectrica SA announces that, on the morning of 13 August 2026, it began the procedures for the controlled shutdown of Unit 2 at the Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant," it said.
Romania has been trying for days to avert a complete shutdown of the plant's two 700MW reactors.
These included blowing up a rock and sinking four barges filled with rocks into the river to try to divert its flows, with total costs are budgeted at more than two million euros $2.3 million.
It is the plant's first shutdown since a 2003 drought, when it had to close for several weeks.
Alternative sources, including from wind power generation, as well as imports, are expected to cover electricity supply, the energy ministry said on Wednesday.
It also reiterating an appeal for "responsible consumption".
Unprecedented heatwaves and rain shortages across Europe this year have caused the level of the Danube to plummet.
Nearly two-thirds of the Danube has recorded flow rates that are the lowest on record for a month of July in 34 years of measurements, according to an analysis published on Monday by the EU climate monitor Copernicus.
The current drought, which is already severe, has been exacerbated by climate crisis, according to a report by the World Weather Attribution group of scientists, who warn that the problem is set to worsen.

Life in Latvia is getting more expensive – study reveals what costs more than elsewhere in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:48:20 UTC
18:48:20 KST

Rising food prices and everyday expenses have become a widely discussed issue in Latvia. The latest Eurostat data on the price level index for household final consumption expenditure also show that Latvia can no longer be considered one of the cheapest countries in the European Union (EU).
For some everyday expenses, prices in Latvia have already overtaken those in some of Europe’s wealthier countries. Nevertheless, the overall price level of goods and services in Latvia remains 17% below the EU average.
The greatest pressure on household budgets comes from essential expenses that people cannot easily avoid. Compared with the EU average, Latvians pay 7.5% more for food, 4.6% more for clothing and footwear, and 5.2% more for alcohol and tobacco products.
The main reason Latvia’s overall household consumption price level remains relatively low, at 83% of the EU average, is the lower cost of domestically provided services, including healthcare, education and transport, as well as housing.
Compared with Western Europe, Latvia still has a significant price advantage in these categories.
Housing costs, for example, are 44% below the EU average, healthcare costs are 31% lower, education 20% lower and transport 16% lower.
“The data confirm that certain essential expenses place a significant burden on household budgets, and for several everyday goods and services we are already paying Western European-level prices or even more. At the same time, lower service costs continue to cushion the overall cost of living,” said Kārlis Purgailis, economist at Citadele Bank.
“However, every year the overall cost of living is moving closer to the EU average. This is largely driven by the rapid wage convergence seen in Latvia and across the Baltic region, which encourages local producers and retailers to raise prices to cover rising labour costs,” he explained.
According to Purgailis,
because food and clothing are easily imported goods, their prices are among the first to converge with European levels,
while Latvia’s domestic services sector is still catching up.
A comparison of the Baltic states reveals two distinct trends. Lithuania’s overall household consumption price level is exactly the same as Latvia’s, at 83% of the EU average, while the cost of living across individual categories of goods and services is also very similar in the two countries.
Estonia, however, is in a markedly different position. Its overall price level is now practically in line with the EU average, reaching 101%. Food, clothing and footwear, alcohol and tobacco products are more expensive in Estonia, while housing costs are also approaching the EU average.
Although the cost of living in Latvia and Lithuania remains lower than in Estonia, neither country can any longer be considered cheap.
Across the EU, household final consumption price levels varied significantly in 2025, ranging from 63% to 140% of the EU average, which is set at 100.
The highest household consumption price levels were recorded in Denmark, at 140% of the EU average, followed by Ireland at 136% and Luxembourg at 132%.
At the other end of the scale, consumers paid the least for comparable goods and services in Bulgaria, at 63% of the EU average, followed by Romania at 65% and Poland at 73%.

TikTok's finfluencers: How reliable is the financial advice reaching young investors?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:47:56 UTC
18:47:56 KST

Young people are increasingly turning to social media for financial information and advice, amid a sea of dubious tips. What do experts say are the warning signs to watch out for?
"Defence stocks make millionaires 95% of the time," a man tells his followers in a TikTok video before pointing viewers towards a handful of companies in the defence sector.
It's one of several videos offering investment tips: some feature creators while others use AI-generated personas to offer stock picks and financial advice to users scrolling through social media in Europe.
But how much of this advice should you actually trust?
A new analysis of 150 popular finance-related TikTok videos by broker comparison website BrokerListings.com suggests that viewers should be cautious.
The videos it studied amassed at least 100,000 views each, covering topics ranging from stocks and cryptocurrency to debt and personal finance.
The platform found more than 70% of the videos' creators did not display a clear relevant background in financial services or suitable qualifications sufficient to provide reliable advice to the public.
In addition, more than 60% of the videos did not adequately explain the potential risks or downsides to the financial products or situations they discussed.
Their findings come as regulators are increasingly grappling with the influence of social media on young investors.
Ulf Linke, a consumer protection expert at Germany's financial regulator BaFin, told The Cube, Euronews’ fact-checking team, that the authority sees a "clear trend" towards investment tips on social media, particularly among younger people.
A 2024 BaFin survey found that more than half of Millennial and Gen Z investors considered social media a reliable source of financial information, while 60% saw it as a good alternative to professional financial advice.
In April, the European Parliament backed calls for minimum standards for so-called "finfluencers" — influencers who provide financial advice on social media — specifically citing risks such as hidden advertising, misleading claims, scams, and AI-generated financial content.
According to MEPs, social media has become a "primary" source of financial information for many younger people.
The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) also issued guidance for finfluencers earlier this year, warning that rules on investment recommendations can apply to financial content posted on social media.
Under these rules, someone recommending an investment may need to make clear who they are, separate facts from opinions and disclose if they could financially benefit from what they are promoting.
Even publicly expressing an opinion on whether a share or cryptocurrency will rise or fall can, in some circumstances, constitute an investment recommendation.
"Disclaimers such as 'This is not investment advice' will not protect you in these cases," ESMA states.
Why can financial advice on TikTok be risky?
The format of social media clips is one of the main reasons why they are a precarious source of financial or budgeting information, researchers say, as their short length can mean that a lot of important context is left out.
According to James Barra, head of content and research at BrokerListings, the nature of short-form videos on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram does not necessarily lend itself to the kind of longer, balanced explanations that financial products can require.
A short video promoting a side hustle or get-rich-quick scheme may be more engaging, he said, than a longer explanation weighing up both the potential benefits and risks.
The advice can also reach people with vastly different levels of financial knowledge and experience.
A particular investment, for example, could represent a relatively small proportion of an experienced investor's portfolio, but be much riskier for a young investor putting a large share of their savings into it.
"And that sort of nuance… you don't necessarily have room for that in these short-form videos on TikTok," Barra told The Cube.
BrokerListings also found that the most concerning content did not necessarily come from TikTok's biggest financial influencers.
Barra said larger influencers and commercial partnerships have attracted greater scrutiny from regulators and social media platforms, while smaller, organic creators can also produce content that reaches substantial audiences, but receive less scrutiny.
TikTok told us that its Community Guidelines on regulated goods, services and commercial activities set out rules that apply to this type of content. The platform said it takes enforcement action, including removing content, when it is found to violate those guidelines.
TikTok also prohibits financial scams and said that 99% of videos it removed for violating its fraud and scams policies in the first quarter of 2026 were taken down proactively before being reported by users.
Is it all unreliable?
Despite concerns, not all financial content on social media is unreliable. BrokerListings says its researchers also found creators sharing useful information on topics such as budgeting, managing debt, building emergency savings and long-term investing.
It can also offer an alternative means for young people learning about personal finance.
"You don't learn about this at school, you don't learn about it at university," Barra said. "A lot of people don't learn about it from their parents.
There are also established financial education channels which take a different approach to the quick stock picks and promises of high returns found elsewhere on social media.
For example, Germany's Finanzfluss ("Financial flow", in English), presented by former investment banking analyst Thomas Kehl, has built a large online audience around financial education, producing content on topics including ETFs (exchange-traded funds), investing basics, saving and retirement planning.
In one recent TikTok, the channel discusses the growth of actively managed ETFs in the US and Europe, explaining the product and market developments rather than directing viewers towards a particular stock and promising them they will make a return.
How can you spot unreliable financial advice online?
Nevertheless, experts warn that users should look closely at who is behind the financial content they are watching.
According to Linke, reputable creators should identify themselves, provide verifiable contact information, disclose potential conflicts of interest and explain the professional background that qualifies them to discuss investments.
If this information is missing, investors should not trust the investment tips, he added.
Linke also warned users to be suspicious of tips promising high returns without explaining the risks, and to not give in to pressure or the fear of missing out on potential returns.
Another warning sign, according to Barra, is content built around displays of wealth, such as expensive cars, luxury hotels or other suggestions that following a particular investment strategy could lead to a similar lifestyle.
Urgency should also raise questions. Barra pointed to videos telling viewers that a stock is about to soar or crash, or those suggesting they have only a short window in which to buy a particular cryptocurrency.
Social media users should also consider if a creator is benefiting financially from what they are promoting, with some creators receiving commission when a viewer signs up to a trading platform through their link.
Such sponsorships or affiliate relationships do not mean the information is unreliable, but European rules require such conflicts of interest to be disclosed.
ESMA recommends that consumers check information from social media against other sources before making financial decisions.
That could mean looking at information published by financial regulators such as ESMA or national authorities such as Germany's BaFin; checking official company reports if a video makes claims about a particular business; and looking for coverage from established financial news organisations.
Investors can also use national regulators' registers to check whether a company or individual offering financial services is authorised to do so.
Ultimately, the speed with which users can move from watching a TikTok to putting their own money at risk makes that scrutiny increasingly important.
Barra described how someone could watch a video recommending several stocks, ask an AI chatbot whether they were good investments and then open a trading app and buy them, all within a matter of minutes.
"The whole journey can be a lot quicker than it used to be," he said.

"Nova Poshta is adapting its logistics operations to work under wartime challenges in order to better protect customers’ shipments and maintain stable delivery," Nova Poshta said in its Telegram channel on Tuesday.
According to the company, Nova Poshta’s network currently has more than 56,000 service points.
"Our goal remains unchanged: to deliver quickly under any conditions," the company said.
At the same time, for security reasons involving employees, customers and logistics processes, Nova Poshta will not comment on details of the reorganization, the specifics of backup routes or the locations of facilities.
The day before, the company reported on the Threads social network that there could be additional delays in parcel deliveries due to the destruction of central sorting hubs and the reconfiguration of logistics processes.
The company said that backup routes and additional sorting centers are being used. As a result, shipments may pass through intermediate facilities that were not previously used for standard routes.
As reported, overnight on August 5, Russian forces struck Ukrainian commercial and logistics infrastructure. The attack destroyed a Nova Poshta sorting center in Kyiv and Rozetka’s largest distribution center in Brovary, damaged a NOVUS logistics center, and destroyed two Fozzy Group distribution centers.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Thursday called for selective conscription and a shift toward a smaller, technology-driven military as the country grapples with a persistently low birth rate.
"We must introduce selective conscription, and quickly and thoroughly pursue defense reforms that transform our military into a smart, elite and strong military centered on advanced equipment and technologies," Lee said at a meeting with senior aides at the presidential palace, according to Yonhap News Agency.
Lee said South Korea's persistently low birth rate makes it impossible and undesirable to maintain an "inefficient military structure" that relies heavily on personnel and infantry.

South Korea requires able-bodied men to serve at least 18 months in the military, while others may be exempt or required to complete alternative forms of service.
Lee urged policies to ensure military service provides pathways to good jobs and education while helping young people build wealth.
"It is a big responsibility of the government to make sure people do not think their time in the military is a waste of their lives or a loss," he said.
Lee's remarks come as the South Korean Army seeks to automate more maintenance and logistics operations using artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous systems.
Last month, the South Korean Navy tested a humanoid robot performing a ship's helmsman duties.

Veteran remembers inscription he left on Reichstag in TASS interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:46:23 UTC
18:46:23 KST

MOSCOW, August 13. /TASS/. Great Patriotic War veteran Yevgeny Znamensky, a participant in the Berlin operation who turned 101 today, recalled the inscription he left during the storming of the Reichstag in the Battle of Berlin, sharing his memories in an interview with TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov for the Victors project.
"I looked and saw guys climbing up across the canal, scratching something on the walls and raising a flag. The guy in front of me was finishing an inscription, perhaps with a piece of shrapnel: either 'Tambov' or 'Saratov', I do not remember. I told him: 'Friend, leave me at least a little space there'. It was quite a gallery! I am from Serpukhov, it is my hometown. I took that thing from him and wrote: 'Serpukhov, Znamensky,'" he said.
The veteran added that he was proud to have made it "to that lair from his hometown." After the interview, he again left the inscription "Serpukhov," this time on a replica of the Reichstag at the Moskino film park.
Znamensky was born on August 13, 1925, and was drafted in January 1943. Serving as a submachine gunner and artillery reconnaissance officer, he fought from Stalingrad to Berlin and participated in the liberation of Ukraine, Belarus, Poland and Germany.
Kondrashov's interview with the veteran was recorded for the Victors project, supported by the Presidential Foundation for Cultural Initiatives and the National Center for Historical Memory under the Russian president. The project features a series of interviews conducted by prominent television presenters, journalists, war correspondents, actors and musicians with the last surviving Great Patriotic War veterans. Filming began during the 80th anniversary of Victory and is continuing this year. The episodes air on NTV's morning broadcasts and are also available online.
TASS is the project's general information partner.

South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:45:56 UTC
18:45:56 KST

South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war.
The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports.
Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million.
It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025.
Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by the US-Iran conflict, which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) was quoted as saying by the Yonhap news agency.
Incheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase.
Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media.
Heathrow, in west London, recorded 40 million passengers in total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle East reportedly fell 16.5% owing to the regional conflict.
Earlier this week Istanbul overtook Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.
Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations.
A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers.
Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”.
South Korea also lays claim to the world’s busiest air route. The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world.

McDonald’s Hong Kong pulls shrimp burgers after Taiwan detects antibiotic residue
Unknown

2026-08-13

McDonald’s Hong Kong pulls shrimp burgers after Taiwan detects antibiotic residue
Fast food chain removes all Ebi Burger products from menu in city temporarily to address potential public concern
McDonald’s has temporarily removed its popular Ebi Burger series from its menu in Hong Kong as a “precautionary measure”, following a similar suspension in Taiwan due to food safety concerns, despite the shrimp patties used in the local items coming from a different production batch.
Taiwan McDonald’s announced on Thursday morning that it had immediately suspended sales of the “Ebi Burger” and the “Double Ebi Burger” after an importer notified it the night before that random batch testing on the shrimp patties used in the products found 0.7 ppb (parts per billion) of nitrofurans and their chemical residues, which did not comply with food safety regulations.
Nitrofurans are a class of synthetic antibiotics banned in many countries.
The Taiwan operator apologised and said it would refund customers who purchased the products on Wednesday and Thursday.
A check of McDonald’s app in Hong Kong on Thursday showed that the Ebi Burger, the Double Ebi Burger and the Ebi Burger with Pineapple were all currently unavailable.
In a media response, McDonald’s Hong Kong said it temporarily removed all Ebi Burger and related products from its menu as a “precautionary measure” to address potential public concern.

Omar Zhanburuaev, who was convicted of taking part in the violent antisemitic riot at Makhachkala airport in Russia’s Dagestan region in 2023, has been killed while fighting in Ukraine.
Zhanburuaev was sentenced in June 2025 to a prison term ranging from five years to six years and eight months after joining the mob that stormed the airport in search of passengers arriving from Israel.
In January, Zhanburuaev released a video saying he had signed a military contract and joined the Russian army in an effort to change his life and atone for his actions. He said his intention during the airport riot had been to show support for the Palestinians, but acknowledged that he had instead caused harm to his homeland.
According to Shamil Khadulaev, head of Daghestan's Public Monitoring Commission, Zhanburuaev is the latest participant in the airport riot to be killed in combat. Of seven people involved in the unrest who later joined the Russian military, five remain alive, one of them seriously wounded, Khadulaev said.
Another participant in the riots, Muhammad Said Murtazaliev, was previously killed while fighting in Ukraine and was buried in January.
The mass riot took place on October 29, 2023, three weeks after the Hamas massacre and outbreak of the Gaza war. Hundreds of antisemitic rioters stormed Makhachkala airport amid rumors that a plane from Israel was arriving, searching the terminal and tarmac for passengers who had flown in from Tel Aviv. The airport was temporarily closed to arriving and departing flights. 
Thirty security personnel and police officers were attacked during the riot, 23 of whom were injured. Following the incident, Russia’s Investigative Committee filed charges against 142 suspects accused of involvement in the unrest.

Germany records highest heat-related death toll since 2016
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:44:27 UTC
18:44:27 KST

Around 12,500 people in Germany have died from heat-related causes so far this year, the country's public health institute said on Thursday, marking the highest annual toll since records began in 2016.
The figure comes from the Berlin-based Robert Koch Institute’s (RKI) latest report on heat-related mortality, which covers the period from April 6 to August 2.
This means that significantly more people have died from heat-related causes so far this year than in an average full year.
Among the past 10 years, 2018 and 2019 in particular saw a high number of heat-related deaths. In 2018, according to the latest RKI figures, 9,400 people died from heat-related causes; in 2019, the figure was 7,700.
The total number of heat-related deaths this year could be even higher than reported. According to the RKI, this is just a conservative estimate.
There were particularly high numbers of heat-related deaths this year in the two German states of Saarland and Rhineland-Palatinate. Heat-related mortality in the two states stood at 43.4 and 38.7 deaths per 100,000 residents, respectively. Nationwide, the figure was 15 per 100,000 residents.
Heat hits elderly hardest
Heat is particularly dangerous for older people. About 6,300 deaths were registered among those aged 85 and older.
More than 3,100 of the people who died were between 75 and 84 years old, and just under 1,900 were between 65 and 74. About 1,200 deaths were registered among people under 65.
The severe heatwave in late June also had a significant impact. The RKI estimates that around 9,600 people died from heat-related causes during the week of June 22–28 alone. In many parts of Germany, temperatures during those days hovered around 40°C.
According to the RKI, a heat-related increase in mortality typically becomes apparent when the weekly average temperature reaches 20°C, calculated using day- and nighttime temperatures over the course of a week.
During the week of July 27 through August 2, the nationwide weekly average temperature was 21.6°C.

Japan protests as Russia’s Putin visits disputed Kuril Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:43:38 UTC
18:43:38 KST

Japan protests as Russia’s Putin visits disputed Kuril Islands
Japanese PM says Putin’s visit to the Pacific island chain, seized by the Soviet Union in 1945, is ‘unacceptable’.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has paid his first-ever visit to a Russian-administered island chain in the Pacific that is also claimed by Japan, drawing condemnation from Tokyo.
Putin visited the Kuril Islands on Thursday, meeting with the regional governor and visiting a fish-processing plant, a hospital and a school on the southernmost isle of Iturup, according to Russian state media.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Putin warns of tit-for-tat seizures of European vessels
- list 2 of 3Russian strike sparks fire at Ukraine port; Zelenskyy seeks interceptors
- list 3 of 3Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s Wildberries ‘aren’t about the front line’
Japan asserts territorial rights to the four southernmost islands of the chain, which it calls the Northern Territories. The isles were seized by the Soviet Union during the second world war and have remained a source of friction between Moscow and Tokyo.
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called Putin’s visit to the territory “absolutely unacceptable”, saying it “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”.
“This visit … by the sitting Russian president goes against Japan’s consistent position on the Northern Territories,” Takaichi told reporters, using the Japanese name for the islands.
Japan’s Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also criticised Putin’s visit, saying the disputed islands “are an inherent part of Japan’s territory both historically and under international law”. He later summoned the Russian ambassador to “strongly protest” against Putin’s visit, according to Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Putin says Russia ‘not threatening Japan’
Ties between Tokyo and Moscow have worsened since the full-scale conflict in Ukraine began in 2022, with Japan joining other G7 countries in sanctioning Russia and giving money and non-lethal defence aid to Kyiv.
Putin on Wednesday called Japan’s sanctions “unprovoked”.
“Japan has identified Russia as a main source of threats. I would like to point out that we are not threatening Japan … On the contrary, it has territorial claims against our country,” Putin said.
The four disputed Kuril isles are part of the volcanic Kuril archipelago, running in a broad arc from Russia’s Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan’s main northern island, Hokkaido.
The islands’ names are similar in both countries – Kunashir, Habomai, Shikotan and Iturup in Russian, while in Japanese they are known as Kunashiri, Habomai, Shikotan and Etorofu.
Their population of about 20,000 Russian citizens lives in a harsh climate, but the islands have mineral deposits including gold and silver, and rich fishing grounds.
After the islands were occupied in 1945, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people.
Thereafter, the islands acquired strategic importance, providing air and sea bases during the Cold War as the Soviet Union confronted the United States and its closest ally in the Pacific, Japan. Moscow over the years has beefed up its military presence on the islands.
Putin travelled to the Kurils after visiting the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin on Wednesday, where Russia’s navy was conducting drills.
In Sakhalin, Putin, held a meeting “on ensuring the security of Russia’s eastern borders,” according to Russian media.

Accommodations up 4% year-over-year as tourism bounces back to pre-crisis level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

Accommodations up 4% year-over-year as tourism bounces back to pre-crisis level
According to Statistics Estonia, 1.66 million tourists stayed at accommodation establishments in the first half of 2026, from January through June, up 4 percent from the same period a year earlier.
During the first six months of 2026, more than 874,900 foreign tourists and nearly 789,400 domestic tourists stayed at accommodation establishments in Estonia.
According to Piret Pukk, a leading analyst at Statistics Estonia, the number of overnight stays also increased compared with the previous year. "There were 5 percent more overnight stays than in the first half of 2025, totaling 3.04 million," Pukk said.
Foreign tourists spent more than 1.72 million nights at accommodation establishments in the first half of 2026, while domestic tourists spent more than 1.32 million nights. Overnight stays by foreign tourists were up 7 percent from a year earlier, while those by domestic tourists increased 3 percent.
Compared with the first six months of 2019, before the crisis, the total number of tourists staying at accommodation establishments and the number of overnight stays were both 1 percent higher this year. The number of Estonian residents staying at accommodation establishments was 16 percent higher than in the same period in 2019, while the number of foreign visitors was 10 percent lower. Overnight stays by Estonian residents were also up 18 percent, while those by foreign visitors were down 9 percent.
In the first half of 2026, 78 percent of foreign tourists staying at accommodation establishments in Estonia were on vacation and 18 percent were traveling for work. Among domestic tourists, 70 percent were on vacation and 21 percent stayed at accommodation establishments for work-related reasons. A small proportion of guests stayed for other purposes.
Finnish visitors decline, Latvia and UK share up
In the first half of 2026, the largest shares of foreign tourists staying at accommodation establishments in Estonia came from Finland (34 percent), Latvia (15 percent) and Germany (6 percent). More than 298,400 tourists arrived from Finland, down 1 percent from a year earlier. Nearly 135,200 tourists from Latvia stayed at accommodation establishments, up 6 percent year over year, while the number of German tourists was nearly 51,200, up 1 percent.
Significant numbers of tourists also came from Lithuania (38,300, up 7 percent) and the United Kingdom (39,000, up 19 percent). More than 24,000 foreign visitors from each of the following — Asian countries, the United States, Poland and Sweden — stayed at accommodation establishments. In the first half of 2026, 78 percent or more than 684,200 of the foreign tourists staying at accommodation establishments came to Estonia from European Union countries. Their number increased 3 percent from a year earlier.
More than half (54 percent) of all tourists staying at accommodation establishments in the first six months of 2026 stayed in Harju County, including 51 percent in Tallinn. In addition, 11 percent stayed in Pärnu (12 percent in Pärnu County), while 8 percent stayed in Tartu (9 percent in Tartu County). In the first half of the year, 6 percent of tourists stayed in Ida-Viru County, while 4 percent stayed in both Saare and Valga counties. Valga County recorded the largest increase in the number of tourists staying at accommodation establishments during the period, at 13 percent.
Nearly three-quarters or 74 percent of foreign tourists staying at accommodation establishments in the first half of 2026 stayed in Harju County, including 72 percent in Tallinn. During the same period, 11 percent stayed in Pärnu County and 7 percent in Tartu County. Ida-Viru and Saare counties each accounted for 2 percent of foreign tourists.
Harju County was also the most popular destination among Estonian residents staying at accommodation establishments in the first half of this year, accounting for 33 percent, followed by Pärnu County at 14 percent and Tartu County at 11 percent. Ida-Viru, Lääne-Viru, Valga, Saare and Lääne counties were also popular places to stay among Estonian residents.

Interview: Uncovering Unit 731's dark history requires broader int'l cooperation, says Singaporean historian
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:40:18 CST
18:40:18 KST

Singaporean historian Lim Shao Bin reviews materials at his home in Singapore, July 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Then Chih Wey)
SINGAPORE, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- "More than 80 years have passed, and only now are we beginning to realize how much Japan still hasn't told us," said Lim Shao Bin, a Singaporean historian who has spent decades tracing Japan's biological warfare activities in Southeast Asia, in a recent interview with Xinhua.
As each new discovery serves as a reminder of how much remains undocumented, Lim said that filling those gaps would require broader international cooperation among governments and scholars -- not only to advance research across disciplines, but also to encourage the release of more historical records.
Since the 1980s, Lim has collected wartime Japanese documents from secondhand bookstores and government archives in Japan. Over the past decade, his research has focused on Unit 9420, a lesser-known biological warfare unit of the Japanese Imperial Army that operated in Southeast Asia.
Unit 9420 was built as part of Japan's broader biological warfare network, with personnel drawn from established units including Unit 731 in Harbin, and other units in Nanjing and the Japanese homeland.
According to Lim, Unit 9420 "created an entire production line for germ bombs in Singapore and what is now Malaysia." Vegetables were cultivated to feed rats. Rats were bred to produce fleas. The fleas were then infected with plague bacteria before being packed into glass bombs and transported to battlefields.
Headquartered in Singapore, the unit maintained branches across present-day Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam and Myanmar.
"The Japanese military came to Southeast Asia because the climate was ideal," Lim said. Japanese researchers had concluded that fleas reproduced most efficiently at temperatures between 27 and 30 degrees Celsius and humidity levels of around 90 percent.
Many of these findings appeared in "Oka 9420 Unit, Japanese South Army BW Troop," a book Lim co-authored with Chinese scholar Wang Xuan and published in 2025.
Yet new evidence has continued to emerge.
Among the most significant is a recently disclosed testimony preserved at Britain's National Archives from a former prisoner of war identified as W. B. Williams, which may offer new clues that British prisoners were also subjected to human experimentation.
Captured in Singapore in February 1942, Williams wrote that he and many other prisoners were vaccinated and inoculated. Blood samples were taken, and "a glass tube was inserted in the back passage."
Within days, he recalled, large numbers of prisoners, including himself, developed severe headaches, diarrhea, dysentery and abdominal symptoms.
According to his testimony, similar procedures were repeated three times over three years at different camps, each followed by the same symptoms.
"If that is not experiments, I don't know what else you call it," Williams wrote.
"Before this, we had not come across any records indicating that British nationals were also subjected to human experimentation," Lim said.
The possibility, however, did not come entirely as a surprise to Lim. In his 2025 book, he had already raised questions about whether Unit 9420 conducted human experiments on British nationals.
In June 1944, he noted, 17 British prisoners of war held in Singapore contracted scrub typhus -- a disease that was not endemic to Singapore at the time -- and three died.
Separately, a medical report produced by Unit 9420 recorded that military doctors had successfully isolated the related pathogen from wild rats and transported it back to "Syonan-to," the name used by Japan for occupied Singapore.
"The disease wasn't native here," Lim said. "It was brought in."
Lim also pointed to another unresolved chapter.
After Japan's surrender, the United States dispatched several teams to investigate Unit 731. The unit reportedly handed over roughly 8,000 pathology slides to the American side. But the materials were never disclosed to the public, nor were any war responsibility proceedings ever brought against members of the unit.
"International cooperation is essential," said Lim, noting that only coordinated efforts by governments and research institutions can encourage Japan, the United States and other countries to release additional archival materials.
"If it's only individual scholars or universities asking for disclosure, it's very difficult to make progress," he added.
For Lim, international cooperation extends beyond opening archives. Understanding the surviving evidence increasingly requires expertise from multiple disciplines.
He recalled discovering a 1942 inventory listing hundreds of chemical agents transferred from Unit 731 headquarters to Unit 9420 for six months of use. Every entry was recorded in Japanese katakana. "If you don't have specialists from that field, it's almost impossible to interpret."
"We need people from many different fields if we are to fully expose this historical malignancy," he said.
In June this year, Singapore's Channel NewsAsia released the documentary Inside Unit 731: Japan's Secret Human Experiments. Lim said many viewers in Singapore were shocked to learn that the country had been connected to Japan's biological warfare program.
"Many people assumed Unit 731 was only a story about China," he said. "Now that Singapore's broadcaster has told this history, audiences, including many in Europe and North America, are realizing that it involved much more."
For Lim, documenting the history of Unit 731 and its affiliated units is not simply an exercise in reconstructing the past. It is also about understanding the warning signs that precede future conflicts.
Japan's history of military expansion, he argued, demonstrates that preparations for war often begin years before open hostilities.
"The international community must remain vigilant," he said. "There should be more effective supervisory mechanisms for former aggressor states to prevent similar tragedies from happening again." ■
Singaporean historian Lim Shao Bin speaks during an interview with Xinhua at his home in Singapore, July 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Then Chih Wey)

Eurovision Bars Warring Countries From Hosting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

Eurovision, the world’s biggest international song contest, will no longer allow countries at war to host the competition.
The winning country typically hosts the next year’s competition, but under the new rules, the winning country will “automatically be ineligible to host the contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region,” Eurovision song contest organizers announced on Wednesday.
The change comes after several European countries boycotted this year’s competition over the inclusion of Israel. Israel came second in both the 2025 and 2026 contests, raising questions about whether it would be allowed to host if it won.
The contest’s governing body approved the amendment after receiving feedback from participating broadcasters.
“These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special,” Martin Green, director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said in a statement.
Eurovision organizers made several more changes to the competition’s rules, including raising the minimum age for performers as of the first day of rehearsal from 16 to 18.
Controversy
Five countries—Spain, Iceland, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Slovenia—boycotted this year’s competition in Vienna, Austria, in May after the European Broadcasting Union refused calls to suspend Israel from the contest. Ireland’s public broadcaster RTÉ said in a September statement that its “participation would be unconscionable given the ongoing and appalling loss of lives in Gaza.” José Pablo López, president of Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE, said that same month that “it was about time to break the silence within the EBU regarding the genocide in Gaza.”
Broadcasters also argued that the competitors of Eurovision are not ordinary performers but representatives of their nations. Eurovision “is not merely a song contest,” López said. It’s “the most politicized festival in existence.”
The broadcasters’ decision to withdraw from the contest marked the largest multinational political boycott in Eurovision history.
The boycott came amid intense backlash from the public over the inclusion of Israel in the competition despite its military occupation and bombardment of Gaza, which has killed more than 73,000 people since Oct. 7, 2023.
Israel has participated in Eurovision since 1973, becoming the first non-European country to join the competition. Because Eurovision is run by public broadcasters that are part of the EBU, it includes EBU members outside Europe, such as Canada, which will be eligible to participate in the song contest in 2027 after its broadcaster joined the union in 2026. Bulgaria is set to host the 2027 competition.
But Israel’s inclusion in recent years raised questions about whether the competition was taking a consistent stance towards countries at war. Eurovision banned Russia from participating in the contest after it invaded Ukraine in February 2022, arguing that its inclusion would bring the contest into disrepute. Later that year, the EBU indefinitely suspended Russian state broadcasters from its governance and membership.
After Israel finished second in both the 2025 and 2026 contests—results that also drew scrutiny over allegations of government interference, which the country denied—some broadcasters reportedly expressed safety concerns if the contest were to be hosted there in the future. (An investigation by Eurovision News Spotlight found that the Israeli government had funded an extensive online campaign for its 2025 entry. The EBU maintained that the result was valid but introduced new restrictions this year prohibiting disproportionate promotion, including state-backed campaigns. It formally warned Israeli broadcaster KAN over videos urging viewers to cast all 10 of their votes for Israel. The broadcaster denied wrongdoing and the EBU said the videos did not affect the results of the competition.)
Eurovision has moved competitions before due to geopolitical issues, although there has not been a formal rule until now. Ukraine hosted Eurovision in 2017 in spite of fighting between Ukrainian forces and Moscow-backed separatists in the east. The country won again in 2022, but the 2023 competition was ultimately hosted in Liverpool, U.K., on Ukraine’s behalf.
The new rule also institutionalizes a process to determine whether a winning country not at war is eligible to host. The EBU said it could commission an independent security assessment to determine whether a winning country can safely host the event, and if not, the EBU will appoint another host country.
Under the new rules, an appointed host country would also organize the contest “in its own right” and “will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another member.” That change differs from the 2023 competition for which British and Ukrainian broadcasters collaborated on the production of the competition.

Malaysia construction sector grows 8.8 pct in Q2
China
Unknown Publisher

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's construction sector continued its steady growth in the second quarter of 2026, with the value of work done rising 8.8 percent year-on-year to 47.8 billion ringgit (11.68 billion U.S. dollars), compared with 8.5 percent growth in the first quarter, official data showed on Thursday.
The performance was driven mainly by the special trade activities and non-residential buildings sub-sectors, which expanded 17.6 percent and 13.3 percent, respectively, the Department of Statistics Malaysia said in a statement.
Residential buildings grew 8.7 percent, while civil engineering increased 2.7 percent.
Civil engineering remained the largest contributor to the total value of work done, accounting for 35 percent. The private sector continued to drive activity, contributing 65.8 percent of the total.
For the first half of 2026, the value of work done increased by 8.7 percent year-on-year to 94.3 billion ringgit, although growth moderated from 14.7 percent in the first half of 2025.
All sub-sectors recorded positive growth, led by special trade activities at 21 percent and non-residential buildings at 13 percent. ■

China revises, repeals administrative regulations for landmark environmental code
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:39:49 CST
18:39:49 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang has signed a State Council decree publicizing a decision to revise and repeal certain administrative regulations as the country's landmark Ecological and Environmental Code is set to take effect on Saturday.
The State Council will revise 12 regulations, including those on the national census of pollution sources and environmental monitoring, to ensure they align with the provisions in the new code.
Another three administrative regulations will be revoked to meet the new requirements for advancing high-quality development and ecological progress.
The move is to ensure a coherent regulatory framework with consistent and well-coordinated rules for ecological and environmental protection.
The decision will come into effect on Saturday.
The Ecological and Environmental Code was adopted by China's top legislature in March. The 1,242-article Code has five chapters, covering areas including pollution control, ecological protection, and green and low-carbon development.
The Code is aligned with China's pledges to peak carbon emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality before 2060. ■

MADRID, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- The 2026-27 La Liga season kicks off this weekend with a reduced list of matches, as teams whose players featured beyond the semifinals of the FIFA World Cup do not start their season for another week.
That means FC Barcelona, Athletic Club, Real Madrid, Real Betis and Real Sociedad will not feature on the opening weekend, while Atletico Madrid will play Malaga on Wednesday.
Deportivo Alaves and Getafe kick off the new season on Saturday, with Alaves coach Quique Sanchez Flores and his Getafe counterpart Jose Bordalas each having previously coached the other side.
Saturday's second match sees Sevilla at home to Rayo Vallecano.
Rayo is unable to play in its Vallecas Stadium for the moment, and pre-season results have not been impressive, while Sevilla has seen players such as Djibril Sow, Akor Adams and Nemanja Gudelj all depart and looks to have a weaker squad than the one that struggled for much of last year.
Racing Santander returns to the top flight for the first time since 2012 with a home game against Villarreal on Sunday.
Villarreal has former Rayo coach Inigo Perez making his debut, while Racing needs to tighten up a defense that conceded 61 goals despite winning the second division.
Espanyol is at home to Levante in a game between two sides that avoided relegation last season, with Levante needing to find a replacement for striker Carlos Espi, who has joined Real Madrid.
Celta Vigo could have postponed its opening day game at home to Osasuna given that striker Borja Iglesias formed part of the triumphant Spain team at the World Cup, but with UEFA Europa League games in the coming weeks, the club opted to play, although the match is reportedly under threat due to a fungal infection on the pitch at its Balaidos Stadium.
There will be a packed house at Riazor Stadium on Monday when Deportivo plays its first La Liga game in eight years at home to Elche.
The home side has spent money to build a squad capable of competing in La Liga, while there are several changes at Elche with Martin Anselmi replacing Eder Sarabia as coach, and Alvaro Rodriguez, Aleix Febas, Rafa Mir and Andre Silva all leaving. ■

MOSCOW, August 13. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin has congratulated World War II veteran Yevgeny Znamensky on his 101st birthday with a personal telegram. Putin commended the veteran's combat path, including the Battle of Stalingrad, the liberation of Europe, and reaching Berlin, and his postwar work for the Motherland.
"A man of special life resilience, a front-line soldier, a courageous and strong-spirited person, you have traversed a glorious combat path," the president wrote.
Znamensky was born August 13, 1925, in Serpukhov. He participated in the defense of Moscow before being drafted into the Red Army in early 1943. He fought on the Steppe, Don, and 1st Belorussian fronts, crossing the Don, Donets, Vistula, Oder, and Spree rivers. He ended the war in Berlin on May 2, 1945, signing the Reichstag wall. He was wounded and shell-shocked twice.

5% of US Patriot stocks gets Ukraine through winter, 10% ends the ballistic threat — and Zelenskyy has just 1%, he tells CNN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:37:53 UTC
18:37:53 KST

Ukraine holds only about a tenth of the Patriot interceptor missiles it needs from the United States to stop Russia's surging ballistic strikes, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN. Selling Kyiv 5% of the current US stockpile would carry the country through winter, he said, and 10% would let it "destroy all the Russians' ballistic missiles" — but he holds 1%.
The plea puts a number on a shortage that has run through Ukraine's diplomacy all summer and left its cities increasingly exposed. It is the concrete cost of near-empty interceptor stocks: on 5 August, Russia fired 28 ballistic and anti-ship missiles at Kyiv and Ukraine intercepted none of them, killing 17 people, and four days earlier launched 27 ballistic missiles with only one stopped. July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, according to the UN.
The arithmetic of a losing race
"This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025," Zelenskyy said, while "Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before."
The interceptor that most reliably stops those missiles, the US-made Patriot's PAC-3, is scarce worldwide: the war between the United States and Iran drained stocks as American and Gulf forces spent dozens against Iranian missiles and drones, and the shortage has fallen hardest on Ukraine.
The bottleneck is structural, not budgetary. Only five or six countries build interceptors capable of stopping ballistic missiles, the US makes around 600 Patriots a year, and orders are placed years in advance — so money alone cannot close the gap before winter, defense expert Marc DeVore told Euromaidan Press in June.
A home-built Patriot, still uncertain
Zelenskyy said doubts remain over whether US President Donald Trump's apparent offer to let Ukraine manufacture its own Patriot interceptors will materialize. At the NATO summit in Ankara, Trump said he would license Ukraine to build the missiles, then days later said he was unsure; the Patriot makers have since sent officials to Kyiv, without result so far. "I hope that I will get it," Zelenskyy said, calling it "one of the biggest [challenges] I had from the very beginning of this war."
He described daily, largely private deal-making to close the gap: "million phone calls ... I try to exchange something to missiles ... I do some things which I can't even share. It doesn't mean that it's outside of the law. But I can't speak about it."
Putin, the Donbas, and the next war
On the stalled peace process, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had put new proposals to the Trump administration and needed "more involvement of the American side," adding that Vladimir Putin "doesn't want to stop this war now and (there's) not enough pressure on him now." He rejected ceding the rest of the Donbas that Putin seeks, arguing security guarantees matter more: "Why he will not come again ... to occupy us?"
He confirmed a recent call with Vice President JD Vance but declined to say whether Vance had asked Ukraine to halt strikes on a Russian Black Sea oil port that were hurting US firms and threatening a spike in global energy prices, as the Financial Times reported. Zelenskyy also endorsed Western assessments that Putin could widen the war toward a smaller NATO state, likely in the Baltics: "He wants quick victory ... occupy or destroy or control."

Germany news: Far-right leader backs left-wing populist

Pay for Germany's top executives rises again
Executives at Germany's 40 largest listed companies have seen their average pay rise again, with a typical DAX board member earning more than €3.9 million ($4.5 million) in 2025.
The annual analysis by the shareholder association DSW and the Technical University of Munich found executive compensation increased by 4% compared with the previous year, with a large share coming from performance-related bonuses.
Across all DAX companies, board members earned on average 42 times as much as ordinary employees at their firms.
The widest gap was at Adidas, where executive board members received 106 times the average employee compensation.
The ratio was 75 to one at Volkswagen and 70 to one at healthcare group Fresenius.
Chief executives of DAX companies received an average of around €6.14 million in 2025.
SAP chief Christian Klein topped the ranking with total compensation of about €10.9 million, around 86% of it variable.
Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing received €10.5 million, with around 64% made up of short- and long-term bonuses linked to business performance.
DSW managing director Marc Tüngler said the €10 million mark had been exceeded in two cases, describing it as a level that remained socially and internally sensitive.
German CEO pay remains well below levels at many major companies abroad.
CEOs of non-German companies in the Euro Stoxx 50 received an average of €9.5 million in 2025, while the average among the 30 companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average was €30.5 million.
German officials warn against nostalgia for East Germany
German officials have warned against romanticizing communist East Germany, saying nostalgia for the former dictatorship risks obscuring its repression and lack of basic freedoms.
The comments came on the 65th anniversary of the construction of the Berlin Wall and just weeks before important state elections in eastern Germany.
Culture Minister Wolfram Weimer said both left-wing and right-wing extremists were trying to play down the crimes of the former East German regime.
He described East Germany as a "brutal dictatorship" without free elections, press freedom or freedom of movement, and pointed to the role of the Stasi secret police, political repression and the fortified border around West Berlin.
Evelyn Zupke, Germany's federal commissioner for victims of the communist dictatorship, also warned against what is commonly known as "Ostalgie" — nostalgia for life in the former East Germany.
"East Germany seems more appealing to some people the further it recedes in history," she told the Rheinische Post newspaper, warning that a nostalgic view could blur the reality of the dictatorship.
Day 3 of 4 in Nathalie Pohl's world record Frankfurt-Cologne extreme swim challenge
Extreme swimmer Nathalie Pohl is continuing her swim up the Rhine River (yes, it is still deep enough for this purpose at least!) towards Cologne.
She trying to set a new world record by covering a 200 kilometer stretch from Frankfurt to Cologne in just four days, raising money for charity en route.
Pohl entered the water in Lahnstein, near Koblenz, shortly before 11 a.m. on Thursday. The day's stretch covers some 58 kilometers, ending in Bad Honnef — a short southerly swim upstream from DW's offices on the Rhine in Bonn.
Wednesday's stretch already took her through some of the shallowest segments of the Rhine amid this summer's drought, particularly the bottleneck at Kaub.
Pohl is raising money to improve awareness on the importance of safe swimming among children, and to fund swimming projects and teaching. Her team says they have raised around €85,000 (almost $100,000) so far.
Steel giant Thyssenkrupp plows on with Duisburg production, for now, despite Rhine river issues
German steel giant Thyssenkrupp says the low Rhine River levels have not yet impacted production at its major facility in Duisburg.
Chief Financial Officer Axel Hamann said that supplies to customers were not presently at risk, as he presented nine-monthly performance figures to the press.
For the moment, he said, the facility was still receiving some deliveries of raw materials — particularly coal for the furnaces — via partially-laden barges on the Rhine.
"If the situation really deteriorates and the ship journeys are stopped altogether, then we could not rule out an effect on results," he said, meaning sales volumes and output.
"We of course do have a few options to adapt the production and the deliveries to our facilities somewhat, so we can continue to work longer with the supplies that we have," Hamann said. He said there were shipping alternatives and that the company was trying to secure more supplies via rail in particular.
"We're still a long way away from letting some of our furnaces run cold," Hamann said.
The company was also looking into potential transport by road networks, he said — but typically coal is seen as a very bulky, heavy and cost-inefficient product to transport using trucks in large quantities. Earlier in the week, a company spokeswoman had suggested that truck transportation was not a realistic option.
Drought causing significant crop losses
The lack of rainfall affecting large parts of Germany has severely impacted this summer's harvest, according to an association representing farming companies.
Around 3 million metric tons (3.31 million US tons) of grain and rapeseed have been lost since mid-June, meaning revenue shortfalls of €600 million ($692 million), the German Raiffeisen Association said.
According to the association's expert for cereal markets, Guido Seedler, "that amounts to economic damage of €10 million each dav during the around 60-day hot-weather period from June till the end of the harvest."
The association estimates that this year's grain harvest will be 40.6 million tons, down from 45 million tons in 2025.
"Only the favorable spring weather prevented greater damage," Seedler said, adding that the harvest was still adequate overall but below average.
The German Raiffeisen Association represents 1,600 cooperative companies in agricultural trade and processing.
Top executives earning 42 times as much as average workers — study
Managers at Germany's top listed companies were paid an average of just over €3.9 million ($4.5 million) in 2025, a study has shown.
That means that executives at the 40 companies in the DAX stock index brought home 42 times the pay of an average employee.
The chief executives of DAX companies received pay of an average €6.14 million in 2025, the study by the German shareholder protection association DSW and the Technical University of Munich.
Pay for two chief executives exceeded €10 million: Christian Klein, chief executive of software company SAP, received around €10.9 million, and Deutsche Bank boss Christian Sewing received €10.5 million.
In Klein's case, almost 86% of that came from variable compensation, while 64% of Sewing's pay was made up of short and long-term bonuses linked to business performance.
As high as these sums may seem to many normal citizens, they are relatively modest in international comparison.
Top executives of companies in the Euro Stoxx 50, excluding German ones, received an average of €9.5 million for the 2025 financial year, the analysis showed.
And for chief executives of the 30 companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the average was €30.5 million.

WATCH — A virtual tour of Germany's inner border and the Berlin Wall
For 28 years, a nearly insurmountable barrier kept people from fleeing East Germany. Today, it is difficult to imagine what was bitter reality just a few decades ago. A computer animation reveals the vast security system of Germany's inner border and the Berlin Wall, both of which were recreated virtually in the greatest detail.
Merz calls for defense of democracy on Berlin Wall anniversary
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called on people to keep up the fight to retain freedom and democracy as Germany marks the 65th anniversary of the construction of the Berlin Wall.
"Sixty-five years ago, the leadership of former East Germany had the Wall built. Today, our country has been united longer than it was divided and we live in freedom and peace," Merz wrote on the platform X.
"The lesson of the Wall remains: Freedom and democracy are not a given. We must always fight for them," he wrote.
Merz's remarks come amid a surge in popularity of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party seen by many as anti-democratic in its ideology.
On August 13, 1961, on what would become known as Barbed Wire Sunday, communist East Germany sealed the border between Berlin’s eastern and western sectors before building a wall that was to divide the city for the next 28 years.
People trying to cross the Wall to leave the authoritarian state were often shot dead, and the barrier came to symbolize the repressive political system behind it.
In remarks to the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, he commissioner for culture, Wolfram Weimer, warned against "positive distortions of former East Germany" by the far-right AfD and the Left Party.
Weimer criticized such "collective forgetting, repression and downplaying of former East Germany" as the biggest challenge to properly commemorating the crimes of the regime there.
Suspicious object halts trains at Bavaria station
Rail traffic through the southern German town of Treuchtlingen has been suspended after police found a suspicious object on the tracks that may contain explosives.
Police in Bavaria's Middle Franconia region said specialist Federal Police units were examining the object, which was discovered in the track bed at Treuchtlingen station.
Police described the item as posing a possible explosive hazard and said specialist officers were carrying out further checks.
The object was being X-rayed late Thursday morning as authorities worked to determine exactly what it was.
Police have also urged people to avoid the area.
Treuchtlingen, a town of around 13,000 people about 150 kilometers (95 miles) north of Munich, is an important railway junction in Bavaria. Regional and long-distance services running through the station connect destinations including Munich and Nuremberg.
Heat-related deaths on the rise — Robert Koch Insitute
Several spates of hot weather across Germany this year have caused an estimated 12,500 premature deaths so far, public health authorities have said.
The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) said its figure, released on Thursday, is a conservative estimate.
The worst-affected states were the western states of Saarland and Rhineland-Palatinate, which had more than double the national average of heat-related deaths.
The most deaths were recorded in the age group 85 years or older, at around 6,300. More than 3,100 of those who died were aged between 75 and 84, and nearly 1,900 between 65 and 74.
The severe heat wave at the end of June was especially deadly, with the RKI expecting that around 9,600 people died as a result of heat in the week from June 22 to 28 alone.
Climate scientists say that heat waves will increase in severity and frequency as the Earth continues to warm, largely owing to the human use of fossil fuels.
AfD firebrand Höcke offers to back Wagenknecht as Thuringia state premier
The leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the eastern state of Thuringia, Björn Höcke, has offered to back left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht as state premier.
"I am extending my hand to you," Höcke said on Wednesday in a video posted on X.
He urged Wagenknecht to become state premier before a regional election in neighboring Saxony-Anhalt on September 6.
Höcke's offer comes as Thuringia's Premier Mario Voigt of the Christian Democrats (CDU) continues to face pressure after his doctorate was withdrawn over plagiarism claims.
The AfD has said it plans to launch another constructive vote of no confidence against Voigt.
Under Thuringia's constitution, a premier can only be removed if parliament simultaneously elects a successor by a majority. The AfD and BSW together hold the necessary majority, with 47 of the state parliament's 88 seats.
Wagenknecht, has indicated that her party, the anti-migrant, left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), could abstain in a decisive vote for state premier in Saxony-Anhalt, potentially helping an AfD candidate take office.
The BSW is currently part of Thuringia's governing coalition along with the conservative CDU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Höcke's AfD is the largest group in the Thuringian state parliament but does not form part of the government.
The move proposed by Höcke would call into question the current consensus among mainstream parties that there should be no cooperation with the far right, known as the "firewall."

Moldova offers rail lifeline for Ukrainian food exports as Russia chokes Black Sea trade
Moldova agreed to transit 600,000 metric tons of Ukrainian foodstuffs via railways by the end of 2026, Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan wrote on social media on Aug. 12.
Ukraine has been unable to export agricultural products through the Black Sea for several weeks due to escalating Russian attacks on its seaports.
Russian agricultural exports are also being affected by Ukrainian attacks, including the Aug. 12 operation against the port of Novorossiysk, prompting fears of a global food crisis similar to 2022.
Tofan hailed the agreement as "Solidarity lanes at their best," explaining the use of Moldova's railways as "helping Ukraine reach regional markets and keeping vital trade routes open."
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked Moldova for the decision and the country's "true solidarity with Ukraine."
"As Russia deliberately targets Ukraine's ports and trade routes, alternative export routes are vital for Ukraine's resilience and global food security," Sybiha said.
The European Commission told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 11 that it had met with Ukraine, Moldova, and Romania "to assess the situation regarding alternative shipment routes through the Solidarity Lanes."
EU-Ukraine Solidarity Lanes were first established in 2022, when Ukraine was similarly unable to get its agricultural produce to world markets as Russia carried out attacks along the country's Black Sea coast.
"The Danube corridor remains the most promising alternative in terms of capacity potential, but is still more limited and costly for bulky cargo like grain than that of the larger ports around Odesa," a Commission spokesperson said.
Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said "there is no real alternative to our own Black Sea ports" in an Aug. 6 interview with the German newspaper Der Spiegel.
He predicts a grain and oilseed harvest of 81.5 million metric tons in 2026, of which 70% to be exported. The agreement with Moldova would cover just over 1% of the total expected exports of those crops alone.
Vysotsky estimates that Ukraine will run out of storage capacity from October onwards, and that the Black Sea region accounts for 70% of global wheat production.
"If the crisis continues for months, the global impact could be even greater than it was four years ago," he said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan called on Russia and Ukraine to stop attacking ships in the Black Sea and is attempting to mediate between the two sides to restore shipping flows.

Etna ash keeps Catania airport shut until Friday, disrupting summer travel
CATANIA, Sicily, Aug 13 - Flights at Catania airport in Sicily will remain suspended until early Friday because of ash from Mount Etna's ongoing volcanic activity, which has forced hundreds of flights to be cancelled or rerouted over the past week.
All arrivals at the island hub, Italy's fifth-busiest airport by passenger traffic, will be suspended through 8 a.m. local time (0600 GMT) on August 14, airport operator SAC said in a statement on Thursday.
It had said on Wednesday that departures would be suspended until 2 a.m. local time on August 14. This information regarding departures was not updated on Thursday.
Passengers were advised to check the status of their flights with their airlines before travelling to the airport.
The prolonged restrictions come at the height of the summer holiday season, affecting thousands of passengers, and have placed additional pressure on Sicily's other airports.
Mount Etna, Europe's highest and most active volcano, frequently disrupts operations at Catania airport, whose operator launched the sale of a stake of at least 51% in May.
Marco Viccaro, president of the Italian Volcanological Association, said the activity at Etna, which began on August 6, is more energetic than previous episodes and is continuing in a sustained way.
"This suggests that deeper, gas-rich magma is playing a more active role, making the fragmentation process more efficient and leading to increased ash production," he added. REUTERS

More than 20 civilians were killed and scores of others injured in clashes in the southeastern Sudanese city of Geisan near the Ethiopian border, the UN humanitarian office said.
“Local sources in Blue Nile state reported that more than 20 civilians were killed, and many others injured, in clashes in Geisan town on Tuesday,” the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in Sudan said on Wednesday in a statement published on the UN website.
The escalation in violence has displaced about 2,500 people from the town, it added.
OCHA “reiterated its call on all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and to allow aid to reach people quickly, safely and without obstruction.”
Local authorities in Geisan, in Blue Nile state, said on Tuesday that the Sudanese army had repelled an attack on the city by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), without providing details about casualties or damage.
Military sources told Anadolu earlier on Wednesday that fighting between the army and the RSF-SPLM-N alliance continued in Geisan for a second consecutive day.
The army controls large parts of Blue Nile state, while the SPLM-N has fought the Sudanese government since 2011, demanding autonomous rule for the Blue Nile and South Kordofan regions.
Attacks intensify
Separately, OCHA said human rights workers reported that a drone struck El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, on Wednesday morning.
No information on civilian casualties was immediately available, but one of the drones reportedly hit a water station, which is of grave concern at a time when access to clean water remains one of the most pressing challenges facing the city, it said.
OCHA said continued attacks and insecurity in northern parts of North Kordofan were forcing more people to seek refuge in El Obeid.
Humanitarian partners estimate that around 15,000 families have been displaced to the city over the past three weeks, placing additional pressure on already overstretched displacement sites and essential services, it added.
Sudan has been engulfed in conflict since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the Sudanese army and the RSF over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the regular military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced millions and triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Swiss parliament can decide on the Compass Initiative

Swiss parliament can decide on the Compass Initiative
The Swiss parliament can decide on the Compass Initiative, which calls significant legislative provisions related to international treaties to be approved by the people and the cantons.
Back in November, the Swiss government decided to recommend a “no” vote on the initiative “For a directly democratic and competitive Switzerland – no passive EU membership”, also known as the Compass initiative, without putting forward a counter-proposal. It has now submitted its message to Parliament. The initiative is backed by a cross-party group of business leaders.
+ Swiss-EU treaties: signatures handed in for Compass initiative
The federal government explained that the initiative calls for an extension of the mandatory referendum on international treaties. The initiative also seeks to subject the Switzerland-EU Bilateral Agreements III to the mandatory referendum, thereby requiring their approval by the people and the cantons.
However, the government does not wish to link the fundamental issue of the extended referendum on international treaties to the Bilateral Agreements III, nor does it wish to intervene in ongoing decision-making processes. In its view, a “yes” vote by the people is sufficient for the EU treaties to be adopted. Discussions are currently taking place in Parliament on whether the cantons, as well as the people, should also approve the treaties.
