U.S. Army trains on IFPC missile defense system in South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:00:38 UTC
18:00:38 KST

- Soldiers from the 35th Air Defense Artillery Brigade trained on setting up an IFPC system at Camp Humphreys, South Korea, on August 5, 2026.
- The Army awarded Dynetics a $4.1 billion contract for IFPC Increment 2, which includes laser and high-power microwave configurations.
Soldiers from the U.S. Army’s 35th Air Defense Artillery Brigade trained on setting up an Indirect Fire Protection Capability system at Camp Humphreys, South Korea, on August 5, 2026, according to Eighth Army.
The unit involved, Delta Battery, 6th Battalion, 52nd Air Defense Artillery Regiment, guided equipment into place during the exercise. Eighth Army said the training prepared soldiers to employ the IFPC system in support of air and missile defense operations.
IFPC is a mobile, ground-based air defense system built to counter subsonic cruise missiles, drones, rockets, artillery and mortars. Analysts have described it as an American version of Israel’s Iron Dome, which intercepts short-range rockets and artillery. Each IFPC Increment Two installation combines a launcher, known as Enduring Shield, with interceptor rounds stored in sealed, ready-to-fire magazines that allow rapid reloading without exposing munitions handlers to hostile fire.
The system uses 360-degree radar and integrates into the Army’s Integrated Battle Command System, the network architecture that links sensors and shooters across multiple air defense platforms. The Army has said IFPC is designed to protect fixed and semi-fixed sites, including forward operating bases and critical infrastructure, and to fill the gap between short-range air defense systems and the longer-range Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense systems.
The 35th Air Defense Artillery Brigade, based at Osan Air Base, has operated IFPC in South Korea since at least September 2025, when U.S. Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George visited the unit and was photographed in front of an IFPC launcher, marking the system’s first confirmed overseas deployment. The Army deployed the system again in March 2026 during the Freedom Shield exercise, positioning it at Camp Humphreys to test its integration into a networked, layered defense architecture alongside Patriot and Avenger systems.
The IFPC program has moved through several stages of Army contracting. Dynetics, a Leidos subsidiary based in Huntsville, Alabama, entered a $4.1 billion indefinite-delivery agreement with the Army in November 2024 covering low-rate initial production, full-rate production and lifecycle support, with an initial order of 18 launchers. Dynetics received a separate $617 million contract in April 2026 for the fiscal year 2026 production buy, covering launchers, magazines, trainers and logistics support, with deliveries scheduled through November 2029.
The Army has also run a separate competition for the system’s second interceptor type, with Boeing and Lockheed Martin both selected in 2025 to continue development of competing medium-range interceptor designs meant to engage cruise missiles and drones alongside IFPC’s baseline interceptor.

Russia attacks Ukrainian port on Danube, Zelenskiy urges US to send Patriots
Aug 13 - Russia struck Ukraine's largest grain export port on the Danube on Thursday, causing damage and starting a fire, authorities said, after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy warned that Ukraine needed more U.S. air defence missiles to get through winter.
The port of Izmail, near the Romanian border in Ukraine's southern region of Odesa, handles exports of grain and other commodities. The Izmail regional state administration said on Telegram the overnight strikes had damaged port infrastructure and taken out power in the southeast of the city.
Romania, a NATO and European Union member, scrambled two fighter jets on Thursday, its defence ministry said on X, when an 'aerial target' spent about two minutes in Romanian airspace before leaving for Ukraine, where explosions were heard.
The attack on Izmail and record-low Danube water levels could complicate Ukraine's plans to use the river to ship grain to Europe. A Russian naval blockade of Ukraine's Black Sea ports sent grain exports tumbling 76% year-on-year so far in August, Valeriy Tkachev, deputy head of state railway Ukrzaliznytsia's commercial department, said.
Ukraine is among the world's largest producers of wheat, corn and sunflower seeds and around 90% of its exports of such crops go through the Black Sea.
It supplies around 6% of the world's wheat and around 11% of its corn, and the blockade has raised fears of shortages in African and Middle Eastern nations that rely on Ukrainian exports. Russian officials have also warned that Ukraine's strikes on its grain export facilities and ships were pushing up global food prices.
Chicago wheat futures were largely flat on Thursday after a sharp rise in the previous session, when Ukraine attacked Novorossiysk, a major grain shipment hub in Russia's part of the Black Sea, raising concerns about disruption to exports.
On Thursday, Ukraine's military said it struck an oil refinery and petrochemical complex in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan, about 1,300 km (800 miles) from the Ukrainian border, causing a fire - the latest in a months-long campaign of attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure.
UKRAINE ASKS FOR MORE AIR DEFENCES
Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Kyiv had handed proposals to U.S. negotiators for a plan to end the conflict, which started when Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022. But there have been no signs so far of a resumption of peace talks, which unravelled earlier this year.
Ukraine has repeatedly called for a ceasefire. Russia says it wants a settlement, but it must involve Ukraine fully ceding four regions Moscow claims - including land Russia does not yet control - something that Kyiv has refused to consider.
Late on Wednesday, Zelenskiy told CNN that Ukraine needs at least 5% of the current U.S. stockpile of Patriot interceptor missiles to ward off surging Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Kyiv has been seeking more PAC-3s, the newest type of Patriot missile capable of downing Russian ballistic missiles. Deliveries of Patriot missiles to Ukraine dwindled after the war on Iran diverted supplies.
In the interview, Zelenskiy said a 10% share of the current U.S. stockpile of Patriots would be enough to stop all Russian ballistic missile attacks.
"Sell us 5%, we will go through the winter and save people's lives. If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians' ballistic missiles. I have 1%," he told CNN.
Because of their speed and steep trajectory, ballistic missiles are much harder to intercept than drones and cruise missiles.
In July, Russia fired over 450 various missiles at Ukraine, more than half of them ballistic, Yuriy Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian air force said on Facebook.
He also said the air force would stop announcing daily figures on downed and suppressed Russian ballistic missiles, and would present them monthly. Ihnat said that daily updates saying no ballistic missiles had been shot down, when Ukraine lacks air defence interceptors, were only providing an opportunity for Russians to celebrate. REUTERS

Chinese carmakers could capture 15% to 30% of European market by 2035: Citi analysts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:00:10 UTC
18:00:10 KST

Chinese carmakers could capture 15% to 30% of European market by 2035: Citi analysts
‘Made in Europe’ requirement in EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act cited as key factor in lowest growth forecast
Chinese carmakers could capture between 15 and 30 per cent of the European automotive market by 2035, up from roughly 10 per cent this year, analysts at Citi said, with the outcome resting on how far Brussels goes in tightening tariffs and made-in-EU rules.
Current European Union rules would allow Chinese carmakers to reach 30 per cent by 2035 – Citi’s base scenario – while extending existing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles to plug-in hybrids would cap the market share at 25 per cent, Citi analysts led by Harald Hendrikse said in a note issued on Wednesday.
They said the sharpest curb in their forecasts would come from the “made in Europe” requirement in the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which would reduce Chinese carmakers’ market share to 5 per cent in the next two years and hold it at 15 per cent by 2035.
A comprehensive “made in EU” framework under the act would require Chinese carmakers to assemble locally and use local supply chains, which would significantly reduce “future market share gains as EU local manufacturing offsets China cost advantages”, the analysts said.
They warned that European carmakers were potentially facing 10 years of volume losses and restructuring. In their base case, other Asian carmakers – mainly those from Japan and South Korea – would also see their market share decline from the 20 per cent recorded last year to below 16 per cent by 2035.
Chinese carmakers have seen their share of the European market expand rapidly, led by brands such as BYD and SAIC’s MG, which has alarmed European politicians and, increasingly, European manufacturers.

More air raid sirens on the way for RAF Akrotiri
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:00:07 BST
18:00:07 KST

The Ministry of Defence is buying additional air raid warning sirens for RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus, capable of covering both the base and the neighbouring Akrotiri village, the department stated in a contract award notice.
The notice, identifier 2026/S 000-077006, was published on 13 August 2026 and records the award decision as taken the same day. The contract is worth £800,000 and runs for five years from 26 October 2026, with the earliest signature date given as 25 August.
According to the notice, the requirement exists to supplement sirens already installed at the base. The new system must produce distinct alert tones, covering an air raid or imminent threat and an all clear, and must carry both live and recorded voice announcement functionality. It has to be portable and able to work independently of any fixed infrastructure, which is what the title’s reference to rapid deployability means in practice.
The award covers supply, commissioning, documentation, training, warranty and through-life support. Two tenders were received under an open procedure, both from small and medium-sized enterprises, with one supplier successful.
The contract went to Acoustic Technologies, trading as ATI Systems, an American company based in Boston. Contracting was handled by British Forces Cyprus headquarters at Episkopi.
RAF Akrotiri sits within the Western Sovereign Base Area on the south coast of Cyprus and is the RAF’s permanent operating base in the eastern Mediterranean. It has supported British air operations across the region for decades, most recently as the launch point for Typhoon strikes against Islamic State targets in Iraq and Syria under Operation Shader, and for the RAF sorties flown against Houthi targets in Yemen during 2024.
Its position roughly 100 miles from the Syrian coast and within reach of Lebanon, Israel and the wider Levant places it closer to regional conflicts than any other permanent British base. The Sovereign Base Areas are British territory retained under the 1960 treaty that granted Cyprus independence, and Akrotiri village lies inside the boundary, meaning the base authorities have a civilian population to warn as well as service personnel.

11 Charged in ‘One of the Largest Marriage Fraud Prosecutions’ in U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

The U.S. Justice Department on Wednesday announced that it had charged 11 people for allegedly conspiring in a multimillion-dollar, decade-long scheme involving more than 1,000 sham marriages to obtain legal immigration status for mostly Chinese nationals.
Newly confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche, in announcing the arrests and the unsealing of the indictment, described it as “one of the largest marriage fraud prosecutions in United States’ history.”
According to the unsealed indictment, foreign nationals allegedly paid a group of “facilitators” as much as $100,000 for their assistance in getting fraudulently married and applying for lawful permanent residency in the U.S.—or a green card. The facilitators paired each foreign national with a willing U.S. citizen, who was onboarded by “recruiters” and whom they usually paid up to about $30,000 to engage in the sham marriage.
Blanche added that the facilitators allegedly employed attorneys, tax preparers, and even marriage officiants.
The indictment contained photos of alleged sham marriage ceremonies that prosecutors claimed were submitted to federal authorities to support their clients’ green card applications.
The indictment also stated that while the facilitators and the recruiters mainly operated in New York, they also orchestrated fraudulent marriages in other states, including Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Tennessee. Prosecutors also alleged that the facilitators oversaw marriages overseas, such as in China and Vanuatu.
Prosecutors charged the defendants with conspiracy to commit marriage fraud and immigration fraud, which is punishable by up to five years in prison, and conspiracy to encourage the unlawful residence of aliens in the United States, which has a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
Blanche said the unsealed indictment shows "how far people will go to cheat our immigration system,” and added that they will go after those who do “no matter how complicated the scam.”
The indictment follows President Donald Trump’s executive orders that attempt to limit birthright citizenship, including one that restricted “birth tourism”—or the practice of pregnant women giving birth in the U.S. solely for their child to obtain citizenship. Blanche, in the Wednesday announcement, said he has ordered authorities to prioritize investigations and prosecutions of those involved in“birth tourism” schemes. The State Department said on Wednesday it opened a task force to identify “birth tourism” practices and “take action to revoke visas of those who engage in or facilitate it.” According to the State Department, the task force has already revoked more than 600 visas of foreign nationals.

New studies show childhood habits' long-term health impact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:59:00 UTC
17:59:00 KST

New studies show childhood habits' long-term health impact
A child's exercise, sleep and screen time habits are linked to their well-being, with the association stronger among children and young people who are overweight or obese, studies have found.
Two studies involving a researcher from the National Institute for Health Development (TAI) examine children's health from different perspectives. Toomas Veidebaum, a senior researcher at TAI's department of chronic diseases, is a co-author of both research papers.
The studies are based on the international IDEFICS/I.Family longitudinal study, which followed European children from early childhood through adolescence. Researchers repeatedly collected data on the children's health, body weight, diet, physical activity, sleep, screen use and living environment.
A child's entire day affects their well-being
A study published in the International Journal of Obesity examined how children's well-being is associated with three daily habits: physical activity, sleep and screen time.
The analysis included 7,359 observations of European children ages 2 to 16. The data was collected over six years in three waves. Researchers assessed how well the children followed age-specific recommendations for physical activity, sleep and screen time.
Psychosocial well-being was lower among children who followed these recommendations less often. The association was stronger among boys and children and young people who were overweight or obese. Body mass index and waist circumference were used to assess body weight. Both measures affected the strength of the association between physical activity, sleep and screen time and well-being.
The study's observational design makes it possible to describe associations that developed over a longer period, but the findings cannot establish that one factor directly causes another.
"Physical activity, sleep and screen time together make up a child's day. If screens take up a large part of the evening, there may be less time for sleep. In turn, too little sleep affects energy levels, mood and the desire to be active. When supporting a child's health, it is therefore worth looking at their entire daily routine rather than just one habit," Veidebaum said.
Psychosocial well-being refers to a child's emotional and social well-being. It is influenced by factors including relationships with family and friends, the school environment, self-esteem and the ability to cope with everyday life.
The study's findings suggest that the daily pattern combining physical activity, sleep and screen use may be particularly important for the well-being of children with excess weight.
"A child with excess weight may face more physical and social barriers to being active. At the same time, regular physical activity supports self-confidence, social interaction and well-being. The right activity should give the child a sense of achievement and take their abilities and interests into account," Veidebaum said.
Only a little over half of young people exercise regularly
The National Institute for Health Development's population health yearbook helps put the international study's findings into an Estonian context. According to a 2022 school-aged children's health behavior survey cited in the yearbook, 57 percent of Estonian children ages 11 to 15 took part in sports, dance or another organized physical activity at least twice a week. The figure was 60 percent among boys and 54 percent among girls.
Regular exercise was also associated with how young people rated their health. Among 11-year-olds who exercised regularly, 91 percent rated their health as good. The figure was 81 percent among those who exercised less often or irregularly.
Active young people were more likely to report greater life satisfaction and to enjoy going to school, and were less likely to experience depressive episodes.
Differences were also seen in health complaints. Around 40 percent of young people who exercised infrequently experienced feeling low, irritability, nervousness or difficulty falling asleep. Among those who exercised at least twice a week, fewer than one-third reported these complaints.
Among young people who exercised regularly, 17 percent were overweight or obese, compared with 24 percent of those who exercised once a week or less.
These findings show that physical activity, well-being and body weight are also closely associated among children in Estonia. However, it is important to bear in mind that the data shows associations and does not establish that regular exercise directly causes better mental or physical health.
Effects evaluated six years later
A study published in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology focused on the long-term impact of the IDEFICS program. Researchers examined whether a health program implemented during childhood was associated with participants' cardiovascular and metabolic health later in life.
Cardiometabolic health refers to the health of the cardiovascular system and metabolism. It can be assessed using measures such as blood pressure, blood glucose metabolism, blood lipid levels, waist circumference and body weight.
The IDEFICS study began during the 2007-2008 school year. A total of 16,229 children ages 2 to 9 in eight European countries took part in health assessments. Around half lived in areas where a community-based health program was implemented. The remaining children lived in comparison areas with similar socioeconomic backgrounds.
The program focused on three areas: nutrition, physical activity and stress management. Children, families, preschools, schools and local communities were all involved in the activities.
The program aimed to encourage water and fruit and vegetable consumption, daily physical activity, sufficient sleep, moderate screen time and health-promoting activities for families to do together.
The children's health indicators were measured at the start of the study, two years later and six years after the program began. The latest analysis included 1,159 children from Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Hungary, Italy and Sweden who had blood-based measurements available both at the start of the study and six years later. Of these, 685 were in the intervention group and 474 in the comparison group.
Biggest differences in blood pressure
Researchers calculated a metabolic syndrome risk score for each participant. The score combined blood pressure, waist circumference, insulin sensitivity and blood lipid measures, allowing researchers to assess changes in these indicators as a whole.
Over six years, the metabolic risk score improved somewhat more among participants in the health program than in the comparison group. The finding remained after researchers accounted for participants' age, sex, country of origin, body weight and parents' level of education.
Systolic and diastolic blood pressure contributed most to the difference. Among boys, the more favorable change in metabolic risk in the intervention group was most pronounced.
Changes in body mass index were similar in the intervention and comparison groups over the six-year period. This means that the health program's potential benefits may have been reflected in blood pressure and other metabolic indicators even without a clear difference in body weight.
"Body weight is one easily visible indicator of health, but the changes taking place in a child's body go beyond that. Blood pressure, blood glucose regulation and blood lipid levels provide early information about cardiovascular and metabolic health," Veidebaum said.
He said the findings also demonstrate the importance of long-term follow-up. "The effects of a prevention program may develop gradually and show up in different health indicators at different ages. A longitudinal study makes it possible to track which changes that begin in childhood carry over into adolescence and which require more sustained support," Veidebaum said.
The study's authors described the finding as modest but potentially significant from a public health perspective. More favorable development of blood pressure and metabolic indicators beginning in childhood could affect the later risk of cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes.
Communities were selected as intervention and comparison areas for practical reasons and matched according to socioeconomic background. The six-year analysis included participants from whom fasting blood samples were collected both at the start of the study and six years later.
Health-supporting environment must be maintained for years
The studies highlight two complementary perspectives. A child's daily physical activity, sleep and screen time habits are associated with their well-being. In turn, a program involving families, schools and communities may affect health indicators associated with the risk of chronic diseases years later.
"Children develop their habits within environments created by adults. Safe opportunities for physical activity, daily routines, the way schools are organized, extracurricular activities and shared family habits largely determine how easy it is for a child to live a healthy lifestyle," Veidebaum said.
TAI's population health yearbook also emphasizes that risk factors for chronic diseases develop throughout a person's life and often begin in childhood. Early prevention means creating opportunities that support health at home, in preschool, at school and in the community.
Longitudinal studies help researchers understand how habits and health indicators established in childhood change over time and at what stage of life their development can be most effectively influenced.
The Population Health Yearbook 2026 provides an overview of the health of people in Estonia and the factors that affect it. This year's yearbook focuses on the development of risk factors for chronic diseases from the perspective of longitudinal studies. It includes data on life expectancy, healthy life years, leading causes of death, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, excess weight, mental health, health behavior and access to health care services, among other topics.

Drought causes Swiss water levels to fall to record lows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:58:19 UTC
17:58:19 KST

Drought causes Swiss water levels to fall to record lows
Rivers and streams in Switzerland have exceptionally low water levels due to the ongoing drought. In July, the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) even recorded historic lows at eleven monitoring stations.
Between April 1 and 31 July 31, around a fifth of the monitoring stations recorded record low levels for this time of year, as the FOEN told the Keystone-SDA news agency. This confirmed a report in the Swiss paper Tages-Anzeiger.
According to the FOEN, water levels in many watercourses north of the Alps are so low that this only occurs once every two to ten years, and in some cases only once every 30 to 100 years or even less frequently. South of the Alps, the situation is less dramatic, partly thanks to glacial melt.
+ Switzerland is water-rich. So why are 151 towns rationing it?
Thunderstorms offered little relief
The Swiss Plateau and the Jura are particularly affected. The drought is clearly evident on the Doubs near Ocourt in canton Jura and on the Rhine near Basel. In Basel, river flows have been below the long-term average since the start of the year – with the exception of February.
Even the thunderstorms in the first half of last week did little to improve discharge levels in the affected watercourses, as the FOEN notes. In Switzerland, the only streams and rivers less severely affected are those whose flow is significantly influenced by glacial melt.
Lakes are also affected
Water levels in numerous lakes are also exceptionally low, including Lake Constance, Lake Walen, Lake Zurich, Lake Zug and Lake Maggiore. Smaller lakes such as Lake Sempach and Lake Hallwil are also affected.
The FOEN emphasises that Switzerland still has “abundant water resources”. However, climate change will alter their availability: the water supply from snowmelt and glacial melt is decreasing. Dry spells are likely to become more frequent and longer, with more water in winter and less in summer. The total volume of water available over the course of the year, on the other hand, is expected to decline only slightly.

'I am just waiting to die' — Gaza cancer patients face rising mortality amid Israeli curbs: medics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:58:03 UTC
17:58:03 KST

Palestinian cancer patients are dying at two to three times the pace they did before the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, as Israel blocks many from travelling for treatment after destroying the only local specialised facility, Palestinian doctors said.
Israel destroyed Gaza's specialised cancer hospital last year, leaving an estimated 17,000 Palestinians with cancer without a local option for chemotherapy or other advanced treatment.
Few Palestinians can afford to travel for treatment, and those who can face Israeli restrictions. The military imposes strict caps on daily crossings to Egypt, despite a 2025 Israel-Hamas ceasefire deal that requires free movement in and out.
Asked for comment, COGAT, the Israeli military unit in charge of administering Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territories, said it coordinates medical evacuations with the World Health Organization. To depart, Palestinians must have a valid request from a receiving country and pass "required security screening," COGAT said.
The WHO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Race against time
For Khuloud Abu Sahmoud, a Palestinian mother-of-two with advanced ovarian cancer, the wait for treatment abroad has become a race against time as her cancer spreads.
"Every day my disease progresses, and my condition is tragic. My fingernails have all fallen out — I have none left. I am just waiting to die."
Abu Sahmoud, 33, said she has been waiting to exit Gaza for treatment in Egypt or further afield since the ceasefire was struck last October. In that time, the cancer has spread to her lungs and bones, she says.
Palestinian health officials said 11,000 people, including patients, had gone through Rafah since it reopened, fewer than half the number that had been expected under the ceasefire deal.
A further 20,000 patients, including 5,000 with cancer, are registered for treatment abroad but not yet permitted to leave, the officials said.
Toxic chemical exposure
Despite the ceasefire, Israeli forces continue to occupy more than half of Gaza, with Israel having since expanded its ground invasion to around two-thirds of the territory. Nearly all of Gaza’s more than 2 million people have been confined to a narrow strip along the coast, mostly in makeshift tents or shelters in damaged buildings.
Before the war, local health services had made advances thanks to investment from abroad and persistence from local doctors, a Reuters investigation found.
But most Gaza hospitals were destroyed or damaged by Israel during the war, and those that remain operational have been stripped of up to 70 percent of essential medical supplies, including those needed for cancer treatment and diagnostic services, doctors said.
Among those killed by Israel during the war were dozens of highly qualified specialists, including cancer experts operating in the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, demolished by Israel in March 2025.
"We have been recording a significant number of deaths, ranging from three to five daily, because patients are not receiving the chemotherapy needed to save their lives," said Mohamed Abu Selmia, head of Gaza's biggest hospital, Al Shifa.
Sobhi Skaik, a Palestinian surgeon who was head of the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, said the death rate before the war was about one to two per day. Some pre-war statistics put the figure at around 1.7 per day, he said.
He said the rising deaths were due mostly to an absence of local treatment and to border restrictions. But he also said that cancer itself may be spreading at a faster rate due to the presence of toxic materials from Israeli explosives dropped on Gaza.
There were some 11,000 registered cancer patients in Gaza before the war started, after which registrations largely stopped, Skaik said.
He estimated that another 6,000 Palestinians had likely developed cancer since.
"Some people can be treated if diagnosed in early stages, but they are wandering around the tents sick, unaware, and with no help," Skaik said.

That leaves the war in a standoff.

"We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," Trump told Axios Sunday.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, effectively blocked by Iran, has become a key issue in the conflict between Tehran and Washington. Iran says it wants to impose a transit fee in coordination with Oman, the strait's other coastal state. The United States has strongly rejected the idea.
Environmental groups have warned that the conflict has increased the risk of ships being damaged or hit. On Wednesday, it emerged that oil from a tanker that ran aground off Oman and is linked to Russia's so-called shadow fleet had reached the Omani mainland.
Greenpeace says the Strait of Hormuz and the surrounding waters contain sensitive ecosystems including coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass meadows. An oil spill could also threaten the water supply of millions of people, as many Gulf states rely heavily on desalination plants.

Total eclipse plunges Spain’s Segovia into darkness for 59 seconds of wonder (4/4)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:56:08 UTC
17:56:08 KST

Total eclipse plunges Spain’s Segovia into darkness for 59 seconds of wonder (4/4)
From our special correspondent in Segovia – A total solar eclipse on Wednesday plunged Spain’s Segovia into daytime darkness for 59 seconds. Perched high up on the city's iconic cathedral bell tower, locals and visitors from and wide watched, in awe, as the moon’s shadow blotted out the sun.
Issued on: Modified:
There are rare occasions in life when time is seemingly suspended by an extraordinary event, unleashing a whirlwind of emotions that, in the moment, transform us.
The total solar eclipse that covered swaths of Spain late on Wednesday offered one such moment – particularly for the lucky few gathered atop Segovia’s majestic Cathedral of the Assumption of the Virgin and San Frutos overlooking the Castile and Leon region's rugged landscape.
Only a handful of people had the privilege of climbing up the 16th-century bell tower, passing through gates and doors that are usually closed to the public at this time of day. And because a view like this must be earned, they climbed the 190 steps leading to the lofty summit on foot.
The 90-metre ascension was a mere formality for Minos, who travelled from Malmö in Sweden with his sister Michelle to witness “the eclipse of a lifetime”.
Read moreEclipse chasers: When chasing totality becomes a way of life (1/4)
As the moon began to hide the sun, the astronomy enthusiast eagerly counted down the minutes leading up to totality – the moment when the sun’s face is entirely hidden from view.
“Ten to go,” he announced, proudly pulling out a state-of-the-art camera fitted with a solar filter, a gift from their father for this very special occasion.
‘Dios mio!’
Like countless other eclipse chasers, the Swedish pair travelled from Madrid through the breathtaking Sierra de Guadarrama mountain range to reach Segovia, known for its iconic Roman aqueduct and majestic Alcazar castle, which is said to have inspired Snow White’s castle in the eponymous Disney movie.
As mainland Europe witnesses its first total solar eclipse since 1999, FRANCE 24 is dedicating a series of articles to this astronomical event – one of the continent’s most anticipated of the decade – with reports from the path of totality in Spain.
• Eclipse chasers: When chasing totality becomes a way of life (1/4)
• From Solar corona to human emotions: What can we learn from eclipses? (2/4)
• ‘First of our lives’: Thousands race for best spot in Spain to watch total solar eclipse (3/4)
Such architectural gems are part of everyday life for locals in the know, who made up the majority of the privileged few gathered at the top of the cathedral. They included Segovian couple Kelly and Yago, who watched the spectacle alongside relatives, strangers and a priest, their eclipse glasses firmly in place and their eyes fixed on the shrinking sun.
Read moreIn pictures: Partial to total eclipse sweeps across much of Europe
At 8:30pm, chiming bells heralded the moment when the moon would completely blot out the sun. “It’s Jesus ringing for us!” joked the priest, provoking a general burst of laughter.
“Dios mio… Dios mio!” (My God!) Kelly repeated as darkness and an eerie silence descended on this ancient city, soon giving way to applause from the crowd gathered at the foot of the tower.
Wonder and fear
As the fifty-nine seconds of total eclipse lapsed, it was hard to recall whether the moment had passed quickly or whether every second had been felt as a unique experience.
It was equally difficult to interpret the passing emotions on people’s faces as they gazed at the celestial alignment.
There was shock and awe as the solar corona appeared in all its glory, but also apprehension at the thought of damaging one’s eyesight, and the fear of missing even part of a fleeting moment that many will never experience again.
“I’ll remember this for the rest of my life,” said Yago as his awestruck partner wiped away the tears welling up in the corners of her eyes. “It’s something you can’t imagine until you’ve experienced it,” he added.
Read moreFrom Solar corona to human emotions: What can we learn from eclipses? (2/4)
Yago spoke of ancient people who would have viewed eclipses as a bad omen or a sign of the gods’ wrath, and for whom such experiences were often a source of both thrill and fright.
Science now offers a simple explanation for why the sun briefly disappears. But gazing at a total solar eclipse for 59 seconds, one can only understand the vertigo experienced by our ancestors who once looked up at the sky without knowing whether our star would return.

We need to think seriously about our agricultural industry so that we don’t pay money for every single little thing. This is a business,” Aleksandr Lukashenko emphasized.

At the same time, there is no question of completely abandoning subsidies. “In some areas, we must provide help, otherwise it will be like in Western Europe: they stopped providing support, and agriculture collapsed,” he added.
The field visited by the head of state belongs to the Zdanovichi agricultural enterprise in Minsk District. Aleksandr Lukashenko inquired in detail about the state of affairs with the enterprise’s head, Grigory Chuiko. According to him, while the farm has enough land, “the city is still encroaching.” In this regard, the president raised the issue of the impermissibility of residential development on agricultural land once again. “We need to densify and build in empty spaces, on small pockets of land. Inside Minsk – by all means, there are plenty of places where we are building,” he emphasized.

ARKHANGELSK, August 13. /TASS/. Under the pretext of "mythical threats from the East," NATO is militarizing the Arctic region and intensively strengthening its offensive capabilities along Russia’s northern borders, Russian Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Department Director Vladislav Maslennikov said.
According to the diplomat, Western countries' approaches toward the Arctic region have increasingly been dominated by a confrontational mindset and scenarios involving the use of force to secure their interests in recent years. "As a result, the high latitudes, which were characterized exclusively by peaceful and constructive cooperation for decades, are now witnessing a rise in military and political tensions and an increased risk of unintended escalation," he noted while speaking at the 4th Arctic Regions Forum.
"Under the pretext of countering mythical threats from the East, NATO is pursuing a course of active militarization of the Arctic Region and is intensively strengthening its offensive capabilities along our northern borders. Large-scale exercises aimed at rehearsing offensive scenarios are regularly held in the region, and non-Arctic member states of the alliance are actively involved in these activities," the diplomat emphasized.
Maslennikov stressed that reducing the overall potential for conflict in the region and committing to international cooperation and law are among Russia’s primary and unwavering priorities. "At the same time, Russia is taking the necessary measures to ensure its national security by developing an appropriate response to emerging challenges and threats, which are growing by the day," he added.
TASS is the forum’s general media partner.

====================================================================================================

Xi Story: The rain, the caves and the quest to preserve Mogao Grottoes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:52:05 CST
17:52:05 KST

LANZHOU, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- In Dunhuang, an ancient Silk Road city in northwest China, even rain has caught the attention of Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The city is home to the Mogao Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage site dating back to the 4th century. The region's arid climate has helped preserve the murals, sculptures and a vast trove of Buddhist art in hundreds of grottoes carved into cliffs on the edge of the Gobi Desert. But increased rainfall and rising humidity, particularly in summer, can accelerate the deterioration of the fragile heritage.
During a visit to the caves in August 2019, Xi asked experts whether Dunhuang had been seeing more rain in recent years. He then turned to another challenge: how to balance growing visitor numbers with the need to protect the grottoes.
"His questions addressed the most pressing challenges facing the heritage," Fan Jinshi, honorary president of Dunhuang Academy, recalled.
Since the Mogao Caves were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987, visitor numbers have risen steadily, increasing the strain on the environment inside the grottoes.
"For a World Heritage site, conservation comes first. Tourism comes second," Xi said, emphasizing that economic benefits should never take precedence over preservation.
The attention Xi has paid to Dunhuang is part of a broader commitment to protecting China's millennia-old cultural heritage. Over the years, he has repeatedly called for the protection of cultural relics, archaeological discoveries and traditional culture, while visiting heritage sites across the country to witness conservation efforts firsthand.
"Protecting and passing on our historical and cultural heritage is a responsibility to history and to the people," Xi has said.
To Xi, China's cultural legacy is not simply a glimpse into the past. It continues to shape the present and inspire the future.
For centuries, Dunhuang stood at the crossroads of the Silk Road, where merchants, monks, artists and travelers converged, bringing with them ideas, faiths and artistic traditions from across Asia.
Standing before a mural in Mogao Cave 323 depicting Zhang Qian's journey to the Western regions, Xi was drawn to a scene of openness and exchange dating back more than two millennia. The Tang Dynasty (618-907) artwork tells a story not only of diplomacy, but also of the encounters and exchanges along the Silk Road.
"Dunhuang culture reflects the cultural confidence of the Chinese nation. Only a civilization that is confident in itself can preserve its own identity while embracing, learning from and drawing on the best of other civilizations," Xi has said.
During his visit to Dunhuang, Xi called for Dunhuang Academy, which oversees the conservation and study of the Mogao Caves and other major grotto sites in the region, to become a model for World Heritage conservation.
Years later, that vision has been transformed into a comprehensive approach that combines craftsmanship, science and technology.
Inside Mogao Cave 454, conservator Yin Zhihong works with meticulous care to remove soot stains from a mural. The burning incense and candles have left the soot deeply embedded in the paint, so even the smallest mistake could cause damage.
Researchers are testing a flexible cleaning technique that uses a nanoscale sponge to lift the soot without harming the pigments. The technology is now moving from the laboratory into the caves, showing how scientific innovation is providing new tools for preserving cultural heritage.
But for Dunhuang, the focus is increasingly shifting from repairing damage to preventing it.
At the grottoes' monitoring center, a wall of screens offers a real-time picture of the caves and the environment around them. Temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels inside the grottoes are tracked alongside visitor numbers. Rainfall and blowing sand are monitored across hundreds of kilometers, helping conservation teams spot potential threats and act before damage occurs.
Smart cave doors turn that data into action. They automatically seal the grottoes when heavy rain approaches or sandstorms threaten, and open in fine weather to allow fresh air to circulate.
Digital technology is opening another path to protect and share the heritage. Dunhuang Academy is building high-resolution digital records that allow the murals, sculptures and manuscripts to be preserved and studied remotely, while online exhibitions allow more people to experience the heritage without adding to the pressure on the sites.
Dunhuang is part of a broader nationwide effort. Under Xi's leadership, China has increasingly prioritized the protection of cultural heritage, while promoting responsible use and minimal intervention. Years of investment, technological advances and painstaking conservation work have strengthened China's capacity to safeguard its cultural and historical legacy.
That expertise is also being introduced beyond China's borders.
In Uzbekistan's ancient city of Khiva, a major Silk Road hub, Chinese heritage experts worked with local counterparts to restore historical sites, helping bring the once-weathered city back to life. ■

17:51:23 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Public Security (MPS) said on Thursday that Chinese and Thai police recently worked together to bust a major cross-border credit card fraud ring targeting Chinese citizens, arresting nine suspects.
The operation, jointly carried out by the MPS and Thailand's Royal Thai Police headquarters, resulted in the arrest of four Chinese nationals and five Thai nationals, the ministry noted in a statement.
The two sides coordinated the timing of the crackdown and dismantled several criminal sites, arresting the suspects, the ministry said.
According to the statement, Chinese police uncovered the transnational criminal ring in 2025 and promptly shared information about the case with their Thai counterparts and sought their assistance.
Investigations found that two of the suspects had conspired, with one allegedly operating a shop in Thailand as a front for illegally obtaining victims' credit card information, while the other allegedly used the stolen data to make counterfeit cards and recruited people to use the cards for fraudulent transactions and launder the illicit proceeds for profit. Authorities have so far identified more than 5 million yuan (about 736,500 U.S. dollars) in financial losses linked to this case.
The operation marked the first coordinated joint law enforcement action by police from the two countries in recent years targeting economic crime, the ministry said.
It added that the two sides will explore establishing a regular cooperation mechanism to combat cross-border economic crimes, with plans to deepen collaboration in areas including information sharing, exchange of expertise, joint analysis, the pursuit of suspects, and the recovery of illicit proceeds. ■

British firm Inzpire to train Ukrainian pilots in air tactics
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:49:43 BST
17:49:43 KST

The Ministry of Defence is to award Inzpire a contract worth £502k to deliver air warfare education and training to the Ukrainian Air Force, covering roughly 20 weeks of instruction a year, the department stated in a contract award notice.
The contract runs for a year from 26 August 2026, with a single 12-month option period available, and the earliest date for signature is 26 August.
According to the notice, the work covers an air tactics and planning course, including the setting of training objectives, course development and delivery. The contract was placed directly rather than through competition, and is classified under the common procurement vocabulary code for technical training services.
The supplier is Inzpire Limited, a company based at Alpha Court in Lincoln and recorded as a small or medium-sized enterprise.
Inzpire was founded in 2006 by former RAF aircrew and has built its business around mission planning software and the provision of experienced military personnel as instructors and advisers. Its GECO mission system is used on British and export aircraft, and the company has held training and evaluation contracts across the RAF and Royal Navy, including work supporting fast jet and rotary wing crews.
Britain has trained Ukrainian personnel continuously since 2022, most visibly through Operation Interflex, the infantry training programme run in the UK with contributions from more than a dozen partner nations, which has put tens of thousands of recruits through basic soldiering courses. Air training has been a smaller and less publicised strand.
Ukrainian pilots began elementary flying training in the UK in 2023 as part of the international effort to prepare crews for the F-16, with the aircraft themselves supplied by Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Belgium since Britain does not operate the type. Language training and ground school ran alongside, with conversion to type handled elsewhere.
Tactics and planning instruction of the kind covered by this contract addresses a different problem from flying the aircraft. Soviet-derived air forces were built around close ground control, with controllers directing aircraft onto targets, while NATO practice places far more responsibility on the aircrew to plan missions, interpret the air picture and make decisions in flight.

Complaint filed in German court over Meta AI glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:48:44 UTC
17:48:44 KST

Berlin-based nonprofit HateAid has filed a criminal complaint against Meta’s AI-powered smart glasses, saying the device violates Germany’s strict privacy laws and should be banned, Politico reports.
In recent months, the Meta glasses have been the subject of a flood of complaints, with reports of people being filmed without consent or having intimate footage captured without the knowledge that Meta’s contractors could be reviewing them.
HateAid has argued that selling Meta’s smart glasses in Germany is a criminal offense because the device allows people to secretly film others. The lawsuit claims that selling the glasses in Germany violates the Telecommunications, Digital Services and Data Protection Act. HateAid’s complaint is against Meta, Ray-Ban, and Oakley, as well as several retailers.
Meta spokesman Matthew Pollard said the smart glasses were approved by German watchdog BNetzA in 2022 and
are designed to be more secure than any smartphone.
Security measures include an LED light that turns on when the glasses are recording video, and technology that prevents the light from being changed.
Meanwhile, HateAid said the glasses should only be marketed if they are clearly identifiable and there should be clear restrictions on where they can’t be used.
European privacy watchdogs have commissioned a report on smart glasses, which is expected to be ready by the end of the summer.

Outside, relatives keep vigil. “My heart is about to burst out of my chest,” said his niece, 16-year-old Sara Loaiza.
Rescue workers in Cali and Pereira are digging through unstable rubble with cranes and hand tools, frequently ordering silence to listen for voices.
President Abelardo de la Espriella has declared an “economic emergency” and three days of national mourning, as thousands of people sleep outdoors in makeshift shelters and volunteers organise food, water and blood donations for the worst-hit communities.

Sweden's right-wing government lags in poll, but gap narrows
STOCKHOLM, Aug 13 - Sweden's ruling right-wing coalition government is lagging centre-left opposition parties ahead of an election for parliament next month, but the gap between the two sides has narrowed since June, a new opinion poll showed.
The July 29 to August 10 survey, published by the daily Svenska Dagbladet, showed Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson may again become prime minister after four years in opposition, replacing Ulf Kristersson of the right-wing Moderates.
Swedes go to the polls on September 13 and the election campaign focuses on cost of living, security, immigration, crime and energy supply.
Support for the four opposition parties, of which Andersson's Social Democrats is the biggest by far, stood at 50.6%, up from the 48.9% they won in the 2022 election, according to the survey of 2,016 voters by pollster Demoskop.
The backing for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's governing bloc, including the closely aligned far-right Sweden Democrats, stood at 46.9%, down from the 49.6% they won in the last election four years ago.
In a blow to the government's chances of staying in power, junior coalition member the Liberals polled just 2.4%, well below the 4% threshold to win Riksdag seats.
Andersson's Social Democrats, Sweden's largest party, was set to win 30.2%, the poll showed, against 30.3% four years ago, while the Moderate Party could see a decline to 16.8% from 19.1% over the same period.
It remains unclear with which opposition parties Andersson would form a government, but a shift in power is likely to entail more welfare spending with no big changes on immigration, defence or support for Ukraine.
The Sweden Democrats, who plan to join the cabinet for the first time if the right-wing bloc wins, had 20.2% support, down from 20.5%. Its leader, Jimmie Akesson, has said his party aims to hold several major ministerial posts. REUTERS

Your takeaway habit is feeding Dutch inflation, says DNB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:45:25 UTC
17:45:25 KST

Your takeaway habit is feeding Dutch inflation, says DNB
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch households are spending so much on takeaway meals that it is impacting national inflation, the Dutch central bank DNB has reported.
Delivery meals have nearly doubled as a share of the average shopping basket, from around 1.6% in 2015 to just over 3% today, DNB said on Thursday.
Prices have climbed fast. With more people spending, delivery firms have also passed on higher wage, energy and ingredient costs, and between 2020 and 2023 the category went from adding less than 0.1 percentage point to inflation to a full 0.35 point.
It has since eased back to 0.13 point – but only because prices stopped rising so fast, not because anyone is ordering less, DNB said.
The bank traces consumer habits back to the Covid pandemic, when locked-down households began using ordering apps much more, especially while working from home.
Dutch inflation has sat above the European Central Bank’s 2% target for years, driven mainly by rents and food prices. The pizza and sushi deliveries are now also hitting the figures.

Drought amid the heat may damage crops and the sowing of winter crops - Ukrhydrometeorological Center
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:44:12 EEST
17:44:12 KST

Drought amid the heat may damage crops and the sowing of winter crops - Ukrhydrometeorological Center
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported that the heat at the beginning of August was caused by African air and broke records in the west. The drought may damage late-season crops and soil preparation for winter crops.
The heat at the beginning of August in Ukraine was caused by African air masses and reached record levels in the western regions, while the intensification of drought against this backdrop could threaten the sunflower, corn, and buckwheat harvests, as well as create unfavorable conditions for preparing the soil for sowing winter crops for the 2027 harvest, the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported, according to UNN.
Details
"The first ten days of August in Ukraine, compared with the climatic norm, proved to be among the warmest in the western regions in terms of the average ten-day and maximum air temperatures for the entire observation period," the report said.
Average daily air temperatures on the hottest days, as noted, "exceeded the climatic norm by 4-9 ℃".
"This temperature pattern was caused by the arrival in Ukraine of hot air masses of African origin. In the second half of the ten-day period, the movement of an active cold front through the western and northern regions caused a brief cooling in this area, uneven rainfall, and locally heavy showers accompanied by hail and squalls," the report said.
During the first ten days of August, as a result of hot weather on most days and predominantly dry conditions, atmospheric and soil drought spread and intensified, creating unfavorable agrometeorological conditions for the completion of the growing season of late agricultural crops throughout the country. In areas where reserves of available moisture had already been depleted, the growing season of late agricultural crops ended prematurely. This was also facilitated by dry winds observed across most of the country
"Such a high-temperature regime may have a particularly negative impact on the yield of sunflowers, which are in the mass flowering phase; on the formation of corn ears and grain filling; and on the amount of grain in buckwheat, which is undergoing grain formation," the report emphasizes.
In the southern regions, as noted, "premature ripening of corn grain and sunflower seeds was observed, resulting in a reduction in the weight of the grain and seeds (a decrease in productivity)".
"As a result of the adverse effect of the heat on late agricultural crops, loss of turgor (wilting of plants) during the daytime and drying of plants were observed; leaves and ovaries fell off, while sunscald appeared on the leaves and fruit," the report states.
In most regions, the prolonged precipitation deficit throughout the summer created unfavorable conditions for preparing the soil for sowing winter crops for the 2027 harvest. First and foremost, winter rapeseed, whose optimal sowing period falls between August 10 and 25
Heat in Ukraine broke records in 13 regions, with a maximum of +39°07.08.26, 13:20 • 21146 views

Six Arab national football associations back FIFA's Infantino
Six heads of Arab national football associations, including Qatar and 2030 World Cup co-hosts Morocco, backed FIFA President Gianni Infantino on Thursday, with football's world governing body in crisis following a failed private investment plan.
Infantino, who is seeking reelection next year, has faced open revolt after three confederations—UEFA, AFC and CONCACAF—called for him to quit over his aborted bid to bring private investment into FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.
The Swiss administrator had proposed carving off the commercial rights to the World Cup and selling 20% to private investors to raise about $4.2 billion.
"Recognising the important role of Arab football in bringing people together and strengthening cooperation among football associations across the Arab world, we ... express our full support for Mr Gianni Infantino, president of FIFA, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide," the heads of the six federations said in a joint statement.
The statement was signed by the heads of the national federations of Qatar, Lebanon, Morocco, Sudan, Egypt and Mauritania. Four of the six signatories are also FIFA Council members.
"We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together," they said.
"We look forward to continuing our close cooperation with him towards a stronger and more prosperous future for world football, expanding opportunities and further enhancing Arab football’s contribution to the global game."
Infantino’s withdrawn proposal came with a $20 million grant for member associations for the next funding cycle, an amount that could have been doubled if they signed the deal.
Despite the opposition of the three confederations, which represent 136 of the 211 member associations who will vote in the FIFA presidential election in March, Infantino still has plenty of allies in the game.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius on Thursday called for cooperation from the Catholic Church and answers on whether it took sufficient steps to detect and prevent child sexual abuse after two priests were charged with sexual offenses involving children.
“I expect open and constructive cooperation between the Church and law enforcement, transparency and a readiness to answer not only who may have committed the crimes, but also the vital question of whether sufficient measures were taken in all cases to ensure that potential abuse was detected early, prevented and reported to the responsible authorities,” Sinkevičius said in a Facebook post.

The cases involving the two priests have been referred to court.

The second priest is charged with possession of child pornography. Authorities say there are no victims in that case, which has been transferred to the Vilnius City District Court. According to Lithuanian news outlets Delfi and Liteko, the accused are Tadas Svedavičius and Ryšardas Peciunas.
The Archdiocese of Vilnius said it learned of the allegations from prosecutors after the pretrial investigations began. The priests have been suspended, and canonical investigations have been opened, the archdiocese said.

Lockheed calls its GRIZZLY containerized launcher production-ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:39:45 UTC
17:39:45 KST

- Lockheed Martin posted video Tuesday describing its GRIZZLY containerized missile launcher as production-ready and reloadable.
- GRIZZLY completed its first Hellfire missile live-fire test in March 2026 and intercepted a Group 3 drone using a JAGM missile in June 2026.
Lockheed Martin posted a new video of live-fire testing for GRIZZLY, its containerized missile launcher, describing the system as production-ready and built to add mobility to distributed weapons.
“Built fast. Built flexible. Built for the mission. GRIZZLY is an affordable, reloadable and production-ready containerized launcher designed to bring mobility and adaptability to the fight. The future of defense is here, and it’s containerized,” Lockheed Martin said in the post.
GRIZZLY packages a missile launcher inside a standard 10-foot Tricon shipping container, a size small enough to move by truck, rail or ship without specialized transport equipment. Lockheed Martin built the system using existing weapon and launcher architecture, including the fielded M299 launcher, completing development in about six months through internal company investment rather than a government contract.
The company completed its first integrated live-fire test of GRIZZLY in March 2026, firing a Hellfire missile from the container in both vertical and angled launch configurations. That test validated the launcher’s ability to load and fire a missile directly from the containerized format, according to Lockheed Martin. The system uses commercial off-the-shelf materials, which the company says lowers logistics costs and shortens acquisition timelines compared with custom-built launcher hardware.
Lockheed Martin expanded GRIZZLY’s role in June 2026, when it used the launcher to intercept a Group 3 one-way attack drone with a Joint Air-to-Ground Missile, or JAGM, for the first time. JAGM is a Lockheed Martin-built precision missile designed to replace both the Hellfire and the TOW anti-tank missile, combining a dual-mode seeker that can lock onto a target using laser guidance, radar, or infrared imaging depending on conditions like weather, smoke, or enemy jamming.
The missile was originally developed for use on helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft to strike armored vehicles, but its guidance flexibility has made it increasingly attractive for counter-drone missions, where a target’s small size and fast, erratic movement make a single-mode seeker less reliable. That June test paired GRIZZLY with the company’s Sanctum counter-unmanned aircraft system, showing the launcher can function for defensive point-defense missions as well as offensive strikes. Group 3 drones generally weigh between 55 and 1,320 pounds (25 to 600 kilograms), covering midsize unmanned aircraft that fall between small commercial drones and larger military systems.
The choice of Hellfire as GRIZZLY’s original interceptor has drawn some skepticism online, where critics have questioned whether a missile originally built as an anti-armor weapon, and one that costs roughly $150,000 per unit, makes sense as a counter-drone tool against targets that can cost a few thousand dollars to build. That criticism echoes a broader debate in air defense circles over cost-per-kill economics, the same imbalance that has driven interest in cheaper interceptor drones and directed-energy weapons. But the case for using an already fielded, thoroughly proven missile family is straightforward from a logistics standpoint. Both Hellfire and JAGM have extensive combat reliability behind them, and pairing either with GRIZZLY means a unit defending a rear base or an expeditionary staging area does not need to stock a separate munition, train a new crew, or add personnel to operate a dedicated interceptor system. That modularity also positions GRIZZLY against one of the cheaper interceptor options on the market today, Russia’s Pantsir-based systems, whose interceptor missiles are estimated to start around $200,000 per unit, putting Lockheed Martin’s missile costs in a comparable range rather than a clear disadvantage.
Lockheed Martin has said GRIZZLY is designed to work with different command, control and sensor systems rather than a single dedicated network, allowing it to integrate into a range of operational setups. The company has also developed a related containerized launcher called Kodiak, which completed its first live-fire test earlier this month using a Reduced-Range Practice Rocket to demonstrate offensive fires with GMLRS-family munitions.
The M299 launcher architecture GRIZZLY draws on is already fielded on Apache helicopters and other aircraft, giving Lockheed Martin an established design base rather than a clean-sheet launcher build. Tricon containers, the standard shipping format GRIZZLY uses, are a military logistics standard already used to transport ammunition, vehicles and equipment worldwide, which is part of why a container-based launcher can blend into existing supply chains without drawing attention as a distinct military system.
U.S. and allied interest in similar containerized systems has grown alongside concerns that fixed launch sites are increasingly vulnerable to satellite tracking and long-range precision strikes, a lesson reinforced repeatedly during the war in Ukraine.

"I really doubt I'll carry on": Messi's stark words in farewell to his father
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:38:23 UTC
17:38:23 KST

The Argentinian footballer has published an open letter bidding farewell to his father and agent Jorge Messi, who died on 8 August in Rosario after a long illness. In it, the Argentina captain admits he is unsure whether he will carry on playing.
Lionel Messi rarely shares details of his private life. Over two decades of his career, the Argentine striker has kept the media at long arm's length and reserved his emotions for his closest circle. That is why it is striking that, after his father's death, he's chosen to publish an open letter on social media in which his grief is all too apparent.
In the message, addressed directly to Jorge, Messi writes that he does not know how to continue without him. "I don't know what I'm going to do without you, I don't know how to carry on. I just played football and nowI have serious doubts that I'll keep doing it for much longer," the letter reads. Coming from someone who has always avoided talking about his retirement, the words carry particular weight.
The Albiceleste captain also laments, through his sadness, that his father was unable to hold on a little longer. "You were by my side from the very start, there was so little left to go. Why didn't you hang on that bit longer so we could finish together?" the statement reads.
Jorge Horacio Messi was not only Lionel's father. He was also his agent from the earliest years and the person who, as the footballer himself has acknowledged on several occasions, shouldered much of the weight of his career off the pitch.
In the letter, Messi recalls that constant closeness and regrets that his father's health, already fragile during the last World Cup, prevented him from accompanying him through to the end of the tournament.
"Dad, I still can't believe you're gone. We still had so much left to enjoy together. You kept insisting that I should play the last World Cup, and just days before it began was when you got worse," he writes. Messi says his mother assured him his father would improve enough to travel and watch him play the final, and that he himself clung to that hope. "I told you we were going to reach the final so you could travel. We made it to the final and you couldn't be there," he adds, referring to the match Argentina played and lost against Spain on 19 July in New Jersey.
"I wanted to win it to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn't; my legs just weren't there any more. This time I tried to push my body beyond its limits, but I couldn't. I never managed to feel right," he concludes in that part of the message, in which he acknowledges the physical wear and tear with which he arrived at the World Cup.
Contract in place and no decision yet announced
For now, Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami and has made no formal announcement about his future, either with the US club or with the Argentine national team.
The letter, however, suggests thathis father's death has triggered a bout of soul-searching he had not previously made public. The player himself admits that his relationship with football was always bound up with his father's figure, which helps explain why uncertainty over his future has emerged precisely at this moment.
Jorge Messi's funeral was held in private at the El Prado cemetery in Rosario, the hometown of both father and son, and was attended by Antonela Roccuzzo and the footballer's children. Clubs and bodies in Argentine football, among them Newell's Old Boys, the team Jorge openly supported, sent messages of farewell in the days that followed.
Six of the best - the most important moments in Messi's career
1. Barcelona first-team debut (2004). Aged just 17, Messi made his league debut for Barcelona's first team, the first step in a spell at the club that would last for more than two decades.
2. First Champions League as a leading star (Rome, 2009). Messi scored the second goal, a header, in the final against Manchester United, in a season in which Barcelona won all six trophies on offer. He has described that goal as the most important of his career.
3. Qatar 2022 World Cup. The one title he was missing. Messi lifted the trophy with Argentina after beating France in a penalty shoot-out, finally becoming world champion after previously losing four finals with the senior national team.
4. Leaving Barcelona (2021). After more than two decades at the club and 35 trophies, Messi tearfully announced his departure, forced by the club's financial and institutional crisis, before signing for Paris Saint-Germain.
5. Latest Ballon d'Or (2023). The year 2023 brought his latest Ballon d'Or, the ninth of his career. The award recognises him as the best player of the year and saw him share the stage with Spain's Aitana Bonmatí, who received the prize on the women's side of the game.
5. All-time World Cup top scorer (2026). During the World Cup staged in the United States, Canada and Mexico, Messi broke Miroslav Klose's record to become the top scorer in the tournament's history, at the same World Cup in which Argentina reached the final and lost to Spain.

The Times of Israel reported that Israeli forces and police attempted to “evacuate the settlers” early on Thursday after a previous failed effort the day before. “He [Qusai Abu Rida] does not want to leave the home. Because if he leaves the home, the settlers will take over immediately,” Ridi said.

Qusra sits in Area B of the occupied West Bank, nominally under Palestinian civil administration. The village has faced a string of recent attacks, including the burning of a newly built mosque last month.
In the neighbouring village of Jalud, a similar two-week siege in July forced two Palestinian families off their land before settlers took over the property.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in the occupied West Bank in settlements that are considered illegal under international law, alongside roughly three million Palestinians. Israel has occupied the territory since 1967.

Solar eclipse 2026 in pictures: The best shots from around Europe
Millions witnessed the most significant eclipse in Europe for decades yesterday evening as the Sun disappeared behind the Moon. Here are some of the best shots taken from the celestial event.
Parts of mainland Europe experienced its full solar eclipse in two decades yesterday evening, with the moon passing directly between the Earth and the Sun.
Considering the next total solar eclipse is not due to occur until 2081 for France, 2090 for the UK and not until the next century for Germany (Spain, on the other hand, get to see one next year), it was an event not worth missing.
