Romania once again scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after a group of drones was detected during russia's attack on Ukraine near the border; an aerial target was detected entering Romanian airspace for approximately 10 minutes, the country's Defense Ministry reported on Wednesday, according to UNN.
Details
As stated, the Romanian Ministry of National Defence's radar surveillance system, at 01:27 local time on the night of August 12–13, "detected a group of five aerial targets in the area of Izmail, over Ukrainian territory, near the river border with Romania."
Measures were taken to alert the population in the northern part of Tulcea County, and an RO-Alert message was sent at 01:30.
"Two F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force from the 86th Air Base in Borcea were scrambled to monitor the situation. Ground-based radars detected an aerial target entering national airspace approximately 2 km south of the town of Pardina. The target remained in national airspace for approximately 10 minutes along the Chilia branch, after which it left Romanian territory in the direction of Ukraine approximately 13 km southwest of the settlement of Chilia Veche," the Romanian Defense Ministry stated.
"Shortly after leaving Romanian airspace, reports of explosions were received on Ukrainian territory," the statement said.
The air raid alert issued for the north of Tulcea County ended at 02:42.
"The Ministry of National Defence is continuously monitoring the situation and informing allied structures in real time about such events," the statement said.
Later, Romania's Defense Ministry issued a new statement: "On Thursday morning, August 13, at 09:02, the radar surveillance system of the Ministry of National Defence detected an aerial target near the river border with Ukraine. Two F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force from the 86th Air Base in Borcea were scrambled at 09:20 to monitor the situation."
The population in Tulcea County was alerted again, with an RO-Alert message issued starting at 09:13.

Taboos to avoid during Taiwan's Ghost Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:40:33 UTC
16:40:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Ghost Month officially began Thursday with the start of the seventh lunar month, when Taiwanese folklore holds that the gates of the underworld open and spirits enter the mortal realm.
During the month, many people observe traditional taboos intended to avoid attracting ghosts, often referred to respectfully as "good brothers" (好兄弟). Numerology expert Tang Chen-wei (湯鎮瑋) and folk custom expert Yang Teng-kei (楊登嵙) shared several customs they said could help people avoid negative energy, per UDN.
1. Avoid extreme sadness or anger
Tang said strong emotions such as grief and anger are believed to increase yin energy. Because Ghost Month marks a seasonal shift from yang to yin, people are thought to be more vulnerable to negative influences if they cannot regulate their emotions.
Maintaining emotional balance, Tang said, is believed to promote steadier fortune throughout the month.
2. Avoid nighttime adventures
Tang advised staying away from isolated or sparsely populated places after dark, particularly locations considered to have heavy yin energy. Exploring abandoned buildings or other eerie sites at night is traditionally believed to disturb spirits and attract unwanted supernatural attention.
3. Avoid moving or renovating at night
Moving house or beginning construction is not strictly prohibited during Ghost Month, Tang said, but such activities should be scheduled during daylight hours and on an auspicious date selected from the traditional farmer's almanac. He recommended completing renovations before 5 p.m. and avoiding last-minute nighttime moves.
Yang offered additional advice on clothing during Ghost Month. He said people born in the Year of the Rat, Ox, Rabbit, and Horse should be particularly cautious this year, per UDN.
4. Do not wear solid black, white, or red
According to Yang, all-black clothing is believed to attract spirits, while all-white attire may signal mourning and draw wandering ghosts. Solid red clothing is said to remind spirits of bloodshed and provoke unrest.
He suggested adding colorful accessories or choosing natural colors instead.
5. Avoid revealing your shoulders
Traditional belief holds that people possess three protective spiritual flames: one on the head and one on each shoulder. Yang said revealing the shoulders, particularly in places associated with yin energy such as cemeteries, hospitals, columbariums, slaughterhouses, and abandoned buildings, is thought to weaken this protection.
6. Avoid ghost-like clothing
Distressed or ripped clothing, wedding dresses, messy hair, and ghost costumes are also discouraged during Ghost Month, Yang said. Ripped clothing may cause spirits to mistake someone for a wandering ghost, while bridal attire and ghost-themed costumes are believed to attract unwanted supernatural attention.
UDN noted that the advice reflects folk belief and cautioned readers against excessive superstition. For many families, Ghost Month remains a time to show respect for ancestors and wandering spirits through offerings, temple ceremonies, and everyday acts of caution.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Bureau of Standards, Metrology and Inspection and Taiwan Intellectual Property Office held a joint press conference Wednesday warning that uninspected or pirated toys can pose safety and intellectual property risks, according to a Standards Bureau press release.
The agencies said toys are products designed for children under 14, with 31 categories subject to mandatory inspection before import or release from factories. Products must bear the Commodity Inspection Mark before they can be sold domestically.
Tests cover chemicals such as plasticizers and heavy metals, mechanical hazards such as small parts and sharp edges, electrical faults, microbial counts, and warning labels.
The bureau said it conducts annual market inspections and sampling tests, focusing in particular on new and trending toys. Vendors selling products that have not completed required inspections can be fined NT$200,000 to NT$2 million (US$6,200 to US$62,000).
If the total value of non-compliant goods is under NT$100,000, fines range from NT$10,000 to NT$100,000. Businesses must also recall or correct the products within a specified period, with failure to comply carrying an additional fine of NT$100,000 to NT$1 million.
The bureau said it posts overseas toy safety alerts, including notices from the US Consumer Product Safety Commission and the EU’s Safety Gate, on its Product Safety Information Network. It also notifies the Ministry of Health and Welfare, warns the public and childcare facilities to stop using affected products, and asks domestic e-commerce platforms to remove them as a precaution.
The Taiwan Intellectual Property Office warned that toys or packaging printed with unauthorized artwork may violate copyright law, while use of identical or similar registered trademarks without permission may infringe trademark rights. The office added that pirated toys may also be of questionable quality.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs urged consumers to buy licensed, age-appropriate toys bearing the inspection mark and complete Chinese labels. It also advised adults not to let children chew toys, to watch for small parts that could be swallowed, and to have children wash their hands after playing.
The bureau said it will continue monitoring emerging toy risks and changes to international standards to update inspection rules as needed. The office added that suspected infringements can be reported with evidence to the Criminal Investigation Bureau’s Intellectual Property Rights Investigation Corps or local police.

Russian Ships Use First and Second World War Camo and Cages Against Ukrainian Drones
Russian commercial vessels navigating the Black Sea during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine have begun adopting physical and optical protective measures to guard against Ukrainian aerial and naval uncrewed systems.
Shipping monitors and maritime observers recently identified several vessels carrying crude oil and general cargo, including a 28-year-old Suezmax tanker laden with approximately 1 million barrels of crude, as reported by The Insider on August 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among these ships is a 119-meter cargo vessel built in 1987, which was spotted outfitted with protective netting, metal cage structures, and geometric camouflage patterns similar to dazzle designs utilized during the First and Second World Wars.
Shipping monitors and maritime observers recently identified several vessels, including a 28-year-old Suezmax tanker carrying approximately 1 million barrels of crude oil and a 119-meter general cargo ship built in 1987, outfitted with protective netting, metal cage structures, and geometric camouflage patterns similar to dazzle designs utilized during the First and Second World Wars.
Monitoring service TankerTrackers.com spotted the Sierra Leone-flagged Suezmax crude oil tanker CARUZO passing through Istanbul with around 1 million barrels of Russian crude oil.
The 28-year-old vessel is subject to sanctions imposed by the United Kingdom, the European Union, New Zealand, Canada, Switzerland, and Australia, though it is not listed on US sanction registers.
Environmental group Greenpeace identifies the vessel as part of the Russian shadow fleet, while Ukrainian military intelligence states that CARUZO has been involved in exporting Russian oil products outside G7 embargo guidelines and price caps since at least October 2023, including ship-to-ship transfers near the Kerch Strait in January 2024.
Crew members on board CARUZO completely enclosed the vessel's superstructure with protective netting, essentially enclosing the crew spaces.
The ship also features metal frame structures hanging from both sides of the stern section, which analysts indicate are designed to protect the engine room from attacks by explosive sea drones.
According to tracking data from Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the ship has regularly turned off its Automatic Identification System upon entering the Black Sea since July 2025 while recording static positions in the Bosphorus for months. Beyond the Black Sea, records list CARUZO visiting ports and terminals across Turkey, China, India, Malaysia, Morocco, Egypt, and Vietnam.
In a separate observation, Turkish merchant captain Murat Fırtına documented a distinct defensive modification on the Russian-flagged cargo ship MECHTA S in the port of Haydarpaşa on August 10.
The 119-meter vessel, built in 1987 as Sormovskiy-3059 and designed for Black Sea and river-sea transport, was photographed displaying bold geometric shapes in shades of blue, dark blue, white, and gray across its hull, bow, stern, and superstructure.
The design mirrors the dazzle camouflage historically used during World War I and World War II to visually disrupt a ship's outline, obscuring its size, orientation, speed, and vulnerable impact points from optical targeting systems. Commenting on the vessel's appearance, Fırtına noted that older photographs of MECHTA S showed standard painting without geometric shapes.
"If considering that today even merchant ships in the Black Sea face threats from unmanned aerial vehicles and naval drones, it cannot be ruled out that such painting has not only an aesthetic purpose, but also represents military camouflage designed to complicate optical detection of the vessel and targeting," he stated, adding, "But it must be admitted: seeing a merchant ship in 2026 in the middle of Istanbul, in Haydarpaşa, looking as if it came off the pages of wartime history, is quite unusual."
The vessel MECHTA S is not currently included in official sanction lists or shadow fleet registries. Tracking records from Starboard Maritime Intelligence spanning 3,294 days—roughly nine years—indicate that Novorossiysk is the ship's most frequently visited port, with 83 recorded port calls totaling over 72 days.
The vessel recently underwent a 26-day maintenance period from July 15 to August 10 in Yalova, Turkey, before appearing in Istanbul.
Starboard data shows that the ship lacked active AIS tracking for approximately 930 days and 6 hours, representing about 28% of the monitored timeframe, while also lacking verifiable insurance coverage through recognized P&I clubs.
Earlier, Russia was seen fitting anti-drone netting to an FSB Coast Guard Project 22460 Okhotnik-class patrol ship based in temporarily occupied Crimea. The improvised protection reflected a broader trend of adding physical drone defenses to Russian naval vessels as Ukraine expanded its use of aerial and maritime drones.

Gaza cancer patients face rising death rate amid Israeli curbs, doctors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:35:16 UTC
16:35:16 KST

Gaza cancer patients face rising death rate amid Israeli curbs, doctors say
CAIRO/GAZA – Gaza cancer patients are dying at two to three times the pace they did before the start of the war in the territory, as Israel blocks many from travelling for treatment after destroying the only local specialised facility, Gaza doctors said.
Israel blew up Gaza’s specialised cancer hospital in 2025 after saying troops found a tunnel used by Hamas militants running beneath it. That means that an estimated 17,000 Gazans with cancer have no local option for chemotherapy or other advanced therapy.
Few Palestinians can afford to travel for treatment, and those who can face Israeli restrictions. The military imposes strict caps on daily crossings to Egypt, despite a 2025 Israel-Hamas ceasefire deal that requires free movement in and out.
Asked for comment, COGAT, the Israeli military agency that controls access to Gaza, said it coordinates medical evacuations with the World Health Organization (WHO). To depart, Gazans must have a valid request from a receiving country and pass “required security screening”, COGAT said.
The WHO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Race against time
For Khuloud Abu Sahmoud, a Palestinian mother of two with advanced ovarian cancer, the wait for treatment abroad has become a race against time as her cancer spreads.
“Every day my disease progresses, and my condition is tragic. My fingernails have all fallen out – I have none left. I am just waiting to die.”
Abu Sahmoud, 33, said she has been waiting to exit Gaza for treatment in Egypt or further afield since the ceasefire was struck in October. In that time, the cancer has spread to her lungs and bones, she says.
COGAT said around 5,800 Gazans needing medical treatment have exited to Egypt since Israel agreed in February to a limited reopening of the Rafah border crossing, largely shut during the war, which began in 2023.
“Medical evacuations are in no sense restricted by the State of Israel but are wholly dependent on the receiving country’s request; without the official request, COGAT cannot coordinate a patient’s leave,” COGAT said.
Palestinian health officials said 11,000 people, including patients, had gone through Rafah since it reopened, fewer than half the number that had been expected under the ceasefire deal.
A further 20,000 patients, including 5,000 with cancer, are registered for treatment abroad but not yet permitted to leave, the officials said.
Toxic chemical exposure
The ceasefire ended major fighting but left Israeli forces in control of more than half of Gaza, since expanded to around two-thirds. Nearly all of Gaza’s more than two million people live in a Hamas-controlled strip along the coast, mostly in makeshift tents or shelters in damaged buildings.
Before the war, local health services had made advances thanks to investment from abroad and persistence from local doctors, a Reuters investigation found.
But most Gaza hospitals were destroyed or damaged in the war, and those that remain operational have been stripped of up to 70 per cent of essential medical supplies, including those needed for cancer treatment and diagnostic services, doctors said.
Among those killed by Israel during the war were dozens of highly qualified specialists, including cancer experts operating in the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, demolished in an Israeli controlled demolition in March 2025.
“We have been recording a significant number of deaths, ranging from three to five daily, because patients are not receiving the chemotherapy needed to save their lives,” said Mohamed Abu Selmia, head of Gaza’s biggest hospital, Al Shifa.
Sobhi Skaik, a Palestinian surgeon who was head of the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, said the death rate before the war was about one or two a day. Some pre-war statistics put the figure at around 1.7 a day, he said.
He said the rising deaths were due mostly to an absence of local treatment and to border restrictions. But he also said that cancer itself may be spreading at a faster rate due to the presence of toxic materials from Israeli explosives dropped on Gaza.
There were some 11,000 registered cancer patients in Gaza before the war started following the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on southern Israel, after which registrations largely stopped, Skaik said.
He estimated that another 6,000 Gazans had likely developed cancer since.
“Some people can be treated if diagnosed in early stages, but they are wandering around the tents sick, unaware, and with no help,” Skaik said. REUTERS

Tokyo issues angry response as Putin makes his first visit to the disputed Kuril islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:32:53 UTC
16:32:53 KST

The four contested islands, seized by Russia during World War II, have gained importance since the end of the conflict, providing strategic military bases to the Kremlin.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visited the far-eastern Kuril islands for the first time on Thursday, prompting a "strong" protest by Japan which also claims the territory.
Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by tensions over the contested islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and seized by the Soviet Union in 1945.
The Kremlin posted a video of Putin in the Kuril Islands, with Russian media saying he visited a fish-processing plant where he was given caviar. Putin travelled to the Kurils after visiting the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where Russia's navy was conducting drills.
In Sakhalin, Putin held a meeting "on ensuring the security of Russia's eastern borders," state-run media outlet RIA Novosti said.
Japan, whose ties with Russia have worsened further since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – just as Moscow's relations with China and North Korea have warmed – objected strongly.
"The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory both historically and under international law, and the government of Japan strongly protests this visit," said Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi in a statement.
The Soviet Union took the strategically located volcanic archipelago north of Hokkaido in the final days of World War II, and has maintained a military presence there ever since.
In 2010 then-president Dmitry Medvedev became the first Russian leader to visit the disputed territory. Medvedev also went there several times subsequently as prime minister under Putin’s presidency.
The four contested isles are part of the volcanic Kuril archipelago, which runs in a broad arc from Russia's Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan's main northern island Hokkaido. The Soviet Union only declared war on Japan on August 8, 1945, after the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima and six days before the end of the conflict.
The islands' names are similar in both countries -- Kunashir, Habomai, Shikotan and Iturup in Russian, while in Japanese they are known as Kunashiri, Habomai, Shikotan and Etorofu.
Their population of about 20,000 Russian citizens live in harsh climates, but the islands have mineral deposits including gold and silver, and rich fishing grounds. After the islands were occupied in 1945, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people.
Thereafter the islands acquired strategic importance, providing air and sea bases during the Cold War as the Soviet Union confronted the United States and its closest ally in the Pacific, Japan.
On several occasions it appeared that off-and-on talks between Tokyo and Moscow were making progress and in 1956, when diplomatic relations were established, where Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev suggested two of the disputed islands might be returned under a peace treaty.
Although the talks resumed after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, no progress has been made and they remain in Russian control.

Germany's dry rivers spark battle on engineering vs restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:28:00 UTC
16:28:00 KST

An empty cargo ship navigates at the Duisburg harbor during low water levels of Rhine River caused by a heat wave and a prolonged drought in Duisburg, Germany. Tuesday. Aug. 11, 2026.
As a heat wave dries Germany’s rivers, government ministers are at odds over what to do about it: Re-engineer the waterways or restore them to their natural state.
The debate has flared as precariously falling water levels have revealed vast sandbanks on the Rhine, Danube, Elbe and other rivers, severely impacting cargo shipping crucial for many industries.
With climate change driving new heat records and longer dry spells in Europe and beyond, scientists warn that the problem will intensify in coming years.
Germany’s new transport minister, Steffen Bilger, convened a recent crisis summit with shipping, port and logistics operators on the problem impacting the European Union’s biggest economy.
The key short-term counter measure he announced was to temporarily lift a ban on truck transports on Sundays and public holidays to help ease cargo bottlenecks.
In the longer term, Germany needs to dredge deeper navigation channels and develop a new class of low-draft ships, argued Bilger, a member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU bloc.
“We must make our waterways more efficient while simultaneously making ships suitable for times of low water,” Bilger said on Aug. 12 after talks with state transport ministers.
“That is why we are pushing ahead with important expansion projects,” he added, vowing that environmental protection would be “kept firmly in mind.” Speaking in Berlin on the same day, Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of junior coalition partner the center-left SPD offered a radically different vision, centered on restoring rivers.
After a campaign over hundreds of years saw rivers tamed for commercial use, he urged a shift back “toward natural rivers featuring meandering branches and floodplains that retain water across the landscape.”
“In past centuries, Germany was a land rich in water,” he said.
“Great effort went into straightening rivers to harness them for our use, but also into enabling agriculture by draining the wetlands.”
Now, however, climate change has turned water into a scarce resource, requiring a shift in thinking, Schneider argued.
His views echoed those of environmental groups that oppose deepening shipping channels. 
“They do more harm than good,” said Beatrice Claus of the WWF.
“Expansion and straightening cause water to drain away into the North Sea and Baltic Sea even faster, rather than being retained in the surrounding area.”
Dredging is not a permanent solution, critics argue, because rivers constantly fill the channels with new sediment.
Environmentalists also say river bank fortifications destroy shallow-water zones where aquatic life and insects breed, and the adjoining natural floodplains that act like sponges at times of excess water.
“Dredging rivers creates the illusion of taking action,” said Olaf Bandt, head of environmental group BUND.
For now, most German states have lifted the Sunday trucking ban, banking on a mode of transport with a far heavier carbon footprint than river boats.
Thomas Puls of the German Economic Institute said he did not expect the move to make much difference, telling news weekly Der Spiegel that it takes at least 150 trucks to replace a single inland waterway vessel.

Rail Baltica’s first phase in Latvia planned with major cost-cutting measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:24:50 UTC
16:24:50 KST

The first phase of the Rail Baltica main line in Latvia is planned within its existing scope, including the creation of a cross-border Rail Baltica connection from Lithuania to the Estonian border, as well as the completion of construction works at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station. This would allow Rail Baltica to be connected to Latvia’s existing railway network, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (New Unity) told reporters on Wednesday following a meeting of the thematic committee overseeing the project.
The minister stressed that this solution applies specifically to the project’s first phase and that the idea of the so-called “Riga loop” has not been abandoned. “We would like to look at it differently, but we are in 2026 and we have to think rationally,” Kozlovskis said.
The committee on Wednesday heard a report on the results of an in-depth review of the Rail Baltica project, which outlined three possible scenarios. “One scenario was to continue what had been started and proceed as before, which is neither acceptable nor possible. The second scenario is to review and reduce the requirements, while the third is to immediately terminate any further activities,” Kozlovskis explained. He stressed that the project must move towards optimisation – building and financing only what is technically essential rather than “funding various visions and, to some extent, dreams”.
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) said Latvia must establish a “minimum programme”, or a basic scenario for the project. According to him, consultants found that, for example, the approximately 600-kilometre Madrid–Barcelona high-speed railway technically has two stations, with one serving as the main stop, whereas Latvia’s roughly 200-kilometre section has been designed with 17 stations.
Station platforms have also been planned at 400 metres in length,
although technically they could be reduced to 200 metres.
The prime minister said the Transport Ministry must prepare proposals by the 15th of September for reducing technical and construction-material requirements for the first phase of Rail Baltica to the minimum level necessary to create a functional and permanently operational railway line. “So we go down to the minimum to understand what we can build and what we cannot,” Kulbergs said.
Taking into account the consultants’ assessment of project costs, the Finance Ministry and State Treasury, together with the Transport Ministry and Economics Ministry, have also been tasked with assessing by the 15th of September how much state budget funding could be allocated to Rail Baltica in the coming years, as well as identifying other sources of financing and opportunities to attract investment.
Kulbergs noted that the law now also recognises Rail Baltica’s role in military mobility, potentially opening the door to military funding that had not previously been explicitly envisaged. “We have to think outside the box about what other opportunities exist, because Europe will not provide enough money in the next funding envelope to implement this project,” he stressed.
A third task involves the State Chancellery and Transport Ministry
assessing proposed changes to the project’s governance. Kulbergs said the project has so far been poorly managed, arguing that Latvia’s interests have not been sufficiently protected in negotiations with contractors.
He also criticised the contract for construction of the main line signed in December 2023, saying it had “put us in a stranglehold” because it was concluded without specialist verification and complete project documentation.
According to Kulbergs, the contract does not set an effective maximum cost ceiling or define the maximum requirements Latvia can afford. “This is a good contractor capable of building the project, but the question is whether we can afford it. This contractor costs a very significant amount every month. If we continue building as we have until now, nobody will know when it will be completed or how it will be financed.
Nor will anyone be able to afford a train ticket,”
Kulbergs said.
The Transport Ministry said the results of the in-depth Rail Baltica review were presented on Wednesday by consultants from Alvarez & Marsal Infrastructure & Capital Projects, who analysed the causes of the project’s previous problems and proposed further steps. The assessment is classified as a restricted-access document.
The review concluded that if Latvia continues implementing Rail Baltica in the same way as before, the full cost of the Latvian section could increase significantly and the project could not be completed solely with available EU funding. Consultants also concluded that successful implementation would be unlikely without clearly assigning overall responsibility and establishing a project management team experienced in projects of a similar scale.
According to the ministry, Alvarez & Marsal recommends first deciding how much annual state budget funding Latvia can realistically allocate to Rail Baltica in the coming years. Latvia should then consult Estonia, Lithuania and the European Commission to agree on minimum technical requirements for the project, particularly regarding maximum train speeds.
The Transport Ministry also presented potential cost-saving solutions
prepared together with Eiropas Dzelzceļa līnijas (EDzL) and contractors for the 33-kilometre Rail Baltica section between Misa and the Latvian-Lithuanian border.
By rationalising the design and introducing standardised solutions for engineering structures, construction elements and environmental measures, construction costs could reportedly be reduced by 24.8%, generating around 108 million euros in savings on future construction works.
Among the proposed measures, the average height of the railway line could be lowered by approximately three metres and the thickness of the frost-protection layer reduced by 37%. This would cut embankment construction volumes by 46% and excavation and soil replacement works by 25%. It could also potentially eliminate the need to construct 13.2 kilometres of noise barriers.
The government launched the in-depth Rail Baltica review on the 3rd of November last year, appointing international consultancy Alvarez & Marsal to carry it out. The value of the consultancy contract is confidential.
The purpose of the assessment is to provide an objective and comprehensive analysis
of Rail Baltica’s implementation, examine risks and the project’s financial and contractual position, and develop recommendations and a practical action plan for more efficient, transparent and sustainable implementation.
At the end of July, the government also established a thematic committee on Rail Baltica implementation comprising ten members of the government. Chaired by Prime Minister Kulbergs, it is intended to coordinate cross-sectoral government decisions on the technically functional and financially sustainable continuation of the project.
In addition to Kulbergs, the committee includes Foreign Minister Baiba Braže, Climate and Energy Minister Jānis Vitenbergs, Education and Science Minister Ilze Indriksone, Finance Minister Māris Kučinskis, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis, Defence Minister Raivis Melnis, Justice Minister Edvards Smiltēns, Smart Administration and Regional Development Minister Edgars Tavars, and Economics Minister Viktors Valainis.
The estimated cost of Rail Baltica’s first phase across the Baltic states could reach 14.3 billion euros,
including around 5.5 billion euros in Latvia, although indexation could push Latvia’s share to approximately 6 billion euros.
According to the latest cost-benefit analysis, the entire Rail Baltica project across the Baltic states could cost as much as 23.8 billion euros. By comparison, the previous cost-benefit analysis conducted in 2017 estimated the total cost at 5.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica is intended to create a European standard-gauge railway connecting Tallinn with the Lithuanian-Polish border and, from there, linking the Baltic states with the wider European rail network. The project envisages approximately 870 kilometres of new 1,435 mm standard-gauge railway across the Baltic states, designed for maximum train speeds of up to 240 kilometres per hour.

Nearly 370 Palestinian children are being held in Israeli prisons, many without having been convicted of a crime, RT’s Charlotte Dubenskij has reported, citing Palestinian and Israeli rights organizations.
The number of minors held under administrative detention – which allows imprisonment without charge or trial – has almost doubled in just over a year, according to the latest figures from Israel’s prison service.

Israeli police also report that around 100 minors are detained each month for entering Israel without a permit.
The detentions have come amid mounting allegations of mistreatment inside Israeli prisons. Former detainees and rights organizations have reported abuse, torture, starvation, physical and psychological harm, sexual violence and denial of medical treatment.
Israel is also holding the bodies of more than 100 Palestinians who died in its custody, according to a recent report cited by RT.
The situation in the West Bank has received comparatively little international attention amid the war in Gaza, where Israeli military operations have caused widespread destruction and displacement.
Gaza’s Health Ministry has put the Palestinian death toll since October 2023 at 73,386, with another 174,250 people wounded. Israel launched its military campaign following the Hamas-led October 7 attack on southern Israel, in which around 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 taken hostage.

The White House has not disclosed the overall cost of the planned construction or detailed the sources of most of the funding.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said the projects are being carried out in a "manner consistent with" Congress's intent.

According to the report, Congress has traditionally approved funding for major White House construction projects.
Budget records cited by the newspaper show the administration has directed $875 million into the Executive Residence maintenance account since Trump took office, compared with annual appropriations of $2.5 million in recent years.

A proposal for an economic future: Gaza needs more than reconstruction - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:21:25 UTC
16:21:25 KST

For more than three years, I have been working on a question that many would consider impossible: What would it take to rebuild Gaza not simply with new buildings, but as a functioning, productive, and economically independent society?
There is no shortage of discussions about Gaza's future. There are proposals for governance, security, humanitarian assistance and reconstruction. What is still missing, however, is a practical economic model capable of turning hundreds of thousands of displaced people from recipients of aid into homeowners, workers, entrepreneurs and participants in a functioning economy. I believe that such a model is possible, and that its foundation must be ownership.
For decades, Gaza's refugee camps have been a symbol of dependency. Reconstruction offers an opportunity to change that reality. Instead of rebuilding homes as publicly funded shelters, families should finance and own their homes, turning housing into the first asset in their economic future.
My proposal envisions approximately 400,000 residential units in high-rise buildings across Gaza, primarily for residents of the refugee camps and people whose homes were destroyed during the war. Construction costs are estimated at $60,000–$100,000 per unit. Rather than relying on donations to finance the housing itself, families would purchase their homes through long-term mortgages of up to 40 years, with the allocated land serving as equity and collateral.
This is more than a financing mechanism; it is a different philosophy of reconstruction. A home can provide shelter while also becoming an asset that gives a family financial security and access to credit. When hundreds of thousands of families own homes and build assets for themselves and their children, they develop a direct stake in the stability and future of the society in which they live. Ownership can therefore become a foundation for economic mobility, civic responsibility, and long-term stability.
From reconstruction to economy
Housing, however, is only the beginning. Gaza cannot become economically viable through residential towers alone. Reconstruction must include industrial zones, transportation infrastructure, reliable energy and commercial centers. Its approximately 40 kilometers of Mediterranean coastline also represents a long-term economic asset, with potential for tourism, hospitality and commerce.
Modern construction technology makes the scale of this ambition more realistic. Over the past several years, we have examined the international companies specializing in modular and industrialized construction, using prefabricated components and factory production. These technologies can allow construction to take place simultaneously across multiple sites and significantly accelerate the delivery of large numbers of homes.
The financing challenge can be addressed through a combination of private and institutional capital. We are examining a structure involving an international banking consortium, potentially supported by institutions such as the World Bank and political-risk insurance mechanisms such as MIGA. These mechanisms could help mitigate risks associated with political instability, renewed conflict and damage to investments, creating a framework in which international capital can participate.
An economic foundation for a different future
No economic plan can substitute for security, legitimate governance and the rule of law. Any successful reconstruction will require guarantees that infrastructure and investment will not once again become instruments of conflict. But security and economic development should not be viewed as competing priorities. A society in which families own homes, businesses can operate, and people can build assets for their children has a fundamentally different foundation from one that remains dependent on temporary shelter and external assistance.
This is the thinking behind the plan developed by the Institute for Structural Reforms, which has been working on the concept for the past three years, well before the end of the war. The proposal has recently been presented to Palestinian officials and has generated interest, while discussions are also taking place with international institutions and senior figures regarding its potential implementation.
I am an Israeli lawyer and entrepreneur. I do not claim that an economic plan can resolve the profound political and security questions surrounding Gaza. But precisely because I am Israeli, I believe we should be willing to think beyond the immediate horizon of war and ask what kind of reality we want to see on the other side of it.
If the day after the war is to be different from the day before, Gaza needs more than concrete, pipes and temporary shelters. It needs the foundations of an economy in which people can own, work, build and invest in their future. Reconstruction should not simply restore what was destroyed. It should create the economic foundations for a different future.
Attorney Shraga Biran is an Israeli lawyer, entrepreneur, and real-estate expert with more than six decades of experience in law, property, and urban development. He founded the Institute for Structural Reforms, which develops innovative structural solutions to social and economic challenges, including housing, land, and urban renewal.

An immigrant from Guatemala who was taken to a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, in July experienced a medical emergency and died after hospitalization, President Donald Trump's administration said.
Jose Chajon-Raxon was detained by ICE at the Delaney Hall detention facility on July 18 and experienced a medical emergency the next day, the Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, said in an emailed statement on Wednesday.
A nurse responded to the medical emergency and "witnessed Chajon-Raxon experiencing seizure-like activity," the DHS said, adding that medical workers were called and Chajon-Raxon was taken to a hospital.
The DHS said Chajon-Raxon was "released from ICE custody on July 22" but did not provide more details on that. The DHS statement did not mention when Chajon-Raxon died.
Delaney Hall in Newark has previously come under scrutiny from human rights advocates and Democrats following the deaths in ICE detention of a man from El Salvador named Edwin Lopez-Cornejo and another from Haiti named Jean Wilson Brutus. The Salvadoran man died this month after a medical emergency, while the Haitian man died in December.
More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide
ICE was not notified of Chajon-Raxon's death as it was "not responsible when an individual passes away weeks after leaving their custody," the DHS said.
Democratic US Representative Rob Menendez said he had been given conflicting information on Chajon-Raxon's death, adding that he went to the ICE facility on August 3 in an oversight visit.
More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since President Donald Trump took office in January last year. Rights groups have repeatedly raised concerns about medical care and living conditions at the facilities.
ICE says detainees are given appropriate medical care.
The agency has been the face of Trump's immigration crackdown. The Republican president says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.
Rights groups say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

Remembering Oren Nahari: The storyteller who brought the world into Israeli living rooms - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:21:15 UTC
16:21:15 KST

When Oren Nahari published what would become his final book, The Great Battles That Changed History, co-written with Yoav Limor, he revealed that the original manuscript contained 50 battles. But the publisher was unequivocal.
“Who is going to read a 400-page book?” they asked him. Nahari was forced to decide which 30 battles would make it into the final book.
That story captures Oren Nahari perfectly. Whenever he began telling you about an event, the depth of his knowledge, the details he knew, and the connections he drew would always leave you with your jaw hanging open. “Where does he get all this knowledge?”
Nahari always had a book in his hand, was a man of facts, details, and stories
The answer would always come between broadcasts, as Oren waited to go on air for a report or commentary: Oren Nahari always had a book in his hand. And he didn’t just carry it – he read it. He read very quickly.
But Oren was not merely a man of facts and details. He was a storyteller.
Whenever the earth shook somewhere in the world, a rebellion erupted, an economic crisis broke out, or any other event occurred – even one that might seem marginal – Oren could focus not only on the question, “Are there Israelis there, and if so, how were they affected?” He would first explain why the event mattered to us even if there were no Israelis there at all.
The smallest events can shape the world, and Nahari knew how to explain why
Because that is the reality of our interconnected world: the flutter of a butterfly’s wings, even the smallest event, can influence history and shape the world – even when there are no Israeli citizens or Jews involved. The wisdom lies in knowing how to explain why.
When he launched the revolution that was the show Ro’im Olam (Seeing the World) in 1988, together with David Witztum, Yaakov Ahimeir, and many other talented journalists, he brought the world to Israeli viewers.
Only recently, he began an extraordinary project on Kan Reshet Bet, a historical radio program called A Year in an Hour, exploring the history of the 20th century. And, as was so often the case with Oren, sometimes a single year required much more than an hour to explain – sometimes even three. Sadly, he never had the chance to complete the project, which ended in 1961.
And Oren had one more remarkable quality: he was a breeding ground for journalists.
When I joined the foreign desk of Israel’s Channel 1 in 2009, I discovered a true journalistic incubator. Oren had an extraordinary ability to teach, but above all, to convey one fundamental message: the most important thing is knowing how to tell a story. There is an audience for it.
That was the message with which he said goodbye to his radio listeners last Saturday:
“Keep watching, keep listening, keep asking questions, never take things for granted, and keep being curious.”

Two railway workers killed in Odesa region
A Russian jet-powered Shahed drone deliberately struck the locomotive of a passenger train in Odesa region, killing the train’s driver and assistant, Ukrainian Railways Board Chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said.
The attack occurred as the train was approaching a station where passengers were supposed to be evacuated after a drone threat was detected.
“Unfortunately, I have to report the most terrible news: according to the information currently available, this strike left no chance for our locomotive crew – the driver and his assistant,” Pertsovskyi said.
The train was carrying 340 passengers. They and the rest of the train crew were evacuated safely, with no injuries reported among them. Passengers were subsequently transported to Odesa by buses.

Venezuela's interim government, opposition complete 1st round of transition talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:20:06 UTC
16:20:06 KST

Merve Berker
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
Venezuela's interim government and opposition representatives have concluded a first round of transition talks aimed at advancing national reconciliation following the US removal of former leader Nicolas Maduro, media reports said Thursday.
In a joint statement issued after several days of negotiations, the two sides said they reached agreement on two key issues: reforming the judiciary and seeking access to frozen international assets to support recovery efforts following the twin earthquakes on June 24 that have claimed more than 6,300 lives, according to TRT World.
The parties agreed to "initiate a process that contributes to the transformation of the justice system," including reforms to the Organic Law governing Venezuela's Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ).
The statement also said they would work toward securing the release of Venezuela's international reserve assets held at the Bank of England to finance earthquake recovery efforts.
It called for the establishment of "mechanisms for transparency, traceability and auditing" to ensure the funds are used appropriately.
The interim government of President Delcy Rodriguez was represented by National Assembly Speaker Jorge Rodriguez, while the opposition delegation was led by Dinorah Figuera, head of the political bloc that won a majority in the 2015 parliament.
The joint statement did not mention the National Electoral Council, an institution the opposition has previously said it wants to reform.
Figuera said during the talks, "We are in this process to achieve a democratic and free Venezuela."
According to the report, many Venezuelans hope the transition process will pave the way for democratic elections.
The talks are led by National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez on behalf of the government and Figuera, who heads the opposition-linked Delegated Commission of the 2015 National Assembly.
Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado is not participating and has rejected the process, arguing that it does not reflect the democratic mandate claimed by the opposition following Venezuela's disputed 2024 presidential election.

The unnamed official’s remarks came in response to Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz’s statement that Israel did not intend to withdraw from southern Lebanon, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
“The US expects all parties to act in a manner consistent with the framework they agreed to, and Israel has made it clear that it has no territorial ambitions in Lebanon,” the official said.

Who is Karoline Leavitt?

Does the clean energy transition need forever chemicals?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:13:00 UTC
16:13:00 KST

Does the clean energy transition need forever chemicals?
August 13, 2026
From solar panels to wind turbines, batteries and hydrogen cells, many renewable energy technologies driving the energy transition share a common ingredient: a class of man-made substances known as "forever chemicals."
The group contains 10,000 synthetic chemicals also known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which persist in the environment and can take thousands of years to degrade.
Widely detected in drinking water, exposure to certain levels of PFAS is linked to increased risk of cancer, suppressed immune function, decreased fertility and developmental delays in children.
These health impacts have inspired bans on well-publicized sources of toxic PFAS such as clothing waterproofing sprays, Teflon non-stick cookware, firefighting foam, packaging and cosmetic products.
While recent bans in France, New Zealand and Denmark target specific PFAS used in consumer products, the European Union wants a broader ban.
The thousands of forever chemicals the EU proposes outlawing includes fluoropolymers, which are valued for their resistance to extreme temperatures, corrosion and UV degradation, and are present in numerous green technologies from lithium-ion batteries to solar panels.
In EV batteries, for example, binders created with PTFE fluoropolymers — also found in Teflon products — are used to coat dry electrodes for greater energy efficiency.
The chemicals industry has pushed back against Europe's mooted ban. An alliance of the world's leading chemical companies, the Performance Fluoropolymer Partnership (PFP) says health concerns about "some types of PFAS" are leading to "unwarranted restrictions" on fluoropolymer production and use.
In a statement on its website describing fluoropolymers as "critical in the fight against climate change," the PFP stated that any bans would "hamstring our climate and energy goals by possibly making the transition more expensive or simply impossible."
Are PFAS necessary to fight climate change?
PFP members include the chemicals arm of US multinational conglomerate, 3M — which is being sued more than $2 billion by the Australian government for its firefighting foam that has leached forever chemicals into the environment — and the Chemours Company, which manufacturers Teflon and was established by chemicals powerhouse, DuPont.
The European Environment Agency says these polymers are considered "relatively less problematic" than the building blocks for PFAS known as monomers. This is due to a larger molecular size that "limits their uptake into living cells" and potential toxicity.
Yet fluoropolymers still degrade over time, raising "additional environmental and human health concerns," according to the agency. Experts say these polymers will inevitably emit PFAS during their life cycle and enter the environment — and living organisms — through weathering and physical stress over long periods.
"I don't think we're going to solve the climate crisis by getting cancer," said Gretchen Salter of US-based Safer States, which lobbies to safeguard the environment from toxic chemicals. "You can't demonstrate that these chemicals aren't going to do harm."
"Since chemical makers cannot escape the fact that these types of PFAS are harming our health, they are trying to claim that they are necessary for the clean energy transition," Salter said, adding that research shows how PFAS themselves fuel climate harm and toxic pollution.
The petrochemical industry accounts for 30% of global industrial energy demand — which is higher than the iron, steel and cement sectors — and generates 18% of the industrial sector's greenhouse gas emissions. Overall, chemicals used to produce everything from pharmaceuticals to fertilizers, plastics, paints, electronics and cleaning products are responsible for around 6% of global emissions.
Salter said PFAS categorized as fluorogases (F-gases) are also being marketed as "climate-friendly" since they are used for clean tech like heat pumps, and in electric car batteries. But PFAS gases, though largely non-flammable, are "now the largest source of PFAS pollution globally," she said.
This is partly due to their global warming impact, which is potentially thousands of times higher than carbon dioxide. F-gas leaks can happen throughout a heat pump life cycle via worn seals and improper maintenance and end-of-life disposal. F-gases are also present in fridges and air-conditioning units as a synthetic coolant, where they can leak too.
Are there PFAS-free green tech alternatives?
According to UK-based Chem Trust, which advocates for safer alternatives to toxic chemicals, a suite of PFAS-free clean energy technology is already on the market, including for heat pumps that are being rolled out across Europe as part of a transition from gas heating.
Instead of relying on F-gases, propane is just one alternative energy efficient refrigerant for domestic heat pumps, and with the right design has a negligible fire risk, notes a 2025 Chem Trust report.
The group also says several companies are now producing solar cells without fluoropolymers. Equally, polymer paint that protects wind turbine blades and makes them more efficient is available PFAS-free.
"We are seeing more companies in the EU and across the world embrace the challenge of developing PFAS-free green technologies," said Shubhi Sharma, scientific researcher at Chem Trust, in a statement.
But plastics and chemical lobby group Plastics Europe released an assessment report of PFAS-free substitutes in May that argued that "in many critical uses" such as transport, electronics and semiconductors, these alternatives are "either not available or simply do not match the necessary criteria to be considered a viable alternative to fluoropolymers."
Salter of Safer States said efforts to exempt so-called critical and low concern PFAS from class-wide bans means "destroying any sort of incentive to switch to safer alternatives."
"As long as the chemicals industry insists that there are no alternatives, there will be no market to develop any," said the campaigner.
Chemours insists its fluoropolymers and F-gases are "made and used with minimal environmental impact," and says it will achieve a 99% PFAS emissions reduction in the manufacture of fluorinated organic compounds by the end of the decade compared to 2018.
Liz Hitchcock, director of the federal policy program at US environment nonprofit, Toxic-Free Future, told DW that the extreme persistence of PFAS in the environment will inevitably lead to human exposure.
"We've heard claims that there are better PFAS, there are safer PFAS, but we haven't seen the proof."

In the morning, Chisinau Airport was evacuated after a report of a bomb threat, which turned out to be false. The checks have been completed, and the airport has resumed normal operations.
Chisinau Airport in Moldova was evacuated in the early morning due to a bomb threat; the report turned out to be false, the country's Border Police said on Wednesday, UNN writes.
Details
Early Wednesday morning, at around 4:30 a.m. local time, the Border Police reported an alert over a bomb threat at Chisinau International Airport named after Eugen Doga.
Border Police officers promptly intervened to evacuate passengers and staff from the airport. Specialized units of the country's Ministry of Internal Affairs were working at the scene. The check-in procedure was suspended, and warnings were issued about possible changes to scheduled flights.

Israeli strikes in south Lebanon a ‘violation of international law’: PM
Prime Minister Nawaf Salam rejects Israel’s claim that villages destroyed in southern Lebanon were military sites.
Lebanon’s government has accused Israel of deliberately destroying homes and civilian infrastructure across the country’s south amid a ceasefire that has grown increasingly fragile.
Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Wednesday said Israel’s “attacks, incursions, demolitions and the systematic destruction of homes represent a serious violation of the principles and rules of international law and international humanitarian law”.

Salam rejected Israel’s claims that villages it had destroyed were military sites, saying the claim “does not stand up to any logic and cannot be used as an excuse for destroying them, displacing their inhabitants and preventing them from returning”.
His statement came hours after Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz visited southern Lebanon and said Israeli forces were “destroying the underground infrastructure” there and “destroying all the houses”.
Katz separately said Israeli troops would not withdraw from occupied zones in Lebanon, Syria or Gaza. Israeli attacks wounded several people in southern Lebanon on the same day.
A US State Department official told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that Washington “expects all parties to act in a manner consistent with the framework they agreed to”, adding that Israel “has clearly stated that it has no territorial ambitions in Lebanon”.
On August 5, Israel launched strikes on the town of Mansouri after accusing Hezbollah of a ceasefire violation that killed two Israeli soldiers near Majdal Zoun.
The Israeli military ordered residents to evacuate Mansouri, the first such order issued in weeks, while a separate attack elsewhere killed one person and wounded 11. A day later, an Israeli strike hit a home in Burj al-Shemali.
Hezbollah did not claim the attack that killed the Israeli soldiers and has made no public statement addressing it directly.
Where the ‘ceasefire’ stands
Lebanon was drawn into the US and Israel’s war on Iran on March 2 after Tehran-aligned Hezbollah launched attacks on northern Israel.
Although a US-mediated ceasefire aimed at halting the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah began on April 17, Israeli forces have continued their attacks and occupy dozens of villages across southern Lebanon, with no timeline set for a full withdrawal.
The latest conditional truce traces back to a framework agreement reached in Washington in June, under which Israeli forces were meant to withdraw gradually from occupied Lebanese territory as the Lebanese army deploys to replace them, starting with limited “pilot zones,” in exchange for Hezbollah’s disarmament.
Lebanon and Israel have since held seven rounds of US-mediated talks, four in Washington and three in Rome, aimed at implementing the agreement.
Hezbollah, which is not party to the talks, has said it will pull back from south of the Litani River but will not disarm to the north,
Lebanese authorities say Israeli strikes and ground operations since March have killed 4,333 people and displaced more than a million – roughly a fifth of the country’s population.
These figures have continued climbing through the summer even after the ceasefire nominally took effect.
In Washington, two US senators have proposed a $1.2bn security assistance package for Lebanon over five years, tying part of the funding to progress on the state’s monopoly over weapons and Hezbollah’s disarmament.
The assistance package highlights how the country’s post-war stability remains bound up with an unresolved political and military standoff that shows few signs of easing.

MP proposes endorsing Tiit Land to Riigikogu independents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:11:00 UTC
16:11:00 KST

MP proposes endorsing Tiit Land to Riigikogu independents
Ex-Reform MP Meelis Kiili has proposed that unaffiliated members of the Riigikogu support the nomination of Tiit Land as a presidential candidate to ensure that at least two viable candidates make it onto the ballot.
"Supporting the nomination of a candidate and voting for that candidate in the presidential election are two completely different things. Supporting Tiit Land's nomination does not mean an obligation to vote for him later. It means creating an opportunity to have at least two viable candidates whose positions can be compared publicly," Kiili explained.
At least 21 MPs are needed to nominate a presidential candidate.
Kiili stressed that the goal of unaffiliated MPs should not be to push through any particular candidate. He said the immediate objective should be very simple: Estonia should get the best possible president, and for that to happen, there first needs to be a genuine choice.
"An election means having candidates to choose between. A process with only one candidate may formally comply with the rules, but it does not provide a meaningful choice. Having at least two candidates would create an opportunity for debate and compel the candidates to explain their understanding of the president's role and Estonia's future," Kiili said.
In his view, presidential candidates should be assessed, among other things, on how they understand the president's role as a balancing force in the political system, supreme commander of national defense, a unifying figure in society and Estonia's representative in foreign and economic relations. The future president must also understand the importance of education, the information space and energy security to Estonia's long-term survival and security.
Kiili said the procedure for electing the president should also be revisited after the presidential election.
Meelis Kiili, formerly a member of the Reform Party, announced on August 10 that he had decided to leave the party and continue serving in the Riigikogu as an unaffiliated MP. Shortly before Kiili, Kalev Stoicescu announced his departure from Eesti 200. This, in addition to effectively leaving Estonia with a minority government, brought the number of MPs unaffiliated with a parliamentary group in the Riigikogu to 20. However, only nine of them have not affiliated themselves with any political party.
Isamaa and the Center Party, which are considering supporting Land's nomination, have eight and seven members in their parliamentary groups, respectively, for a total of 15. Adding MPs who do not belong to those parliamentary groups but have joined the parties would give them another four votes, bringing the total to 19 — two short of the number needed to nominate Land.
That means at least two additional votes from independent unaffiliated MPs would be needed. Stoicescu, for example, who initially supported Ülle Madise, has already indicated that he may also support Land. If both he and Kiili were to do so, Land would have the 21 signatures needed for his nomination.
Stoicescu said Thursday that MPs who do not belong to a Riigikogu parliamentary group, commonly known as unaffiliated MPs, will meet with Land on Friday and with Ülle Madise on Monday. He said he will decide after the meetings which candidate's nomination he will sign in support of.
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise remains the potential presidential candidate with the best chances, having secured the backing of 55 MPs from the Reform Party, Eesti 200 and Social Democratic Party groups as at Wednesday evening, according to Riigikogu Deputy Speaker Toomas Kivimägi.
Key dates:
• Aug. 21-24: Candidate nominations
• Sept. 2: First round of voting in the Riigikogu
• Sept. 3: Second and third rounds of voting in the Riigikogu, if necessary
The article was updated to add a comment from Kalev Stoicescu.

Lukashenko travels to Minsk District to thank top-performing harvester operators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:11:00 UTC
16:11:00 KST

MINSK DISTRICT, 13 August (BelTA) - Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko met with harvest leaders in Minsk District who have achieved outstanding results during the ongoing harvest campaign, BelTA has learned.
The head of state arrived at a field of Agrokombinat Zhdanovichi. Here, the president received a gift - a symbolic sheaf marking the threshing of 2 million tonnes of grain in Minsk Oblast. However, Aleksandr Lukashenko emphasized that there should be no stopping there.
“With an eye on three million,” he said accepting the gift.
 
 
Speaking with the harvest leaders, the president thanked them for their excellent work during the campaign. At the same time, he noted that there should be far more such people and made a request to share the experience and train a worthy successor generation.
“Please consider how you can help. Having a dozen harvester operators who have threshed 4,000 tonnes and one who has reached 8,000 tonnes is not sufficient. We need one hundred or even two hundred such individuals - people eager to take on the challenge,” the president stressed. “Help us create a reserve of young specialists. The state will provide support and assistance in this effort.”
As Minsk Oblast Governor Aleksei Kushnarenko reported to the head of state, a harvest leaders’ club, Golden Wheat Ear, is being established in the central oblast, which will include harvester operators who have threshed over 4,000 tonnes. A young harvester operators’ school, Little Wheat Ear, will operate under it.
Among the leaders is Pavel Shutilo, who works at the Kukhchitsy agricultural enterprise in Kletsk District. In early August, he became the first in Belarus to thresh 4,000 tonnes of grain, and has since surpassed the 5,000-tonne mark. This impressive result was achieved on a harvester manufactured by Gomselmash.
 
 
 
The harvester operator from Kletsk District regularly achieves high harvest results on Belarusian-made machinery. In 2024, Pavel Shutilo threshed 3,200 tonnes of grain, and in 2025, he surpassed 8,400 tonnes, becoming one of the main heroes of the harvest.
Addressing the harvester operator, the head of state shared a story from his own experience as a manager in the agricultural sector. At the time, about 20 harvester operators worked at the enterprise, and their combined annual harvest was around 4,000 tonnes of grain. By contrast, Pavel Shutilo alone threshed over 8,000 tonnes last year. However, the machinery in the 1990s was vastly different in both quality and power.
The president asked Pavel Shutilo what improvements could be made to the domestically produced harvester. According to the harvester operator, the machine is good and equipped with all the necessary conveniences. “You should always tell me the truth about our cars and harvesters: what needs to be improved? The machines are good, and they look like the best global models,” said Aleksandr Lukashenko. “But now we need to push the quality further, so everything is perfect, and no one tells me we need to buy CLAAS or John Deere because Gomselmash doesn’t measure up. And here I have an example: Pavel is working, and he measures up. Neither CLAAS nor John Deere can match that.”
 
 
 
The head of state has previously recognized the harvester operator’s achievements. At the second meeting of the 7th Belarusian People’s Congress, Aleksandr Lukashenko called Pavel Shutilo a hero. “There is a hero sitting here - a young man. He threshed over eight thousand tonnes!” the president said at the time. The entire hall applauded the harvester operator, who was among the participants of the congress.
Vitaly Kishko, who works at the same farm hauling the harvest, has also achieved high results. During this year’s harvest campaign, he has already transported over 6,100 tonnes of grain, legumes, and rapeseed, breaking his own previous records. Last year, Vitaly Kishko transported over 4,600 tonnes of crops, and in 2024, over 4,200 tonnes.
 
 
 
 
 
Another employee of Kukhchitsy, Andrei Alekseichik, transported 7,700 tonnes of grain last year. This year, he is participating in the harvest as the specialist responsible for organizing the campaign.
 
 
 
The president also expressed gratitude to Sergei Zdrok, Director of Kukhchitsy, who supervises the leading harvest workers. The head of the agricultural enterprise assured the head of state that experienced harvester operators and drivers are transferring their expertise to young farmers.
 
 
 
The farmers received well-deserved gifts from the president, who presented them with keys to new BELGEE vehicles. “Men, I am deeply grateful to you for what you are doing. How can the president meet with the agricultural sector’s finest and fail to thank them for their efforts?” Aleksandr Lukashenko stressed. “You’ve deserved it.”

How to store honey properly so that it does not spoil: advice from a beekeeper technician
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:10:54 EEST
16:10:54 KST

How to store honey properly so that it does not spoil: advice from a beekeeper technician
Kyiv • UNN
Beekeeper technician Mykola Maliarchuk said that honey is best stored in a clean glass container with an airtight lid, avoiding moisture and temperature fluctuations. He noted that freezing helps preserve its liquid consistency, while a change in the top layer is a sign of spoilage.
Proper storage of honey depends on many factors. A technician and beekeeper, Mykola Maliarchuk, told UNN journalist in more detail how to store honey properly and what signs may indicate that it has begun to spoil.
According to the specialist, glass containers are best suited for long-term honey storage. They must be clean and completely dry, and the honey itself must be protected from moisture. It is also important to avoid sudden temperature fluctuations.
It is advisable to use clean and dry glassware. Under such conditions, honey can be stored at room temperature. At the same time, significant temperature fluctuations should be avoided. It is better to place the container in a cooler spot, such as on the floor, where there is no excessive heat
Honey also does not necessarily need to be kept in complete darkness if it is stored in an ordinary room, but the expert does not recommend leaving the jar in direct sunlight.
There is no need to specifically hide honey from the light in a room. If it is kept in a normally lit room, this does not affect its quality. However, honey should not be left in direct sunlight, because the temperature there can fluctuate significantly. It is also important to protect honey from moisture, so the container must be tightly sealed
Mykola Maliarchuk also explains that an open container can lead both to the honey drying out and to moisture getting into it. Therefore, for long-term storage, the jar must be tightly sealed.
If the container remains open, honey gradually loses moisture and may dry out. Moisture from the surrounding environment can also enter the product through the open container. If there is enough of it, the honey may begin to ferment. Therefore, it must be hermetically sealed for long-term storage
If the goal is to preserve the liquid consistency of fresh honey for as long as possible, the beekeeper names freezing as one possible method. In this case, the product may remain liquid for a long time.
Fresh liquid honey can be placed in a freezer. In that case, it may remain liquid for a long time and retain the state of fresh honey. It is important to do this before it begins to crystallize. It can be stored in a freezer for even one or two years
At the same time, for ordinary storage, it is important to choose the right container material. Mykola Maliarchuk emphasizes that glass is best suited for long-term honey storage.
I would not recommend storing honey for a long time in plastic buckets or canisters. Aluminum containers are also not the best option. Stainless steel may be used, but the container must be hermetically sealed. A glass jar with an airtight lid is best suited for long-term storage
The specialist also refutes the widespread claim that honey supposedly never spoils at all. According to him, moisture entering the container can lead to changes in the upper layer of the product.
The claim that honey never spoils at all is false, because some moisture still gets into the container, even through a loosely closed lid, so the top layer of the honey may gradually change. It becomes fluffy and soft, although the lower part may remain normal
According to Mykola Maliarchuk, a sign that honey has spoiled may be a change in its structure specifically at the top. In solid honey, the top layer becomes soft, while in liquid honey the consistency may also change, becoming significantly thinner.
When solid honey begins to spoil, its top layer changes first - it becomes soft. If the honey below remains solid, this means that the changes began at the top. The consistency of liquid honey may also change: it becomes as runny as water because it loses its viscosity and begins to ferment
The beekeeper separately draws attention to the ripening of honey before it is extracted. If unripe honey with a high water content is purchased, it may begin to ferment very quickly.
Unripe honey is essentially nectar that the bees have not yet had time to process. They gradually evaporate the water from it, and when the honey matures, they seal it in the honeycombs. You should not rush to extract it, as unripe honey contains a lot of water, which can cause it to begin fermenting
Another important stage is cleaning the honey after extraction. According to the expert, the product should be strained through special sieves to remove foreign particles. This should also be done with purchased honey to make sure that there is nothing unnecessary in the product.
After extraction, honey should additionally be cleaned and strained through special sieves. This helps remove pieces of honeycomb, bees, brood and other foreign particles that may have gotten into the product. I try to extract honey without brood, but if any gets into the honey, it must be strained
The cleanliness of the container is also quite important. According to the beekeeper, old honey left on the walls of a jar or other vessel can affect a new batch of honey.
If old honey remains in the vessel, it must be completely removed, and the container thoroughly washed and dried. You should not pour fresh honey into a vessel containing remnants of old honey, as this can cause fermentation. The container must be clean, dry and free of foreign substances
