A bungled bomb plot in Poland exposed a spy – but whose spy was he?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
04:00:49 UTC
13:00:49 KST

The police came for Igor Rogov because someone had mailed him a bomb-making kit. The eclectic mix of items – a chrome vacuum flask, a pair of marker pens, a power bank and a bottle of antifreeze fluid – might have seemed innocuous to an untrained eye, but Poland was on high alert in July 2024. Two months previously, a shopping mall in Warsaw had burned down in an arson attack; an Ikea in neighbouring Lithuania was also set on fire. Authorities believed it was a sabotage campaign masterminded by Russia’s intelligence services, intended to sow panic and undermine support for Ukraine. They feared it was only a matter of time before the Kremlin escalated further.
A security officer at the parcel company’s warehouse was suspicious enough about the package to call in the authorities, who arrived with sniffer dogs and special equipment. X-rays of the marker pens showed they had 1980s Soviet-produced detonators concealed inside, while the flask had a false bottom containing a sachet of metallic powder. The power bank appeared to have been tampered with in some way, and a probe of the bottled liquid showed it contained a highly volatile nitroglycerine solution. With the right expertise, the items could be turned into a powerful bomb.
Police ascertained that Rogov, the parcel’s addressee, was a 27-year-old Russian political activist, who in the past had campaigned for the opposition leader Alexei Navalny and other anti-Kremlin groups. He had fled Russia two years previously, fearing arrest for his activities, and been granted asylum in Poland. He won a scholarship to attend university in Sosnowiec, an industrial city in the south-west of the country. His wife, Irina Rogova, followed him to Poland and also enrolled at the university; the couple lived in a student dormitory. It was there that authorities arrested him.
Rogov’s phone, when searched, contained photographs of urban scenes in the vicinity of Sosnowiec overlaid with red arrows, apparently indicating places to hide or retrieve items. One photo was of a gas pipeline on the outskirts of town, an appealing potential target for a Russian bomb attack. The chance discovery of the package, it seemed, had led authorities to a participant, perhaps even a coordinator, of Russia’s sabotage campaign against Poland, living under deep cover as a brave opponent to the Kremlin.
More than a year later, in October 2025, Polish authorities revealed they were also accusing Rogov of longstanding collaboration with the FSB, Russia’s feared security service. This suggested that his whole career as an anti-Kremlin activist might have been a cover story for his FSB work. When the case came to court, however, the judge closed proceedings to the public and press on national security grounds, fuelling further speculation and rumours about what exactly Rogov had done – especially among Russia’s exiled political opposition, where infighting, suspicions and accusations are commonplace.
Although Rogov’s trial was closed, I discovered thousands of pages of documents about him and his wife in the court papers of a related case. (Some of the files were previously reported on by the Polish news site Wirtualna Polska). Those files, as well as interviews in several countries with intelligence sources and with those who knew Rogov, helped piece together a tale of exile and espionage that involved blackmail, deception and a marital crisis with dramatic consequences. (In accordance with Polish law, people mentioned in court files are identified in this story by first name only, except where they have given their consent to be interviewed and named in full. Rogov and his wife are named as they have already been widely identified as protagonists in the case.)
Many who knew Rogov were shocked by his arrest. They described their friend as likable, easy-going and somewhat hapless, and struggled to imagine him as a cunning superspy, or a bomb courier with a secret life blowing up European cities on behalf of Vladimir Putin. “This is a guy who once accidentally sent half-naked photos to the group chat,” said Milia Kashapova, who was Rogov’s campaign manager when he stood in city council elections back in Russia and worked with him at close quarters for several months. “It’s hard for me to believe that all that time he was playing a double game, that he didn’t once come unstuck. If he was really collaborating all along, well, then I’d have to say that Igor Rogov is a genius.”
At the beginning, the only thing Polish investigators had on Rogov was the fact that someone had mailed him the suspicious package. In his first jail interrogations, Rogov maintained it was all a big misunderstanding. He denied any knowledge of the package’s contents and insisted he would never have knowingly done anything to harm his new homeland. “I’m very grateful to Poland for taking me in and I’m ready to help you in any way I can,” he told investigators.
Rogov gave his version of how his name had come to be on the package. His friend Emil, also a Russian opposition activist, had told him that a contact was bringing a parcel from Ukraine and needed someone in Poland to leave it with. Emil said the package contained “presents from Ukraine” and Rogov said he would be fine to pick it up. Some days later he received a call from a woman who introduced herself as Kristina. “I’ve got a package for you from Diesel,” she told him, adding that she had just arrived in Kraków from Ukraine. Rogov had no idea who Diesel was, but assumed this was the package Emil had asked him about. He told Kristina he was away visiting friends, but gave her his address in Sosnowiec and explained how she could mail it to him using a courier service.
Polish authorities soon identified Kristina as a Ukrainian model from Odesa and put out an international arrest warrant for her. She was detained in late August at Amsterdam airport, just before boarding a plane to the US. Once delivered to Polish custody, she explained her side of the parcel story. “Diesel” was her old acquaintance – the nickname was because he worked with secondhand cars. He had found out she was planning to drive to Poland and asked if she might take a package with her. “He said he needed to distribute this stuff to poor people and was helping women and families,” Kristina told investigators. “I did think it was a weird set of things, but Diesel is a pretty weird guy.”
Kristina told investigators that Diesel had put the flask, power bank and other items in her Mercedes before she embarked on the long drive to Kraków. There, she had a rendezvous with a Czech businessman who had offered to pay her €3,000 if she would spend a week with him at a luxury hotel. She ate oysters and drank champagne with the Czech, though at night they retired to separate bedrooms, the case files suggest.
After she bade farewell to her new Czech friend, Kristina remembered the package. She was meant to hand it off in person, but when she called the number Diesel had given her, the man on the other end – Rogov – told her to send it via parcel courier instead. She retrieved the empty shoebox from a pair of €500 Golden Goose sneakers the Czech had bought her and filled the box with Diesel’s items. Then she wrapped it in paper and took the package to a bank of automated parcel lockers as instructed by Rogov.
Having addressed the package, she shoved it into a locker that was a shade too small, causing the packaging to tear. That damage meant the courier company opened the parcel when it reached their sorting facility, discovered the suspicious contents and raised the alarm. This set in train the arrests of Rogov and Kristina. Had she picked a larger locker, the package might have gone undetected and the bomb been assembled and detonated. But by whom? Rogov, or someone else? And on whose orders?
In the days after she sent the package, but before she was arrested, Kristina said she received a call from Diesel’s number. “I’m going to speak. You listen and stay quiet,” said a male voice she did not recognise. He told her the person she had mailed the package to had been detained, and that if she were also detained, she should invent a story about how she had come by the package. “All the correspondence between you and Diesel has been erased; don’t mention Diesel to anyone,” said the man.
The mysterious Diesel was emerging as the key to the parcel plot. Could he be a Russian agent working in Ukraine? Polish authorities had already arrested several Ukrainians recruited by Moscow to carry out arson in Poland, and it was possible that Diesel was part of a Russian sabotage ring with Rogov, using easy access to explosives in Ukraine to source the raw materials before they were assembled and detonated in Poland. Polish authorities issued an international arrest warrant for Diesel and one for Emil, who had told Rogov about the package.
Whoever Diesel was working for, one thing became clear as the questioning continued: Kristina knew nothing about the parcel’s purpose or final destination. In one of her interrogations, as investigators scrolled through her phone demanding ever more details of her encounters with various men in her contacts list, she lost her cool and asked them how this could possibly be relevant to the matter at hand. “All you’ve managed to achieve through your investigations is to prove that I’m a breaker of men’s hearts,” she told them.
Kristina was released in summer 2025, after a brief trial in which the prosecutor accepted that she had carried the items without realising they were dangerous and agreed to soften the charges. She was sentenced to time already served – 304 days – and fined. She did not respond to my requests for further comment.
As for Rogov, it was starting to look as if he, too, could be a tangential player in the bomb plot. He insisted he knew nothing of Diesel, and that the package had his name on it only because he had agreed to help out Emil. The biggest red flag suggesting he might be lying was the set of photographs of various urban scenes in Sosnowiec, marked with arrows, found on his phone. But he had a convincing explanation for that, too. He had sometimes ordered recreational drugs via a Telegram bot, he admitted, and would receive a photo of the pickup location with an arrow marking the drop spot. The only reason some of the locations were close to pipelines or other infrastructure was because these were desolate, empty places where hiding or retrieving a package would draw less attention, he said.
The investigation, which had initially seemed like it would uncover a major Kremlin terror plot against Europe, was not going to plan. There was no proven link to Russia, and the only two arrests were of a clueless Ukrainian model and a young Russian who was apparently guilty only of the occasional purchase of recreational drugs.
But something else was about to come to light about Rogov. Polish investigators were to learn that he had been credibly accused of working for the FSB for years, spying on his friends and colleagues in the Russian opposition. The source of the accusations made them hard to dismiss: it was Rogov’s wife, Irina.
Igor met Irina when they were teenagers. They were both studying veterinary medicine in Saransk, a drab city about 500km (310 miles) south-east of Moscow, where they lived their whole lives before emigrating. Rogov had a cheeky smile and easygoing demeanour that made him friends easily. He got into activism as a student, though to start with he was mostly drawn to local environmental issues. He was then one of thousands of young Russians who helped out with Navalny’s ill-fated attempt to stand against Putin in the 2018 presidential election, and he later became part of Open Russia, the opposition movement set up by the exiled oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
Rogov won respect in opposition circles after an incident in Minsk, in neighbouring Belarus, in August 2020, when Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Putin, declared victory after a rigged presidential election. Protesters took to the streets and Lukashenko launched a violent crackdown. Rogov was in Minsk as part of an informal monitoring mission organised by Open Russia. On the second evening of protests, Rogov and a fellow activist, Artem Vazhenkov, got caught up in an ambush outside a shopping mall. Black-clad riot police grabbed anyone they could lay their hands on and tossed them into armoured trucks; Rogov and Vazhenkov ended up at Minsk’s notorious Okrestina jail with hundreds of others. They were kept in a courtyard, hands tied and face-down on the ground, then moved to a packed cell holding about 40 men. “There was no attempt to get any information, like in Russian prisons. They just beat you for the hell of it,” Vazhenkov told me. The riot police broke Rogov’s ribs and fingers and left his body covered in bruises. The repeated kicks to his head in custody gave him migraines that recurred for years.
After three days of beatings, Rogov was released and deported to Russia. At the Open Russia office back in Moscow, he alternated between laughing and crying as he recounted the ordeal, still moving gingerly from the bruises. “We sent him to a holiday guesthouse for a couple of weeks to recover,” said Andrei Pivovarov, Open Russia’s executive director at the time.
A few weeks later, Igor and Irina, then 23 and 24 years old, got married in Saransk. Vazhenkov, who attended, said it was a “typical Russian wedding”, with vodka, toasts and lots of dancing. Rogov also became more active in Open Russia; the organisation felt partly responsible for the Minsk debacle and supported him to become the official head of their Saransk branch. But a few months later, Open Russia officially dissolved itself, because its designation as “undesirable” by Russian authorities meant activists could be arrested just for being linked to it. So when Rogov ran for a seat on Saransk’s city council in the summer of 2021, he stood as an independent candidate. Getting registered to stand, even in such a low-level vote, required organised and sustained campaigning. Milia Kashapova, a 26-year-old activist formerly associated with Open Russia, moved to Saransk for a few months to be his campaign manager.
The campaign was low-budget – Kashapova lived in the apartment of Rogov’s grandmother – but inventive. They spent long days canvassing on the streets and made Instagram reels featuring Igor and Irina’s cats. In the evenings they sat in bars, often with Irina, and discussed strategy. The police showed up at most public events to intimidate supporters, but this was standard practice in Russian regional politics, and Rogov ploughed on. He and his team went door-to-door, promising those who agreed to hear them out that, if elected, he would bring a breath of fresh air into the corrupt city council. In a campaign post on Telegram, he posted a picture of him and Irina with one of the cats, accompanied by the slogan: “Love and fidelity are the foundations of my family.”
When polling day came, Rogov won 16% of the vote in his district, finishing third behind two broadly pro-Kremlin candidates. He thanked his supporters and announced that he planned to launch several court cases to protest against procedural violations. “Think this is the end? It’s just the beginning,” he wrote on his Telegram channel. But in the following weeks, with a political crackdown on opposition groups under way, the Rogovs decided to leave Russia. They went to Georgia, then to Poland, after winning scholarships on a programme for Russian opposition activists. They arrived in Sosnowiec on 28 February 2022, four days after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Over the next few months, Russia would take a dramatic turn for the worse, as wartime censorship laws kicked in. Henceforth there would be only two choices for most political opponents: jail or exile.
The Rogovs’ new home was a boxy room in a student dormitory, where their neighbour was Danila Buzanov, another exiled Russian activist. Buzanov had spent several years working as a Navalny coordinator in Balakovo, a gritty industrial town known for its nuclear power plant. He had done multiple stints in jail and fled Russia in late 2021, packing a bag and slipping out of the country overnight after police showed up at his mother’s house with another arrest warrant for him.
Buzanov was also starting a new life from scratch in Sosnowiec, and he bonded with Igor and Irina over stories from Russia. “Igor was just a solid, straightforward guy, always joking, always pleasant to talk to, just like the kind of friends I had back at home, the ones I knew since school,” Buzanov told me. The trio’s closeness was amplified by the living arrangements: they shared a bathroom and a kettle, and the doors to their bedrooms were usually left open so the cats – which Irina had managed to exfiltrate from Russia – could roam freely.
Rogov always seemed to have money to go out and socialise. “Absolutely any meeting, with anyone, he was always there, always ready to have a beer and talk,” said Buzanov. Irina worked long hours doing manicures at a beauty salon to supplement her miserly university stipend – but Igor had no job. When Buzanov asked him where the money came from, he said he had sold his car before leaving Russia and was living off the proceeds. Rogov was also ever-present at the political demonstrations organised in nearby Katowice, where the small community of Russian exiles would gather to protest against the war in Ukraine or commemorate the death of Navalny in a Russian jail. Irina rarely joined. “She was completely apolitical; she’d rather go clubbing than go to a rally,” said Buzanov.
Over time, the psychological pressures of a life in exile began to take their toll on the Rogovs’ marriage. Irina found Igor distant and moody, and he was increasingly using recreational drugs. One of the dormitory’s administrative staff later described him in a police interview as a “nice polite boy” who was “rather hapless and seemed as though he wasn’t very good at dealing with things”. The couple’s arguments got progressively worse, and at some point Irina moved out to a room on a different floor, taking the cats with her. Igor grew a moustache and started working out more. He began spending time with another Russian exile studying at the university, named Polina. In April 2023, Irina walked in and caught him and Polina having sex on their old bed. She shouted at them and stormed out. A few minutes later, Buzanov’s phone buzzed with a Telegram message from Irina: “Did you know that Igor has been informing on you and others to the FSB?”
Irina sent a similar message to a group chat of her husband’s old political contacts from Russia, and within minutes, Igor’s phone was lighting up with queries that could be loosely summarised as: “WTF?” After a frenzied discussion between the couple, Igor persuaded Irina to give him her phone and he unsent her message. Later, she and Igor both messaged the group to say it had been a bad joke, apologising for any confusion. But Rogov swiftly confessed to his neighbour, Buzanov: “He was close to tears, and he didn’t try to justify himself, he just began apologising. ‘I’m so sorry, I was forced to do it,’ that sort of thing,” Buzanov told me. Too shocked to ask many follow-up questions, Buzanov put a password on his laptop and warned other friends to be careful around Rogov.
The marriage crisis put Irina in a difficult position, as her Polish residence permit was tied to Igor’s asylum status. She was furious that the whole dormitory knew about his affair, and told him he had humiliated her and ruined her life. She even discussed with friends whether it would be safe for her to move back to Russia, given that she had never directly been involved in opposition politics, and had once gone back to Saransk for a short trip to visit relatives without encountering any problems. But she was still in Sosnowiec in July 2024, when Igor was arrested.
When the news broke, the friends from the group chat assumed it was confirmation that Irina had been telling the truth about Rogov’s FSB collaboration, and that Polish authorities had found out. In reality, for the first few months of his detention, investigators were focused only on the explosive parcel, and had no idea about anything else.
From the files I was given access to, it is not clear how Polish authorities first became aware of Rogov’s alleged FSB links – whether Igor confessed, Irina told them or information was volunteered by someone in the group chat. But on 13 November 2024, roughly four months after Rogov was arrested, investigators added a second charge to his file: along with the charges linked to the explosive, he was also now under investigation for espionage. On the same day, Polish authorities arrested Irina, grabbing her as she crossed the street in Sosnowiec and accusing her of being her husband’s accomplice. Through a series of interrogations of both, the story of Rogov’s collaboration came into focus.
Rogov said he had been recruited during his university years, before he even started out in opposition politics, by a local Saransk FSB officer he knew as Yevgeny. To start with, he was proud of the collaboration, believing the FSB to be a patriotic organisation and grateful for the small amount of extra income it provided. After some time, Yevgeny gave Rogov a burner phone, and told him to keep it hidden at home; it would be their way of communicating. Irina was suspicious of these conversations, and demanded to know who Igor was speaking to so regularly on the secret phone. At first, he told her it was “a person who helps me with studies, deals with various bureaucratic issues and helps me financially”. Later, he confessed that he had been recruited by the FSB. He never told her the details of his conversations with Yevgeny, he claimed, and she never pushed. “It was enough for her to know it wasn’t another woman,” he said.
It is not clear from the files if the initial impulse to get involved in opposition politics came from Rogov or from Yevgeny, but once Rogov started his political activism, the FSB man pushed his recruit to make as many contacts as possible. “I was supposed to keep doing the things I wanted to: climb up the ladder in opposition circles, meet new people, help people, and then at the end tell the FSB about everything,” Rogov recounted. Whenever he came back from a trip to an opposition conference in Moscow or abroad, he told Irina he needed to spend some time working up a report to pass to Yevgeny.
The ideal scenario, Yevgeny told Rogov, would be if on one of these trips abroad, he was approached and pitched by a western intelligence agency. “The point was, I was supposed to become a double agent,” said Rogov. That plan never worked out, but it suggests Yevgeny had big plans for his agent. In every Russian region, one European intelligence official told me, there were numerous FSB operatives focused on infiltrating opposition groups, and these officers would look for ways to elevate their cases beyond local interest. “The low-level officer who did the recruitment will be trying to prove himself by pushing the case as far as possible,” said the source.
This may also explain Rogov’s trip to Minsk in August 2020. A report detailing the mood on the Belarusian streets would have been attractive currency for Yevgeny, an FSB man in the provinces, with his superiors in Moscow. Irina had begged Igor not to go, as they were due to be married a few weeks later, but after several conversations with Yevgeny on his burner phone, Rogov had told her he had no choice.
A few days after Rogov left for Minsk, he went dark. There were widespread reports of mass arrests, and Irina was in such a panic that she retrieved the burner phone and called the single number saved in it. When a man picked up, she said: “I’m Igor’s fiance and I know he talks to someone on this phone. I know that Igor went to Belarus because of you, and I need to find out what happened to him.” The man on the other end said little, then hung up. Soon after, Belarusian authorities released Rogov. It is not clear whether the FSB intervened with Minsk to facilitate his liberty, but his fellow activist Vazhenkov, who was detained at the same time, was not freed for another two days.
When Rogov returned, shaken and bruised from the beatings in Minsk, he was angry with Irina for contacting Yevgeny. He told her she should not poke her nose into his business and that she should never use the secret phone again. Then he hid it somewhere she could not find it.
In the months after Minsk, Rogov could sense that Yevgeny was delighted as he rose to prominence in the local opposition scene, he recalled. But he also claimed to have become genuinely engaged in the opposition struggle, and regretted he had ever agreed to collaborate. “If I had a choice I wouldn’t have done it … but to function in politics and maintain relationships I had to pass information on, because [Yevgeny] could have made everything impossible with one click of his fingers,” he said. On one occasion, when Rogov was at a hospital appointment for his migraines, he was presented with a military draft notice. When he discussed it with Yevgeny, the FSB man suggested he could make it go away. “Yevgeny knew everything about me and he blackmailed me … I had no choice, I felt under constant psychological pressure,” Rogov claimed. It was not clear from the files whether Yevgeny supported or had input into Rogov’s 2021 city council run, nor was it clear whether Rogov continued to receive regular payments from the FSB.
In Rogov’s telling, when he arrived in Poland in February 2022, he thought he had finally escaped Yevgeny’s clutches. He broke off contact, he claimed, and was focused on building a new life in Poland. But three months later, he got a message from an unknown number on Telegram and guessed immediately it was Yevgeny. “In a very veiled way he asked me to bring him some car parts, and I knew that he was demanding I pass on information,” Rogov told investigators. He ignored the message, but Yevgeny kept sending new ones. “Each of his messages caused huge stress for me, because I had family in Russia and I was really afraid of that,” he said. Rogov claimed that his father, still in Saransk, had been approached and told he could be mobilised into the army to fight in Ukraine, even though he was over 50 and should not have been eligible. Rogov assumed it was Yevgeny cranking up the pressure.
Eventually, Rogov said, he collected some fairly mundane information about Buzanov and a few other exiled opposition activists he knew, wrote it up into a Word document, and put it on a USB stick that he gave to Irina, who was taking a trip to Russia in summer 2022 to visit her parents. “I was convinced that the information could not really harm people, that this data could be partially found on the internet,” he claimed to his interrogators. Rogov said he had hoped the information transfer would placate Yevgeny, and also that he believed it could have been useful insurance for Irina: if she was given any trouble by Russian border guards for her links to opposition figures, she could say she was carrying important information for the FSB. (Irina claimed he did not tell her what was on the stick or who it was for until after she arrived in Russia.)
In the end, Irina entered Russia with no trouble. Back in Saransk, she visited the couple’s old apartment, which was now empty, and on her husband’s instructions, retrieved his old burner phone from the back of a kitchen cupboard, where it had remained undisturbed since their emigration. She charged it and called the one number saved in its contacts, as Igor had ordered her to, but there was no reply. She left Russia without handing over the USB stick. When she returned to Poland, she asked her husband if he was still in touch with Yevgeny. “He said no, and that he doesn’t want to maintain contact with him but he doesn’t know how to get out of it,” she said.
Some months later, around the time the marriage started disintegrating, Rogov got a message from another of Yevgeny’s alias accounts. By now, the couple’s asylum papers had come through and Rogov said he had been ready to start a new life, without Russian politics and without the FSB. “I wrote back saying I don’t work in politics any more and I won’t be passing any more information,” he said.
Later in 2023, Vazhenkov – the activist who had also been arrested in Minsk – visited Rogov in Sosnowiec and found his old friend to be a changed man. “We hardly discussed politics … he said he’s no longer political, he’s focused on studying hard. And he was really upset about the breakup with Irina,” Vazhenkov told me. Irina seemed to be adjusting better, having apparently moved on from the dark period immediately after the separation: “She had a lot of plans and she had learned good Polish.”
But neither Igor nor Irina would get to live the new lives they had envisioned. Before long, both were in jail. Last month, three years after Rogov claimed he had broken off contact with Yevgeny and two years after his arrest, a court in Sosnowiec sentenced him to seven years for espionage. Irina was sentenced to three years for aiding him by taking the USB stick to Russia.
The trial was held behind closed doors, and even information about how the defendants pleaded is classified. But lawyers for Igor and Irina told me they were planning appeals. Both lawyers said they would have preferred an open trial, suggesting that if the public knew the facts of the case, they might be less inclined to view the couple as Kremlin superspies. “It’s a shame my client’s case couldn’t be looked at in a more transparent and nuanced way,” said Irina’s lawyer, Katarzyna Matejczyk. However, at a time when Moscow is waging war in Ukraine and organising sabotage attacks in Europe, Polish authorities have little time for shades of grey when it comes to Russian spying. “In the current geopolitical situation, there is no chance of any verdict other than a conviction,” she said.
There was one remaining loose end – the explosive package that had set the whole story in motion. Rogov was found guilty on charges relating to the package, but there were few details in the short public verdict. Jacek Dobrzyński, a spokesperson for the Polish minister who coordinates the country’s security services, told me the parcel’s trail had led back to Moscow. “There is no doubt that this was a Russian plot orchestrated by the Russian secret services,” he said.
However, something did not quite add up. The court files I was able to see yielded no evidence of a Russian link and in fact pointed to a different possibility. During the investigation, one source told Polish authorities they believed “Diesel”, the Odesa car salesman who had given the package to the model Kristina to bring to Poland, actually had links to Ukrainian military intelligence.
This suggested the package might not have been a Russian bomb after all, but a Ukrainian one, transiting Poland and eventually destined for Russia. Since 2022, Kyiv has been running its own campaign of sabotage inside Russia, targeting military officials or pro-war cheerleaders. The latest such attack came this month, when an improvised bomb exploded in a Moscow restaurant during the birthday celebrations of a Russian army general. Three people were killed. My Ukrainian intelligence sources claimed no knowledge of the package sent to Rogov, but one said Kyiv’s sabotage campaign was a delicate issue with allies and usually organised behind their backs: “Almost every European country agrees that it’s legitimate for us to do this, but almost none of them want to cooperate on it.”
The person who could best solve the puzzle of the package, I thought, was the man who sent it, the mysterious Diesel – real name Yuriy Kovalenko. Finding him was easier than expected: he replied to my Facebook messages and agreed to meet at the offices of his lawyer in Odesa, on condition that she also be present. When we met, he was wearing a shell-suit jacket, blue jeans and New Balance trainers, and a kippah – he had rediscovered his Jewish identity in recent years, he said. He told me his nickname was due to his longstanding love of cars, but that these days most people just called him Yuriy.
Kovalenko told me he made a living by importing, fixing up and selling secondhand cars. He categorically denied any links to the Russian intelligence services. He also denied links to the Ukrainian services, but made it clear through his answers that he believed the explosive package had been Ukrainian, not Russian. The final destination was meant to be Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave that borders Poland, he said. However, he insisted he had only found this out later, and that he, too, had been merely a link in a chain of unsuspecting couriers. He claimed he had been given the collection of items by a friend who “possibly had some kind of link” with Ukrainian intelligence services. That friend, he said, asked him to send some items to Poland, so he asked an old acquaintance in the Russian opposition, Emil, if he knew anyone reliable there. Emil gave him Rogov’s name.
Kovalenko was evasive on the specifics: he refused to give further details about the person who supposedly gave him the package and he would not say how he knew the explosives were bound for Kaliningrad. Nor could he explain how they were meant to get there. In addition to his lawyer, he was accompanied to the interview by a man who sat silently next to him and did not introduce himself, claiming to be there “by chance” when asked.
In the shadow world of intelligence games and sabotage plots, it can be hard to discern where the true loyalties of each individual player lie. To add a final complication to the tale, Emil is suspected by many former colleagues in the Russian opposition of being an FSB informer just like Rogov. The full story of the bomb and its various couriers might be lost to history, but the very fact that Ukraine has not arrested Kovalenko, given Poland warned Kyiv of his role in the bomb plot and requested his extradition, points in the direction of the explosives being Ukrainian, not Russian.
And if that is indeed the case, it would be a further strange twist in the story of Igor Rogov, making him at once a Russian FSB informant and a would-be Ukrainian bomb courier.
In the two years since Rogov’s arrest, his old roommate Buzanov has been conflicted over what to think about his former friend. At the start, he felt sorry for Rogov and wrote him letters in prison. Then he was angry that Rogov’s treachery had led to Irina also being jailed, simply for carrying the USB stick into Russia. He also fears the story could prompt unfounded doubts, among Polish authorities or his friends, about his own loyalties. “Our biographies are so similar, and that’s uncomfortable,” he said, as we chatted in a cafe in a city not far from Sosnowiec. Many of Rogov’s friends rejected my interview requests, saying they did not want to be linked publicly to a convicted spy, but Buzanov was happy to talk for hours, keen to show he had nothing to hide.
This is one of the most damaging consequences of Rogov’s collaboration: it has intensified suspicions about Kremlin infiltration among the thousands of Russian opposition and civil society activists who have fled the country in recent years. These suspicions further corrode the effectiveness of the exiled opposition, already weak and divided, as they struggle to remain relevant from their new homes in Warsaw, Berlin or Vilnius.
Rogov was certainly not the only one among their ranks to have been recruited. “I am convinced there were hundreds of us,” a former FSB informant in Navalny’s organisation told the Guardian in 2022. Increasing the sense of paranoia among the opposition is likely part of the FSB strategy in making these recruits in the first place. Kashapova, Rogov’s former campaign manager, told me she used to brush off concerns about infiltration but had become “suspicious of everything and everyone” since Rogov’s arrest.
If the FSB’s goals are clear, Rogov’s motivations remain more elusive. From the testimony I saw, it is hard to say for sure just how reluctant his cooperation was, where his real loyalties lay or whether the information he passed on caused anyone real harm. His friends, without access even to that testimony, have drawn a range of conclusions: some refuse to believe the charges, others accept he may have been an informant but presume he was subjected to unbearable pressure by the FSB, while a third group are furious at him and believe there can be no excuses for collaboration. None can quite square the idea of Rogov as a long-term FSB plant with the young man they thought they knew.
Buzanov, who testified as a witness at the trial, imagines Rogov’s collaboration was likely down to his trademark poor decision-making, which had always got him into scrapes. He is convinced that Rogov was genuinely against Putin, but suspects he was so weak-willed that he was co-opted into working for the FSB, thinking he could make some money without doing anyone much harm. In the same vein, he assumes, Rogov agreed to receive the suspicious package without asking too many questions. “I don’t think he’s some superspy, sent on a special mission to Poland,” he said. “I think he’s just a fool.”
Additional reporting by Ada Petriczko

Zambia elections haunted by ghost of incumbent president’s arch-rival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
04:00:49 UTC
13:00:49 KST

As Zambians go to the polls on Thursday, the ghost of the current president’s predecessor hangs over the elections.
Hakainde Hichilema, 64, is bidding for a second term leading the southern African country after defeating his arch-rival Edgar Lungu by a landslide in 2021.
A feud between the two men, their families and supporters has dominated Zambian politics, to the extent that the quarrel has continued even after Lungu died in South Africa in June 2025.
Zambia’s government went to court to try to stop the burial of Lungu by his family, who did not want Hichilema presiding over a state funeral. In June, South Africa’s supreme court of appeal ruled in favour of Lungu’s family, overturning a previous high court decision in favour of the government.
In this election, Hichilema is facing the Tonse Alliance of opposition parties led by Brian Mundubile, 55, who was a government chief whip under Lungu. Mundubile’s running mate Makebi Zulu acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson during the burial row, and on the campaign trail the two men have promised to bring Lungu’s body back to Zambia for a dignified burial.
The way death is dealt with is very important in Zambia, said Christopher Vandome, a senior research fellow at the thinktank Chatham House. “Even Hichilema supporters want to see due respect given to those that have died,” he said. “When it appears things get messy, it just makes the incumbent look disrespectful.”
The shadow of Lungu has also hung over allegations by the Tonse Alliance that Hichilema has deployed authoritarian tactics during the election campaign, including raiding its offices and detaining 36 members of Mundubile’s team.
Hichilema’s team furiously denied the claims, invoking Lungu’s treatment of Hichilema during the last election. “Zambians know what repression looks like. In 2021, the opposition leader [Hichilema] had been arrested 15 times, Prime TV [a private station] and the Post [a newspaper] had been shut down, and on election day the internet was switched off,” said a spokesperson for the ruling United Party for National Development. “Today the opposition campaigns freely across all 10 provinces, no media house has been closed and the airwaves are open.”
Transparency International Zambia monitors have recorded incidents of police interrupting opposition rallies, said Tamika Halwiindi, a coordinator at the organisation. “Disruptions from the police citing issues to do with safety have been noted to be more biased against the opposition and independents, as opposed to … the ruling party,” she said.
During Hichilema’s term, activists have also reported having peaceful demonstrations shut down. Mputa Ngalande of the Fight Inequality Alliance said he was among a group detained for more than 12 hours in July 2024 when they were protesting against the state power company during a period of 22-hour-a-day blackouts.
Vandome said: “[Hichilema’s] prospects of winning are very high. But his … personal lived experience of how complicated Zambian elections can be has given him this insecurity which is actually counting against him … denting his image in a way he doesn’t have to.”
Zambia’s economy has stabilised since an economic crisis, which was triggered when it defaulted on its debts in 2020 under Lungu. Annual inflation is now 6.5%, compared with 24.6% in July 2021. The government made primary and secondary education free in 2022.
Meanwhile, Zambia has attracted more international investment in recent years due to its huge deposits of copper, a key material in green technologies.
At the start of the month, in a giveaway to young voters, Hichilema, also known by his initials HH and nickname Bally (a slang word for an elder), told a crowd of jubilant university students that he was increasing their accommodation allowance by 50% with immediate effect.
However, the cost of living could still count against Hichilema in the elections, in which almost 8.8 million registered voters will also choose MPs and local councillors. The average annual income rose from $1,127 to $1,318 between 2021 and 2025, according to World Bank data. But prices almost doubled over the same period.
“What people are asking is: ‘If we are doing well economically, why are we not feeling impact on the ground?’” said Ngalende. “Because you will find on the ground that it is very difficult to access three meals a day.”

India fuels worldwide jump in planned coal production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
04:00:48 UTC
13:00:48 KST

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.
The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.
Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.
Wind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to a separate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.
China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.
Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.
“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”

Victims of road crime feel ‘forgotten by system’, official review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
04:00:47 UTC
13:00:47 KST

Bereaved families or seriously injured victims of road crime feel “forgotten by the system” with offences not treated with the seriousness they deserve, an official review has found.
The victims’ commissioner for England and Wales found that many of the thousands afflicted each year by criminal driving felt that “the harm they had suffered mattered less” than that from other serious crimes.
Almost 30,000 people were killed or seriously injured on roads in England and Wales in the year to June 2025, including 1,579 fatalities – more than three times the number of people killed in homicides.
An estimated 25-30% of collisions involve criminal driving, such as drink or drug use or speeding.
The report, based on interviews with injured victims and bereaved families, found many faced long waits without support while police determined whether a collision would be treated as a crime.
They faced “lengthy police investigations, poor communication, court delays and difficulties accessing support” after life-changing criminal collisions, it said.
Some victims told researchers they had waited more than two months for witness statements to be taken. Many were left dissatisfied with eventual sentences, particularly when offenders were not jailed after a road death.
The victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said: “Behind every road death or serious injury is a victim, a grieving family and lives changed for ever. Yet too many victims told me they felt road crime was not treated with the seriousness it deserved and that the harm they had suffered mattered less than other serious crimes.
“Many spoke of lengthy investigations, poor communication, repeated delays and a lack of support at the very time they needed it most. Some were forced to fight for basic information, answers and recognition while trying to cope with unimaginable loss and trauma.”
In her report, she said victims had repeatedly said that “they feel forgotten by the system that is meant to support them”. She said that where victims had received informed support from dedicated officials and specialist charities, “the difference was profound”.
Waxman urged the government to ensure stronger national standards, oversight and accountability for road traffic collision investigations, and more consistent training for police in dealing with trauma, among other recommendations to improve investigations and strengthen support for victims.
The road safety charity Brake said it hoped the report could be a catalyst for change. Ross Moorlock, the chief executive, said: “We bear witness every day to the devastation victims experience in the aftermath of a crash, when too often the criminal justice process adds further trauma.
“This report highlights what we have known for a long time – that road crime is not treated with the gravity it demands, and that road victims are swept aside by systemic failings of a process that is meant to support them.”
The Parliamentary Advisory Council for Transport Safety (PACTS) said it welcomed the report and it urged the government to ensure that all victims get the support they needed, regardless of criminal charges, citing the difficulty in getting evidence after most serious collisions.
Jamie Hassall, the executive director of PACTS, said the testimony in the report showed “the devastating impact of uncertainty, lengthy investigations, poor communication and inconsistent access to support, often at a time of profound grief and trauma”.
He said it made “a compelling case for a more victim-centred approach, with timely and thorough investigations, stronger national standards, trauma-informed practice across all victim-facing agencies, and sustainable funding for specialist support services”.
The government was approached for comment.

China’s ‘brain chip’ drive accelerates with slew of state-backed initiatives
China is throwing the power of the state behind efforts to overtake Elon Musk in a vital frontier technology: brain-computer interfaces
For years, Elon Musk has dreamed of conquering a range of chronic health conditions by inserting computer chips into the human brain. But that vision could become reality fastest in China, where state authorities are launching a coordinated effort to accelerate the nascent industry’s development.
The past few days have seen a string of initiatives related to brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) announced in China, involving parties ranging from state insurance companies to investment banks and local governments.
On Wednesday, PICC Property and Casualty – a major state-owned insurer – announced it had signed the nation’s first commercial insurance policy covering the invasive surgery often needed to implant a BCI in a patient’s brain.
The news sent ripples through the markets, with BCI-linked stocks in Hong Kong climbing as investors bet the insurance breakthrough would help speed up the technology’s commercialisation.
Shares of BCI-related companies rose by 1.59 per cent on Wednesday. Shanghai Heartcare Medical Technology, a maker of neuro-interventional medical devices, was up 1.28 per cent, while software developer BrainAurora Medical Technology rose 1.65 per cent.
PICC Property and Casualty has launched its scheme in partnership with a hospital affiliated with the Zhejiang University School of Medicine in Hangzhou, a tech hub in eastern China home to leading start-ups including AI firm DeepSeek and humanoid robot pioneer Unitree Robotics.
BCI technology, which conventionally requires open-skull surgery to implant electrodes in a targeted region of the brain, allows patients to control digital devices using their thoughts alone.

Meta says it has taken down 756,000 Australian teen accounts as ban enforcement looms
SYDNEY – Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said on Aug 13 that it had taken down more than 750,000 accounts it suspected were held by Australians aged under 16 since a world-first ban on such accounts, and promised more action in the face of possible regulatory intervention.
The company said it had deactivated 462,000 suspect Instagram accounts and 294,000 suspect Facebook accounts from just before the Australian social media ban went live in December to June, up from the 331,000 Instagram accounts and 173,000 Facebook accounts it said it had removed by January.
The world’s largest social media company has said it wants to comply with a law that it and other platforms have vocally opposed, just as Australia’s internet regulator considers an enforcement lawsuit against platforms, including some owned by Meta, that it says have failed to take sufficient steps to comply with the law.
No other platforms have released compliance data that matches the date range given by Meta, but Australian government figures and multiple independent studies have shown more than eight in 10 under-16s were still on social media in the ban’s first three months.
The Australian government proposed the landmark law, which came into force on Dec 10, on concerns about social media’s impact on the physical and mental health of children and young teens.
With other countries around the world considering similar age restrictions, Australia has accused the platforms of intentionally setting the ban up to fail and has introduced a law to double the maximum penalty for non-compliance to A$99 million (S$89 million) and give the regulator greater document discovery powers.
Parliamentary hearing on Aug 14
Representatives of Meta, TikTok, YouTube owner Google and Snap’s Snapchat are scheduled to give evidence in a parliamentary inquiry about the changes on Aug 14, as are regulatory and government officials.
“Enforcement is ongoing, and these numbers will continue to grow,” Meta said in a statement.
“We share the Australian government’s goal of ensuring young people have safe, age-appropriate experiences online, and we are meeting our obligations under the law,” the company added.
A 2025 Australian trial of age assurance technology found products on the market could effectively support a ban. Most large platforms, including Meta’s, rolled out photo-based age estimation software, although they say they typically first subject users to age inference, or assuming a person’s age based on their online activity.
Meta said it was using AI to analyse user profiles for “contextual clues that an account may belong to someone under 16, such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades” and to analyse reports about suspected underage accounts.
The company added that it had removed the option for a person to make more attempts to set up an account if the previous account had been deleted. REUTERS

Child dies without medical assistance in Hola Prystan community in occupied Kherson region — Military Administration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
03:59:00 UTC
12:59:00 KST

Child dies without medical assistance in Hola Prystan community in occupied Kherson region — Military Administration
Svitlana Lynnyk, head of the Hola Prystan Military Administration, reported this to Ukrinform.
"There are only two pharmacies left in the community — one in the city and one in Nova Zburivka. There was some supply while people were still being transported, but now they are simply selling what remains. Hospitals are not operating, and first-aid medical centers have not been operating for a long time. In the village of Tavriyske, there is still someone from the medical staff at a medical facility. In Nova Zburivka, there was an ambulance for some time that had been transferred from Hola Prystan, but they have not been there since last year," Lynnyk said.
She added that the nearest places where residents can receive at least some medical assistance are Bekhtery, Zaliznyi Port and Skadovsk. Skadovsk has the nearest hospital.
"The quality of treatment there is at the lowest level. Mortality from 'treatment' has increased, complications arise, and people work unprofessionally. From there, people travel to Henichesk, Kalanchak and Crimea to seek medical care," Lynnyk said.
She said that a mother in the community was unable to take her 12-year-old child to a hospital, and there was no one available to provide medical assistance locally.
According to Lynnyk, the child had a high fever, but there were neither medicines nor medical personnel available. To receive medical assistance, the child would have had to be taken out of the settlement to an intersection, where an ambulance could pick them up. The mother had no way to do this, she added.
The head of the military administration noted that the occupation authorities, including Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-appointed head of the occupied part of Kherson region, only talk about a "difficult situation" and "give instructions," but these are empty words.
The Russians have not distributed humanitarian aid in the villages of the community's administrative districts for at least eight months, while residents of the city have not seen such aid for more than a year.
"The occupation authorities do not go anywhere near Hola Prystan. From time to time, a priest from the Moscow Patriarchate comes and distributes humanitarian aid, but only to those who have a Russian passport. And even then, for the aid to be delivered, people had to contribute 100 rubles each for some time," she said.
According to Lynnyk, during the winter the occupation authorities did not even pretend to be trying to help the population. Another winter will once again bring the challenge of surviving the cold, as there is no gas supply, heating or electricity.
Lynnyk said that residents are installing outdoor summer stoves known as kabytsias in their yards. There is no firewood available to heat homes, and there are no places where residents can safely cut wood because Russian forces have mined the forests.
The head of the military administration, who managed to evacuate members of her family from the occupied territory three months ago, said that they had been forced to survive the winter in apartment buildings where the temperature was as low as 3°C, resulting in frostbite to their toes.
As Ukrinform reported, the bodies of two children were found on a city beach in occupied Henichesk.

Israeli settlers besiege Palestinian families in West Bank’s Qusra

03:54:09 UTC
12:54:09 KST

Israeli settlers’ siege of Palestinian homes in West Bank enters fourth day
Dozens of settlers besiege three Palestinian families in Qusra, cutting off water, power and essential supplies.
Israeli settlers have besieged three Palestinian families inside their homes in the occupied West Bank, cutting off water and electricity in a campaign residents described as an attempt to steal their land.
Security camera footage from the village of Qusra, south of Nablus, on Wednesday shows Israeli settlers surrounding one of the houses.

Trapped residents said Israeli soldiers had failed to disperse the settlers despite intervening earlier in the day.
Aisha Abu Rida, one of the residents under siege, told Al Jazeera that the siege began on Sunday, with settlers blocking all entrances to her home.
“We are surrounded by settlers, but we are steadfast, God willing. We will not leave our home, no matter what happens. Despite the water and electricity being cut off, we will remain steadfast,” she said.
“Despite their repeated attacks, which are aimed at displacing us, God willing, we will remain steadfast and stay in our homes, even if we are martyred,” she added.
Turkiye’s Anadolu news agency reported that the mayor of Qusra had been told by the Israeli army that the military operation will continue until Sunday morning.
‘Living in fear’
Loai Ridi, an American-Palestinian who owns a house in the village, said his brother Qusai Abu Rida and 18-year-old nephew, Ahmed, were among those trapped.
Speaking to Al Jazeera from Toledo, in the United States, he said the family was relying on a temporary solar power system and leftover well water from the winter after supply lines were cut.
“He [Qusai Abu Rida] does not want to leave the home. Because if he leaves the home, the settlers will take over immediately,” Ridi said. “It’s really very, very difficult. He just told me, ‘I only have supplies for two to three days left. And if no one is able to provide us with food, I am not sure what else I can do’.”
Ridi said Israeli forces had done little to intervene when his brother had called for help on Sunday, and alleged the soldiers had knelt to pray alongside the settlers at the scene, in footage that has since circulated on social media.
“They basically did nothing,” he said.
Earlier on Wednesday, more Israeli forces arrived on the scene, dismantled the settlers’ tent and clashed with about 50 to 60 of the group before withdrawing. “They were unable to evacuate the settlers because they were not firm with them,” Ridi said. “They should have picked them up in vans and taken them away.”
The Israeli military said later on Wednesday that it would deploy an additional infantry battalion to the area, with its chief of general staff ordering continued efforts “to strengthen order and operational control” and prevent further incidents.
A day earlier, the Israeli military had said it received reports of settlers entering and seizing Palestinian homes and land in the area, describing the activity as “illegal, reprehensible and unacceptable” and disruptive to residents’ daily lives. It added that disciplinary action would be taken against security personnel filmed at the site in preceding days.
Ridi said his family was “living in fear”.
“They are being harassed and attacked by the settlers,” he said. “I cannot do anything about it.”
‘Ethnic cleansing’
Qusra sits in Area B of the occupied West Bank, nominally under Palestinian civil administration. The village has faced a string of recent attacks, including the burning of a newly built mosque last month.
In the neighbouring village of Jalud, a similar two-week siege in July forced two Palestinian families off their land before settlers took over the property.
Violence and land seizures in the occupied West Bank have intensified over the past months, with Jewish settlers emboldened by the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, which has overseen a rapid expansion of settlement construction in the territory.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in the occupied West Bank in settlements that are considered illegal under international law, alongside roughly three million Palestinians. Israel has occupied the territory since 1967.
According to the Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now, there are 146 illegal settlements in the West Bank and a further 390 smaller outposts.
Breaking the Silence, an Israeli rights group, said on X that while settlers commit “daily terror against Palestinian men, women, and children … neither this terror nor ethnic cleansing would be possible without the [Israeli] army’s support”.
The United Nations has also warned that the situation in the occupied West Bank has reached a “breaking point”.
According to UN figures, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 76 Palestinians, including 18 children, in the occupied territory so far this year. About 3,800 Palestinians, nearly half of them children, have also been displaced by settler violence, demolitions and evictions.
UN’s Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov said on Tuesday that the UN has documented more than 1,430 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across roughly 260 Palestinian communities in 2026, with many carried out in the presence of Israeli forces.
He also noted that Israeli authorities have also advanced or approved roughly 12,360 settlement housing units across the West Bank this year, including 5,160 in occupied East Jerusalem.
“These are interconnected steps, not isolated developments,” Alakbarov said, warning that they were reshaping the occupied West Bank, weakening Palestinian governance and advancing “de facto annexation”.

US stocks tick toward records as oil prices drop and inflation gets less bad
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. stock market is ticking toward an all-time high Thursday following the latest sign that inflation is getting less bad. Stocks also got a lift from easing oil prices in their latest yo-yo move.
The S&P 500 climbed 0.5% and was on track to top its record set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 123 points, or 0.2%, as of 11:30 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.6% higher.
Wall Street relaxed after a report showed prices at the U.S. wholesale level were 4.7% higher last month than a year earlier. While that’s still very high, it’s not as bad as June’s 5.5% inflation rate at the wholesale level, and it was slightly better than economists expected.
If inflation continues to trend that way, the Federal Reserve could decide to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money.
Fed officials are split on whether they should have already begun hiking interest rates. But Thursday’s report, following a similar update on inflation at the U.S. consumer level the day before, has traders now betting on just a 34% chance that the Fed will raise rates at its next meeting in September. That’s down from the roughly 50% probability seen two days ago, according to data from CME Group.
U.S. stocks are rising toward an all-time high.
Any increase by the Fed would be the first in more than three years. It also could anger President Donald Trump, who has been lobbying for lower interest rates.
Treasury yields sank in the bond market, which eases pressure on stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64% from 4.68% late Wednesday and from 4.72% on Monday, though it’s still well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran sent oil and gasoline prices surging.
Oil prices eased back on Thursday, helping to limit worries about inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 1.1% to $88.03.
It’s been swinging sharply recently and pinballed between $72 and $102 last month as hopes rose and fell that a deal in the war could allow oil tankers to freely exit the Middle East again and deliver crude worldwide.
On Wall Street, stocks in the real-estate industry helped lead the way. When interest rates are lower and bonds are paying less in yield, the dividends that many real-estate investment trusts pay look more attractive. Lower mortgage rates could also drive more activity in the housing market.
AvalonBay Communities, which owns apartments across the country, rose 2.5%. Builders FirstSource, which sells countertops and other building materials, added 1.3%.
Fossil Group rose 4% after the seller of watches and jewelry became one of the latest companies to report better results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Such reports have helped drive Wall Street to its records because stocks tend to track the path of corporate profits over the long term.
They helped offset a drop for Cisco Systems, which fell 8.6% even though the tech giant reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than Wall Street expected. Analysts said investors may be worried about its profit margins going forward, and its stock has been shaky through the summer amid worries that AI-related stocks in general shot too high.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi again had one of the world’s biggest moves and jumped 3.6%. Seoul has been home to the world’s sharpest swings for artificial-intelligence stocks because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

FSSAI warns influencers of legal action over unverified food claims
NEW DELHI: From "boosts immunity" to "rich in nutrients", food claims endorsed by celebrities and social media influencers are now under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India's (FSSAI) scanner. In a significant move aimed at curbing misleading promotions, the regulator has warned influencers and celebrities that endorsing unverified food claims could invite legal action, even as it cracked down on manufacturers selling unsafe food products.The advisory comes at a time when food brands are increasingly relying on digital creators and celebrities to market health drinks, protein supplements, snacks and packaged foods to millions of consumers online. FSSAI has asked influencers to verify that every claim made by a brand is truthful, scientifically substantiated and compliant with food safety regulations before lending their name or credibility.The regulator said endorsements are more than advertisements because consumers often trust the people promoting them. It cautioned influencers against amplifying claims such as "boosts immunity" or "rich in nutrients" unless they are backed by evidence and permitted under food laws.
Misleading food advertisements and endorsements, it said, can attract action under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018.Alongside the advisory, FSSAI prohibited the manufacture, sale and distribution of food products made by M/s Shree Shyam Foods, M/s Bharat Food Products and M/s KDP Food Industry after government laboratories found their ghee and mustard oil products unsafe for consumption.
The regulator also penalised Dharwad Mishra Pedha and Food Processing Industry in Karnataka after its Motichoor laddoos were found to contain Tartrazine at 2,670.5 mg/kg, more than 26 times the permissible limit of 100 mg/kg. Shree Chemfood Pvt Ltd of Gujarat was similarly penalised after samples of iodised salt were found to be substandard and misbranded.FSSAI has also urged consumers to report misleading food advertisements and celebrity endorsements through its Food Safety Connect platform.

Use medical tourists' money to treat poor Indians: Panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
03:48:21 UTC
12:48:21 KST

NEW DELHI: Revenue earned from foreign patients and affluent Indians should help fund treatment for poorer patients, a Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare has recommended, proposing that corporate hospitals adopt a cross-subsidisation model to make advanced healthcare more affordable.The panel said hospitals that benefit from government concessions such as subsidised land, tax incentives and 100% foreign direct investment (FDI) should earmark part of the revenue generated from medical tourism and high-paying patients to provide advanced tertiary care to economically weaker Indians.The recommendation is part of the committee's report on the affordability and accessibility of healthcare, which noted that India's corporate hospital sector has recorded strong growth driven by high-value procedures, rising medical tourism and increasing revenue per occupied bed. While acknowledging India's emergence as a global healthcare destination, the panel said the benefits of this growth must also reach patients who cannot afford expensive treatment.Observing that private health insurance penetration in India remains low and out-of-pocket expenditure continues to push many families into financial distress, the committee said a structured cross-subsidy mechanism could improve access to life-saving tertiary care for poorer patients.
It said hospitals receiving government support should share part of the gains from medical tourism and premium-paying patients with economically weaker sections.The panel also recommended that corporate hospitals reserve a defined quota of beds under government-funded health insurance schemes such as Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY at standard package rates to ensure that beneficiaries have access to advanced treatment at leading private hospitals.
To address the uneven distribution of healthcare infrastructure, the committee proposed linking government incentives, including subsidised land, tax benefits and FDI facilitation, to investment in tier-2, tier-3 and rural areas. It also recommended expanding public-private partnerships and extending financial and technology support to smaller hospitals in underserved regions.The recommendations form part of a broader roadmap to make healthcare more affordable. The committee has also proposed capping private hospital room rents in major metropolitan cities at the average tariff of nearby three-star hotels, standardising treatment package rates, improving price transparency and expanding government health spending to reduce out-of-pocket expenditure.

US senator demands answers on USS Abraham Lincoln’s extended deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
03:46:52 UTC
12:46:52 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
US Sen. Richard Blumenthal on Wednesday demanded answers from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has remained at sea for more than 250 days.
"There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months," Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, wrote in a letter.
The senator said the Lincoln departed Naval Base San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, for what was initially planned as a seven-month deployment. Its deployment was scheduled to end in May but has since been extended, with no publicly announced return date.
Blumenthal said the carrier has gone more than 200 days without a port call, setting a record for consecutive days at sea.
The extended deployment has raised broader questions about whether the Navy can sustain the operational demands being placed on its aircraft carrier fleet while maintaining crew welfare, equipment readiness and scheduled maintenance, according to Blumenthal.
“These reports warrant immediate attention, but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force,” he wrote.
The senator said the Lincoln's prolonged deployment is particularly significant because it comes amid continuing US military operations involving Iran and the possibility that American naval forces could remain in the region for an extended period.
“If the Administration intends to maintain a prolonged military campaign or an elevated carrier presence in the region, it must explain how it intends to ensure today's operational requirements do not create tomorrow's readiness crisis,” Blumenthal wrote.
He also warned that prolonged deployments can compound the inherent risks of operating an aircraft carrier, where sailors work around jet engines, fuel, weapons, heavy machinery and electrical systems while facing potential threats from adversaries. 
Questions over soldiers' fatigue, morale, mental health 
According to Blumenthal, fatigue, deferred maintenance and reduced opportunities for rest and recovery can further increase those risks.
Blumenthal asked the Pentagon to explain how it intends to maintain carrier strike group operations in the Middle East over the next 12 to 24 months if current requirements continue.
He also requested details about each extension of the Lincoln's deployment, including who authorized them and what operational requirements were cited.
The senator asked the Navy to provide a list of significant habitability and quality-of-life problems identified aboard the carrier, including issues involving hygiene supplies, mold, toilets, laundry facilities and water supplies, along with the corrective measures taken.
He also requested information about metrics used to monitor fatigue, morale, mental health and crew readiness, as well as any increases in safety incidents, medical issues or disciplinary problems associated with the deployment.
Blumenthal further questioned whether the Navy’s current force structure and deployment model can sustainably meet the demand for aircraft carriers.
Finally, he asked the Pentagon to explain the military objective behind the Lincoln's continued deployment in relation to Iran and how officials determine whether its presence remains necessary.
Sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have reportedly attempted to go overboard during the aircraft carrier’s prolonged deployment in the Middle East, raising fresh concerns among military families and lawmakers about the mental health and living conditions of its crew.
Reports by Navy Times and Stars and Stripes describe multiple incidents involving sailors attempting to jump overboard as the ship enters its ninth month at sea. The carrier, carrying roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines, has spent more than 250 consecutive days without a port visit, according to reports.

NEET-PG aspirants get wrong exam city texts after NBEMS glitch
Unknown

Several candidates reported receiving two different SMS messages within hours, each mentioning a different test city (representative image)
NEW DELHI: Hundreds of NEET-PG 2026 aspirants were left confused after receiving incorrect SMS alerts about their allotted examination cities, prompting the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) to issue a clarification that a technical glitch had led to wrong messages being sent to some candidates.Several candidates reported receiving two different SMSes within hours, each mentioning a different test city. In one such case, an aspirant was first allotted Gudur (Andhra Pradesh) and later received another message assigning Noida (Uttar Pradesh) as the examination city.In a public notice issued on Wednesday, NBEMS said the test city allocation had been completed as scheduled and uploaded on the official applicant portal. However, "due to some technical issues", the test city conveyed to some candidates through SMS was incorrect. It said fresh SMSes and emails carrying the correct test city had subsequently been sent to the affected candidates.
The Board advised candidates not to rely on SMS messages and instead verify their allotted examination city through the NBEMS applicant portal, which it said contains the correct details for all candidates.
It also urged aspirants to rely only on official communications and beware of fake websites and misinformation.The clarification comes just days before the conduct of the national postgraduate medical entrance examination, with candidates already making travel and accommodation arrangements based on their allotted test cities. The confusion triggered anxiety among aspirants, many of whom took to social media to seek clarification after receiving conflicting messages.NBEMS maintained that the applicant portal carries the correct examination city details and asked candidates to refer to it for authentic information. It said corrected SMSes and emails have been issued wherever required.
