====================================================================================================

Montana State University launches a new Wool Lab to revive an old industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:53:01 UTC
03:53:01 KST

Montana State University launches a new Wool Lab to revive an old industry
On a hot August afternoon, wool expert Brent Roeder strode among sheep, combing his fingers through their fleece to assess color, length and uniformity. Roeder, an extension specialist at Montana State University, tends to the college-owned flock at an old off-campus cavalry barracks called the Fort Ellis Research and Teaching Farm. The flock exists to give agriculture students hands-on experience. That includes learning how to raise high-quality sheep for sales like the one in Miles City that Roeder plans to take six animals to this September.
“You’re taking your best of your best,” Roeder said.
Roeder is on a mission to revitalize the regional wool industry. He manages the university’s new Wool Lab, a facility dedicated to making wool production more efficient and more profitable for Montana’s sheep ranchers. He has spent a lifetime watching synthetic fiber undermine demand for wool. Now, Roeder hopes the new facility can show students “why the wool industry is still important and relevant.”
“I’m a little gray-haired. Finding this next generation was part of the investment in this lab, to be able to teach that next generation so they could innovate,” Roeder said.
The new building opened in July. The on-campus facility also contains the Montana Department of Livestock’s Veterinary Diagnostic Lab and the Montana Department of Agriculture’s Analytical Lab. The Wool Lab cost about $10 million, funded by a combination of legislative appropriations and donations from private industry.
The Wool Lab’s previous home, located about a mile from the new one, dates back to the 1940s. The Montana Legislature first approved funding for that lab in 1945, when the industry was mid-boom after years of substantial government subsidies for the wool industry during World War II. In the mid-twentieth century, wool labs were common at land-grant universities. But today, the only similar facility outside of Bozeman is at Texas A&M, according to Roeder.
The disappearance of wool labs tracks with the wool industry’s slow and steady decline. Over the last 80 years, the U.S. sheep herd has decreased by 90%. That’s partly driven by rising agricultural input costs, regional drought and an increase in imported lamb.
Montana has not been immune to the squeeze. Over the last 30 years, in-state wool production has dwindled by two-thirds, and sheep-ranching operations have declined by half. As of 2024, Montana was home to about 190,000 sheep and about 1,100 wool operations.
Synthetic fabric has overwhelmed the market share that wool once ruled, according to Roeder.
“It’s really only been over the last 70 or 80 years that synthetics have come in. And they’ve completely dominated the whole fabric manufacturing system,” Roeder said.
So Roeder has aligned himself with the natural-fiber industry, which includes cotton and wool-based clothes. He decries synthetic clothing’s environmental cost — it’s made from fossil fuels, releases microplastics when washed and doesn’t biodegrade — and describes natural products as more comfortable to wear.
“I’m not against plastic or the oil industry, because I have a lot of friends in that industry, but maybe we shouldn’t be making $5 plastic shirts and importing them from China,” Roeder said.
Roeder wants the Wool Lab to innovate cheaper ways to produce and process wool. Montana ranchers help steer the direction of the lab’s research. Every two years, 25 sheep producers come to campus to grade Roeder’s work.
Those assessments aren’t public. But Stefanie Leach, executive assistant with the Montana Wool Growers Association, which wrote a $100,000 check for the new lab, told Montana Free Press the facility is doing necessary work.
“Without the research there, our industry stays stagnant. Without them doing research, we have no new innovation,” Leach said.
One way the lab hopes to boost the regional market is by helping ranchers breed animals that produce wool that can be worn comfortably next to human skin. That requires that wool fibers be less than 30 microns (0.001 inches) thick. Next-to-skin wool doesn’t itch. And most of the country’s domestic supply of next-to-skin wool comes from Idaho, Utah, Wyoming and Montana, according to Leach.
Becky Weed, a sheep rancher near Belgrade who utilized Wool Lab resources during her early days in the business in the 1980s, said modern ranchers don’t just need help producing a particular grade of wool — they need help processing and selling it. She said the market was different when she got into the wool industry four decades ago.
“The mainstream wool growers at that time weren’t paying as close attention to what happened to their fiber, who was using it, who was marketing it, and how much they were getting paid for their wool,” Weed said.
But that changed as the industry shrank. Now, sheep ranchers have to be more intentional, Weed said.
She said she’s glad the Wool Lab is getting “a shot in the arm” and praised Roeder as “a real leader amongst the wool growers.”
Roeder said conditions for wool producers are improving — the commodity price has doubled in the last two years and is currently at a six-year high — but the industry still suffers from years of economic neglect.
“We have not had enough profitability in the industry for so long, there’s been no investment in facilities, structures, new barns and handling equipment. There just wasn’t the revenue to do it,” Roeder said.
As Roeder herded and handled sheep at the Fort Ellis farm, he wore a hat decorated with an American flag in the shape of a lamb, a token of thanks from the Teton County Fair, where he’s spent more than a decade helping 4H participants raise and show their sheep and goats. His belt buckle, emblazoned with “Texas A&M,” commemorates his 1993 championship in intercollegiate wool judging.
He said he’s confident the wool industry isn’t going anywhere, and that a next generation of Montana sheep ranchers has plenty to learn, and to teach.
“Don’t ever put your fingers inside,” Roeder said, dropping his hand between a sheep and the pen’s metal railing. He pulled away just before the animal’s head butted the rail where his fingers had been.
“That’s instinct,” he said.

Eurovision bars countries at war from hosting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:53:00 UTC
03:53:00 KST

Eurovision bars countries at war from hosting
August 12, 2026
Eurovision Song Contest organizers announced rule changes that would prevent countries involved in an armed conflict from hosting the event.
Israel and Ukraine are among the countries the rule could affect, with both having enjoyed recent success in the competition.
What did the Eurovision organizers say?
Eurovision is typically staged by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition as part of a co-production involving members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," the EBU said.
The EBU may commission an independent security assessment if necessary. If the winning broadcaster is deemed unable to stage the contest, another broadcaster will be selected.
Why is the Eurovision changing the rules?
The EBU did not name any particular country as the reason, but Israel finished second at Eurovision in both 2025 and 2026.
Five countries — Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland — boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna, saying they could not participate alongside Israel because of the war in Gaza. Israel is currently involved in the war in Iran.
The new rule formalizes a challenge Eurovision has faced before.
Ukraine hosted the contest in 2017 despite fighting in the east of the country, but after winning Eurovision in 2022 it was unable to stage the following year's event because of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Liverpool instead hosted Eurovision 2023 in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf.
Russia has been excluded from Eurovision since 2022, when the EBU banned it following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
What else is changing about the Eurovision?
Under the new rules, the EBU is raising the minimum age for performers from 16 to 18 to reduce pressure on young artists.
Lead vocals must also be performed live and cannot be supported by pre-recorded voices.
The EBU said the clarification was intended to protect the integrity of performances and ensure audiences hear the lead singer live.
Eurovision director Martin Green said the contest's rules were reviewed each year to keep the competition fair and transparent.
Next year's contest will be held in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas following Bulgarian pop singer Dara's victory in Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with "Bangaranga."

Former Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:46:30 UTC
03:46:30 KST

The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.
Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.
On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.
A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”
Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.
The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.
On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.
But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.
The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.
Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.

A country in a state of war will not be able to host Eurovision – updated contest rules
Kyiv • UNN
The European Broadcasting Union has updated the Eurovision rules, according to which the winning country automatically loses the right to host the contest in the event of an armed conflict or geopolitical tensions. An alternative host will be determined after a security assessment.
The European Broadcasting Union has updated the rules for holding the Eurovision Song Contest. Now, the winning country automatically loses the right to host the contest if it is involved in an armed conflict or faces a tense geopolitical situation. This is stated on the official Eurovision website, reports UNN.
The winning broadcaster automatically loses the right to host the contest if an armed conflict, a tense geopolitical situation, or any other circumstance significantly affects the safety, security, or stability of its country or the immediate region
If necessary, the European Broadcasting Union may commission an independent security assessment of the winner’s region. Following such an assessment, the Union will consult with the Advisory Group to determine whether the winning country is capable of safely hosting the contest.
If it is determined that the winner cannot serve as the host, the EBU will appoint an alternative host broadcaster. The appointed host broadcaster will assume all rights, obligations, and responsibilities related to staging the Contest, including responsibility for organizing, producing, and staging the event. The host broadcaster will organize the Contest in its own name and will not be required to hold the event on behalf of another participating country
It should be noted that in 2022, the Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra won the international song contest "Eurovision 2022" with the song Stefania. The contest was held in Turin, Italy.
The following contest was supposed to take place in Ukraine, but it was relocated to the United Kingdom because of the hostilities.

Bulgaria became the winner of the Eurovision Song Contest 2026 for the first time in history; it was represented by DARA with the song Bangaranga. The contest final took place on Saturday evening, while Ukraine’s representative Leleka finished in ninth place.

Israelis approached me with Hunter Biden’s laptop – Tucker Carlson to Rick Sanchez (VIDEO)
US journalist Tucker Carlson has said that people linked to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approached him with material from Hunter Biden’s laptop ahead of the 2020 US presidential election.
The laptop belonging to the son of then-presidential candidate Joe Biden became the focus of a major controversy weeks before the vote after the New York Post published material from it pointing to alleged influence-peddling involving the Biden family. The story was widely questioned by US media at the time, while dozens of former intelligence officials suggested it bore the hallmarks of a Russian information operation.
Speaking to RT’s Rick Sanchez on Wednesday, Carlson recalled that he was working at Fox News at the time and said he sent one of his producers to meet a person connected to Netanyahu.
“People connected to Netanyahu came to us,” he said, adding that they claimed to have information from Hunter Biden’s laptop.
“It was the Israelis who were pushing that,” Carlson said, referring to the laptop allegations. “They called me.”
Carlson said he believed the material from the laptop had been circulating before the device was reportedly left at a Delaware computer repair shop and suggested that somebody had obtained it from cloud storage.
Asked who originally obtained it, Carlson said he did not know. “Some people claim it was the Russian security services that did that. Maybe. I have no idea.” he said.
Carlson went on to suggest that Netanyahu did not want Joe Biden to win the 2020 election, pointing to the Israeli leader’s close relationship with Donald Trump. He characterized the episode as Israeli interference in US politics.
The laptop scandal erupted in October of 2020, weeks before the US presidential election, when a Delaware computer repair technician released copies of a hard drive containing emails suggesting foreign influence peddling by the Biden family. The New York Post was the first outlet to publish the story.
Thereafter, CNN published an analysis titled ‘The anatomy of the New York Post’s dubious Hunter Biden story.’ Talking heads and hosts frequently asked if Donald Trump was spreading ‘Russian disinformation’ by bringing up the scandal during presidential debates.
Politico published a breaking story of a letter from 51 intelligence officials, running the headline: ‘Hunter Biden story is Russian disinfo, dozens of former intel officials say’.
The Washington Post published multiple opinion pieces downplaying the scandal, while the New York Times published an article titled ‘Trump Had One Last Story To Sell. The Wall Street Journal Wouldn’t Buy It’. US federal broadcaster NPR refused to cover the story at all, while the British Guardian published pieces criticizing social media platforms for allowing the story to circulate, citing “likely misinformation.”
The authenticity of significant amounts of data from the laptop was subsequently confirmed by major US news organizations, including the NYT and WaPo, reversing their initially dismissive stances.

Russia: Why is the Yabloko party barred from the elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:37:00 UTC
03:37:00 KST

Why is Russia's Yabloko party barred from upcoming election?
August 12, 2026
On Monday, Russia's highest court upheld a lawsuit against the anti-war opposition party Yabloko. Its candidates will now be barred from taking part in the parliamentary election from September 18 to 20.
The case against Yabloko was brought by the pro-Kremlin party Rodina, which accused it of infringing copyright with its election campaign materials. Rodina also made the claim that Yabloko had engaged in extremist activities and had received illegal financing from abroad.
The verdict was pronounced by presiding judge Vyacheslav Kirillov. This was the same judge who, in April, banned the Russian human rights organization Memorial and designated it an extremist organization. Kirillov also previously dismissed legal complaints against the Russian prison service filed by the prominent opposition politician Alexei Navalny. Navalny spent many years in Russian prisons prior to his death in jail in 2024.
At least 500 people gathered in front of the court to show their support for Yabloko, distributing apples and sang songs. The name Yabloko — "apple" in English — derives from the initials of the party's three founders, Grigory Yavlinsky, Yury Boldyrev and Vladimir Lukin (YaBL). The apple is now well-known as a symbol of the party.
At the end of the nine-hour court session, security services threatened the people gathered outside the courthouse with arrest, also warning young men that they could be taken to an army enlistment office.
"You are mistaken if you believe that, with a stroke of a pen, you can write off millions of people who want peace, freedom and a normal future for their country," Nikolai Rybakov, the leader of Yabloko, wrote on Telegram that evening.
He insisted that the party had not broken any Russian laws, and announced he would appeal the judgement.
Kremlin 'got scared'
Yavlinsky, one of Yabloko's founders, said those in power were afraid of Yabloko's program, which calls for an election "for peace, freedom and a life without fear" — because, he said, "removing a party with a platform like this from the election, without any real grounds, is the political system exposing itself."
The lawsuit came at the same time as an appeal by Russian opposition and cultural leaders living abroad for people to support Yabloko.
They include the politician Yulia Navalnaya, Alexei Navalny's widow, as well as Lyubov Sobol, Ilya Yashin and Andrei Pivovarov. The writer Dmitry Bykov, human rights activist Oleg Orlov and other prominent people also voiced their support for Yabloko.
Navalnaya, who now leads the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) her husband set up in 2011, responded to the verdict. The Kremlin was originally going to let Yabloko stand in the election, she said, but those in power "got scared" and had the party blocked.
Navalnaya wrote on Telegram that the powers-that-be had observed a development they wanted to stop at any cost: People were starting to join forces. This, she wrote, was less about support for Yabloko than the possibility for millions of Russians to express how they really felt about President Vladimir Putin and the war in Ukraine.
Andrei Pivovarov, a political activist who lives in exile in Germany and is a coordinator of the Russian Antiwar Committee, explained that the opposition had not believed supporting Yabloko would bring about swift political change or an end to the war. The aim, he said, had been to make visible the extent of anti-war sentiment in Russia.
"There would have been a dozen parties on the ballot who are pro-war, and one that is pro-peace. The war wouldn't end even if Yabloko were to get representatives into the State Duma. But we would have seen that a lot of Russians oppose the war," said Pivovarov. This view, he added, would not simply disappear now Yabloko has been barred from standing.
What were Kremlin's plans for Yabloko?
In an interview with DW, Political scientist Ivan Preobrazhensky speculated that the banning of Yabloko could be a consequence of a power struggle between different interest groups in the Kremlin. He suggested that the security bloc allied with the federal security service, the FSB, may have wanted Yabloko to act as a counterweight to the New People party. This is regarded as a project of Sergey Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of the presidential administration.
Another version of events is that Kiriyenko himself may have tried to create the impression of political rivalry, and underestimated the potential of anti-war feeling in the country.
Preobazhensky said the government underestimated the number of people in Russia who oppose the war and are ready to support a political force campaigning for an end to the war in Ukraine. Surveys, he said, indicate that there is substantial demand for such a political alternative. He also believes the Kremlin initially intended to let Yabloko run in the election but changed its mind when it saw how much support the party was getting.
Another political scientist, Mikhail Vinogradov, thinks there was a different calculation behind the move. If Yabloko had scored very few votes in the election, the Kremlin could have painted a picture of a population solidly behind the war. A poor result would also have served to disillusion those who oppose it.
Barring Yabloko makes independent election monitoring more difficult. The party is now no longer allowed to send representatives to monitor polling stations. Roman Udot, a Russian specialist in electoral observation, explained that Yabloko has also enabled access for independent observers in the past.
Does the Kremlin have situation under control?
The State Duma election is taking place at a time of growing uncertainty in Russian society, said Margarita Zavadskaya from the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. She pointed to data from the Russian Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), which regularly records the population's prevailing view of the situation in the country: optimism or alarm?
At the end of July, 57% of those surveyed said that they were worried. This is the highest level since mobilization in the autumn of 2022. FOM surveys should be taken with a grain of salt, but Zavadskaya said an increase like this in high summer indicates that "something is not going according to plan."
She gave the increase in drone attacks, deaths, fires in warehouses and rumors of a fresh mobilization as reasons for the prevailing sentiment, and added that the summer of 2026 has been the most unsettling for the people in Russia since the beginning of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine almost five years ago. She also believes the number of people who support the war is going down rather than up.
Russia's leadership, therefore, has good reason to be nervous.
"For the Kremlin, the ideal scenario would be a boring election with low turnout and no noteworthy events," said Zavadskaya. "Right now, though, this seems unlikely, as the situation in the run-up to the election does not appear normal, nor does it give the impression that the government has the situation under control."

The statement means Vienna police believe that, at this stage, there are no signs that a crime is being or has been committed in the case. “Everything is crazy,” an Israeli official told ynet, describing the disappearance.
In addition, Vienna police spokesman Markus Dittrich told the Austrian newspaper that “an internal investigation, inquiries with hospitals and the like have been opened in cooperation with the Israeli diplomatic mission in Austria.” He did not say what direction the investigation is focused on.
It was also reported Wednesday that cellphone location tracking carried out by police in Israel and Austria indicates that the two women, who are Sabbath-observant, were last seen during Shabbat near the city train station, an open area that includes, among other things, a municipal park. The family says it did not receive an update from police about the location tracking.
Family members went Sunday to the Modi’in police station, where they filed a missing persons report and provided the information they had. The station forwarded the report to the police’s international division in the investigations branch, which activated police officials in Austria. Family members also said Mali and Liel had contacted them Friday before Shabbat began, but did not respond to messages after Shabbat ended.

Air Force Moves Ahead with Plan to Put HH-60W at Andrews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:31:27 UTC
03:31:27 KST

Editor’s Note: This story was updated Aug. 13 with additional comment from the 316th Wing.
New helicopters, a new unit, and more Airmen are primed to move to Joint Base Andrews, Md., as the Air Force upgrades to modified HH-60Ws for its executive transport needs around the nation’s capital.
In an Aug. 12 announcement, the service said it has selected Andrews as the “preferred location” for 26 HH-60Ws to replace 26 UH-1Ns now serving the executive airlift mission for Air Force District of Washington. The mission includes contingency response for the government and senior leadership transportation. Some 60 new Active-Duty jobs will also relocate to the base.
Before the move can take place, however, the Air Force must conduct an environmental impact analysis. Assuming no issues emerge, initial operational capability is expected in early 2029, an Air Force spokesperson said, with full operational capability in 2030. Andrews’ 316th Wing is already moving forward with plans to stand up a new 5th Helicopter Squadron later this month to prepare for the transition.
A spokesperson for the 316th told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the 5th Helicopter Squadron will fly the UH-1N while it waits for the HH-60W. The spokesperson added that the wing will use unmodified HH-60s to train and qualify aircrew ahead of the modified aircraft’s arrival.
Andrews has long hosted presidential and executive airlift, and the existing 1st Helicopter Squadron has flown from there since 1967, according to a unit fact sheet. Its UH-1N “Huey” helicopters went into service there in 1971.
Now, 55 years later, those Vietnam-era helicopter are nearing the end of their service lives. The Air Force said in 2018 it would replace those birds with MH-139 Grey Wolf helicopters, but last year revamped those plans and opted for modified HH-60Ws instead.
Opting against the MH-139, which is based on the civilian AgustaWestland AW139, was surprising, but the Air Force determined it would be more cost efficient to modify HH-60Ws already in the backup inventory than buying new MH-139s.
Modifications detailed in budget plans include reconfiguring the cabin to accommodate 11 passengers and removing specialized equipment for combat search and rescue, such as the gun system, chaff/flare buckets, armor, and personnel litter.
Members of the House Armed Services Committee voiced skepticism in their version of the 2027 National Defense Authorization bill, indicating they may yet object: “The committee remains concerned regarding the justification for transitioning these missions to an alternate rotary-wing platform and seeks additional details on cost and operational implications.”
Regardless, the Air Force continues to push ahead with its plan. Budget documents indicate the HH-60W modifications would be made in fiscal 2028 and continue into 2030.

Drag moves to the silver screen in Stop! That! Train!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

May the light of RuPaul shine upon me. I was gagging when a sweet moment of sincerity spiralled into a hilarious smackdown between RuPaul's Drag Race superstars Ginger Minj (AKA Joshua Allen Eads) and Jujubee (AKA Airline Inthyrath).
We've hopped online, tragically too early for cocktail hour at my end, to chat about their top billing in comical disaster movie, Stop! That! Train!
Think Leslie Nielsen in Flying High! but much queerer.
It all started so innocently.
"Juju and I have been very close friends for 11 years now," Ginger says.
"We practically live together on tour. We know each other's nuances, when we should be there, and when we should back off. We've definitely grown through our pain together."
And then the 'bye, girl,' moment erupts, as Jujubee pulls a theatrically affronted face thunderous with shade.
"I never knew we had any pain," Jujubee intones faux-imperiously.
"I'm just discovering this in this interview. Thank you so much, Stephen A Russell, for allowing me to hear the truth come out of Ginger Minj. What are you saying? What kind of pain?"
Ginger blinks: "Are you saying I told the truth?"
To which Jujubee responds: "Finally. Put it all over the internet. That needs to be the headline."
Chemical reaction
Watching Ginger Minj and Jujubee spar playfully is a hoot, as is Stop! That! Train!
They play Tess and DeeDee, two employees of the unglamorous Stank Rail who smuggle their way into a better gig aboard the Glamazonian Express.
Facing the wrath of snooty first-class attendant Amber, played by fellow Drag Race queen Brooke Lyn Hytes, is only half the battle. There's also the small matter of the once-in-a-generation 'stormaganza' that's bearing down on the train, in the face of which even RuPaul's President Gagwell is powerless.
Director Adam Shankman tasked Ginger and Jujubee with playing Tess and DeeDee (relatively) straight, anchoring the movie’s outrageous misfortune.
"The rest of the cast is in Airplane! but the two of us are in Thelma and Louise," Ginger says. "That was so great, because with Drag Race, the acting challenges are about being as big as possible. Being a scene-stealer.
"But this was an opportunity to be the antithesis of that, and it was such a challenge, but so much fun."
Jujubee concurs. "There's a beauty in how grounded their comedy plays."
Shankman directed The Wedding Planner. He also officiated Stop! That! Train! co-star and Buffy alum Sarah Michelle Gellar's union with Freddie Prinze Jr and is a Bob Fosse Award-winning choreographer.
"That's why the shots are so beautiful," Jujubee says. "He's always thinking about the movement behind the scenes."
The film features a sweet and saucy romance for DeeDee in the compact shape of M3GAN actor Brian Jordan Alvarez's hunky train conductor, Cal.
"I'm three times bigger than him and begged to be put in the background," Jujubee laughs. "Can I just hold his hand from back here, so I look a little smaller? If we were floating in the ocean and there was a door, I'd let him on."
But the real love story is the friendship between Tess and DeeDee.
"There's no faking chemistry," Jujubee says. "You can't act it. You either have it or you don't. It's science. I don't know what chemical we make, but it's explosive."
Ginger grins. "It's probably a chemical imbalance."
Canadian club
Canadian Drag Race host Brooke Lyn Hytes (aka Brock Hayhoe) relished embracing Amber's queen bee energy as the antagonist to Tess and DeeDee.
"I feel like I was typecast," she cackles. "I have that face."
The hardest part of getting into character was letting go of control over costume, hair and makeup, allowing Salvador Pérez Jr, Jeri Baker and Kerry Herta do their thing.
"Drag queens are so used to driving the bus when it comes to their career and what they look like," Hytes says. "We're self-made creatures, so to give that over to somebody else's vision takes a lot of trust. But it turned out so well."
As did Stop! That! Train!'s ritzy dance numbers, choreographed by Jamal Sims.
"He's amazing," Hytes says. "I'm a bit of a backseat everything, giving suggestions, and have a hard time not stating my opinion. But it was a very collaborative environment."
Hytes knows her moves, having been a ballet dancer as a kid.
"I was in the boys' class, doing the male steps, and I realised pretty quickly they weren't for me," she says. "I wanted to be the swan, not the prince. And if I'm not interested in something, I'm putting zero effort in."
Instead, Hytes headed to the drag troupe Les Ballets Trockadero de Monte Carlo and on to Drag Race, now hosting the Canadian edition. It's an opportunity she does not take for granted.
"Drag Race has changed all of our lives," Hytes says. "It's changed popular culture. There aren't enough words to describe how grateful I am for everything it's given me. None of us would be here doing anything without RuPaul and World of Wonder. So please don't fire me."
Movie stars
Ginger Minj is equally effusive about the power of her president. “I grew up in a little Southern Baptist town where all the good Christians knew each other,” she recalls.
"When The Brady Bunch Movie (1995) came out, my mom took me to see it. The cinema was full of people I would see at church on Sunday, and I remember holding my breath when RuPaul came on the screen."
She needn't have worried.
"Everybody laughed. They bought into it. And in my head, when my mom looked at me and smiled, I was like, 'Oh, I can do that. I can be that. It gave me hope."
That young queer kids can look up to her and Jujubee as movie stars alongside Gellar brings them both such joy.
"All I ever dreamed, as a kid, was to be a movie star," Jujubee says. "So sharing this queer joy with the masses is really cool. The film's full of people who have always been othered. Who felt like the odd one out.
"And now they get to be a fabulous star in this equally fabulous disaster movie that explodes like a confetti cannon with particles that go everywhere for all eternity."
Stop! That! Train! is in cinemas now.

EU 'bringing great dangers upon itself' by seizing vessels: Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:29:33 UTC
03:29:33 KST

Russia has warned that the EU, by seizing Russian vessels, "is bringing great dangers upon itself."
The Russian foreign ministry said on Wednesday in a statement that European forces are carrying out "unlawful inspections" of foreign vessels under a "corrected" mandate of Operation Irini, established to help enforce the UN arms embargo on Libya.
The Russian diplomatic service cited the August 2 inspection of the Cameroonian-flagged Tao Payoh in the Mediterranean, carried out by Italian military personnel assisted by a Polish patrol aircraft and a Greek patrol vessel.
After about two hours, the vessel was allowed to continue its voyage, it noted.
“The suspicions against the vessel, obviously, were not confirmed,” the ministry stressed.
The ministry said Europe cited its Operation Irini as legal grounds for the inspection.
The ministry pointed out that the UN-backed mandate expired in May 2026, arguing that the operation is now being used by the EU to intimidate commercial carriers and restrict freedom of navigation.
It said the EU is trying to use Irini to counter maritime shipments of Russian oil and other goods, calling the practice "an abuse of international legal norms" and "an overly broad interpretation of the operation's powers."
The ministry also rejected EU attempts to identify vessels allegedly belonging to a so-called “shadow fleet”, accused of carrying shipments of Russian oil banned under EU sanctions – saying such inspections have no legal basis.
“No internal decisions by the EU can abolish the fundamental freedoms guaranteed by the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea,” it stressed.
The ministry further criticised EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas for condemning routine maritime shipments serving the energy and food security needs of developing countries.
The ministry said the EU's actions amounted to using Irini as a tool for political pressure and warned that Brussels is creating serious risks for itself by interfering with international commercial navigation.
"By resorting to such actions, the European Union, as a result of the measures it has taken that are absolutely inconsistent with the norms of international law, is bringing great dangers upon itself," the ministry warned.

Analyst explains what makes Belarus’ development path unique
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:27:00 UTC
03:27:00 KST

News of the story 
        
                "On Point"
        
    
                                                              
            
                                                                              
            
                                    
                    MINSK, 12 August (BelTA) - What the Belarusian development path means was explained by military analyst Aleksandr Alesin in a recent episode of BelTA’s V Teme [On Point] project.
 
 
  
  
 
“People often talk about the American, Japanese, Scandinavian, and other development paths. But there is also a Belarusian path, which means that we preserved the potential created during the Soviet era and built on it,” Aleksandr Alesin said. 
 
The expert noted that Belarus’ development strategy was based not on natural resources or transit potential, but on the knowledge, skills and expertise of Belarusian specialists, as well as the development of the education system, design bureaus, and engineering schools.“This allowed us not to start from scratch by destroying what had been achieved before, but to move forward and overcome the crisis that emerged in the first years after the collapse of the Soviet Union,” he said. 
 
Aleksandr Alesin noted that in the early 1990s it was often said that all the necessary goods could simply be purchased. Based on this logic, there was supposedly no need to focus on developing industry, agriculture and other sectors. Belarus chose a different path, demonstrating that such assumptions were wrong. 
 
“Moreover, by preserving and developing our potential, we have been able to become a technology provider for countries of the Global South. Their former colonizers never shared their technological developments with them, so that these countries would not be able to rise from their knees,” Aleksandr Alesin said. “Belarus, meanwhile, is ready to share cutting-edge technologies, provide professional training, and set up assembly facilities. These countries come to us because we cooperate with them on an equal footing,” he added.

Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk, damaging several warships and other vessels.
The Exilenova+ community reported the damage following an analysis of satellite imagery conducted jointly with the CyberBoroshno OSINT community.
The Project 11356R frigate Admiral Makarov, one of the Black Sea Fleet’s key Kalibr cruise missile carriers, was damaged in the attack. Analysts identified a strike near the eight-cell vertical launch system, as well as structural damage in the aft superstructure area housing radar systems.
The Project 11356R frigate Admiral Essen, which belongs to the same class, was also damaged. Analysts identified structural damage in the area where its Kalibr missile launchers are located.
A Project 266M minesweeper, designed to search for and destroy naval mines in coastal and ocean waters using specialized minesweeping gear and sonar, was also among the damaged vessels.
The attack also damaged the Project 20360 OS research vessel Viktor Cherokov, which Russia uses to test weapons, conduct torpedo launches and support the fleet’s submarine operations.
Damage was also identified on the unidentified Project 22160 patrol ship Vasily Bykov, designed to protect territorial waters and conduct patrol and escort missions.
The aft section of the Project 864 medium reconnaissance ship Priazovye, equipped with electronic intelligence and radar surveillance systems, was also likely damaged.
In addition to the warships, an unidentified dry cargo vessel moored in the harbor was also damaged.
During the attack on the oil terminal, an Aframax-class oil tanker was also damaged. Signs of fire, firefighting foam and an oil spill were observed in the water.
The Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Russian naval base and port in Novorossiysk overnight on August 12 with Neptune missiles, Palianytsia missile-drones and unmanned surface vessels.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces hit designated targets, including air defense positions, berths and port infrastructure.

What Living Through the Hottest July Ever Looked Like Across the U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:25:59 UTC
03:25:59 KST

This July was the hottest month ever recorded in United States history. Last month’s average temperature was 3.3°F (1.8°C) higher than the 20th century average for the contiguous United States, according to new data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. This was the warmest July—and warmest month—in the 132-year record, 0.1–0.2°F warmer than the previous records seen during the Dust Bowl in July 1936 and in July 2012.
The reality of this extreme heat was experienced through three separate heat dome events, with several states, including Idaho, Utah, and Montana setting all time temperature records on July 12. Salt Lake City, UT, saw temperatures reach 109°F, while in Montana, Billings saw temperatures reach 111°F and Miles City 115°F. Wyoming recorded its warmest July and warmest month on record.
Extreme heat wasn’t the only notable climate event Americans were dealing with. Wildfires in eastern Oregon burned through 140,000 acres, forcing thousands of residents to evacuate. Federal fire resources were stretched thin as other fires burned in Colorado, Washington, and beyond.
The smoke from the blazes, coupled with fires in neighboring Canada, worsened air quality for millions across the country. By mid-July, Chicago was reporting the worst air quality in the world.
Though the month ranked as the third driest July of the 132-year record, with about 48.5% of the contiguous U.S. in drought, mid-month flash floods in Central Texas along the Guadalupe River brought over 28 inches of rainfall. The floods killed two people in the same area which saw catastrophic flooding over last year’s July 4th weekend.
The month showed just how varied the impacts of climate change can be. Residents in Texas and Oregon saw their homes damaged or destroyed by flooding or fire, while those in the Midwest found themselves digging out N95 masks to walk their pets or commute to work while facing some of the worst particulate air quality the region has seen in over 25 years. Many others found creative ways to take respite from the heat—seeking shade in tree-lined streets or cooling off in fire hydrants and lakes alike. Here’s what it was like to live through the hottest month on record.

Al-Zaidi: September 30 is the deadline for US withdrawal from Iraq
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:25:29 UTC
03:25:29 KST

ALBAWABA- Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi reaffirmed Wednesday that September 30 will remain the “final and irrevocable” deadline for ending the U.S.-led international coalition’s military mission in Iraq, as Baghdad seeks to assert full state control over weapons amid difficult relations with both Washington and Tehran.
Al-Zaidi made the remarks during a meeting in Baghdad with U.S. Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper, according to the Iraqi prime minister’s office. He said the coalition’s military mission would end by September 30 and that October 1 would mark the beginning of a new phase in which Iraq would have no foreign military presence and would rely on its own security and military institutions to protect the country.
The meeting comes as the planned U.S. withdrawal coincides with another highly sensitive deadline: Baghdad’s effort to bring all weapons under state control. The Iraqi government has set the end of September as the deadline for armed factions to surrender their weapons or place their activities under state authority.
The process has faced resistance from powerful Iran-aligned groups, raising concerns about whether Baghdad can enforce the policy without triggering a confrontation with armed factions.
The issue also underscores the delicate position Iraq occupies between Washington and Tehran. For years, the presence of U.S. forces has been a central justification cited by Iran-backed factions for maintaining their weapons and military structures. Washington, meanwhile, has pressed Baghdad to ensure that Iraqi territory is not used by armed groups to threaten U.S. forces or regional partners.
The timing has become particularly sensitive following reports of a recent visit to Baghdad by Ismail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force. According to media reports, Qaani urged Iraqi authorities to postpone the implementation of the weapons-confinement policy, warning that immediate enforcement could have broader implications for Iran-linked armed groups across the region. The reported visit highlighted the competing pressures facing Baghdad as it attempts to strengthen state sovereignty while maintaining its relationship with Tehran.
For Washington and Baghdad, the end of the coalition mission does not necessarily signal an end to bilateral security cooperation. Al-Zaidi has said Iraqi-U.S. relations will move toward a broader partnership focused on economic development, investment and security cooperation rather than the presence of foreign combat forces. During his July visit to Washington, he and U.S. President Donald Trump discussed expanding economic ties and investment in Iraq.
At the same time, Baghdad is attempting to maintain working relations with Iran. Al-Zaidi traveled to Tehran shortly after his Washington visit, reflecting Iraq’s difficult effort to balance relations with the two rival powers whose influence has shaped its political and security landscape since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. He subsequently visited Turkey, where talks focused on trade, energy, security and infrastructure, including efforts to strengthen Iraq’s oil-export routes.
Since taking office, Al-Zaidi has presented his government as seeking to restore state authority, strengthen Iraq’s institutions and move the country toward economic development after years of conflict and political instability. His agenda has included efforts to combat corruption, with the prime minister saying there would be no “red lines” or exceptions in pursuing those accused of misappropriating public funds. His government has also sought to engage armed factions in a process aimed at moving their activities into political and social spheres.
The convergence of the September 30 deadlines therefore places Al-Zaidi at the center of one of Iraq’s most consequential political and security tests in years: completing the U.S. military withdrawal while persuading or compelling powerful armed groups to accept the state’s exclusive authority over weapons. How Baghdad handles the two challenges could define the next phase of Iraq’s relations with both Washington and Tehran, and determine whether Al-Zaidi can turn his promises of stronger state institutions and an anti-corruption drive into lasting reforms.

UK, Italy could deploy in Lebanon to check Hezbollah disarmament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:24:39 UTC
03:24:39 KST

Breadcrumb
UK, Italy could deploy troops in Lebanon to verify Hezbollah disarmament
Lebanon and Israel have agreed on Britain, Italy, Switzerland and Indonesia as potential contributors to a proposed mechanism that could see foreign troops deployed to Lebanon to verify Hezbollah's disarmament, people familiar with the matter said.
The shortlist emerged from US-mediated talks in Rome last week, the latest round of negotiations between Israel and Lebanon on implementing a June agreement that ties Israel's phased withdrawal from Lebanon to the disarmament of Hezbollah.
The countries could help define the mechanism's scope, provide personnel to oversee its implementation or contribute troops to observe or take part in inspections verifying disarmament, three sources said.
A Lebanese official told Reuters on Friday that Israel and Lebanon had agreed on a list of potential countries that could send troops to verify disarmament, but declined to identify them, saying the US would decide which of them would take part.
Lebanon and Israel in late June agreed to a US-mediated framework as part of Washington's efforts to end the latest round of conflict between Israel and Hezbollah, triggered in March when the Lebanese armed group attacked Israel following US and Israeli war against Iran.
A source with direct knowledge of the matter said discussions surrounding the shortlisted countries were in the early stages but said that they were "cautiously optimistic" the effort would proceed.
Switzerland's foreign ministry told Reuters it was exploring ways to support "various stabilisation processes", but declined to provide details. A British foreign ministry spokesperson said Britain was ready to support efforts to de-escalate tensions and long-term security, particularly in southern Lebanon, without elaborating.
The Israeli prime minister's office had no immediate comment. The Lebanese presidency and Indonesian foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel wants raids on private homes
Israel's military occupies what it describes as a security zone extending 10 kilometres into southern Lebanon and has said it will not withdraw unilaterally until Hezbollah is disarmed.
Two sources said that under the proposed mechanism, villages in southern Lebanon would be inspected and verified as being free of weapons. Israel wants those inspections to include private homes, they said.
Lebanon's army has resisted pressure over the last year to search private properties, fearing such searches could spark tensions in the south and with Hezbollah more broadly. Security officials have told Reuters the army would need warrants for each house.
A foreign security official said the question of private properties would need addressing, including how and by whom they would be searched. The official said the extent of foreign troops' freedom of movement would also need to be clearly established.
A mandate for the presence of foreign troops in Lebanon would have to be agreed, the sources said, with the most likely scenario being that they would be formally invited by the Lebanese government under a framework endorsed by Israel.
The US and Israel were unlikely to accept UN involvement, the sources said, while European nations may oppose oversight by US President Donald Trump's so-called Board of Peace.
(Reuters and TNA staff)

Criminal gangs in western Sweden are using valuable Pokemon cards to launder money, police said Wednesday.
Investigators have found large quantities of Pokemon cards during criminal investigations and at border checkpoints, according to Swedish Police.
Rare and vintage cards can sell for tens of thousands of euros on the secondary market, making them an attractive way to move illicit funds.
Police said gangs can use criminal cash to buy valuable cards through private transactions on online buying and selling platforms. The cards can then be resold to legitimate collectors or auction houses, allowing the proceeds to enter the financial system.
Police have recovered sealed and graded Pokemon cards alongside other contraband during raids targeting organized crime networks.
Tamara Fuentes, a spokesperson for the West Police Region, told the Sweden Herald that trading on unregulated platforms allowed criminals to conduct private deals without receipts.
“Trading is taking place unregulated on buying and selling sites, which gives criminals the opportunity to make private transactions without receipts,” she said. "We urge holders of valuable cards to be extra vigilant and ask questions of the buyer, especially if the purchase is to be made with cash.”
Authorities are urging collectors to be cautious, particularly when dealing in cash transactions.
The warning highlights concerns about the use of alternative assets to move illicit money, as criminals seek ways to avoid traditional financial systems.

Eurovision to exclude countries at war from hosting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:23:51 UTC
03:23:51 KST

The organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest have announced a rule change, excluding any country engaged in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
Eurovision is organised each year by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition and is a co-production of public broadcasters belonging to the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region", they said in a statement on Wednesday.
As the EBU includes members from outside Europe, the contest is not limited to European countries.
The EBU said it could commission an independent security assessment before deciding whether a winning country is capable of hosting the event safely.
The statement did not mention any country by name, but Israel came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.
Five countries, Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland, boycotted the 2026 edition in Vienna, a first for the contest.
They said they could not take part alongside Israel because of its genocide in Gaza.
If a winning country is found unable to host the contest, the EBU will appoint another host nation.
Under the new rules, that country will organise the concert "in its own right" and "will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another Member".
Ukraine hosted Eurovision in 2017 despite its ongoing conflict in the country's east.
But after Ukraine won the contest in 2022, it was unable to host the following year's edition because of war with Russia.
Eurovision 2023 was instead held in Liverpool in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf.

DR Congo Ebola outbreak set to become deadliest on record, WHO warns
Outbreak to eclipse West Africa’s Ebola outbreak of 2014 to 2016 if it continues at current pace, WHO chief says.
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) is spreading faster than health authorities can contain it and is on track to become the deadliest on record, according to the World Health Organization.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Wednesday that at its current pace, the outbreak is on track to eclipse the West African Ebola outbreak of 2014 to 2016, a crisis that killed more than 11,000 people and accelerated the push to develop a vaccine.

The outbreak in eastern DR Congo has killed more than 2,000 people out of more than 4,300 recorded cases, making it the fastest-moving Ebola outbreak on record. It was formally declared on May 15, though genetic sequencing later revealed the virus had actually begun circulating in February.
The outbreak is being driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which no vaccine or treatment has yet been approved.
Containment efforts have been hampered by the region’s remoteness and ongoing conflict near Congo’s borders with South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda. Many infections and deaths are occurring in communities that health teams have struggled to reach. Weak infrastructure, under-resourced clinics, circulating misinformation, and strikes by health workers over unpaid wages have further slowed the response.
Dr Abdirahman Mahamud, WHO’s director for health emergency alert and response operations, said the agency’s moderate projection has the outbreak peaking within six months. Under a more severe scenario, he said, it could stretch on for nine to 12 months.
The 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa remains the deadliest on record, having claimed more than 11,000 lives out of roughly 28,000 cases and prompting a major international push towards vaccine development. WHO officials say the current crisis could surpass that toll if access to affected communities does not improve soon.

Pope hats, bloody shirts and so many bobbleheads: The creative ways MLB teams lure fans to the park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

Pope hats, bloody shirts and so many bobbleheads: The creative ways MLB teams lure fans to the park
CHICAGO (AP) — It started as a limited promotion for a specialty theme night. Then the Chicago White Sox heard from their fans.
Everyone wanted a pope-themed hat.
“When things go bananas ... that’s when it gets really fun,” said Brooks Boyer, Chicago’s chief revenue and marketing officer.
Fun is the overarching theme when it comes to stadium giveaways, and business has been good at major league ballparks this year.
An array of creative promotions — everything from the New York Mets handing out fake glasses and mustaches for a Bobby Valentine Disguise Night to the Texas Rangers giving away a Nolan Ryan bloody lip jersey — has played at least a small role in an MLB-wide average attendance of 29,618 through Tuesday’s games, the highest such number for a full season since 2017.
Bobbleheads remain popular — like the Brandon Nimmo Bull Riding bobblehead in Texas, or the butter-churning Nick Kurtz “Big Amish” bobblehead with the Athletics — but it’s not just those iconic figurines that are drawing big crowds. The Brewers handed out 25,000 bar dice sets to fans 21 and over on Saturday, and they had a crowd of 40,625 at American Family Field.
The pitch clock and other innovative rules introduced by MLB in 2023 are often credited for spurring fan interest. But it’s clear from the long lines — and occasionally astronomical resale prices on eBay — what a clever giveaway can do for ticket sales, too.
“I definitely think across the league, there’s been an increase in demand and desire, and even necessity, to do things that are outside of the box,” said Meagan Hermosillo, the director of marketing and promotions for the Arizona Diamondbacks. “For us, we can’t really do a standard bobblehead or a standard anything. It has to have some kind of unique factor if we want it to move the needle.”
Chicago’s pope hats took creative — and careful — planning
The White Sox ended up giving the pope hats — shaped like the Pope’s miter, with the team’s sock logo in the middle — to everyone in the crowd of 38,113 for Tuesday night’s 5-4 loss to the Cincinnati Reds. The tribute to Pope Leo XIV, a Chicago native and longtime White Sox fan, helped push the club’s season-long attendance to 1,460,383, surpassing its total of 1,445,738 for all of 2025.
The team leaned into the theme. There were signs posted in the ballpark that read “LEO KNOWS MUNE” and “LEO KNOWS KONERKO,” referring to current White Sox first baseman Munetaka Murakami and former slugger Paul Konerko. Sister Mary Jo Sobieck threw out a ceremonial first pitch, and former White Sox pitcher Donn “The Pope” Pall kicked off the game with the “play ball” announcement.
“I thought it was a great idea, knowing that the Pope is from Chicago and he’s a Sox fan, which is great,” said Edward Lopez, 58, a truck driver from the south side of the city.
Lopez was supposed to go to the game with his girlfriend, but she wasn’t able to make it. So he went through two different gates to make sure he secured two pope hats.
“It was worth it,” he said.
Promotions for the White Sox go through a committee led by senior director of marketing and promotions Mike Downey. They throw out ideas and concepts, and they also look at samples from different vendors.
The team also is handing out wooden domino sets to 10,000 fans on Aug. 22 and magic wands to 20,000 fans on Sept. 4, a nod to the viral wand-waving dugout displays of injured reliever Mike Vasil.
“We’ve always looked to have our giveaways be something that we know people would wear or use or value because it adds value to the ticket,” Boyer said. “So it starts with that.”
While planning the pope hat night, religious sensitivities were part of the conversation for the promotions committee.
“We haven’t done items that would be Pope Leo’s likeness,” Boyer said. “We wouldn’t do that without the permission of the Vatican. ... We’ve been very careful. There is a little bit of nuance and finesse that needs to be done. And items, you know a lot of items may not be for everybody.”
Teams are eagerly jumping on larger cultural moments for eye-catching promotions
The Baltimore Orioles handed out a Tupac Shakur bobblehead in May. The New York Yankees gave out a “ KPop Demon Hunters ” bobblehead on Tuesday night, and they have a George Costanza calzone bobblehead — paying tribute to a 1996 “Seinfeld” episode — coming up on Aug. 27. Every MLB team except Toronto had a Star Wars Night this season.
Following in the footsteps of the minor leagues in many cases, it’s not enough anymore to just feature a popular player for a giveaway.
“You can see that teams are doing a much better job with their understanding (of) who they’re trying to target,” said Jim Strode, an associate dean and professor at Ohio University’s College of Business. “When I think of the ‘Seinfeld’ one, I’m thinking, you know, they’re targeting Gen X, they are targeting some, you know, younger baby boomers to try to get out to the ballpark.”
There is also what Lauren Anderson, the director of the Warsaw Sports Business Center at the University of Oregon, described as the “collector chase game.” There were multiple fans looking to buy additional pope hats at Tuesday night’s game, and there were several listings for the giveaway and the “KPop Demon Hunters” bobblehead on eBay on Wednesday.
“You want something that’s unique and cool and something that you can, you know, I’m one of 5,000 people to get these, I’m one of 10,000,” Anderson said. “I mean, there is also a bit of the game of people want something that’s limited so they can flip it and sell it, like on an eBay.”

Radiation vest tested on NASA moonshot can cut astronauts’ exposure in solar storms, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:23:01 UTC
03:23:01 KST

Radiation vest tested on NASA moonshot can cut astronauts’ exposure in solar storms, study suggests
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — A new study suggests a protective vest tested on a manikin during NASA’s first Artemis moonshot could drastically cut the radiation exposure of lunar astronauts during severe solar storms.
Scientists reported Wednesday on the radiation-shielding vest worn around the moon by a female test dummy in 2022. No one was aboard that Artemis I debut flight, which paved the way for humanity’s long-awaited return to the moon in April by a flyby crew of four.
Radiation remains one of the biggest threats to astronauts as NASA works toward a moon base. Shielding garments could keep lunar crews safe when solar storms strike and even allow them to venture beyond their shelters if necessary, the U.S., German and Israeli team reported in the journal Science Advances.
A version of the vest was previously tested on the International Space Station. It didn’t travel with the Artemis II astronauts since it was a short 10-day mission with limited room, but may wind up a carry-on for future moon crews.
Meant to be worn only during high-radiation and potentially cancer-causing solar events, the vest covers the most vulnerable human organs and tissue: lungs, stomach, bone marrow, breasts and ovaries. Women are believed to be especially susceptible to radiation-induced cancer.
Artemis I carried two female manikins that spent nearly a month flying to the moon and back. Dubbed Zohar and Helga, the manikins — each a life-size 3 feet from head to lower torso — were strapped into the passenger seats of NASA’s Orion capsule.
Zohar wore the 57-pound (26-kilogram) AstroRad vest, developed by the U.S.-Israeli startup StemRad and Lockheed Martin. The companies had already tested a prototype on the space station for comfort and function, modeling it after gear worn by nuclear disaster teams.
Helga flew vest-less, but like its companion contained thousands of radiation sensors.
The study’s lead author, StemRad’s Jordan Houri, called it “the largest experiment ever conducted to determine astronaut radiation exposure beyond low-Earth orbit.” NASA, the German Aerospace Center and the Israel Space Agency provided the funding. Radiation exposure is much less for space travelers closer to home, thanks to Earth’s protective atmosphere and magnetic field.
Artemis I encountered no major solar outbursts. But based on measurements gathered as NASA’s Orion capsule zipped through the inner Van Allen radiation belt, Houri and his team simulated how much protection the vest would provide during extreme solar particle events like those in 1972 and 1989 that detonated magnetic sea mines and collapsed a power grid.
Lucky for NASA, the 1972 solar outburst occurred in between that year’s two moon landings, keeping the crews of Apollo 16 and 17 safe from potentially lethal radiation exposure.
The latest findings showed the vest could reduce an astronaut’s radiation dose by about 60% in a solar storm as fierce as the one in 1972 and by nearly 40% in a calamity mirroring 1989. That’s equivalent to 193 days and 131 days, respectively, of unnecessary deep space radiation exposure, the scientists noted.
While none of the Apollo moonshots exceeded two weeks, the moon-base stays envisioned by NASA will likely last weeks, if not months, driving up the risk of enduring a dangerous solar storm. Mars expeditions will last even longer — months, years and possibly entire lifetimes if SpaceX CEO Elon Musk achieves his goal of building a city on the red planet.
The scientists are using their observations to trim more weight from the vest without sacrificing protection. They’re also investigating how to make radiation shielding from items already aboard a spacecraft — recycling that could save the lives of crews.
Houri doesn’t anticipate a need for further deep-space testing anytime soon, since Zohar and Helga “provided us with an exceptionally large, high-fidelity dataset.”
Zohar and her vest are now on display at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center, where their journey to the moon began.

Beyond keeping out bugs, the screen door safeguards Americans’ trust in others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Beyond keeping out bugs, the screen door safeguards Americans’ trust in others
ANN ARBOR, Mich. (AP) — The metallic screech followed by a sad excuse for a bang. The tap-tap-tap of a cat eager to come in before dusk. The erratic thumping of moths doomed by the siren-pull of the kitchen light. Morning brings the soft knock of a neighbor, friend or relative who knows there is no need for the formality of ringing a doorbell.
The screen door, despite — or thanks to — its modest making, is fundamental to the American home, to the suburban and rural soundscape and to what remains of our collective innocence.
The door that is barely a door. Made of lightweight aluminum or wood, with a wire mesh and a latch lock that gives under a thumb nudge, it is about as shabby as a barrier gets. Its mission to let the breeze in and keep the mosquitos, pesky flies and assorted vermin out appears simple, but its impact goes beyond that.
Semi-transparent, a screen door is an invitation, allowing a peek inside. It says someone is there. In architectural terms, it means this threshold wants breaching.
The screen door creates a liminal space, a quasi-open passage where one can see, hear and even smell what nature and the local community offer on the other side.
Its sieve-like surface gives way to the semi-private backyard. It allows a grandmother to leave the sturdy, opaque real backdoor wide open, almost forgotten, until it is time to go to bed. In the meantime, she can listen to songbirds, contemplate her flowerbeds or keep an eye on her grandchildren at play.
Fittingly, there exists what appears to be an apparently apocryphal origin story of the screen door. It says it was invented by a woman in Iowa in the late 19th century. Accurate or not, it is one of those modern myths worth embracing.
As if it were a symbol of good behavior, the screen door resists being slammed. Its closing mechanism cushions the blow, gently pushing back against the tug of a human hand, wheezing as it finally gives in.
At best, the creaking of a screen door announces a loved one’s arrival. It demands our trust in the outside world. It tempers our anger, quells our suspicions.
Once shut, the quiet says you are home.

US strikes targeting Houthis killed 153 civilians in Yemen last year, Pentagon review says
Washington (AP) — U.S. airstrikes targeting Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen last year killed more than 150 civilians, according to a Pentagon review of the attacks, which comes as concerns rise over civilian casualties during military campaigns under the Trump administration.
The unclassified assessment, obtained by The Associated Press, was sent to Congress as part of an annual report on civilian casualties and reported earlier by NBC News. A Pentagon official, who was not authorized to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said the department will submit the report in the coming months but had nothing more to announce.
Civilian casualties from U.S. military operations have drawn concerns, including from lawmakers in Congress, after a U.S. missile struck an Iranian primary school in the opening days of this year’s war, killing up to 168 people. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is said to have slashed the size of an office focused on reducing civilian harm, the AP has reported.
The Pentagon review focused on three airstrikes in April 2025 that were launched during the U.S. campaign against the Houthis. The militants were attacking commercial ships in the Red Sea, a crucial global trade route that leads to the Suez Canal and into the Mediterranean, as well as Israel.
Those strikes targeted hostile forces in or near Yemen’s rebel-held capital city of Sanaa as well as the Ras Isa port, the report said. A total of 153 civilians were killed and 243 were injured.
The strike on the port was the most deadly, killing 80 people and injuring 171 others. It sent massive fireballs billowing skyward and turned tanker trucks into burning wrecks. The Houthis aired graphic footage of the aftermath on their al-Masirah satellite news channel, showing corpses strewn about the port.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said at the time that the “strike was not intended to harm the people of Yemen.”
“U.S. forces took action to eliminate this source of fuel for the Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and deprive them of illegal revenue that has funded Houthi efforts to terrorize the entire region for over 10 years,” U.S. Central Command said in its statement in April 2025.
The command determined that the three strikes “more likely than not” resulted in civilian harm, the review said. The information was based on U.S. intelligence sources, imagery and open-source reporting.
It was determined that condolence payments were not appropriate for the three strikes, according to the Pentagon’s review, which did not explain why that was the case.
Such payments may be one of several responses when U.S. military operations injure or kill a civilian, the review stated, adding that they’re not required by law and not an admission of wrongdoing.
Such payments are not unheard of. Following an errant drone strike in Afghanistan that killed 10 people, seven of them children, in 2021, the Pentagon said it was committed to offering condolence payments to relatives.
The U.S. military first launched attacks against the Houthis in 2023, during the Biden administration, after the militants started launching drones and missiles at commercial ships in the Red Sea. The Houthis said the attacks were aimed at stopping Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza and supporting the Palestinians, though they occurred as the Houthis tried to strengthen their position in Yemen.
The U.S.-led campaign against the Houthi rebels turned into the most intense running sea battle the Navy had faced since World War II, U.S. military leaders and experts told the AP in 2024. American fighter jets and Navy destroyers shot down Houthi drones and missiles that were launched at commercial vessels and U.S. warships.
The Houthis now are carrying out a growing number of strikes against government forces in Yemen and oil facilities in neighboring Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, and the kingdom’s shipping in the Red Sea.
Fears are growing that the renewed violence could reignite Yemen’s civil war following a 2022 truce and open a new front in the Middle East war.

Beyond the headlines, Pakistan and Russia are drawing closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
