03:22:20 KST

Beyond the headlines, Pakistan and Russia are drawing closer
Sometimes trust develops gradually in settings that most people are unaware of, such as a working group, a ministerial handshake, or an agreement made on the fringes of a summit that garners national attention for a single day.
For the better part of a decade, Pakistan and Russia have been developing this kind of trust. In the summer of 2026, there were a number of quiet episodes in quick succession that essentially focused on security, diplomacy, energy, education, and trade, with Afghanistan running through almost all of them as a shared concern.
Work behind the scenes
On June 23, Russian and Pakistani officials gathered in Islamabad for the 12th edition of their Joint Working Group on Countering International Terrorism, led by Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Dmitry Lyubinsky and Pakistan’s additional foreign secretary, Ambassador Khalid Jamali. The discussion focused on regional terrorist threats, with a particular emphasis on those originating in Afghanistan. The 12th such meeting – a number which indicates that the relationship is designed not for headlines, but for continuity, the kind that can withstand changes in government and the overall geopolitical climate. The two parties agreed that further intelligence sharing and international cooperation would be critical.
Let us get the practical logic right: Bilateral channels like this one fill a void that slower, more bureaucratic multilateral organizations like the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the UN cannot cover on their own. Pakistan values Russia’s counterterrorism experience, particularly in urban warfare and counterinsurgency, while Russia is interested in Pakistan’s own operational experience along its western border. It is not a formal alliance, but it benefits both parties.
A few weeks earlier, the two countries’ interior ministries had already been busy. On June 6, Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi met his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Kolokoltsev, on the sidelines of an SCO gathering in Bishkek, signing agreements on curbing illegal immigration, repatriating citizens, and countering narcotics trafficking. It wasn’t bilateral-only: Naqvi held similar meetings that week with the interior ministers of Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Kazakhstan. Pakistan used a regional platform to navigate several bilateral conversations in a few days. One element is worth noting: Participating ministers estimated that approximately 25 terrorist organizations are now functioning in Afghanistan. That single figure explains why Islamabad and Moscow continue to find reasons to communicate more effectively than any communiqué wording about “shared concerns” can.
Common problems, varied approach
There is undoubtedly a shared concern for both nations. Nearly every issue on this bilateral agenda includes Afghanistan, although Pakistan and Russia approach it in different ways. Islamabad’s main worry is groups that it claims operate from Afghan territory against targets in Pakistan, primarily the Balochistan Liberation Army and the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which Pakistan firmly believes the Taliban authorities are harboring. This is denied by Kabul, which views the issue as an internal one in Pakistan. The Islamic State – Khorasan Province (ISKP), which has claimed assaults far beyond Afghanistan’s borders, even inside Russia, is Moscow’s top concern.
Where the two countries converge is on engagement rather than isolation as the way to manage that risk. In April 2025, Russia removed the Taliban from its list of designated terrorist organizations, and in July 2025 it went further, becoming the first country to formally recognize the Taliban administration as Afghanistan’s government. This was a historically loaded step, given that the Soviet Union fought and lost a nine-year war there against the mujahedin forebears of today’s Taliban. Moscow’s own explanation leaned on both security and economics: continued cooperation on counterterrorism and counter-narcotics, alongside stated interest in energy, transport, agriculture, and infrastructure projects inside Afghanistan. That recognition was formalized further in January 2026, when Russian President Vladimir Putin accepted the credentials of the Taliban government’s ambassador in Moscow.
The Shanghai spirit
Here comes the question as to why the SCO is important. None of this happens in isolation. Pakistan joined the SCO as a full member in 2017, and the group has become one of the more useful platforms on which Islamabad and Moscow meet as equals. They are two states with overlapping headaches: porous borders, extremism that ignores maps, and narcotics routes that have outlived several governments on both ends. Pakistan’s interior minister has repeatedly invoked the “Shanghai spirit”: mutual trust, equality, and respect for sovereignty as the most suitable or perhaps the only framework for shared security challenges.
Kyrgyzstan has held the SCO’s rotating chairmanship since the Tianjin summit in September 2025, with a year focused on long-term stability, including a proposed International Center for Combating Organized Crime in Bishkek. The 2026 SCO Heads of State Summit will be held there from August 31 to September 1. Pakistan is set to assume the chairmanship immediately afterward. Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has said Pakistan will use its chairmanship year to emphasize economic ties, connectivity, and regional security, ahead of hosting the next Council of Heads of State summit in Islamabad in 2027, which will be Pakistan’s first time hosting the organization’s flagship leader-level gathering.
Economy and trade: Still a work in progress
The economic relationship between Russia and Pakistan is still finding its footing and both governments now talk about that gap openly. In June, they agreed to work toward a Program of Economic Cooperation running through 2030, aimed at expanding trade and investment and clearing longstanding barriers to bilateral business. Pakistan’s energy minister described the relationship as having moved from Soviet-era ‘unfriendly country’ status to that of a ‘trusted friend’ across trade, energy, defense, and technology, pointing to four recent meetings between Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and President Putin as evidence of sustained high-level attention. A Russia-Pakistan Readmission Agreement signed in Bishkek is also expected to ease visa procedures for business travel.
Connectivity is a specific focus: Pakistan has agreed to explore joining Russia’s International North-South Transport Corridor, a roughly 7,200-km sea, rail, and road network linking India, Iran, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Central Asia, with Gwadar Port floated as a possible link point in Pakistan, complementing rather than competing with Chinese-backed infrastructure in the country.
Slow and steady progress
It would be easy to see all of this as background noise – working groups, sidebar signings, chairmanship handovers, and pipeline negotiations that have run for over a decade. But the pattern holds together. Pakistan and Russia have built a security relationship with real institutional depth, anchored in shared (even if not identical) worries about Afghanistan; a diplomatic calendar that gives Pakistan a bigger regional platform through 2027; and an economic relationship that both sides now describe candidly as underdeveloped and in need of exactly the kind of patient, unglamorous work on trade corridors, pipelines, and payment mechanisms that rarely makes the front page but is usually what determines whether a partnership becomes durable rather than merely symbolic.
Pakistan and Russia have come a long way from a relationship shaped largely by history to one sustained by regular dialogue and practical cooperation. Today, the engagement extends well beyond political exchanges to include security, trade, energy, education, and cultural contacts. Progress has been gradual, but that is what has given the relationship greater depth and resilience. As both countries continue to engage with realism and mutual respect, the real measure of success will not be the number of agreements signed, but the steady implementation of shared initiatives and the stronger institutional and people-to-people links they leave behind.
Not every diplomatic story needs a dramatic turn to be worth telling. Sometimes the story is simply that two neighbors who once had little to say to each other now have a standing appointment across several tracks at once and keep it, year after year, one number, one agreement, one pipeline at a time.

Britain, Italy, Switzerland, and Indonesia considered for Hezbollah disarmament verification mission - report
The proposal marks the latest step in implementing a June framework tying Israel's withdrawal from Lebanon to Hezbollah's disarmament
Israel and Lebanon have agreed on Britain, Italy, Switzerland and Indonesia as potential contributors to a proposed mechanism that could see foreign troops deployed to Lebanon to verify Hezbollah's disarmament. According to people familiar with the matter who told Reuters, the shortlist emerged from US-mediated talks in Rome last week, the latest round of negotiations between Israel and Lebanon.
The countries could reportedly help define the mechanism's scope, provide personnel to oversee implementation, or contribute troops to observe or take part in disarmament inspections.
A source with direct knowledge of the matter said discussions were in early stages but described organizers as "cautiously optimistic" the effort would proceed. Switzerland's foreign ministry said it was exploring ways to support "various stabilization processes" without elaborating. A British foreign ministry spokesperson said the UK was ready to support de-escalation and long-term security efforts in southern Lebanon.

- Israel and Lebanon make ‘structural’ progress toward framework: US official tells i24NEWS the details | Mike Wagenheim
Israel's prime minister's office had no immediate comment, and the Lebanese presidency and Indonesian foreign ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
Israel's military occupies a declared security zone extending 10 kilometers into southern Lebanon and has said it will not withdraw unilaterally until Hezbollah is disarmed. Two sources said the proposed mechanism would involve inspecting southern Lebanese villages to verify they are weapons-free, with Israel seeking to include private homes in those searches. Lebanon's army has resisted pressure to search private properties over the past year, fearing such searches could inflame tensions with Hezbollah, and security officials have said warrants would be needed for each home.
Sources said the US and Israel were unlikely to accept UN involvement, while European nations may resist oversight by the US-backed Board of Peace.

Brazil pushes spending curbs in bill before Congress as debt concerns mount, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:19:53 UTC
03:19:53 KST

Brazil Congress approves spending curbs as debt concerns mount
BRASILIA - The Brazilian Congress approved on Aug 12 spending-control mechanisms proposed by the government in an effort to rein in the country’s debt.
The finance and planning ministries included the proposal in an unrelated Bill as investors question President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s willingness to pursue a more forceful fiscal adjustment amid rapidly rising public debt.
The country’s lower house and the Senate approved the text on Aug 12, with the Bill heading to presidential sanction.
The proposed changes are expected to generate about 10 billion reais (S$2.5 billion) in savings in 2027 by slowing mandatory spending growth, Finance Minister Dario Durigan told journalists in Brasilia.
Mandatory spending is widely viewed as a key vulnerability of Lula’s leftist administration. Reuters had reported the government proposal earlier in the day, citing sources.
Lula, who is seeking reelection in October, does not explicitly address the need for a more ambitious fiscal adjustment in his campaign platform for the next four years.
Under the proposal, if the government’s revenue and spending report preceding the annual budget Bill projects a primary deficit, spending mandates created by ordinary legislation would be capped in the following fiscal year.
Because the latest fiscal report projected a 52 billion reais primary deficit in 2026, the measures are expected to apply to next year’s budget.
That means programs tied to non-constitutional rules could not grow faster than the real spending limit under Lula’s fiscal framework, which allows annual increases of 0.6 per cent to 2.5 per cent.
The government also proposes excluding oil revenue transferred to the Social Fund from the calculation of mandatory health spending, preventing windfall oil revenue from automatically boosting some expenditures tied to net current revenue.
The triggers would remain in effect until the government posts an annual primary surplus.
The government inserted the changes into a Bill that approves offsetting tax breaks adopted to cushion the impact of higher oil prices with additional government revenue generated by the commodity’s rally.
“We took the opportunity to introduce permanent measures that help us in controlling mandatory spending,” Durigan said. REUTERS

Millions of people gathered in Spanish cities to see the first total solar eclipse

Millions of people gathered in Spanish cities to see the first total solar eclipse
Kyiv • UNN
On Wednesday, millions of people in Spain gathered to see a total solar eclipse that lasted less than 2.5 minutes. This is the first such phenomenon in the country in more than a hundred years.
On Wednesday, millions of people filled Spain’s cities and towns in search of the best views of a total solar eclipse, when the alignment of the Sun, Moon and Earth will briefly plunge part of the planet into darkness, reports UNN, citing AP.
Details
Crowds brought folding chairs, umbrellas and hats, eagerly awaiting the celestial spectacle, which began in the early evening. It is the country’s first total solar eclipse in more than a century.
Across a wide area of northern and central Spain, millions of people expected to get some of the best views of the eclipse in continental Europe. A small part of Greenland and Iceland may witness the eclipse — weather permitting.
Additionally
The total eclipse — when the Moon completely blocks the sunlight — was expected to last less than 2.5 minutes, reaching its maximum duration off Iceland’s western coast. By the time it reached a small part of Portugal and then Spain, shortly before sunset, the total phase would be reduced to about a minute. The eclipse would then end over the Mediterranean Sea.

US dismantles decade-long multi-million dollar marriage fraud scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:18:25 UTC
03:18:25 KST

Yasin Gungor
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
The US Justice Department unsealed a two-count indictment Wednesday, charging 11 individuals for their roles in a massive criminal network that arranged more than 1,000 sham marriages to bypass immigration laws.
“This Department of Justice is rooting out fraud everywhere — including in our immigration system,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. He characterized the elaborate scheme as a "deliberate affront" to national laws and emphasized that the actions will not be tolerated under the Trump administration.
The network operated an international business model from 2016 through July 2026, primarily helping citizens of China obtain fraudulent permanent residency, according to the indictment. Some customers reportedly paid up to $100,000 for a sham marriage, while the US citizens recruited to participate received payments of approximately $30,000.
The network allegedly operated in multiple US states, including Connecticut, Florida, and Georgia, as well as in China and Vanuatu. It also relied on marriage officiants, attorneys, tax preparers, insurance providers and other service providers.
Participants executed the fraud by staging wedding ceremonies and photographs to make the unions appear legitimate. To further deceive US Citizenship and Immigration Services, the conspirators manufactured evidence such as joint bank accounts, insurance policies and tax returns. The defendants also coached participants on how to provide false answers during immigration interviews.
The 11 defendants each face charges of conspiracy to commit marriage and immigration fraud, alongside encouraging unlawful residence. If convicted, they face combined maximum penalties of up to 15 years in prison.
US Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York noted that the arrests dismantled a central component of "one of the largest marriage fraud schemes charged in United States history."

UEFA Champions League winners Paris Saint-Germain will face Europa League holders Aston Villa in the UEFA Super Cup in Salzburg, Austria, on Wednesday.
The match at Stadion Salzburg, also known as Red Bull Arena, will kick off at 1900GMT.
PSG secured their place in the Super Cup after retaining the Champions League title with a 4-3 penalty shootout victory over Arsenal following a 1-1 draw after extra time in Budapest.
Aston Villa qualified by defeating German club Freiburg 3-0 in the Europa League final in Istanbul. Youri Tielemans, Emiliano Buendia, and Morgan Rogers scored as Villa lifted the trophy for the first time.
PSG are seeking to become only the second team in the modern era to retain the Super Cup, following Real Madrid’s back-to-back triumphs in 2016 and 2017.
The French club defeated Tottenham Hotspur on penalties in last year’s edition after the match ended 2-2.
Aston Villa, meanwhile, will make their second Super Cup appearance. They won the trophy in 1982 after beating Barcelona 3-1 on aggregate.
The teams last met in the 2024-25 Champions League quarterfinals. PSG won the first leg 3-1 in Paris before losing the return match 3-2 at Villa Park, advancing 5-4 on aggregate.
PSG players return from World Cup duty
PSG have had limited time to prepare for the match following the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
Six of their players were involved through the tournament’s final weekend, including five members of the France squad and Spain midfielder Fabian Ruiz, who lifted the trophy.
Only 24 days separate the World Cup final and the Super Cup, leaving some players with a short recovery period before the new European club season.
Despite the disrupted preparations, head coach Luis Enrique included his leading players in the squad traveling to Salzburg.
Villa reshuffle squad after notable departures
Villa manager Unai Emery has been forced to reshape his squad after guiding the club to fourth place in the Premier League and the Europa League title last season.
Morgan Rogers joined Chelsea in a British-record £117 million ($158 million) transfer, while Youri Tielemans completed a £35 million ($47 million) move to Manchester United.
Lucas Digne left Villa for PSG and could face his former club Wednesday.
Amadou Onana and new signing Johan Manzambi are unavailable through injury, while World Cup participants Ezri Konsa, Ollie Watkins, and Emiliano Martinez remain on extended leave.
Villa strengthened their squad with several additions, including Joao Gomes, Alejandro Garnacho, and Modou Keba Cisse, all of whom were named in the squad for Wednesday’s match.
Somali referee who was denied US entry set to officiate match
Somali referee Omar Artan will become the first non-European official to oversee a UEFA Super Cup match.
Artan had been selected as a match official for the 2026 World Cup but was denied entry to the US after arriving on June 6, despite holding a valid visa.
UEFA appointed him to officiate the Super Cup five days later, following discussions with the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Trump administration pulls support for annual Arctic environmental report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:17:51 UTC
03:17:51 KST

The Trump administration has pulled its support for an annual report on the environmental changes across the Arctic, a region that is already heating up four times faster than the global average due to the climate crisis.
On Tuesday, Kim Doster, the communications director of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), said the federal agency was withdrawing its support for the Arctic Report Card, which has provided environmental updates on the region to scientists and the public since 2006.
Without explaining why the government stopped its support, Doster told the New York Times: “Coordination of the 2026 Arctic Report Card will not be facilitated through NOAA … All data historically contributed by NOAA to the product will continue to be collected and will remain publicly available.”
Doster told the outlet that other Noaa programs would continue to support research in the region that contributes to “national security, weather prediction, safety of navigation and the economic vitality of coastal communities”.
The Guardian has approached Noaa for additional comment.
Over the last 20 years, the peer-reviewed report has tracked crucial changes across the Arctic’s atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere and tundra. The climate crisis has made the Arctic the world’s fastest-warming region. In recent years, the region has experienced severe sea ice decline, carbon sink reversals and ecosystem upheavals.
In the 2025 Arctic Report Card, scientists found that surface temperatures across the Arctic from October 2024 through September 2025 were the warmest recorded since 1900. It also found that in March 2025, Arctic winter sea ice reached the lowest annual maximum extent in the 47-year satellite record.
Meanwhile, on land, the report noted that ongoing glacier loss contributes to steadily rising global sea levels, threatening Arctic communities’ water supplies, driving destructive floods, and increasing landslide and tsunami hazards.
It also found that in more than 200 Arctic Alaska watersheds – large land areas where rain and melted snow drain northward into the Arctic Ocean – iron and other elements released by thawing permafrost have turned rivers and streams orange in the last 10 years. The “rusting rivers” have in turn increased acidity while elevated levels of toxic metals have degraded water quality, in turn affecting aquatic habits, rural drinking water supplies and subsistence fishing.
Rick Thoman, the lead editor for this year’s report, said: “We are scrambling to pull the pieces together. I am optimistic that we can find a path forward for 2027 and beyond. Given the late date, whether we can pull it together for 2026 is an open question, but we’re trying to make it happen.”
Meanwhile, Twila Moon, one of the report’s editors and a scientist at the Colorado-based National Snow and Ice Data Center, said: “The US is an Arctic nation. It’s not just a distant place. It’s also our national place. So many of the changes there have impacts that reach down into our mid-latitudes, even further south.”
Moon added: “Even if we’re able to move the Arctic Report Card forward in a way that brings information to people, there’s still a real loss in this not being a US federal effort. That’s a real stepping back of US leadership in the science arena, in the environmental intelligence arena, and that kind of has a whole other flavor of harm as well.”
Rick Spinrad, the former Noaa administrator under Joe Biden, called the decision “really unconscionable”.
“It provides the baseline of what’s happening in the Arctic,” Spinrad said, referring to the report. “Then in terms of value for future planning, you can imagine anybody who’s dependent on Alaskan infrastructure – for example, like the oil pipeline, or the fishing community, or local communities that are worried about changes in weather conditions that are going to affect frost heaves on their roads,” he added, highlighting municipalities like Anchorage and Fairbanks.
“Now we will not have that tool, and it will be up to them to try to ferret out where the data are, and then to find somebody who can do the analysis to tell them what the trends have been and what they can expect in the future.
“It’s not clear to me why the administration made this decision. I can only infer that it’s tied to their aversion to anything associated with having a better understanding of climate change,” Spinrad added.
The funding cancellation is the Trump administration’s latest move to impede government-led studies on the climate crisis and its global effects.
Since retaking office last January, the Trump administration has stripped away support for scientific research that mentions “climate”, dismantled a key climate research center in Colorado in a move that the governor, Jared Polis, warned would put “public safety at risk”, attempted to scrap a $368m crucial deep-sea observation system, as well as removing key climate change reports from government websites.
Other federally led environmental rollbacks include Noaa’s decision to stop tracking the costs of climate crisis-fueled disasters, as well as the dismissal of all contributors to the US government’s flagship report on climate crisis preparedness.

Claiming that villages and towns "are entirely 'military facilities' does not stand up to any logic and cannot be used as an excuse for destroying them, displacing their inhabitants and preventing them from returning," he said in a statement.
Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz visited southern Lebanon on Wednesday, vowing to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" there and saying the Israeli military was "destroying the underground infrastructure" in the area and "destroying all the houses".
Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March by attacking Israel, which responded with heavy airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanese authorities say have killed more than 4,300 people.
Israeli officials vowed to carry out similar levels of destruction to Gaza and the military subsequently razed entire villages to the ground.
A framework deal reached in late June between Lebanon and Israel involves the disarmament of the Iran-backed group, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in "pilot zones".
While violence has significantly decreased since the signing of a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June and the Lebanon-Israel deal, Lebanon still reports intermittent Israeli strikes and ongoing demolitions.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) on Wednesday said Israeli troops carried out detonations in southern villages including in Zawtar al-Shariqya, which abuts one of the "pilot zones".
Lebanon's army said Israel had blown up "the municipal building in Zawtar al-Shariqya" as well as "a public school, a health clinic, a children's nursery and a number of homes".
Also on Wednesday, Lebanon's army chief Rodolphe Haykal met visiting US General Joseph Clearfield, who heads a coordination group involved with the June agreement.
The pair discussed "developments in the south and security arrangements" relating to the deal, the Lebanese military said, as well as "the difficulties the army faces in carrying out its missions, primarily due to the continuing attacks, bulldozing and destruction by the Israeli occupation".
President Joseph Aoun also met Clearfield, his office said, and discussed the implementation of the framework deal.
Israel and Lebanon are to hold an eighth round of US-sponsored negotiations next month, in Rome.
(AFP and TNA staff)

Spain rejects discussing sovereignty of enclaves with Morocco
The status of the North African enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla as Spanish territories is not up for discussion, Spanish officials said on Wednesday, after Morocco's justice minister reiterated Rabat's sovereignty claims over the cities.
Tuesday's remarks by Abdellatif Ouahbi to Asharq TV marked the first time Rabat has publicly raised the contentious issue since Ceuta's border crisis in late July, during which an estimated 72,000 migrants briefly crossed into the enclave. At least 96 people died in the mass border rush.
Ouahbi said his country always raised the issue of the cities' status in negotiations with Spain, with a long-term goal of achieving a resolution through dialogue.
Since its independence in 1956, Morocco has regarded Ceuta and Melilla as occupied by Spain, arguing sovereignty over them should ultimately be transferred to Rabat. Madrid considers them integral parts of its territory since the 17th and 15th centuries, respectively.
"Ceuta and Melilla aren't just Spanish; they're super-Spanish and cannot be touched," Spanish Defence Minister Margarita Robles told reporters in Ceuta when asked about Ouahbi's comments.
"Any attack on Ceuta and Melilla is an attack on Spain as a whole. It must never happen again," she added, referring to the border crisis.
The Spanish government has largely praised Moroccan authorities for their cooperation in repatriating the migrants, blaming the crisis on people-smuggling mafias.
In a separate statement, Spain's Foreign Ministry said Spain's territorial integrity "has not been, and will never be, discussed with anyone".
Separately, Morocco's Interior Ministry said on Wednesday it had stepped up security near the borders with Ceuta and Melilla over online calls for another mass crossing attempt on August 15, warning it would prosecute organisers and participants.
"The ministry calls on everyone to remain vigilant and responsible and not to be drawn into such suspicious and misleading calls, given the risks they may pose to people's lives," it said in a statement, also urging Spain to accelerate the return of unaccompanied Moroccan minors in Ceuta.
Last week, Spanish Youth Minister Sira Rego said Madrid would evaluate Morocco's offer to repatriate the children on a case-by-case basis.

Trump sued over plan to sell access to Truth Social posts
NEW YORK – Two US media groups on Aug 12 sued President Donald Trump over his move to charge for early access to his often market-moving Truth Social posts.
The lawsuit, filed in New York by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation, states that the scheme is “extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional.”
Subscribers to the paid service are supposed to get almost instantaneous access to Trump’s messages on the Truth Social platform – crucial seconds ahead of the general public.
The billionaire Republican often uses the platform to announce huge news, ranging from developments in the Iran war to trade tariffs, all of which can instantly send market values tumbling or soaring.
Early access to the service can cost up to US$100,000 (S$128,016) per month, or US$60,000 per month if users commit to three years, according to the Aug 12 lawsuit.
“This scheme is profoundly corrupt. The President stands to gain financially by giving ‘market-moving’ government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company,” a court filing says.
Trump Media & Technology Group, the company running the platform, has dismissed concerns over the product, which is called Truth API and was first unveiled in mid-July.
Calls for probe
The Intercept, a nonprofit US news outlet, and Freedom of the Press Foundation, which operates a database tracking Truth Social posts, argue that the paid service hinders their ability to properly cover Trump.
“Timely access to the President’s posts is critical for both groups,” the filing states, asking the court to declare Truth API as unlawful and block future posts.
Several Democratic lawmakers have called for a probe into the service by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates US markets.
Trump Media interim CEO Kevin McGurn said this week that Truth API is already generating revenue with 10 customer agreements signed, though he did not identify the clients.
The Wall Street Journal has reported that trading companies were among the first to subscribe to the service.
On Aug 10, Trump Media posted a ten-fold jump in losses for the second quarter of 2026, linked to declines in values of its digital assets.
Trump, like his close relatives, is alleged to have made billions of dollars in his second White House term through cryptocurrency ventures, property deals, stock trades and payouts from lawsuits.
Forbes, a financial media outlet, has estimated that Trump’s net worth shot up from US$2.3 billion to US$6.5 billion since 2024, when he won the election over Kamala Harris. AFP

Eurovision to exclude countries at war from hosting contest, EBU says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:06:46 UTC
03:06:46 KST

The EBU said it could commission an independent security assessment before deciding whether a winning country is capable of hosting the event safely.
The organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest announced a rules change on Wednesday excluding any country in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
Eurovision is organised each year by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition and is a co-production of public broadcasters belonging to the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region", the EBU said in a statement.
As the EBU includes members from outside Europe, the contest is not limited to European countries.
The EBU said it could commission an independent security assessment before deciding whether a winning country is capable of hosting the event safely.
The statement did not mention any country by name, but Israel came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.
Five countries, Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland, boycotted the 2026 edition in Vienna, a first for the contest.
They said they could not take part alongside Israel because of its war in Gaza, triggered by Hamas' 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
If a winning country is found unable to host the contest, the EBU will appoint another host nation.
Under the new rules, that country will organise the concert "in its own right" and "will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another Member."
Ukraine hosted Eurovision in 2017 despite its ongoing conflict in the country's east between Ukrainian forces and Moscow-backed separatists.
But after Ukraine won the contest in 2022, it was unable to host the following year's edition because of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Eurovision 2023 was instead held in Liverpool in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf.

Anti-migration measures begin to deliver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:05:05 UTC
03:05:05 KST

Anti-migration measures begin to deliver
Despite facing a record labor shortage, an economic slowdown and surging inflation, the Russian authorities are continuing to restrict migrant labor. The measures are having a clear impact. In the first half of 2026, the number of immigrants from Central Asia moving to Russia to work decreased by 15%.
- Uzbekistan, the leading source of migrant workers, sent 1.1 million people — down 13.2% from the previous year. Next was Tajikistan, down 18% to 494,500 people. Kyrgyzstan saw a drop of almost 17%, with 289,000 arriving.
- Uzbek and Tajik citizens must obtain a work permit (known as a patent) to work officially in Russia (this requirement was waived for Kyrgyz citizens under the EAEU agreement). Prices for patents vary in different regions. Fees rose sharply for 2026. Krasnodar set the highest price at 27,300 rubles ($350) — a hike of around 10,000 rubles.
- The migration crackdown started after the terror attack on Crocus City Hall in March 2024. At the time, police raided dormitories and construction sites where labor migrants lived and worked, forcing many to sign army contracts and sending them to the front lines.
- Since then, the State Duma has implemented a range of laws aimed at restricting the flow of migrant workers from Central Asia and imposing greater controls on them once they arrive. The interior ministry has been authorized to deport immigrants without trial and to maintain a “register of controlled persons” — a database of migrants subject to expulsion for various reasons (usually overstaying their permit). In certain regions, migrants are completely banned from working as taxi drivers, or in the retail and service sectors. Fees for residence permits increased fivefold, and payments for temporary residence permits increased eightfold.
- Putin last week signed a law to double (from 22 to 45) the number of administrative offenses for which migrants can face deportation as well as the usual fine.
- All this is happening amid historically low unemployment that has hovered around 2.2-2.3% since 2024. According to labor ministry estimates, by 2030 the labor shortage could reach 3.1 million people. Approximately 11 million positions are due to become vacant in the next five years as current employees retire. This pressure is compounded by the rapid expansion of the military-industrial complex, which drains already scarce personnel from civilian sectors. At the same time, as previously reported, recruiting contract soldiers into the army acts as a non-market mechanism to drain the labor market: it removes individuals from the workforce not because the economy has expanded, but because the state offers a contract where no other options exist.
Why the world should care
Labor shortages — exacerbated by the war — are one of the major systemic problems facing Russia’s economy. A lack of workers limits the potential for economic growth and fuels persistent inflationary pressure due to rising salaries that are not matched by increased productivity. According to Bloomberg Economics estimates, since the start of the war wage growth has outpaced productivity growth by about 5 percentage points.
By 2040, Russia risks confronting a labor shortage on two fronts: an aging population will place a growing burden on the pension system, while a shrinking cohort of new workers will fail to replace those retiring. Migration inflows are not enough to compensate for natural population decline (there’s a reason why demographic statistics are classified), leading to an overall reduction in the number of workers — all in a country where, amid export sanctions, people are becoming the new “oil”.

Russia builds 3,000 jet drones monthly to counter Ukrainian interceptors, HUR says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:02:12 UTC
03:02:12 KST

Russia has ceased producing its Geran-3 jet-powered attack drone, Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) told the Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi. The agency estimates Russian industry now makes about 3,000 newer Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month.
Russia is shifting toward faster jet drones because Ukraine’s low-cost interceptors have become more effective against slower Shaheds. The Geran-4 and Geran-5 leave defenders less time to react, requiring faster interceptors or short-range air defenses. At the reported production rate, these newer Geran models, previously used in limited numbers, could become a regular feature of Russian attacks.
HUR said Russia has established serial assembly of the two newer models at the Alabuga complex in Tatarstan, with other Russian companies supplying components. The agency also said Russia’s Defense Ministry wants to expand Alabuga’s capacity. Construction began in May. Satellite imagery showed large-scale work by early July 2026, although the purpose of the new buildings remains unknown.
From Geran-3 to newer jet drones
Russia first used Geran-3 drones in large numbers during a combined nighttime attack on Ukraine on 30 July 2025. At least eight flew alongside propeller-driven Shaheds and decoys. The model retained the Geran-2 airframe but replaced its piston engine with a Chinese Telefly JT80 turbojet. HUR gave it a speed of 300–370 kilometers per hour and a range of up to 1,000 kilometers.
In May, then-Defense Ministry adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said Ukrainian defenses stopped 95% of incoming Shaheds during the most recent documented strike and predicted Moscow would produce more jet-powered Geran variants.
The newer Geran-4 has a more robust airframe than the Geran-3 and is designed for high-speed flight and maneuvers. It can reach 500 kilometers per hour.
The larger Geran-5 carries a roughly 90-kilogram warhead and has a stated range of up to 1,000 kilometers. HUR has said Russia may equip it with R-73 air-to-air missiles, potentially threatening aircraft sent to intercept it.
The Chinese engines that Russia itself can't build
The Geran line combines Iranian designs, Russian assembly, and imported technology. HUR described the Geran-3 as a localized version of Iran’s Shahed-238. It found 45 foreign components inside, including parts from the United States, China, Switzerland, Germany, Britain, and Japan.
Russia depends on China for the turbojet engines in newer Geran models. HUR deputy chief Vadym Skibitskyi told RBC-Ukraine that Russia remains fully dependent on Chinese turbojet engines for the Geran-4 and Geran-5. Each costs about $35,000–$40,000, he said.
A Chinese XK-F358 mesh radio recovered from a Geran-5 also helps Russian drones resist jamming. Its manufacturer remains outside the US, EU, UK, and Ukrainian sanctions, according to a review by Euromaidan Press.

The former ambassador argues that the current president, Min Aung Hlaing, the general who plunged Myanmar into conflict and economic chaos, is illegitimate and had no power to ask him to leave the property.
Min Aung Hlaing’s pro-military party won a landslide victory in elections earlier this year that have been widely condemned as a sham. Min Aung Hlaing is wanted by the international criminal court for crimes against humanity against the Muslim Rohingya minority.
Kyaw Zwar Minn’s lawyer, David Perry, told the court: “The military authorities could not lawfully terminate his licence at the address. Nor could they legitimately use the property.”
Prosecutors said Myanmar’s authorities instructed the former ambassador to “hand over state-owned properties” in April 2021, and that the Foreign Office also told him to leave the residence, but he did not comply.
They argue that his view of the Myanmar government – which is not formally recognised by most democratic countries, including Britain – does not provide a defence.
“Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed from that position means that he is guilty of the offence of diplomatic trespass,” the prosecutor Louise Oakley told the court.
Kyaw Zwar Minn previously told the Guardian he spent a night in his car outside the embassy in April 2021 after his then deputy, Chit Win, and a military attache, Soe Aung, locked him out of the building on the regime’s orders.
He said at the time that he no longer felt safe at the north London residence and had contacted the police after former staff delivered a letter ordering him to move. Friends and relatives in Myanmar had been forced into hiding fearing reprisals as a result of his stance, he said.
The 68-year-old became a diplomat under Aung San Suu Kyi after a long career in the army and has called the “Rohingya issue” very important. Before his removal as ambassador, he had been told by a source in Myanmar’s foreign ministry that his staff were spying on him.
He anticipated in 2021 that the crisis would lead to civil war. “You can see the military government is not going to step back,” he said. “More people will die and the economy is going to collapse. Then anything can happen in our country.”
The court case comes as the war enters its sixth year. More than 100,000 people have been killed and more than 5 million displaced, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.
Aung San Suu Kyi, now 81, has been detained on a range charges since the military took power. She was previously held under house arrest for 15 years under a past junta, and was awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1991. After her election as state counsellor in 2015, she became a pariah for leading a regime that excused a genocide, jailed journalists and locked up critics.

A Ukrainian railway engineer spied on Lyman’s defenses for Russia using Google Maps

A Ukrainian court sentenced the former chief engineer of Lyman’s locomotive depot to 15 years in prison with property confiscation for helping Russia target the frontline city, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said on 11 August. Investigators report he sent a Russian handler the locations of Ukrainian positions intended for guided-bomb and artillery strikes.
Lyman blocks Russia’s northern route toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, which are part of Ukraine's fortress belt in the Donbas. As attacks on supply lines intensify, information about Ukrainian positions can help Russia direct bombs and artillery. The case fits a broader pattern of Russian intelligence recruiting people inside Ukraine to locate targets. Russian services have used money and blackmail, including threats against recruits’ families, to secure their cooperation.
According to the SBU, the former engineer traveled around Lyman and its outskirts to record Ukrainian military bases. He marked possible targets on Google Maps, then sent screenshots to a handler in Russia through a messaging app.
The collaborator operated from basement
The agency said an acquaintance whom it described as a “DNR deputy” in occupied Donetsk Oblast connected him with Russian intelligence. The SBU said the man moved into an apartment building’s basement to shelter himself while directing Russian strikes on the community.
SBU officers detained him in Sloviansk in May 2026. The agency said a seized smartphone contained evidence of his reconnaissance and contacts with the Russian side.
The SBU did not identify the man, the court, or any specific strike enabled by his information.
How Russia turns locals into spotters
The Lyman case involved an acquaintance of the former engineer, but Russian services also use money, blackmail, and online platforms to find recruits. The SBU says minors may initially receive simple assignments, such as taking photographs or painting graffiti, before being directed toward more serious sabotage.
Other recruits have allegedly answered Telegram offers of “easy money.” These include a Zaporizhzhia man later convicted of building bombs and a Dnipro suspect accused of activating more than 1,000 Starlink terminals for Russian forces.
Ukraine has prosecuted similar cases before. In November 2024, a court sentenced another Russian agent to 15 years for guiding missile and drone strikes in Zhytomyr Oblast.
More recent cases remain at the allegation stage. The SBU has accused a Kharkiv Oblast man of installing hidden cameras near military sites and a Poltava student of mapping energy facilities while filming air-defense units.

ICE Is Getting Body Cameras. But Will They Help Hold Agents Accountable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:01:25 UTC
03:01:25 KST

All Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field agents will be equipped with body cameras by the end of the month, acting ICE Director David Venturella said. However, the footage acquired by the devices would only be released to the public if it is in “the best interests of the agency,” according to ICE. The policy raises questions about how body cameras are meant to be used in law enforcement, as well as whom they are meant to protect.
Venturella said in his statement last week that the body cameras would help the agency uphold its commitment to “transparency and accountability.”
However, a spokesperson for ICE tells TIME that the body cameras are needed because “the media and sanctuary politicians consistently spread smears about our law enforcement.”
This raises the question: Are the cameras meant to hold ICE agents accountable—or protect the agency?
White House “border czar” Tom Homan indicated that the cameras could be useful for both purposes, saying “body cameras are the way to go” to increase transparency between the agency and the public—but they can also provide insights about split-second behavior under high pressure in the field.
“I think body cameras let the American people know what that officer sees when he takes that action,” Homan said on CBS’s Face the Nation in July. On Fox & Friends Weekend that same month, he went further, saying that body cameras “exonerate more law enforcement than they convict.”
Who they ultimately benefit largely depends on how they are used—in theory and in practice, experts tell TIME.
“Body-worn cameras are only as good as their policies,” says Christopher Schneider, sociologist and professor at Brandon University.
The policies governing body cameras must determine not only when agents are recording, experts say, but also what happens to the footage the cameras collect.
Kirk Burkhalter, a New York Law School professor and former detective with the New York Police Department, believes it is a smart move toward course-correcting after multiple fatal shootings this year by ICE. He calls the rollout of body-worn cameras a “very important first step.”
Why did ICE start using body cameras?
Body cameras became a point of contention after two protesters were killed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers in Minneapolis in January. The deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti both led to disputes about what transpired and whether the use of force was warranted, leading DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to promise in February that agents would be equipped with body cameras going forward.
A policy regarding their use was established that same month, and Congress approved $20 million in funds for purchasing and operating ICE body cameras in April.
Read More: The Chaos and Cruelty of ICE
Body cameras had been issued to more than half of field offices by July, when agents shot and killed two people within the span of a week: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas, on July 7, and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 in Biddeford, Maine. Neither of the incidents were captured by body cameras, though The Intercept reported that the officers in Maine were equipped with recording devices that they were unable to use.
Members of Congress promptly called for stricter oversight.
“In shooting after shooting, we are told that there is no body-worn camera footage of the incident and asked to accept DHS’s account of the incident. Time and again, that account turns out to be a blatant falsehood,” a letter signed by dozens of senators on July 18 said.
But putting cameras in agents’ hands is just a start; they must also be recording when it matters.
When are ICE agents required to turn on body cameras?
The policy says agents should activate cameras “as soon as practicable” at the beginning of an enforcement activity and deactivate them once the activity concludes. Agents who fail to activate their cameras must provide a written explanation, but the policy does not spell out disciplinary consequences for failing to record an encounter.
This is not dissimilar from policies used by other law enforcement agencies, which also typically stop short of codifying disciplinary steps, Schneider says.
“You would think that if an officer was found after an investigation to have intentionally turned the camera off or not turned it on, to engage in misconduct or pretend, you would think they would be fired for that,” he says. “You won't find that in a policy.”
Phillip Atiba Solomon, professor at Yale University and co-founder of the Center for Policing Equity, says that comprehensive policy should not leave key questions unanswered, such as: “What are the consequences if you disobey those rules?”
“A piece of legislation without an enforcement mechanism is a polite request,” he tells TIME.
The policy does require “Field Responsible Officials” to provide operational training to their agents “at least yearly,” focusing on their handling of recordings, privacy compliance, procedures for redacting and sharing data, and civil rights considerations.
But knowing how to use the cameras is different from establishing how useful they actually are in the field.
How effective are body cameras in law enforcement?
Schneider says there is a presiding belief that the presence of body cameras will influence what transpires between civilians and law enforcement officers. Specifically, there is an assumption that they serve as a deterrent.
“The idea is that if a camera is on, of course the officer is not going to engage in misconduct or brutality, and of course people are going to comply with police,” Schneider says. “That's profoundly untrue.”
He points to the murder of George Floyd in 2020 as an example, since the police officers involved were wearing active cameras while the incident unfolded.
Studies show mixed evidence. Some found that body cameras reduce use-of-force incidents and civilian complaints. But when 70 such studies were analyzed together, they showed “no consistent or statistically significant effects,” according to the National Institute of Justice.
Part of the reasoning for this discrepancy, according to Solomon, is that people must believe that what they are doing is wrong in order for them to change their behavior when being observed. In a randomized controlled study that involved thousands of police officers in 2019, researchers wrote that “cameras did not meaningfully affect police behavior on a range of outcomes, including complaints and use of force.”
“Officers—who are not ICE but are regular municipal law enforcement—didn't think that what they were doing was a problem, so we didn't see significant reductions in use of force,” Solomon says of the study.
They must also believe that there will be consequences for their actions, he says. But the Trump Administration’s staunch defense of ICE in the aftermath of this year’s deadly shootings suggests that this component might also be lacking.
In addition to deterrence, body cameras also offer point-of-view documentation.
“The reason why it's so helpful is because it gives the vantage point of the law enforcement officer who's wearing the camera, and you can kind of see and hear what they see and hear,” Burkhalter says. This can give judges, juries, legislators, and the general public a clearer sense of why they responded the way they did at the time.
Read More: When ICE Kills, We Cannot Look Away
Without such video evidence, the public could be left with difficult questions about what exactly transpired in the critical moments of officer-involved fatalities.
When Silverio Villegas González was killed by ICE agents in September 2025 in Illinois, body camera footage captured by local police officers revealed key details about the incident. DHS claimed its officer was “seriously injured” during the altercation and feared for his own life. However, the footage later showed that the officer said his injuries were “nothing major,” undercutting his explanation of events.
Third-party video evidence was similarly instrumental in showing what transpired when officers shot and killed Good in Minneapolis in January. DHS claimed that Good was a “violent rioter” who had tried to run over agents with her car. It said that its officer then fired “defensive shots.” But cell phone footage captured by bystanders contradicted that account.
“The cameras dispel the rumor mill, preventing us from looking at some footage from someone's doorbell cam 50 feet away and trying to decipher what someone had in their hand or what they didn't have in their hand,” Burkhalter says.
Experts have acknowledged, however, that body camera footage is limited—for example, it does not show officers’ facial expressions and may miss key details that are just out of frame.
That makes how it is reviewed, edited, and distributed even more essential.
Who will have access to footage?
When deterrence fails, and use-of-force incidents take place, the footage is paramount in determining who is responsible and paving a path for justice. That raises the question of who has access to the footage and how it can be used.
ICE’s body camera footage will be immediately available to internal personnel and investigators, its policy says, but public access will be strictly restricted and controlled.
“Footage will be available as appropriate for official purposes,” a spokesperson wrote in a statement to TIME. “Body camera footage must be reviewed on a case-by-case basis due to privacy concerns for innocent bystanders.”
Burkhalter says that the agency’s approach aligns generally with existing law enforcement policies.
“I haven't reviewed all local law policies, but I can assure you that very few agencies have an administrative regulation that says we will release all body cam footage within ‘X’ amount of hours,” he says. “That would just be impossible, given most of those cases involve some type of criminal investigation.”
Policies vary by municipality. For the NYPD, for example, it is codified that body-worn camera footage will be released within 30 calendar days of a critical incident, which includes “incidents involving the discharge of a firearm by an officer that result in a member of the public being struck, as well as police use of force that results in serious injury or death.” Other cities require the police commissioner to personally sign off on the release of footage that may be of interest to the public.
The ICE policy says that when serious bodily injury or death in custody is captured on camera, ICE must “expeditiously review the footage,” and if it is determined it is in the “best interests” of the agency, then it must publicly release within 72 hours of the event or “as soon as operationally feasible.”
Given how the policy is written, and how ICE has operated in recent years, Burkhalter says, “I don't see … the agency releasing footage that is going to seriously harm their public image.”
The footage is also subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), giving members of the public another avenue to seek recordings regardless of whether the agency chooses to release them. But a FOIA request does not guarantee disclosure: Footage may be withheld or redacted under applicable exemptions, and requests can take considerable time to resolve.
Schneider’s concern is that, without more explicit guidelines about what acting in its own “best interests” means, the agency could be inconsistent and selective about releasing records. For example, it might prioritize the distribution of footage that puts the agency in a good light or supports the Trump Administration’s deportation agenda.
“Probably they're going to release some of those videos that involve undocumented immigrants who are armed and are also criminals,” he says. “Some people might start assuming because of what's being shared that, ‘Oh well, maybe all these undocumented immigrants are criminals and have weapons—because this is all I see.’”
Who else are the cameras watching?
The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other activist groups generally support the use of body cameras, but they have also warned that without good guardrails, “They risk becoming just another police surveillance device—and one with very real potential to invade privacy.”
Many municipalities require law enforcement officers to turn off their body-worn cameras during sensitive encounters, such as meeting with a confidential informant. ICE does not address such circumstances head-on, but it outlines exceptions for when body-worn cameras would not be worn or turned on, including when an agent is engaging in undercover activity; conducting interviews inside jails, prisons, or detention centers; and aboard commercial flights.
Solomon notes that privacy is one of his biggest concerns—especially because the Trump Administration has not ruled out the presence of ICE officers at voting sites in November.
Although DHS previously told election officials that ICE would not target polling locations, both Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Trump have since declined to categorically rule out a federal immigration enforcement presence at the polls.
ICE officers with recording devices could deter voters from turning out, he explains: “If you're not sure, or if you've got a record, and you just don't want to be on the grid, you are not going to the polling place.”
Those concerns come amid a broader debate over how law enforcement agencies use the data collected by surveillance technology. Recently, that has been expressed through a widening concern about the use of Flock cameras: automatic license plate readers that are cropping up in major cities in the U.S. Residents worry about the technology being used to identify and track people traveling to sensitive locations like protests and specialized health care facilities. There have already been reports from watchdog organizations that officers have used the cameras to stalk their romantic interests.
Solomon therefore expressed skepticism about equipping thousands of DHS field agents, across the country, with even more advanced surveillance tools.
“We are giving folks who have been tasked with terrorizing vulnerable communities the ability to further surveil those communities,” Solomon says. “That's not much of a step forward, if you ask me.”

Ex-Marine Robert Gilman tried to get out of a Russian prison by volunteering for the invasion of Ukraine. He got out on humanitarian grounds instead — so what does Putin want in return?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:01:11 UTC
03:01:11 KST

Ex-Marine Robert Gilman tried to get out of a Russian prison by volunteering for the invasion of Ukraine. He got out on humanitarian grounds instead — so what does Putin want in return?
Russia has released Robert Gilman, a 32-year-old American whom a court had sentenced to 10 years in a penal colony. Gilman was detained in Voronezh in January 2022. According to the Russian authorities, he kicked a police officer in the leg after being pulled off a train for causing a drunken disturbance. The court first gave him four and a half years, then raised the term to 10 over claims that he had attacked guards and an investigator behind bars.
Gilman said his troubles began with poisoned vodka. He said he remembered little about the incident with the police officer in Voronezh. He acknowledged drinking vodka and said something may have been added to it. There were at least five attacks on officers of the Federal Penitentiary Service and the Investigative Committee, Russia’s main federal investigative agency. One sent someone to the hospital. Gilman cited abuse in prison and attempts to keep his conditions from worsening.
Gilman’s family has insisted that he ended up behind bars solely because of his citizenship. His father, Vladimir Gilman, said in 2024 that his son had struck the officer accidentally while he was sick, had caused no serious injuries, and had still received a near-maximum sentence. The accusations of fights in the penal colonies and the pretrial detention center, he said, were the result of provocations meant to bring new charges against his son. He was convinced Robert had been convicted unlawfully so that Russia could later trade him for one of its citizens imprisoned in the United States, and he urged Washington to press for his son’s release.
Robert Gilman has Russian roots. According to his family and to Gilman himself, his parents are from St. Petersburg, he was born in Poland, and he had spent his entire life in the United States. He served in the U.S. Marine Corps and then taught English. He ended up in Russia in transit: he was flying to Moldova for work when he fell ill at the airport and had to stay to get treatment and replace his passport. Somewhere in the process, he got the idea of applying for Russian citizenship. In court, he spoke both English and Russian, and he once quoted, perhaps unwittingly, a meme well known to Russian speakers. “I really regret it. I was just walking toward success. And I find that from now on I will keep walking toward success,” he said in Russian.
Gilman asked to be sent to fight in the war against Ukraine, and he said staff at his pretrial detention center had put him up to it. At a hearing in April 2026, he abruptly announced that he wanted to be sent to fight in the “special military operation,” the Kremlin’s official term for the war. “My father served in Russia, his father served in Russia. My great-grandfather was a captain third rank and took two bullets at Stalingrad. So I believe I’m fully fit for service and am following in their footsteps,” he told the judge. She advised him to take the matter to a military enlistment office. Gilman replied that detention center staff had suggested he make the statement in court specifically. He had said earlier that he had pleaded guilty in the case involving the police officer because he had been promised a lighter sentence that never came.
Gilman’s family has long expressed concern about his health. A week ago, news broke that he might be dying. Global Reach, the human rights group that represented the family, said that Gilman had long been pumped full of unidentified drugs and that in June 2026 he had been admitted to the psychiatric ward of a civilian hospital in a state of dissociative stupor. He could not communicate, was being fed through a tube, and his life was in danger, the group told Reuters. The Reuters report also showed that U.S. officials were already working on the case: on July 23, Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised Gilman’s release with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Gilman was released soon afterward. On August 12 — six days after the Reuters report on the threat to his life — Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump’s special envoy, posted photos of Gilman and his family aboard his own plane. Witkoff has flown to Russia repeatedly for talks with Vladimir Putin. Gilman looks severely emaciated in the pictures, but he is conscious and smiling. After arriving in the United States, he was scheduled to be sent to a military hospital in Texas for a medical and psychological evaluation, Global Reach representatives told The New York Times.
Trump said Putin had released Gilman on humanitarian grounds and had asked for nothing in return. Ivor Bennett, the Moscow correspondent for Sky News, found that suspicious. “For now it’s a gift, but Russia will undoubtedly be hoping for something in return,” he wrote, suggesting that Moscow wants to win back Trump’s support in its negotiations with Kyiv. Dmitry Drize, a political commentator for Kommersant FM, also said the release could be groundwork for a new round of talks with Washington on peace in Ukraine.
Five more Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, according to Global Reach. One of them is Steven Hubbard, 73, who was detained in 2022 during Russia’s occupation of Izium, in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, and accused of taking part in Ukraine’s territorial defense. A Russian court sentenced him to nearly seven years in prison. Ukrainian prisoners who were held with Hubbard and later released have described how he was mistreated.

Greenland forces Trump-linked US oil firm to delay drilling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:00:41 UTC
03:00:41 KST

Greenland authorities have forced a US oil company connected to Donald Trump to postpone drilling wells in the Arctic territory, defying claims by the US president’s envoy that Americans could be extracting crude by next year.
Amid Trump’s imperialist threats, tensions have been rising on Greenland’s eastern coast after the oil company brought drilling equipment ashore in July without permission, drawing a “strong warning” from the government.
Just week before Greenland Energy intended to sink its first wells into the tundra, the government said on Thursday: “The necessary regulatory process cannot be completed, and the necessary approvals cannot therefore be obtained before the planned start of drilling.”
It said that during talks Greenlandic officials had expressed concern that the timetable was too tight to assess the environmental and social impact.
The authorities will have to decide whether to sanction drilling in a protected wetland that is home to rare birds and the muskoxen on which local hunters depend. At the earliest, drilling could now commence in the winter of 2027, the government and the company said.
That is a long way off the prediction made as recently as May by Jeff Landry, the hard-right Louisiana governor whom Trump named as his envoy to Greenland. He said after a visit that oil supposedly lying under Greenland could ease the energy crisis caused by the US attack on Iran.
Landry, whose stated goal is to “make Greenland a part of the US”, said: “We could have those barrels on production within 10 months or so.”
Robert Price, the Greenland Energy chief executive, who maintains that oil worth $1tn could lie under the remote Jameson Land region, said: “Greenland Energy remains committed to advancing its oil exploration programme responsibly and in accordance with Greenland’s regulatory process, and in full compliance with Greenlandic authorities.”
Price added: “We will use this time to refine our plans and deepen relationships with local communities, strategic partners and relevant authorities.”
Since a rich friend put the idea of acquiring Greenland in Trump’s head during his first term, the president has threatened to do so by buying it from Denmark, seizing it with military force or cutting a deal.
Shareholders in Greenland Energy had been hoping for a “Trump pump”, a presidential endorsement that could send the New York-listed stock rocketing. But on Wednesday the price fell by more than a third after the drilling delay was announced.
Price had said a ship bringing 300 containers of drilling kit would set sail from Canada for Greenland in September, with a first well to be sunk the following month. He told a community meeting – falsely – that Greenland had granted permission for the company to start landing equipment.
Greenland Energy’s British partner 80 Mile said in an update for investors on Wednesday that the delay was due to the need to “complete the permitting and regulatory approval process”.
80 Mile holds exploration licences granted before Greenland stopped issuing them in 2021, citing the climate crisis.
Greenland Energy, formed last year, has announced plans to spend $60m (£44m) raised from investors to fund drilling in exchange for a majority stake in the project.
Its representatives have said its oil venture is “not related to American annexation”, yet the company has established multiple connections to the Trump administration.
Phil McGraw, better known as the chatshow host Dr Phil, has a deal with Greenland Energy to “capture the mission of these modern-day wildcatters” for a documentary series to be broadcast on television and social media. He recently appeared in the Oval Office alongside Trump, having served on the president’s religious freedom commission.
A US navy veteran who is working on Golden Dome, the missile defence plan for which Trump says controlling Greenland is “vital”, sits on Greenland Energy’s board. And Kenneth Griffin, a Wall Street billionaire who gave $1m towards Trump’s second inauguration, bought 9% of Greenland Energy’s shares in April.
Rod McIllree, 80 Mile’s boss, said: “While we are disappointed that the timing of the Jameson drilling programme has been impacted, the company remains fully committed to advancing this highly prospective project.”

Russia uses four main narratives regarding POWs and missing persons — CCD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:59:00 UTC
02:59:00 KST

Russia uses four main narratives regarding POWs and missing persons — CCD
Kyrylo Viktorov, head of the Department for Countering Information Threats to National Security at the Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD), reported this during a press conference at Ukrinform.
According to him, the study covered the period from January 1 to August 11, 2026. Using specialized software, analysts examined more than 94,000 publications from nearly 24,000 sources. The study covered both Ukrainian- and Russian-language segments of the information space, while the total number of views of the analyzed materials reached 419 million.
The Center's representative emphasized that not all of the publications analyzed contained destructive narratives. Analysts identified messages that Russia uses to carry out information operations, as well as the corresponding narratives and their objectives.
"The main pattern revealed by our analysis is that Russia often does not need to invent the event itself. It is enough to use a real event and impose the desired interpretation of it on the audience," Viktorov said.
According to him, the first main direction is the dissemination of claims that Ukraine allegedly does not want to return its prisoners of war. Russian and pro-Russian sources systematically promote the idea that Ukraine supposedly refuses to conduct exchanges, does not want to return certain prisoners, or is interested only in bringing back specific categories of servicemen.
"In this way, they try to shift responsibility for the difficulties or delays in the exchange process onto Ukraine, onto the Ukrainian side," the Center's representative explained.
The second direction, according to Viktorov, concerns manipulation of the issue of missing persons. Russian sources attempt to fill the information vacuum with their own explanations, including claims that the missing-person status is supposedly used to conceal the actual number of people killed or to avoid making payments to their families.
The third direction involves creating a positive image of Russian captivity. To this end, Russia uses videos and statements by Ukrainian prisoners of war that emphasize allegedly good treatment by Russia, an alleged unwillingness to return to Ukraine, or reluctance to go back to the front.
"A person who is being held captive cannot be considered a free participant in information communication, especially when we are talking about Russian captivity," Viktorov stressed.
He described the fourth direction as discrediting Ukraine by spreading fake information and disinformation about allegedly inadequate conditions for Russian prisoners of war, lack of medical care, poor food, beatings, or other forms of cruel treatment.
The Center's representative noted that this ultimately creates a distorted narrative: "Russia supposedly treats Ukrainian prisoners of war humanely, while Ukraine, on the contrary, allegedly treats Russians brutally."
He emphasized that these narratives are interconnected and have a common goal — to undermine trust in Ukraine. This includes undermining servicemen's trust in the state, families' trust in institutions responsible for searching for and returning people, citizens' trust in verified information, and international partners' trust in Ukraine.
Viktorov concluded that periods when public attention to the issue rises sharply are particularly favorable for such information operations — including during prisoner exchanges and negotiations, as well as when lists or new information about prisoners of war and missing persons emerge.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian law enforcement agencies currently have information on more than 114,000 missing civilians and military personnel.

Under new rules, countries affected by war will not be able to host Eurovision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:57:57 UTC
02:57:57 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Under new Eurovision rules announced Wednesday, countries affected by war or serious geopolitical instability will no longer be able to host the song contest if safety and security are at risk.
Eurovision said in a statement that its governing Reference Group approved the changes following its annual review and feedback from participating broadcasters after the 2026 contest in Vienna, ahead of next year's edition in Bulgaria.
"The Rules of the Contest now say the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," it said.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) may commission an independent security assessment and appoint an alternative host broadcaster if necessary.
The host broadcaster, it said, will organize the contest in its own right and will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another member.
Under other revisions, starting next year, all competing artists must also be at least 18 years old on the day of their first rehearsal, up from 16, according to the statement.
Eurovision also clarified that lead singers must perform the main melody live. Pre-recorded elements and backing tracks remain permitted but cannot replace or unduly assist the lead vocal.
Eurovision Director Martin Green said the changes aim to strengthen clarity, artist protection, and safety while preserving the contest's “spirit and integrity.”

Russia says Britain must take first step to restore direct military contacts with Moscow

The Russian Foreign Ministry said Wednesday that Britain must take the first step to restore direct military contacts with Moscow.
Commenting on British media reports that claimed UK defense chiefs were under pressure to “reboot” communication channels with their Russian counterparts, the ministry said it had taken note of the claims.
“It was London that initiated the curtailment of dialogue through the defense ministries,” said the ministry.
Russia noted that Britain expelled the Russian military attache in May 2024, which Moscow said disrupted the traditional channel of communication between the two defense establishments.
“Therefore, it is precisely they who should take the first step to ‘fix’ it,’” said the ministry.
Moscow added that it had periodically received signals from the British side indicating an interest in restoring contacts, but said no practical steps had followed.
There has been no direct communication between the British and Russian military chiefs since September 2022, when then-Chief of the Defense Staff Admiral Tony Radakin spoke with Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov following a serious incident involving a Russian aircraft and an RAF surveillance plane above the Black Sea, according to British media reports.
Subsequent British attempts to re-establish contact were reportedly unsuccessful, and now British officials are facing pressure to restore high-level military communication amid concerns that the absence of direct channels could increase the risk of miscalculation and unintended escalation.
