Donovan’s Deep Dives: Splinters, snubs and the ‘one-term curse’: The chaotic fight for central Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:51 UTC
01:38:51 KST

Candidate registration for this year’s elections kicks off on Aug. 31 and ends on Sept. 4, meaning that unless a candidate is unexpectedly disqualified, we will know the final shape of the race in just three weeks. In several key races, breakaway candidates from the two big parties are threatening to run as independents, splitting the vote and threatening each camp’s chances of winning.
For a look at how the races are shaping up in the north and for more general context, see “Donovan’s Deep Dives: Northern Taiwan’s races come into focus” (Aug. 8, page 12).
This column focuses on central and south-central Taiwan. Unfortunately, there is no polling for this region, but expectations outside of Changhua remain fairly stable.
Photo courtesy of Yang Tsu-hsien
THE CENTRAL BATTLEGROUND
There are a few political traits that make central Taiwan unique. In national elections, it is considered the key swing battleground between the pan-green, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP)-leaning south, and the pan-blue, Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-leaning north.
In local elections, a different picture emerges. A pattern that has held steady across the region is the DPP’s “one-term curse”, whereby the party can win, but never wins re-election as Taichung City mayor, the former Taichung county commissioner (the city and county merged in 2011) and the Changhua and Nantou county commissioners. This is odd in a country that typically rewards incumbents.
Photo courtesy of Chiu Chien-fu
This makes the region more pan-blue than pan-green at the local level if looked at in number of years governing, yet the parties alternate regularly in Taichung and Changhua. In Nantou, the DPP has only won once, in 2001.
In theory, this pattern should boost the DPP’s chances this time around, but for various reasons might not.
TAICHUNG
Photo: TT file photo
Despite being Taiwan’s second-most populous city, the Taichung mayoral race is getting surprisingly little press attention and pollsters are ignoring it. It appears they have collectively decided that this will be an easy KMT win. It is not on the short list of races the DPP is optimistic on swinging this election cycle.
The KMT candidate, Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), is a party heavyweight, having previously served as party chair and is currently the legislature’s deputy speaker. He was even on the 2021 TIME100 Next list. He is a moderate, which works in Taichung.
The KMT’s primary was contentious, and KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) appeared to try and weigh the primary to benefit his challenger, but he still won. This did not cause any major splits in the party, and Chiang emerged largely unscathed.
Photo: Chang Tsung-chiu, Taipei Times
Like Chiang, the DPP’s Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純) is beloved in her legislative district, but is less well-known than her rival in the rest of the city. She got an early start advertising heavily, which may have given her a boost.
I saw Ho speak recently. Her speech was so-so, but in the Q&A afterward she shone. She demonstrated a strikingly granular knowledge of issues far from her own district and was willing to take unpopular but practical stances. More than any other politician I have ever met, she conveyed a sense of genuine, warm enjoyment in engaging with people. The catch is that these might be her best skills, which are great at the retail level, but hard to scale in a city of 2.8 million.
The DPP claims that she trails Chiang by 7 or 8 points in internal polling and is catching up fast. That is possible as her name recognition rises, but there is no independent polling to back that up.
CHANGHUA
As explored in previous columns, the Changhua race is a wild soap opera full of intrigue, intense rivalries, intra-family feuds and bitter animosities. The only other race that comes close in the drama is Hualien.
With factional feuds ripping the party apart, KMT Chair Cheng decided to bypass the entire primary process and picked Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政), a mid-level party official and former failed independent candidate running for mayor of tiny Shetou Township. The response was a collective “huh, who?”
The backlash within the party was openly hostile. The KMT’s current county commissioner for Changhua, Wang Hui-mei (王惠美), has refused to endorse him and, until a few days ago, reportedly was not willing to meet with him. Wei has all but been openly begging for Wang’s support in the press, and Cheng has admitted the Changhua race will be “most challenging.”
The DPP has nominated local powerhouse lawmaker Chen Su-yueh (陳素月), and one would assume they are already reaching for the Champagne, but no.
Former DPP Changhua City mayor Chiu Chien-fu (邱建富) lost the primary. He accused the party of bias and has quit the party and is running as an independent. Typically, the party would try and get him to change his mind by registration day, but at this point it looks like they will fail.
Not only could Chiu split the pan-green vote, he claims he will do well with moderate voters. Over half of the Changhua City borough chiefs recently came out to support him, pitting Chiu’s northern Changhua County base against Chen’s southern base.
Though no one has formally come forward, considering the animosity towards Wei in the KMT, it is still possible someone will quit and run as an independent on the pan-blue side, further complicating the race.
NANTOU
Incumbent County Commissioner Hsu Shu-hua (許淑華) is running in a strongly pan-blue county, has strong name recognition, and is widely expected to win re-election. She gained national recognition during Han Kuo-yu’s (韓國瑜) campaigns for Kaohsiung mayor and president at his MC at rallies, which she sometimes did dressed as Wonder Woman.
The DPP has nominated Wen Shih-cheng (魏世政), who is apparently legendary in dentistry circles. Nantou’s population is elderly, so maybe that will appeal to them.
THE CENTER-SOUTH
This is a very traditional region with an emphasis on retail politics and clan or factional affiliations.
There is a saying that “south of the Jhuoshuei River all politics is the same,” and that there is little differentiating politicians from either party. That may be exaggerated, but there is some truth to it. Traditional factional politicians can come from either the KMT or DPP, and corruption and sleaze cross party lines.
In national elections, this region is thought of as pan-green, but locally there are strongholds for both parties.
YUNLIN
Though not unbeatable, the famous Chang clan headed by Chang Jong-wei (張榮味) is the most powerful of KMT patronage factions and a formidable force. Four members of the legislature are associated with his faction, including Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu. The faction dominates agricultural-related industries nationwide.
Chang’s sister is being term-limited out as county commissioner, so this time his daughter, legislator Chang Chia-chun (張嘉郡) is running.
The DPP is running legislator Liu Chien-kuo (劉建國), but Yunlin gets little press coverage and the county is not on the short list of places the DPP is excited about flipping.
CHIAYI COUNTY
Chiayi County, unlike Chiayi City, is considered a pan-green stronghold, and was one of only five governments the DPP held in their 2022 electoral bloodbath. Even the most powerful of the old school KMT patronage factions defected to the DPP.
The DPP is running lawmaker Tsai Yi-yu (蔡易餘), who goes by “Chiayi One Fish” on social media, with “one fish” being a homonym for his given names.
The KMT is not even running a candidate, and is backing independent candidate Puzi Mayor Wu Pin-jui (吳品叡), dubbing her part of the “great opposition alliance,” along with another independent in Hsinchu City and the Taiwan’s People’s Party (TPP) candidate in Chiayi City. Her father was formerly a local KMT official.
Chiayi County is not on the KMT’s “great opposition alliance” list of possible wins, nor is it currently on the list of counties the DPP is worried about losing.

Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.
It is forest fire season in Europe and North America, and the news is filled with harrowing images of disastrous fires filling the air with smoke. What about Taiwan? Taiwan has a unique forest fire profile. Unlike other nations, where the threat peaks in the dry summer months, that period is wet. Instead, major forest fires typically occur during October to April, when the country is drier. Moreover, “high temperatures are not the primary drivers of forest fires” as a study in Theoretical and Applied Climatology noted. Rather, the consensus is that dryness is the trigger of forest fires here, with
When Gary Melyan, a longtime Taiwan resident who died on July 7 at age 83, arrived in Taipei for the second time in 1971, he was a graduate student trying to complete a doctoral thesis on the Taiping Rebellion. Then, sometime in 1974 or 1975, it became a weekly Wednesday night meal. Melyan never finished his PhD, but the weekly Wednesday dinner, now known as the Wednesday Night Old Farts (WNOF), has continued for more than half a century

The only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record on Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.
British driver Andy Green reached 653.908kph in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Federation Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.
The 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot rocketed across the crystalline crust at Utah’s famous Bonneville Salt Flats in a 9.75m car engineered by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The engines, adapted from those used in the company’s heavy machinery, mix pressurized hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create bursts of power.
Photo: AP
“It’s magic to be able to showcase this technology and to showcase how good the engineering is on the best racing surface in the world, Bonneville Salt Flats,” Green said after the run.
To be clear, Tuesday’s feat did not come close to approaching the overall land-speed record, which Green set with jet power in 1997. That year, he climbed into the Thrust SSC, a black needle sandwiched between two cartoonishly large jet engines, and hit 1,227.985kph, breaking the sound barrier and achieving a feat no one has come close to matching. His runs in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert produced sonic booms that shook the nearby town of Gerlach.
In 2006, Green also set the land-speed record for a diesel-powered car — 563.4kph — at the Bonneville Salt Flats. He returned there on Tuesday with the goal of beating that mark using hydrogen power, which he has called the “fuel of the future.”
In targeting his diesel speed, Green easily topped the previous hydrogen combustion world record of 298.5kph. He had a 16km straightaway to build speed. A few dozen JCB staff members and reporters watched from a distance through cameras and binoculars.
Green said the cockpit of the car he used on Tuesday was “probably a little hotter” than in the jet-powered vehicle from 1997, with temperatures routinely above 50?C.
“But I have been training four months for that, both training in the gym and actually just getting used to it with hot baths,” he said.
A remnant of a prehistoric lake bed, the Bonneville Salt Flats are about 160km west of Salt Lake City and sit atop a shallow aquifer that cools the tires. The low-friction surface and dry desert air are conducive to speed and have beckoned drivers since the first race there in 1914.
“It looks like snow, and it behaves a bit like packed snow — it is surprisingly slippery,” Green said.
Green was no stranger to speed when he took his first racing job. He had been flying supersonic military jets when he spotted a 1994 British newspaper ad seeking a high-speed driver to break the sound barrier.
Green did not approach supersonic speeds on Tuesday, but JCB engineers hope his feat with hydrogen power would shake up the clean-energy industry.
The company’s chairman has argued that hydrogen can better handle the demands of heavy industries than electric power.
Hydrogen is only as clean as its source, and the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels. JCB signed a deal to buy green hydrogen, which is created using renewable energy, but makes up a tiny fraction of global hydrogen production.
The concept and development of such technology has been around for decades, but has had a resurgence over the past few years, said Greg Keoleian, a professor of sustainable systems at the University of Michigan and co-director of the school’s MI Hydrogen initiative.
Many major automakers have already developed hydrogen internal combustion engines or hydrogen fuel cell technology, but the higher cost of hydrogen production compared with gas and diesel is a barrier to wider usage, Keoleian said.
“It represents an important energy carrier for decarbonizing areas of the economy,” he said. “As far as its deployment, it’s influenced heavily by the cost.”
An emerging focus is extracting hydrogen from natural deposits instead of separating it from water, a prospect that could significantly reduce costs, he said.

The hard reality of climate change is hitting Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

For anyone in Europe who still thought climate change was a problem for future generations, this summer’s sweltering heat waves have brought home the reality that its costly and life-altering economic impacts have already arrived. Record heat and droughts this summer — which scientists say are exacerbated by global warming — have wreaked havoc in power production, shipping and public health systems, while this wildfire season is on track to be Europe’s biggest ever.
Together, the hit to the region’s economy can already be measured in the hundreds of billions of euros, economists and academics estimate. However, they said this is just the beginning, as costs are set to rise faster than temperatures.
The climate is changing more rapidly in Europe than on any other continent and the damage is already stretching public finances, setting off wild swings in inflation, redrawing the tourism map, and forcing the bloc to rethink how power is produced and how goods are transported.
“What makes 2026 particularly worrying from an economic perspective is that there are multiple episodes of extreme events,” University of Mannheim economist Sehrish Usman said.
“Take heat waves, droughts, wildfires... these events are taking place at the same time and mostly in the same regions, compounding their impact,” she said.
RECORD DAMAGE
Temperatures hit records in June and July, and the economic damage would likely exceed all past records, economists say.
Traffic on the Rhine and the Danube rivers, key cargo arteries, is severely limited because of low water levels, more than a half dozen nuclear power plants have shut or curtailed production due to cooling difficulties. Agricultural yield estimates have been cut with crops harvested late, such as maize and sunflower, suffering a 6 to 7 percent loss last month. Heat curtails human productivity and has already killed tens of thousands of people, with Germany alone reporting more than 10,000 heat-related deaths.
The costs of the emergency response, such as fighting fires or curtailing power use, further stretch budgets.
ING estimates that the halt of traffic on the Rhine would lower the GDP of Germany, the world’s third-largest economy, by 0.3 percentage points this year, while Hungary’s MBH Bank sees a 0.1 percentage point GDP hit for every week the country’s largest nuclear generator is offline.
Allianz, the German insurer, estimates the June heat wave alone would cut the GDP of Europe by 0.3 percentage points, and climate change would shave 5 to 7 percent off growth by 2030 for the most exposed economies such as Spain, France and Italy.
“The total bill for this year will be much larger,” said Hazem Krichene, an economist at Allianz. “This figure doesn’t account for the fires, droughts, different flood events or the expected El Nino.”
Given that the eurozone is expected to grow just 1 percent this year, that hit is substantial.
Yet Usman says the full extent of the economic damage would only be felt several years down the line.
“You’d expect the damage to be largest in the year an extreme event happens and then to fade but we find the opposite,” Usman said. “The economic impact grows over the following years because the extreme weather sets off a chain of slow economic consequences.”
TOURISM AND INFLATION
Southern Europe could take the biggest hit, as temperature spikes are the largest there, cutting tourism income, worsening crop failures and inducing outward migration.
“Can you see tourists marching through southern Italy or Spain in 45 degrees? I can’t. So, I think the nature of tourism will change,” ING economist Carsten Brzeski said.
The south might get more year-round tourists but summer peaks could drop as vacationers move north, hitting the southern hospitality industry, Brzeski said. The south would take a bigger food price hit from extreme weather, complicating life for the European Central Bank (ECB), which is already struggling to keep inflation at target.
“You see bigger effects of extreme temperatures on food prices in places that are already hotter, so if you’re in southern Europe, you’ll see a bigger effect,” said Maximilian Kotz, a researcher at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center.
Extreme heat in 2022 lifted eurozone inflation by 0.34 percentage points via higher food prices, with the south taking a disproportionate hit, Kotz estimated.
Meanwhile, a halt in river transport is making it harder for fuel to reach parts of Europe, widening regional price differences.
HEAT STRAINS
“The fiscal consequences fall most heavily on the economies least able to absorb them,” Allianz said in a research note.
Reductions in annual tax revenue from lost output could reach 1.8 percent in France, 1.3 percent in Italy and Spain as progressive tax systems mean revenues fall faster than output, it estimates.
Business profit margins would decline, depressing investment and exacerbating the economic loss.
Costs would surge, both because governments have to fund the emergency response and must invest, such as in future-proofing power generation or transit routes.
“A key concern is that countries still rely far too much on ad hoc emergency response, which is both expensive and also often quite inefficient,” said Heather Grabbe, a senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank.
But investors might push back if governments try to spend more. Debt levels are already high — especially in France and Italy — and countries need to invest in defence and the green energy transition.
The dilemma could draw in the ECB, which bought up trillions of euros worth of countries’ debt in the past decade to keep borrowing costs depressed when inflation was too low.
“With such a long list of spending needs, the trend will be towards higher government debt,” Brzeski said. “This will then mean pressure on the ECB to step in and do more quantitative easing, if there is a sudden selloff in bond markets.”

Report outlines errors at hospital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:46 UTC
01:38:46 KST

Several major errors at Antai Hospital in Kaohsiung last year led to two deaths after weight-loss surgeries, the Ministry of Health and Welfare said in a report released last week.
Chinese-language media in September last year reported that Wang Ming-yu (王銘嶼), a surgeon at the hospital who is an online influencer, was being investigated by the Kaohsiung District Prosecutors’ Office over the deaths of two people who underwent weight-loss surgeries.
The Kaohsiung Department of Health in August last year — following the completion of its investigation into the deaths, which occurred in a span of 10 days — revoked Wang’s medical license, and suspended the hospital’s surgical outpatient clinic and inpatient services for three months.
Photo: Screen grab from Wang Ming-yu’s Facebook page
The Department of Medical Affairs in the 57-page report on its separate investigation detailed its own findings and suggestions for improvement based on the Medical Accident Prevention and Dispute Settlement Act (醫療事故預防及爭議處理法).
The physician performed two surgeries last year — on a 33-year-old woman with a BMI of 37.89 on June 30 and a 41-year-old woman with a BMI of 31.79 on July 9, the report said. The women died on July 3 last year and July 12 last year respectively.
The primary direct contributing factors that caused the incidents were “the operating surgeon’s overly lenient criteria for determining indications for bariatric surgery, which constitute overtreatment, contravening Article 25 of the Medical Act (醫療法),” it said.
Other main factors were “inadequate surgical risk assessment, and the medical team’s insufficient vigilance and emergency response capabilities regarding post-operative care,” the report said.
A woman with a BMI of 31.79 does not meet the criterion for weight-loss surgery, and the surgeon had only met once with her in an outpatient consultation, with most of the communication conducted via phone messages, it said, adding that the woman’s medical records were not consulted to enable a comprehensive risk assessment.
The two patients were not fully informed by the doctor about potential surgical risks and complications, the hospital facilities were inadequate and the medical team lacked the expertise to manage patient emergencies, it said, citing its finding that the nurses involved in the surgeries had only attended one session of bariatric surgery education and training.
Indirect contributing factors to the incidents included organizational-level and supervisory issues, the hospital’s partnership with an external bariatric team that caused problems in oversight, including personnel qualifications, medical workflows and clinical outcomes, the report said.
The hospital was also negligentin medical practice management resulting in a patient’s death, a contravention of Article 108 of the Medical Care Act, it said.
Taiwan does not have official clinical practice guidelines for bariatric surgery, but there are indications explicitly stipulated in the National Health Insurance’s reimbursement standards, the report said in its recommendations for improvements.
Clinical procedures must strictly adhere to the principle of “medical necessity” to prevent overtreatment and bariatric surgery must not be classified or treated as cosmetic medicine, it said.
Patient health and pre-operative evaluations must be thorough, including verifying the validity of diagnostic and test reports from external institutions, and all stages of decisionmaking — from registration and outpatient consultation to surgery — are critical clinical care records that should not be conducted through social messaging, unless they strictly comply with regulations governing telemedicine, it added.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan’s real existential threat isn’t across the strait — it is happening in the workplace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

This week a flood of news on the great divide in Taiwan. Not the Blue-Green one, but the other divide, between the haves and the have-nots.
The government announced that real wages (wage growth after inflation) grew 1.16 percent in the first six months of this year, marking the strongest real wage growth in six years for the same period, according to the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS). Good news!
The statistics also mapped the demographic strain on the workforce: average monthly overtime hours was 17.8 hours per employee in the first half of the year. That was the highest level in 22 years. Overtime in the electronics and component manufacturing sectors reached its highest level in 47 years of statistics-keeping. The economy cannot be sustained without either rising birthrates or rising in-migration.
Photo: Reuters
Employers are also reluctant to hire because laying off employees is legally difficult. That gives firms a good excuse to substitute overtime for new hires.
K-SHAPED GROWTH
Consumer confidence, which had improved in June, fell again last month. This occurred despite the booming economy and rising economic forecasts for the near future. The Taipei Times quoted National Central University’s Research Center for Taiwan Economic Development (RCTED) executive director Dachrahn Wu (吳大任): “This reflects a K-shaped growth, in which some industries are benefiting while others are being left behind.”
Indeed, technology workers account for less than 10 percent of the workforce, while, as the DGBAS also reported, over 70 percent of employees earned less than the average regular monthly wage in the first six months of this year, another record high. The number of lower-paid foreign industrial workers and part-time employees grew faster than the number of full-time workers.
Why are average wages high? Because that tiny slice of tech workers yanks the average up. The median monthly regular wage was just NT$39,283 in the first half of this year, nearly NT$10,000 below the average wage, DGBAS said.
Despite the gaudy GDP numbers, the average Taiwanese is experiencing an economy in deep trouble. An excellent piece from the Taiwan Political Economy Collaborative runs the numbers. In 2024, it observes, nominal GDP grew by 9.1 percent, but total nominal wages increased by only 4.4 percent, while the number of employed people increased by 0.6 percent. Since output growth was twice wage and employment growth, labor’s share of GDP fell from 44.3 percent in 2023 to 43.1 percent. The collaborative estimates that the labor share of GDP will collapse to just 35.1 percent in the first quarter of this year. Workers are being shut out of the economy as returns increasingly go to capital. Even tech workers don’t earn what they should.
DGBAS statistics show that the share of GDP accruing to the traditional economy fell 2.2 percent in 2024 and slid again last year. The economy that ordinary workers are experiencing is an economy in long-term recession, not the economy that people on the outside see. The “real wage growth” of 1.16 percent is an illusion created by high average wages in the tech sector. As the above collective observes, roughly half of all industrial subsectors are experiencing real wage declines. Workers accept overtime because they experience their own wages shrinking.
A savage editorial from Storm Media strongly criticized the administration of President William Lai (賴清德) and its fixation with the stock market. Taiwan’s elders often criticize the young for being lazy and having no financial skills, Storm said. “Why aren’t you investing in TSMC?” is something younger workers hear all the time from their elders. Of course, younger workers don’t have the cash for that, it is all they can do just to survive. Storm observes that while wages are what the real economy pays for a worker’s productivity, a stock price is the market’s bet on a firm’s future, two completely different things. It thunders: “When a society begins to treat the gap between the two as a personal investment failure rather than a structural policy problem, it has quietly declared that the value of work no longer matters.”
GENERATIONAL DIVIDE
The long-term slump in the labor share of GDP also reflects another great divide, the generational one. Taiwan’s economy is increasingly aging, with returns accruing to older people who no longer work. As Storm Media noted, the old in that economy frequently criticize the young on moral grounds. When a group failure is explained as a moral failure, a structural issue is being hidden, because it favors the group making the criticisms.
A puzzling issue, especially to outsiders, is why there isn’t more rebellion among ordinary workers. The increasingly lopsided economy seems to have few political consequences for the major parties. Part of this is a function of overwork: people who work 50-60 hours a week don’t have the time or energy to engage in political action. The Martial Law economy compelled a six-day work week for precisely that reason: it suppresses political opposition. That is why as the nation democratized it moved to a five-day work week. The authoritarianism is gone, but its attitudes and effects linger.
The Storm Media nod to the behavior of older people provides another clue: younger workers who are victims of structural policy failure internalize that policy failure as their own inadequacy. If someone hears “It’s your fault you are poor!” often enough, they may start to believe it.
The tide of overtime and overwork also suppresses responses to other urgent issues. Workers cannot have children, they lack the time and money. They can’t respond meaningfully to the threat from the thugs across the strait. Indeed, for many it may be rationalized away as a change of masters that will have no meaningful effect on their own lives. Some survey data shows this. A February seminar at Stanford given by Academia Sinica scholar Wen-chin Wu (吳文欽), Wu said that survey data shows that “younger respondents exhibit substantially lower willingness to fight than older cohorts.”
Taiwan’s apparent success also suppresses ordinary workers’ reactions to their economic struggles. Whatever their economic status, people take pride in Taiwan’s economic accomplishments. The ordinary person, despite the slumping domestic economy, is much better off under Lai, following eight years of incremental improvement under president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文), by almost any measure. The convenience of life in Taiwan also helps suppress sustained political response to declining real wages.
Will the long-term decline in the non-export economy manifest itself in the next election? Perhaps, but more by voter absence than by swings in the vote. And by the babies who are never born to vote for the pro-Taiwan parties because elites in both major parties have decided to let the nation die rather than address the political economy of labor and land development.
All the democracy and resilience and economic growth in the world won’t matter one whit if that decline isn’t reversed.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.
It is forest fire season in Europe and North America, and the news is filled with harrowing images of disastrous fires filling the air with smoke. What about Taiwan? Taiwan has a unique forest fire profile. Unlike other nations, where the threat peaks in the dry summer months, that period is wet. Instead, major forest fires typically occur during October to April, when the country is drier. Moreover, “high temperatures are not the primary drivers of forest fires” as a study in Theoretical and Applied Climatology noted. Rather, the consensus is that dryness is the trigger of forest fires here, with
When Gary Melyan, a longtime Taiwan resident who died on July 7 at age 83, arrived in Taipei for the second time in 1971, he was a graduate student trying to complete a doctoral thesis on the Taiping Rebellion. Wanting to assemble some fellow academics for a regular meal, he initiated a Saturday lunch, which quickly shifted to Saturday dinner. Return budget review to experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:43 UTC
01:38:43 KST

On July 30, 53 frontline producers from Taiwan Broadcasting System (TBS) issued a rare joint statement. With lawmakers proposing to freeze or cut more than NT$1 billion (US$31 million) from the budget for Public Television Service’s (PTS) main channel and other platforms including Taiwan Plus, the appeal to the legislature came from behind-the-scenes teams who usually keep their heads down while focused on their creative work.
If nearly half of the budget is frozen or cut, the impact would be felt far beyond broadcaster operations. It would directly affect the production of local documentaries, quality Taiwanese dramas and children’s programming. Incredibly, the main reason given by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) for freezing and cutting the budget is that the delay in the PTS board appointment of new members.
The eight-member PTS board review committee — which is made up of members recommended by each legislative party caucus in proportion to their seats — resigned en masse in April. That brought the review process to a standstill.
The political deadlock caused by partisan struggles and a breakdown in communication is something neither frontline production teams can resolve, nor is it the responsibility of program directors, producers or journalists. Cutting the budgets of frontline creative teams is punishing the wrong people for the wrong reasons.
PTS receives about NT$2.1 billion in government funding each year. That works out to less than NT$90 per citizen annually. Compared with the amount allocated annually to the BBC in the UK (the equivalent of more than NT$200 billion), Japan’s NHK (NT$130 billion) and South Korea’s KBS (NT$31.7 billion), Taiwan’s public broadcaster has long operated with relatively limited resources.
According to the Digital News Report published by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at the University of Oxford, while overall trust in the news media in Taiwan remains low, PTS is still trusted by more than 54 percent of the public, putting it among the leading Taiwanese media firms. Its programs include the likes of Slow Travel Adventures (浩克慢遊), which explores Taiwan’s towns and natural landscapes, the long-running environmental program Our Island (我們的島) and Taiwanese dramas exploring contemporary issues, such as The World Between Us (我們與惡的距離).
PTS has accompanied generations of Taiwanese across different backgrounds, while providing a foundation for Taiwan’s film and television industry.
As educators working on the front lines, we have seen firsthand how short-form videos and algorithms are eroding children’s ability to concentrate and think critically. In an era of commercial saturation, PTS provides a viewing environment completely free of advertising, making it one of the few educational resources that parents and teachers can trust. Through programs covering science, the arts and Taiwan’s local languages, it has consistently produced content with strong educational value and introduced children to diverse perspectives from around the world, helping them develop media literacy and critical thinking from an early age.
The development of culture and the film and television industry requires stable, long-term funding. When budgets are repeatedly frozen and stalled as bargaining chips in partisan struggles, it is ultimately local film and television workers who suffer.
In the legislature, the KMT and the TPP have invoked oversight as a pretext to obstruct PTS’ operations. By orchestrating resignations to block the formation of the PTS board and using the deadlock to justify massive budget cuts, they are effectively turning a public media institution into a bargaining chip for their own ends. This is a heavy-handed assault on Taiwan’s film and television industries, as well as on the rights of children and young people.
We sincerely urge lawmakers to return the budget review process to its proper professional course, give frontline creators the space they need to do their work, and preserve for Taiwan’s children a public platform that offers an international perspective and genuine educational value.
Yang Chih-chiang is a teacher.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

Book review: How to fix the system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:40 UTC
01:38:40 KST

In 2009, the tech billionaire Peter Thiel published an essay with the portentous title The Education of a Libertarian, in which he announced: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” Since the 1920s, he wrote, “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” had rendered the notion of “capitalist democracy” an oxymoron. To be fair, Thiel still seems happy to exercise his freedom to extract money from democracies, via his co-founding of Palantir, which was lately given lots of money by the government.
Thiel calls himself, as many such do, a “classical liberal,” but Daron Acemoglu argues that his ilk still has much in common with left-liberals. All of them, he writes, agree on “the desirability of basic individual rights and freedoms (including the right not to be coerced and the freedoms of expression, religion, association and choice); constraints on power, especially political power; and broad protections for equality before the law.”
On his telling, by the mid-20th century democracy with liberal characteristics had amply proved its worth: blue-collar labor was generously rewarded, and there was a sense of “shared prosperity.”
But now, he argues, liberal democracy is in a crisis, largely owing to the abandonment of the working class by liberalism’s “progressive” wing. In post-industrial Europe and the US, the left ceased to speak of economic class and spoke instead of identity. It is a similar diagnosis to that offered by the French sociologist Didier Eribon in his Retour a Reims, and indeed by Bernie Sanders, who has spoken of “a Democratic party which has abandoned working-class people,” but Acemoglu is happier to wield culture-war rhetoric even as he deplores the culture wars. He accuses the left, for example, of being obsessed with both “social engineering” (via diversity initiatives) and “thought policing,” which is impossible (he means speech policing).
His solution is a new contract of “working-class liberal democracy,” which concentrates on improving the standard of living of the least educated or skilled. This is to be done by focusing on economic growth (reducing, for example, the regulatory hoops one must apparently jump through to become a hairdresser or a masseur), encouraging more community decision-making (possibly imitating the citizens’ assemblies used in the Republic of Ireland) and making social media companies responsible, as publishers, for the messages they promote to users (good luck!). He suggests legislating in favor of “worker AI,” by which employees could use expert systems based on machine-learning to help them be more productive, so that nurses, for instance, could take more medical decisions. (He doesn’t report having consulted doctors on this idea.)
Acemoglu is a smooth and intelligent writer, and there is much in here to fascinate, particularly when he is on home turf: there is a brilliant explanation of why the American tax code perversely incentivizes automation and job destruction, and how the enviable happiness of Norway and Sweden, far from being a result of some innate Nordic wisdom, followed deliberate economic reforms enacted as recently as the 1930s. He is also laudably ready to admit when there is no “ready-made answer” to liberalism’s tensions — between, say, a value of community cohesion and a value of welcoming others who are different.
But his expansive rhetoric does lead to some internal inconsistencies. Acemoglu denounces throughout the progressive-liberal elites in exactly the same way as modern populists do (Farage-like, he even says liberalism’s troubles have reached “boiling point”). Yet, having eased the reader through a potted history of the ideas of Rousseau, Hobbes, Locke, Mill, Kant, Voltaire et al, he concedes that liberalism itself was the invention of a small bunch of clever people: “an ideology created by a highly learned group of philosophers.”
So maybe elites are good, sometimes? And Acemoglu can hardly escape the charge that his own book — one written by a Nobel-winning economist, no less — is itself an example of the kind of top-down “elite debates” he claims to think are sterile. Nor should he try to, because the charge would be stupid; indeed, the kind of thing that an elite billionaire like Peter Thiel would say.
It is forest fire season in Europe and North America, and the news is filled with harrowing images of disastrous fires filling the air with smoke. What about Taiwan? Taiwan has a unique forest fire profile. Unlike other nations, where the threat peaks in the dry summer months, that period is wet. Instead, major forest fires typically occur during October to April, when the country is drier. Moreover, “high temperatures are not the primary drivers of forest fires” as a study in Theoretical and Applied Climatology noted. Rather, the consensus is that dryness is the trigger of forest fires here, with

Trump downplays threat in jet switch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:37 UTC
01:38:37 KST

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he slipped away from Air Force One after a trip last month in Turkey because the US Secret Service and military wanted him on a “different plane” due to a threat that he said did not scare him.
Trump downplayed the nature of the subterfuge involved in his flight, which saw him stow away in an airport catering container to sneak onto another plane while Air Force One was sent into the sky, essentially as a decoy.
He also downplayed the risk to the people — White House officials, security and support staff, and reporters — he left on the plane.
Photo: AFP
“They wanted me to go on a different flight, different plane,” Trump told reporters after returning from an event in Ohio, saying he had little choice in the matter.
“I guess there was a threat out there. I didn’t really ask too much about it,” he said. “I get a lot of threats.”
His comments confirmed a report that first appeared in the Washington Post saying that Trump, following a NATO summit last month, was spirited onto a different plane because of a credible threat from Iran.
The action was kept secret for weeks, until the newspaper’s story.
“I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” Trump said on Tuesday.
He did not provide many details about the action, but said the incident did not scare him.
“I don’t worry about anything, to be honest,” Trump said. “Whatever it is. You know my attitude? Whatever.”
US presidents have sometimes kept overseas trips covert for security reasons, with schedules and logistics kept classified until after for safety reasons. That Trump’s whereabouts were concealed at the time and for weeks afterward is believed to be unprecedented.
“We have absolutely seen the president fly on unmarked or decoy planes before, into Iraq, Afghanistan, other war-zone-like places,” said Garrett M. Graff, author of Raven Rock: The Story of the U.S. Government’s Secret Plan to Save Itself — While the Rest of Us Die. “But this was an ongoing secret that I don’t think we’ve ever seen before.”
After hiding in the catering vehicle and being moved to the other plane, Trump stopped in the UK, sneaked back aboard the presidential plane undetected, and even later scoffed when asked about potential danger.
“If I go, you go, right?” he told reporters then — gliding past the fact that if the plane had been shot down, the president would not have been aboard.
Many details about what happened remain unknown
The president’s flight out of Turkey made headlines at the time because he had arrived aboard a luxury jet gifted by Qatar, which was not equipped with some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems found on older presidential jets.
Trump ended up traveling in a smaller government aircraft from Turkey to the UK, only to secretly reboard the decoy jet, then descend from it and climb back aboard the Qatari plane.
Presidents have regularly tested the confines of their office, pushing their security advisers to visit war zones as a show of US presence and their own leadership. Usually, that happens in the form of trips that are not announced until the president is deemed to be out of harm’s way.
What was different this time was that Trump was covertly separated from the rest of his travelers — including the press pool meant to provide independent coverage of the president and his actions — and, instead of informing the public about what occurred once the risk had passed, the White House still has not fully revealed what took place.
Graff said the presence of the White House press corps is as much about protecting “the presidency and democracy” as it is about covering the story.
“This shows that the White House just fundamentally doesn’t understand how important that role is,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Global tax reform is the key to a fair AI economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:35 UTC
01:38:35 KST

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and the resulting popular backlash have lent new urgency to an old question: How can we promote equitable economic growth from technological innovation while mitigating the negative social and environmental consequences? Domestically and globally, the answer starts with corporate tax policy.
Anxieties about AI have less to do with philosophical unease than with the societal effects. Financial gains are increasingly concentrated among a handful of firms and their shareholders, while the costs — from job displacement to rising energy prices — are borne by everyone else. In democratic societies, taxation is the primary mechanism for translating private gains into public benefits. When that mechanism breaks down, backlash is inevitable.
Distributive justice is an equally salient concern at the global level. While the global north is preoccupied with the significant public pushback against AI, the global south faces a pressing need to mobilize domestic tax flows from multinational corporations, particularly tech firms, in the wake of drastic aid cuts. These problems stem from the same source: When companies shift profits out of the countries where they are generated to tax havens, that reduces public revenues for all governments.
Illustration: Mountain People
The digitalization of the global economy has demonstrated the insufficiency of the international tax system. However, the need to shatter the status quo has never been clearer. AI has supercharged the trend of taxable value being decoupled from physical corporate presence — long a prerequisite for a country’s right to tax. Training data, compute and intellectual property can be scattered across many jurisdictions, far from where workers or users are, fueling debate about where value is created.
US-based multinational tech giants, some of which are poised to win big from the AI revolution, have created a playbook that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic could follow. Because their profits are mostly generated from intangible assets such as software, they can shift them to tax havens, manipulating decades-old norms to pay rock-bottom rates. It is no wonder that so many Big Tech firms have been embroiled in tax controversies.
A 2013 US Senate investigation and a subsequent 2016 European Commission investigation proved that Apple had shifted a large portion of its billions of dollars in global earnings to its Irish subsidiaries, which then paid a tax rate on Apple’s European profits as low as 0.005 percent. The uproar culminated in EU authorities ordering Apple to pay Ireland a staggering 13 billion euros (US$15 billion) in back taxes and sparked a major international tax overhaul at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
The inability to tax the profits of digital companies demands an overhaul of the international tax system. Policymakers have attempted to arrest the global tax race to the bottom by introducing minimum taxes at the national and global levels. The US enacted a corporate alternative minimum tax in 2022, but it has since been diluted. The same is true of the global minimum corporate tax adopted under the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting, whose planned reallocation of taxing rights from headquarters to market countries has stalled.
Tax-justice groups have criticized the Apple court decision and the OECD reforms for failing to consider developing countries’ interests. To create a fairer and more predictable system, African governments have proposed a Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation under the auspices of the UN, with negotiations under way in New York.
The world ultimately needs a robust and durable multilateral tax framework (whether at the UN, the OECD or elsewhere) to capture the value of AI-driven economic activity where it occurs. However, a global minimum corporate tax and the reallocation of taxing rights, while necessary, would not help governments tax AI companies in the near term, as many have yet to turn a taxable profit. That is why a growing number of jurisdictions are looking beyond taxes on net income and introducing digital-service taxes (DSTs) on gross revenues.
More than 20 countries are considering or have already implemented DSTs, prompting threats of retaliatory US tariffs. Moreover, different versions of such taxes are in effect or have been proposed in several US states. In all these cases, policymakers recognize that DSTs are a valuable release valve, be it globally or at the subnational level.
While not a long-term substitute for reforming an obsolete global tax system, DSTs are at least a stopgap. They provide proof of concept by normalizing the once-radical idea that taxing rights should align with where users are, not just where companies choose to incorporate or play accounting games. DSTs might not be the final destination, but they are an important and necessary first step toward a fairer international tax order.
DSTs, like broader multilateral tax reforms, have come under fire from short-sighted politicians and analysts who insist on defending the status quo. These leaders fail to recognize that the status quo is fiscally and politically untenable. This was the case before AI arrived but has come into sharper focus as the technology spreads.
If AI-driven profits are subject to the same asymmetric global tax architecture that has allowed digital activities to be undertaxed, there is a good chance that Big Tech’s outsized power would only grow. There is also the risk of resistance to AI hardening into a legitimacy crisis, which means that society might miss out on its benefits. Corporate tax policies are the battleground where public trust in this new technology, and our governing institutions, will be won or lost.
Zorka Milin is co-director of the Financial Accountability and Corporate Transparency Coalition.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

01:38:32 KST

Taiwan and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines (SVG) yesterday marked the 45th anniversary of diplomatic relations at a reception in Taipei, where leaders of the two countries pledged to deepen cooperation in the years ahead.
“In many other ways you may know, our relationship has grown stronger over those 45 years,” Vincentian Prime Minister Godwin Friday said in an address at the reception.
“It has evolved from one of the formality of establishing diplomatic relations to engaging in technical missions, to fostering stronger economic ties that involve the private and public sectors, and to massively expanding educational opportunities,” he said. “My hope is that when our two countries gather for the 50th anniversary of our relationship, we will be able to say that that relationship has grown.”
Photo: CNA
Friday said that he hoped to see more Vincentian and Taiwanese businesses working together to create opportunities, “enriching our two nations.”
President William Lai (賴清德) again welcomed Friday and his delegation to Taiwan, a day after receiving them at the Presidential Office. This visit is Friday’s first to Taiwan since he took office late last year.
Lai said that the trip was a “demonstration of strong friendship with Taiwan and an opportunity to witness this important historical milestone.”
The world has faced many new challenges over the past 45 years, “but no matter how things change, our nations have always supported one another and walked shoulder to shoulder, upholding the spirit of mutual trust and mutual benefit,” Lai said.
Lai also told Vincentian students attending the reception that the Taiwanese government hoped more young people would bear witness to and participate in the two countries’ diplomatic relationship, bringing new energy to bilateral collaboration.
“I do hope that you make Taiwan your home away from home, and I want to tell you that we are all a family,” he added.
Located in the Caribbean, SVG is one of Taiwan’s 12 diplomatic allies. The two sides established diplomatic relations on Aug. 15, 1981.
Friday and his delegation arrived in Taiwan early on Tuesday for a visit that concludes on Saturday.
During the visit, Friday is also scheduled to participate in an investor roundtable bringing together the Vincentian delegation and prospective Taiwanese investors, as well as a gathering with Vincentians living in Taiwan, the two governments said.

Taiwanese stocks are gaining favor over South Korea’s on steadier earnings prospects, as the two artificial intelligence (AI)-bellwether markets look to recover from last month’s rout.
Foreign investors turned net buyers of Taiwanese stocks last week, ending a six-week selling streak, data compiled by Bloomberg showed. They have accumulated US$1.7 billion so far this month, while net selling US$6.2 billion from South Korea over the same period.
The flows suggest that as investors consider a return to AI stocks amid doubts about companies’ spending payoffs, they might opt more for markets they consider less volatile and more diversified. Some investors view Taiwan as less likely to deliver the spectacular surges seen in South Korea but as offering more even-keeled returns and less dependent on leveraged trades.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
Taiwanese “companies are very, very high quality,” Grantham Mayo Van Otterloo & Co portfolio manager Warren Chiang said. The market “will obviously move with the business of the world economy, but certainly it is not excessively risky from a fundamental sense.”
After steadily beating Taiwan as Asia’s best-performing market for the year, South Korea recently conceded that title, although both are up more than 50 percent.
Recent flows show a divergence that highlights how investors are considering multiple factors as they assess the two markets’ outlooks and potential.
South Korea’s Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc dominate in flash memory chips that have been traditionally cyclical, while Taiwan’s broader presence in the tech hardware supply chain could work to its advantage. “Everything in your iPhone, every part comes from Taiwan,” Chiang said.
Analysts’ earnings estimates for TAIEX companies, on a 12-month forward basis, rose by 9.5 percent last month, while the same measure for the KOSPI was revised 7.4 percent higher, Bloomberg-compiled data showed. That is the first month in nearly a year when Taiwan’s revision moved ahead of South Korea’s.
Meanwhile, South Korea also faces the issue of leverage, particularly the market impact of single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds.
“Korea trades with much heavier leverage and speculative positioning, so even a small wobble in expectations can trigger an outsized move without any meaningful deterioration in fundamentals,” Vantage Global Prime Pyt Ltd senior analyst Hebe Chen (陳碧菲) said.
With last month’s rout only days old, it is still too early to determine how firmly this week’s modest rebound in the region — if it proves sustainable — would shape investor preference.
Despite its volatility, which has eased in the past few days, the KOSPI continues to trade at lower valuations than the TAIEX and is at a record discount following the sell-off.
“Korea looks relatively attractive given where valuations sit, because Taiwan didn’t correct as much,” Aberdeen Asian Income Fund Ltd senior investment director Isaac Thong (董子維) said.
In the end, the key Asian tech hubs’ equity performance could ultimately depend on how the AI sector delivers — whether heavy research and development spending pays off and the supply chain’s momentum continues.
“The longer-term picture is the monetization of AI,” Benzimra said. “That is the long-term risk.”

EDITORIAL: Reality of travel to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

China’s new exit and entry regulations might signal an increase in the risk that Taiwanese travelers will face, an analyst said on Tuesday last week. The new rules, which take effect on Sept. 15, expand the power of authorities to restrict travel on national, industrial and technological security grounds, question travelers about their reasons for leaving and inspect electronic data.
Taiwanese who do not support the ruling party should not dismiss the warnings as fearmongering or propaganda. Beijing applies its “anti-secession” laws indiscriminately, an official said recently while presenting a report on proposed amendments to combat China’s efforts at transnational repression.
Chinese laws such as the so-called “22 guidelines to punish Taiwanese independence” and the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress can be used against people other than supporters of Taiwanese independence, the official said on condition of anonymity.
A Mainland Affairs Council report found that 415 Taiwanese had gone missing, been detained or imprisoned in China over the past two years. Some were reportedly detained for activities as innocuous as belonging to a religion not sanctioned by the Chinese government.
Chinese border officials are empowered to search travelers’ phones at ports of entry and seemingly harmless online activity could potentially be interpreted as evidence of political wrongdoing. This is the danger for Taiwanese accustomed to speech and press freedoms: They might assume they are safe from harassment simply because they identify as Chinese, belong to an opposition party or have never openly criticized the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
The CCP can interpret seemingly harmless actions or speech as threats to the party or national interests — even when they come from Chinese, let alone Taiwanese. The political system under Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) provides ample evidence that even top members of the CCP can find themselves on the wrong side of an expansive definition of political loyalty.
Xi has overseen the downfall of some of China’s top political and military figures. Former security chief Zhou Yongkang (周永康), a member of the Politburo Standing Committee, was expelled from the CCP and sentenced to life in prison in 2015. Former Chongqing party chief Bo Xilai (薄熙來), once considered a potential national leader, was expelled and sentenced to life in prison for corruption in 2013. Sun Zhengcai (孫政才), another former Chongqing party chief and Politburo member viewed as a potential future leader, was removed in 2017 and sentenced to life in prison.
The authorities formally cited corruption and other offenses in those cases, and there is no need to minimize the allegations, but the examples illustrate the dangers of operating within a political system in which the boundaries of acceptable conduct are ultimately determined by the party leadership. Officials with extensive connections and years of CCP service were not immune to political downfall.
For Taiwanese, the lesson is clear: Avoiding overt criticism of the CCP does not guarantee safety. In a system in which political loyalty is ultimately determined by the party, conduct that appears harmless today can be interpreted differently tomorrow.
Hong Kong provides another example of how quickly the boundaries can shift. After the 1997 handover from Britain to China, Beijing said it was prepared to honor its promise to preserve the territory’s autonomy under the “one country, two systems” framework. Hong Kong residents, despite being Chinese citizens, retained freedoms that allowed them to openly criticize the CCP.
Those arrangements were supposed to remain in place for 50 years. Yet less than two decades after the handover, the limits of Hong Kong’s autonomy were becoming increasingly apparent.
The case of Gui Minhai (桂民海), who disappeared from his apartment in Pattaya, Thailand, was particularly startling. It suggested that Beijing was prepared to enforce its political will beyond its own jurisdiction, foreshadowing the increasingly comprehensive transnational repression that has since become a feature of the Chinese state’s efforts to silence critics abroad.
Taipei must tackle the issues head-on, working with countries that share its concerns to protect Taiwanese abroad. In the meantime, the government must do more to educate people traveling to China about the risks they face.
Taiwanese should understand one basic reality: Once they enter China, they are beyond the reach of Taiwan’s authorities, who have little ability to intervene if Chinese authorities detain or restrict them. Supporting an opposition party, identifying as Chinese or simply keeping political opinions private is no guarantee of safe passage.

Two former Chinese military servicemembers were arrested in South Korea for alleged espionage, accused of acts including intercepting communications between fighter jets and ground control and collecting information on movements of US armaments, police said on Tuesday.
One of the suspects, a Chinese national in his 60s, set up an interception device consisting of a software-defined radio receiver, an antenna and a laptop at a hotel near an air base used by South Korean and US air forces in southern South Korea, police said in a statement.
Police said the man is accused of intercepting communications between fighter jets flown by South Korean and US pilots and air traffic controllers at the base several times since 2024.
Photo: Yonhap News Agency via EPA
He previously served in the Chinese military, but refused to disclose further details about his identify, police said.
The man was arrested on Monday for violating laws on aiding the enemy and protecting communication secrets, the statement said.
Police said they were conducting a forensic examination of his laptop to find if he relayed any of the intercepted communications to Chinese authorities.
The man told investigators that it was his hobby to listen to communications between civilian planes and air traffic controllers and he wanted to listen to communications involving fighter jets as well.
Police said they also arrested another Chinese man in his 40s on Monday on accusations of illegally collecting information from the US military headquarters near Seoul, including information on US-South Korean military drills, photos showing the movements of weapons at the headquarters and personnel changes of top US military officers.
He obtained some of the information from a South Korean woman working at the US command, police said, adding that he gave her money in return for the information and they suspect the pair had a romantic relationship.
The man, who runs a military supply store near the US command, said during questioning that he sought the information believing it would help his business.
Police said the man, who also previously served in the Chinese military, violated laws on aiding the enemy and protecting military installations in South Korea.
The statement came a day after South Korean and US militaries said they would start large-scale annual exercises next week.

New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie said he knew before a 54-0 tour victory over the Sharks in Durban, South Africa, on Tuesday that former All Black Ma’a Nonu would perform a solo Haka. After the All Blacks performed a traditional pre-match Haka, 44-year-old Sharks substitute Nonu stepped forward and delivered a response.
“We knew the Ma’a Haka was coming,” said Rennie, whose team scored eight tries in wet and chilly conditions for a second straight win since the South African tour kicked off last Friday.
“Ma’a came and saw our defense coach Tana Umaga last night and said he wanted to be respectful and queried about the right way to respond to the haka,” Rennie told reporters.
Photo: AP
Nonu later told SuperSport TV: “On behalf of myself and my family, I thought it was the right thing to do, to answer the boys and the All Blacks.
“It was such a privilege and an honor, and to do the Haka, showing my respect on behalf of my family to the team I love.
“I got nearly 20 minutes off the bench. I tried my best. It was great to see the New Zealand boys,” he said.
“The All Blacks opened up in the last 30 minutes and I was chasing my tail. Credit to them, they are improving, and all the best to the brothers for the next game,” he said.
Double Rugby World Cup winner Nonu joined the Sharks as a mentor last month, but Springbok call-ups and injuries led Sharks coach JP Pietersen to include him among the substitutes.
“Ma’a has been good for the guys, especially the backs. He is a great addition off the field, helping the youngsters prepare, warm up and get their mindset right,” Pietersen said.
“He spoke to Tana about how to respond to the tradition of the Haka, but was nervous about doing it by himself,” he said.
Nonu came off the bench after 62 minutes, by which stage the Sharks were trailing 35-0. Just one minute later, scrum-half Kyle Preston scored the sixth try for the tourists.
“Conditions made it challenging to shift a lot of ball, but it was a really solid defensive effort,” said Rennie, who succeeded Scott Robertson as head coach last March.
“The last 40 minutes were very positive. I thought we kicked really well, our kicks in the central area of the field found a lot of space. Our option taking was pretty good,” he said.
“We gave away a lot of early penalties, so we struggled to get our hands on the ball. In the second half we were a lot more clinical and kicked really well,” he said.
New Zealand inside center Jordie Barrett was voted man of the match. He scored a try and set up several others with superb cross-field kicks.

Photo courtesy of the Taipei Department of Information and Tourism
Visitors entering the riverside area through gates 3 or 5 in the riverside wall are encouraged to head to the lawns in front of the main stage at Gate 4, which offer the best viewing spots, it said.
Traffic controls would be in effect on roads near the site from 7pm to 11pm on Saturday, with the restricted zone subject to expansion depending on traffic conditions, the department said.
People should use public transportation, it added.
Beimen Station is the closest MRT access point to the site, the department said.
People should not park illegally on elevated highway shoulders or in the restricted zone, it said.

Spanning Plaza 1 (near exits Y27 and Y28) through Plaza 6 of the mall near Taipei Railway Station, the indoor event is to feature Japanese summer festival attractions, including yukata clothing services, cultural exchanges, musical performances, craft markets and floral displays.

Taoyuan to expand free milk program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

Taoyuan is to expand its free milk program to include junior-high school students beginning with this school year commencing on Aug. 31, the Taoyuan City Government announced yesterday.
With the addition of about 67,000 junior-high school students, the program would benefit about 280,000 students ages two to 15, from preschool through junior high school, Taoyuan Mayor Simon Chang (張善政) said in a statement
The expansion is intended to provide essential nutrients to junior-high school students during a critical stage of their growth and development, the city said.
Photo courtesy of Taoyuan City Government
The program was launched in February and provides one free milk or soy milk product per week to every preschool and elementary-school student in Taoyuan. The city said the take-up rate had reached about 70 percent.
The announcement came a week after Taipei expanded its free milk program to include junior-high school students, making Taoyuan, Taipei and Tainan the only special municipalities to provide free milk to junior-high school students. Tainan provides one free milk product per week alongside school lunches.
New Taipei City and Taichung also offer free milk programs for preschool and elementary-school students, while Kaohsiung provides one free milk product per week with school lunches to students at public preschools and elementary schools.
Taoyuan also announced that its free school lunch program would be expanded to cover homeroom teachers and school meal coordinators at all elementary and junior-high schools, benefiting 7,465 faculty members beginning this school year.
Taoyuan was the first of Taiwan’s six special municipalities to introduce free school lunches for elementary and junior-high school students in February 2023, Chang said, adding that the city has increased its annual budget to keep pace with inflation and expanded the use of high-quality local produce to improve school lunches.
The latest expansion would extend the program’s benefits to frontline education workers, Chang said.

CWA warns of hot and unstable weather
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

Temperatures might hit 36°C in parts of Taiwan, while the nation’s southwest faces the threat of heavy rain, with unstable weather expected over the next few days, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
The CWA issued an “orange” heat alert for parts of Taipei and New Taipei City yesterday, indicating that temperatures could reach 38°C or exceed 36°C for three consecutive days.
A “yellow” heat alert — warning of highs of 36°C — was issued for parts of Taoyuan, as well as Changhua, Hualien and Taitung counties.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
As of 1:42pm yesterday, the highest daytime temperatures were 36.9°C in New Taipei City’s Sindian District (新店), 36.2°C in Taitung County’s Luye Township (鹿野) and 36.0°C in other parts of New Taipei City and Taitung.
The CWA also issued a heavy rain advisory, warning that southwesterly winds could bring short-duration downpours to Tainan and Kaohsiung, as well as Chiayi city and county, and Pingtung County, including the Hengchun Peninsula.
The agency issued a strong wind advisory for Green Island (綠島), and Hsinchu city and county, warning of sustained winds of 41 to 51kph (six on the Beaufort scale) and 63 to 75kph (eight on the Beaufort scale).
Independent meteorologist Wu Der-rong (吳德榮) said forecasts showed that southwesterly winds would bring moisture from the South China Sea through tomorrow, making atmospheric conditions unstable.
Intermittent rain in windward areas in southwestern Taiwan are expected through tomorrow, while localized afternoon thunderstorms are expected in central and northern Taiwan, some of which might bring heavy rainfall, Wu said in an online weather column.
Outside of rainy periods, daytime temperatures would be high, especially in eastern Taiwan, and parts of central and northern Taiwan, he said.
From Saturday through Aug. 21, seasonal winds are expected to weaken and give way to a broad low-pressure system near Taiwan, Wu said.
Although moisture would remain abundant, the main weather threat is expected to shift to frequent afternoon convective storms capable of producing lightning, strong winds and intense short-term rainfall, he said, urging the public to monitor short-term weather advisories.
Meanwhile, the CWA said that Tropical Storm Nangka formed at 8am yesterday over waters south of Iwo Jima after strengthening from a tropical depression.
The storm is forecast to move northeast and not affect Taiwan, the agency said.
Chan-hom, the 15th typhoon of this year, has weakened into a tropical depression, while Tropical Storm Peilou in moving away from Taiwan and also poses no threat to the nation, the CWA added.

Asia Vital Components’ Q2 earnings and margins surpass expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:26 UTC
01:38:26 KST

Thermal solutions provider Asia Vital Components Co (AVC, 奇鋐) yesterday reported better-than-expected profit margins and earnings per share in the second quarter, thanks to a better product mix, driven especially by artificial intelligence (AI) server-related products, and scaled-up automated production.
Gross margin climbed to a record high of 32.57 percent last quarter, up 2.8 percentage points from the previous quarter and rising 8.16 percentage points from a year earlier, the company said.
Operating margin also improved to 27.44 percent from 24.51 percent in the previous quarter and 17.21 percent a year earlier, according to the company’s financial statement, which was released after its earnings conference.
Photo: CNA
In the second quarter, net profit increased 20.86 percent quarter-on-quarter and 139.35 percent year-on-year to NT$9.57 billion (US$296.78 million), the company said.
That brought earnings per share to a record high of NT$24.37, compared with NT$20.17 in the previous quarter and NT$10.3 a year earlier.
Analysts had estimated earnings of NT$22.38 per share on average, data compiled by Yahoo Finance showed.
With more contributions from its thermal and chassis businesses, the company’s revenue for last quarter rose to a record NT$49.12 billion, representing a quarterly increase of 0.17 percent and an annual expansion of 65.98 percent, the statement said.
Asia Vital Components specializes in advanced water cooling plates and liquid cooling systems for AI servers, data centers and high-performance computing hardware.
In the first half of this year, the company’s net profit surged 142.5 percent annually to NT$17.48 billion, with earnings per share of NT$44.54, while gross margin rose 6.13 percentage points to 31.17 percent and operating margin climbed to 25.97 percent from 17.86 percent, the statement said.
With shipments of server-related products continuing to increase and more production capacity coming online, Asia Vital Components expects its revenue in the second half of the year to surpass the NT$98.16 billion registered in the first half, the company said.
In the first half, sales of thermal and chassis products totaled NT$81.88 billion, up 104.26 percent year-on-year and accounting for 83.42 percent of the company's total, the statement said.
By application, server- and networking-related revenue came in at NT$64.92 billion, an annual increase of 153.38 percent, accounting for 66.1 percent of the total, up from 48.41 percent the previous year and a key driver of higher gross margin, it said.
The company would continue to expand its production capacity in Vietnam to meet robust demand from major cloud service providers, Asia Vital Components said.
The company has budgeted capital expenditure of about NT$15 billion for this year and expects the figure to be higher next year, it said.
